Commentary on Ezekiel

Latin source: Jerome's commentary on Ezekiel, in fourteen books, with a prologue and a preface to each later book, all addressed to Eustochium (written at Bethlehem about 410–414), from the critical text of F. Glorie, Corpus Christianorum, Series Latina 75 (Turnhout, 1964), pp. 3–743, verified against the page images and collated with Vallarsi's edition (Venice, 1768), with the edition's evident misprints corrected. Each lemma gives Ezekiel in Jerome's own version from the Hebrew and then, after "LXX:", in his Latin of the Septuagint, in quotation marks; all Scripture is translated as Jerome quotes it, from his own Latin. Italics mark the lemmata and the other Scripture and authors he quotes. Psalms keep the Latin (LXX) numbering, with the Hebrew number in parentheses where it differs. Greek is kept as printed, and Hebrew in Jerome's Latin transliterations, with an English gloss in square brackets; the Origenian signs of the Septuagint lemmata are kept. Glorie's supplements are read into the text, the words he brackets as spurious are omitted, and his critical apparatus is not translated. This English translation is released into the public domain.

Prologue

Having finished the eighteen volumes of explanations on Isaiah, I was eager to pass on to Ezekiel, which I had often promised to you and to your mother Paula of holy memory, O Eustochium, virgin of Christ, and to put the final hand, as the saying goes, to the prophetic work; and behold, suddenly the death of Pammachius and Marcella, the siege of the city of Rome, and the falling asleep of many brothers and sisters were announced to me. And I was so dismayed and stunned that day and night I thought of nothing else but the safety of all, and considered myself a captive in the captivity of the saints, nor could I open my mouth until I learned something more certain, while I hang anxious between hope and despair and torment myself with the misfortunes of others. But after the brightest light of all the earth was extinguished, nay rather, after the head of the Roman empire was cut off and, to speak more truly, the whole world perished in one city, I became mute and was humbled and kept silent from good things, and my sorrow was renewed; my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze up; nor did I think that saying should be neglected: Music in mourning is an untimely tale. But since you too demand this unceasingly, and a scar is gradually drawn over the great wound, and the Scorpion is pressed down beneath the soil of Trinacria between Enceladus and Porphyrion, and the Hydra of many heads has at last ceased to hiss against us, and a time has been given in which we ought to devote ourselves not to answering the snares of heretics but to the exposition of the Scriptures, I shall take up the prophet Ezekiel, whose difficulty the tradition of the Hebrews proves. For among them, unless someone has completed the age of priestly ministry, that is, the thirtieth year, he is permitted to read neither the beginnings of Genesis, nor the Song of Songs, nor the beginning and end of this volume, so that the full time of human nature may come to perfect knowledge and to mystical understandings. If by the mercy of the Lord I bring this work through to the finish, I shall pass on to Jeremiah, who in his Lamentations, under the type of Jerusalem, laments the four quarters of the world with a fourfold alphabet.

Book One

1:1a

And it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth, on the fifth of the month. The thirtieth year is spoken of not, as most suppose, with reference to the age of the prophet, nor to the jubilee, which is the year of remission, but counting from the eighteenth year of Josiah king of Judah, when the book of Deuteronomy was found in the temple of God, up to the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, surnamed Jeconiah, who was led into Babylon with his mother and with Daniel and the three youths and Ezekiel — this is the first captivity of the tribe of Judah, when the wrath of God dripped down upon Jerusalem —. According to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], however, the Lord and Savior is prefigured, who at thirty years of age came to baptism, which is the perfect age in a man. Hence also in the book of Numbers, according to the Hebrews, the priests begin to minister in the tabernacle not from the twenty-fifth year of age, as is contained in the Seventy, but from the thirtieth. As a sign of this Joseph too went before, when in Egypt he bestowed grain on the hungry people, and John the Baptist came to the streams of the Jordan and preached the baptism of repentance. In what is written, 'in the fourth', with the sentence left hanging, 'month' is understood; for at once there follows 'on the fifth of the month'. To make this plainer, the Seventy added it above.

1:1b-2

When I was in the midst of the captives beside the river Chebar, the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God. On the fifth of the month, that is the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin. That the captive people sat by the river of Babylon, David prophesies in the spirit: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept; Chebar, moreover, is either the name of a river or certainly, according to its interpretation, by which it is rendered 'heavy', it signifies the Tigris and the Euphrates and all the great and very heavy rivers which are said to be in the land of the Chaldeans; and understand the opened heavens not by a division of the firmament but by the faith of the believer, because the heavenly mysteries were unlocked to him. Hence also at the baptism of the Savior, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, we read 'the heavens opened'; and when these are unlocked, visions are laid open, not one vision but many, as the Lord says through the prophet: I will multiply visions, and in the hands of the prophets I have been likened. These are the visions which the whole prophecy of Ezekiel has woven together. And more meaningfully, according to the Hebrews and the other translators, Jehoiachin's is called an 'exile', and not a 'captivity', as the Seventy translated; for he was not captured when the city was overcome, but, surrendering himself of his own will, was led to Babylon: therefore let that of Jehoiachin, that is, of Jeconiah, be called the first 'exile', and that of Zedekiah the second or final 'captivity'.

1:3a

The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel the son of Buzi, the priest, in the land of the Chaldeans beside the river Chebar. Both to Daniel and to Ezekiel, who were in Babylon beside the rivers, the mysteries of things to come are laid open above the waters, nay rather in the purest waters, so that the power of baptism might be shown. Besides, the apostle Paul too, when he was washed in the Lord by Ananias, scales having first covered his eyes, was freed of blindness. And in Genesis the first things that lived came forth from the waters. This too is to be understood: that the Lord came to baptism in the thirtieth year of his age; in the fourth month, which among us is called January and stands first at the beginning of the year, apart from Nisan, the month of new things, in which the Passover is celebrated — for among the eastern peoples, after the gathering of the crops and the winepresses, when the tithes were brought into the temple, October was the first month and January the fourth —; and he adds the fifth day of the month, and it signifies the baptism in which the heavens were opened to Christ, and the day of the Epiphany is venerable to this day — not, as some think, his birth in the flesh, for then he was hidden and did not appear. This fits that time when it was said: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Further, 'Buzi' is rendered in our language 'spurned' and 'despised', 'Hiezechiel' [Ezekiel] 'strengthened by God'. This will be fitted to the Lord thus, that we may say that the Creator of the world, because he is the Father of the Savior, is spurned and despised by all the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament. Nor is it surprising that the Lord is the strong one of God, since he himself is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

1:3b

And the hand of the Lord came upon him there. (LXX: "And the hand of the Lord came upon me.") In order that we may be able to discern and understand the visions of God, we need the hand and strength of God upon us. By this hand and arm the people of Israel was led out of Egypt; its mighty works even the magicians partly understood, saying: This is the finger of God; and the Savior in the Gospel: If I cast out demons by the finger of God, in place of which it is written in another Gospel: If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God.

1:4a

And I saw, and behold, a wind of whirlwind was coming from the north, and a great cloud, and a fire enfolding, and brightness round about it. (LXX: "And I saw, and behold, a spirit carrying away — or lifting up — was coming from the north, and a great cloud in it, and fire flashing, and brightness round about it.") For the consolation of the exiled people and the revelation of the sentence of God, the prophet saw a very great vision. In its interpretation all the synagogues of the Jews are mute, saying that it is beyond man to wish to attempt anything either concerning this or concerning the building of the temple, which is written at the end of this prophecy. We, however, entrust to kindly and faithful readers what we have received from our elders and what, according to the small measure of our poor talent, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, we can surmise rather than explain, begging pardon, that they may look with favor on our rashness — nay rather, on a faith that does not know its own measure — rather than be angry. And first it must be known that the 'spirit lifting up or carrying away', which we, following Aquila, have translated 'wind of whirlwind', and, following Symmachus and Theodotion, 'blast and spirit of tempest', is taken by some in a good sense, by others in the contrary sense. For the Hebrew word 'ruha', according to the character of the passages, is taken either as 'spirit' or as 'soul' or as 'wind'. Spirit, as there: You will send forth your spirit and they will be created; soul: His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth; wind: With a violent spirit you will shatter the ships of Tarshish, and elsewhere: Fire, sulphur and the spirit of storms, the portion of their cup. Those who read 'wind' and 'blast of tempest' understand this: that the wrath and fury of God comes from the north, that is, Nebuchadnezzar, and that Jerusalem was to be taken six years after this vision. For the vision is seen in the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin, which was also the fifth of Zedekiah, reigning in Jerusalem, who, we read, likewise after six years, that is, in the eleventh year of his rule, when the city was taken, was led into Babylon. To those, therefore, who dwelt beside the river Chebar and had surrendered themselves to the king of their own accord, it is revealed that they did well to obey the sentence of God: for in a short time both the province of Judea and the city of Jerusalem would be taken. And as for a great cloud being described, we understand that it carries showers and rains over Judea; and the enfolded fire shows the punishments to come and the evils of captivity; and the brightness round about it signifies the open judgments of God. But those who take it in the contrary sense, that is, the good one, understand the spirit carrying away or lifting up as the Holy Spirit, who carries away vices and sins from men, or lifts up those who lie low to the heights, and makes them withdraw from the north, that most frigid wind, from which: Evils blaze up upon all the earth; and in Jeremiah that terrible pot is kindled from the face of the north. The great cloud too they refer to the person of Christ, who came into the Egypt of this world upon a light cloud, and they say that it is properly called great by comparison with lesser ones, namely the prophets and the apostles and all the saints, of whom it is written: And your truth even to the clouds, and: I will command the clouds not to rain a shower upon Israel, and elsewhere: The clouds, the dust of his feet, and again: Clouds and darkness round about him. The flashing fire also, and the brightness round about it, they take according to what is written: God is a consuming fire. To send this upon the earth the Savior says that he came, and he desires it to burn in us and in all believers; and though it brings terror and punishments upon sinners, yet it glows red with brightness and is full of light and radiance. Therefore it refines us, so that it may bestow more joyful things on us when we are pure and cleansed.

1:4b

And from the midst of it as it were the appearance of electrum, that is, from the midst of the fire. (LXX: "And in the midst of it as it were a vision of electrum in the midst of the fire." And what follows: ÷ And brightness in it ⁚, is to be marked beforehand with an obelus.) Had Scripture not added, saying: That is, from the midst of the fire, we could have erred because of the ambiguity of the word, so as to think that the appearance or vision of electrum was in the midst of the wind or spirit. This, therefore, is to be understood: that in the midst of the fire, or of the torments of God, there is the likeness of electrum, which is more precious than gold and silver; and that after judgment and torments, which seem rough and hard to those who suffer them, the gleam of electrum appears more precious, since all things are governed by the providence of God, and what is thought a punishment is a medicine.

1:5

And in the midst of it the likeness of four living creatures, and this their appearance: the likeness of a man in them. In the midst 'of it': 'of the electrum' is indeed understood, but it is better that we understand 'of the fire', which is light to believers, punishment to unbelievers. In the midst of this fire, therefore, was the likeness of four living creatures — a likeness, not a nature —, and of the four living creatures, which are afterwards called fourfold in form, there is one likeness, that of a man, so that all the rational beings in the world may be pointed out: Let us make, he says, man after our image and likeness — now the image and likeness of God is not a form of the body but of the mind, drawn after the likeness of the true image, Christ, which is the image of the invisible God —. These rational creatures dwell in four places, either because of the four hinges of the world by which the globe is enclosed, or because of the four places of the heavenly, the earthly, the infernal and the supercelestial beings, of which the apostle Paul also speaks: That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things heavenly, earthly and infernal. For three there is the testimony of Paul; let us see the fourth too: Praise God, heavens of heavens, and let the water that is above the heavens praise the name of the Lord; and again the Apostle speaks of heavenly things and of others that are supercelestial.

1:6-8a

Four faces to one and four wings to one; and their feet, straight feet, and the sole of their foot as the sole of a calf's foot, and sparks as the appearance of glowing bronze. And the hand of a man under their wings on the four sides. (LXX: "And four faces to one and four wings to one, and their legs straight, and their feet winged. And sparks as flashing bronze, and their wings light. And the hand of a man under their wings on their four sides.") Concerning the four living creatures whose appearance was the likeness of a man, but in such a way that each had four faces and four wings, and straight feet, and the sole of the foot 'as the footprint of a calf's foot' or, as Aquila translated, 'round' — which the Seventy omitted entirely —; concerning the sparks also, glowing red with the brightness of bronze, and their light wings, which is not found in the Hebrew; concerning the hand of a man too under their wings on the four sides, and the rest that the prophetic discourse describes, we shall try to say what seems right to us, once we have briefly summed up the opinions of individuals. Some, whom we too followed in the preface of the Commentaries on Matthew, think that the four Gospels are designated by the names of these living creatures: Matthew's, because he described as it were a man: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham; that of the lion they refer to Mark: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight; that of the calf to the Gospel of Luke, which begins with the priesthood of Zechariah; that of the eagle to the opening of John, who, flying up to the height, began: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word: on which we said in the above-mentioned work what seemed right to us; and more fully in the Revelation of John the forms and names of these living creatures are referred to the four Gospels: how the description of all the living creatures can be fitted to them, we shall try to say in its place. Others, however, who follow the foolish wisdom of the philosophers, surmise the two hemispheres in the two cherubim of the temple, and ourselves and the antipodes as men lying, as it were, on their backs and falling. Most, following Plato, refer the rational, the irascible and the concupiscible part of the soul, which he calls λογικὸν and θυμικὸν and ἐπιθυμητικὸν, to the man and the lion and the calf: placing reason and thought and mind and counsel, the same being virtue and wisdom, in the citadel of the brain; ferocity, however, and wrath and violence in the lion, which resides in the gall; further, lust, luxury and the desire of all pleasures in the liver, that is, in the calf, which clings to the works of the earth; and they posit a fourth, which is above these and beyond these three, which the Greeks call συνείδησιν — the spark of conscience which is not extinguished even in the breast of Cain, after he was cast out of paradise, and by which, when we are overcome by pleasures or by fury, and at times deceived by the very likeness of reason, we perceive that we sin —; this they assign properly to the eagle, not mingling itself with the three but correcting the three when they stray; and we read that in the Scriptures it is sometimes called spirit, which intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings. For no one knows the things that are of a man, except the spirit that is in him; and Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, prays that it be kept whole together with soul and body. And yet we see this very conscience too, according to what is written in Proverbs: The wicked man, when he has come into the depth of sins, despises, cast down in some and losing its place, who have not even shame and modesty in their offenses and deserve to hear: The face of a harlot has become yours, you do not know how to blush. This four-horse chariot, then, God guides after the manner of a charioteer; and when it runs with disordered steps he reins it in, makes it docile and compels it to obey his command. This discussion of the parts of the soul, that is, of man, who is called the lesser world by the same philosophers, we too shall touch upon. There are those who think, simply, that in the four living creatures, according to the opinion of Hippocrates, the four elements are shown of which all things consist: fire, air, water, earth; how these are mixed with one another and, though each is single, are seen joined to one another and touch one another, and have in the one person of the living creatures four forms and figures, is not the business of the present work. The four wheels too, rising from earthly things to the heights, joined to the single and fourfold living creatures, they reckon to be either the mingling of these same elements, or the cycle of the four seasons, each completed in three months, and the turning year, which has taken its name from the fact that it is always turning and returns into itself; of which it was beautifully said in a single little verse: Spring, summer, autumn, winter, and month, and year. And what is said, 'There was a wheel in a wheel', they think signifies 'a year in a year', of which another poet says: And the year rolls back into itself along its own footsteps. The likeness of the firmament too, which is compared to crystal, they would have understood as this heaven which we look up at, under which the four living creatures roll and pass. And the throne of the color of sapphire, and the man seated upon it in human likeness, they assert describe the dominion of him who rules all things and has all things under his feet, of the Omnipotence; and that at the end it is said: This, the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord, through which, as through a kind of painting and image, providence is shown. And as to the feet of the living creatures being called straight, and the sole of the foot a calf's, or round, they hold that every earthly thing flies up to heavenly things and, all angles being cut away, follows roundness, which is the most beautiful of all figures; that the glowing sparks indicate that all things are full of light; and that the hand of a man under the wings, of the man himself as well as of the lion and the calf and the eagle, means that reason should sustain all things and lift them up from earthly lowliness to heavenly things. These things we can refer both to the Gospels and to all that we have set out above. I remember having heard that the four passions, which Cicero discusses most fully in the Tusculans — of joy, of distress, of desire and of fear, of which two concern things present, two things to come —, are signified by the four living creatures — of which Vergil too says briefly: Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice —; that these ought to be ruled by reason and the power of God; and that against them are set — nay rather, set over them — four virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, so that they may be governed by their judgment; but how these are fitted to the faces of the man, the lion, the calf and the eagle, they have said nothing at all; on these the same philosopher and orator discourses in his three books of Duties addressed to his son. I have read too a short little discussion of a certain Catina, whom the Syrians call λεπτὸν, that is, 'sharp' and 'ingenious', who thinks that the order of the camp of the twelve tribes in the wilderness is described, to the east, west, north and south, which are joined to one another both by love and by kinship, and that this is the wheel in a wheel; which are led by the spirit and protected by the cloud in the desert and lit by the pillar of fire at night, so that they may not return to Egypt but may always hasten to go to the land of promise. The likeness of electrum in the midst he interprets as the Holy of Holies, and he refers the face of the man to all Israel, that of the lion to the royal scepter of Judah, that of the calf to the priestly and Levitical tribe; outside these is the eagle, the vengeance and retribution of God, looking out over all things from heaven and ready to tear the sinner, of which it is said also in Hosea: As an eagle over the house of God, that is, the temple; and he holds that in this same prophet the great eagle with great wings and talons, which has the course for entering into Lebanon, is understood as Nebuchadnezzar, whom it signifies even now to be about to come; and that God sits upon a chariot of this kind like a charioteer and commands what is to be done and what is not to be done. This, moreover, he says, is said to the people who live in Babylon: that if it submits its neck to God and obeys his reins, it will again merit his help and recover the land which it had lost.

1:8b-9

And they had faces and wings on the four sides; and its wings were joined, one to the other. They did not turn back when they advanced, but each one proceeded before its face. The Gospels are joined to one another and cling together, and, flying through the whole world, they run hither and thither; they have no end to their flight, nor are they ever overcome and retreat, but they always advance to higher things; hence Paul also says: Forgetting what is past and stretching myself out toward what is to come. This same thing we can say both of the virtues of the mind and of the flight of the seasons and the mingling of the elements: that, leaving the past behind, they always hasten toward what lies ahead. That the seasons glide and flee is shown in a short little verse: But meanwhile it flees, irretrievable time flees, and in a lyric poem: Alas, Postumus, Postumus, the fleeting years glide by ...

1:10

Now the likeness of their countenance: the face of a man, and the face of a lion on the right of the four of them, and the face of an ox on the left of the four of them, and the face of an eagle above the four of them. By the faces he means the beginnings of the Gospels, of which the man and the lion, that is, the birth of Christ and the voice of the prophet thundering in the desert, hold the right side; but that of the calf, that is, of the victims and the priesthood of the Jews, is on the left, because, abolished, it has passed over to the spiritual priesthood of which it was said: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek; yet only in such a way that all cling to one another and are reckoned as one body; the eagle, however, which is above the birth, is also above the prophecy which is fulfilled by the coming of the Lord, and above the priesthood which has passed away, and is outside all these, telling of the spiritual birth, how the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, of which it is most rightly said: His generation who shall declare?. These are, according to the Revelation, as we have already said before: Four living creatures full of eyes before and behind, of which one living creature like a lion, and the second like a calf, and the third having a face as of a man, and the fourth like a flying eagle; and there they are said, after the manner of the seraphim, to have six wings each, covering their face with two and their feet with two, and flying with two, and ceasing neither by day nor by night, and saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who was and who is and who is to come.

1:11

And their faces and their wings stretched out above; two wings of each were joined, and two covered their bodies. We said above too that the Gospels and the seasons and all rational creatures and the four virtues are joined to one another, so that whoever lacks one lacks all. That two are stretched out and lift themselves on high signifies the heavenly preaching, and that all things tend toward the majesty of God. By the two, however, by which the bodies are covered, human knowledge is shut out, and no perfect view is granted, as the Apostle says: We know in part and we prophesy in part. But when what is perfect has come, the things that are in part will be destroyed.

1:12

And each one walked before its face. Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went, and they did not turn back when they walked. He who holds the handle of the plough ought not to look back behind him, nor imitate Lot's wife, lest he fall into the plague of Deuteronomy and perish by an incurable ὀπισθοτόνῳ [opisthotonos, a spasm that bends the body backward], by which Eli too fell, because he had offended God through the fault of his sons; how much more the four living creatures, which were full of light and winged, which follow the Holy Spirit going before them, which so fly through the world and raise themselves to the heights that they cover their bodies with the wings of history and do not grant us a fuller view? That it is said a second time: They did not turn back when they advanced, points to the mystery of both Testaments: that in these four living creatures both the Law and the Gospel hasten toward things to come and never take a backward motion.

1:13-14

And the likeness of the living creatures: their appearance as of burning coals of fire, and as the appearance of lamps. This was the vision running about in the midst of the living creatures: the brightness of fire, and lightning going forth from the fire. And the living creatures went and returned in the likeness of flashing lightning. (LXX: "And in the midst of the living creatures a vision, as of burning coals of fire, as the face of lamps running about in the midst of the living creatures; and the brightness of fire, and from the fire there went forth as it were lightning." And what follows: And the living creatures ran and returned as the appearance of 'bezec', was added in the Seventy from the edition of Theodotion; for they, lest the prophet should seem to utter two statements rather contrary to each other, thought that what they supposed to be contrary, that is: And the living creatures ran and returned, should be passed over in silence, lest it cause the reader to stumble; but it is better in the divine books to translate what has been said, even if you do not understand why it was said, than to take away what you do not know; otherwise many other things too, which are ineffable and which the human mind cannot grasp, will be deleted by this license.) We, however, say this: that, just as in Proverbs it is written in the same place: Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him, and again there is set down what seems to us to be contrary: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself, and both agree according to the difference of times and persons, since the fool is both despised because he does not receive wisdom, and foolish pride is knocked down by another folly, according to what the Apostle also says: I have become foolish; you compelled me, so in this place too we ought to ask why above it was said twice: The living creatures did not turn back when they advanced, and now once: The living creatures ran and returned; and there would be a problem were it not followed by: In the likeness of flashing lightning, which in the Hebrew tongue is called 'bezec', and which Symmachus translated: As the appearance of a ray of lightning. As the sky flashes with frequent fires, and in the twinkling of an eye and in a moment the lightnings dart about and return, not losing their womb and, so to speak, the source and matter of the fire, so these living creatures too, when they proceed with unstumbling foot, hasten toward what lies ahead. But if they see something set against their effort, they do not so much turn back as draw themselves in, to stretch out again and to offer the light which they had hidden for a little while, so that they may give the servants their rations in their season, and not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine; hence Paul too says: I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able to take it; and the choosing of Judas and the anointing of Saul do not convict God of ignorance of things to come, but show that he is the judge of things present; hence also the apostles are commanded that, if they perceive a house to be unworthy of their greeting, they should first shake off their running feet, and the peace which they had given to the house should return to them. The coals of burning fire, however, and the lamps running about in the midst of the living creatures are to be interpreted from that passage in Isaiah: And the fire devoured the matter like hay, and he will sanctify them in burning fire; of which it is also written elsewhere: Coals of fire will fall upon them; and against deceitful lips it is said in another psalm: What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against the deceitful tongue? Sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals; and in another place: You have coals of fire, you will sit upon them; these will be a help to you. Whatever creature we look at flashes forth the knowledge of God, since from the creatures the Creator is recognized; and from the midst of the living creatures the brightness of fire and lightning goes forth: for if the Gospels have struck against one another, in the midst of the letter and of the lowly history you will find the mysteries of the Holy Spirit.

1:15-18

And when I looked at the living creatures, there appeared one wheel upon the earth beside the living creatures that had four faces. And the appearance of the wheels and their work as the vision of the sea, and one likeness of the four of them; and their appearance and works as if it were a wheel in the midst of a wheel. Going by their four sides they went, and they did not turn back when they walked. The wheels had also stature and height and a dreadful appearance, and the whole body full of eyes round about the four of them. (LXX: "And I saw, and behold, one wheel upon the earth following the four living creatures. And the appearance of the wheels and their making as the appearance of tharsis. And a likeness in the four, and their work as a wheel is wont to be in a wheel. On their four sides they walked, and did not turn back when they walked. And their backs, and they had height. And I saw them, and their backs full of eyes round about the four of them.") Thus far the picture of the four living creatures that had four faces each is described, following the spirit and the cloud which was in the midst of the spirit; now for each living creature a single wheel is set, which were not joined to the living creatures but followed them; or one wheel appeared upon the earth, which, divided into four, had as many faces as the living creatures it followed. And so great was the likeness of the four wheels following the four living creatures that they were most truly believed to be one wheel. And their work and making was as the vision of 'tharsis', which we have rendered 'sea'; Aquila put 'hyacinth', a stone which has the likeness of the sky. And their appearance was as a wheel in a wheel, not so that you would believe it one wheel, but one coupled to another. They went on the four sides and were not dragged, nor did they turn backward; for how could it happen that they turned back, when they were following the living creatures, which always stretched themselves toward what lay ahead? The stature too and height of the wheels was so great that it caused wonder in those who saw them. And the whole body and the backs were full of light round about, so that you would see no member that did not have eyes of light — of whatever kind the fables of the poets describe Argus to have been, hundred-eyed or of many eyes, whom Juno turned into a peacock for his negligent guarding —, so that what is a marvel of God the Creator was the condemnation of an unavenged adultery. All things heavenly and earthly, and whatever falls under human understanding, roll on their own wheels; the moon runs through the yearly circuit of the sun in each month; the Morning Star, which is itself the Evening Star, while it gleams ruddy in the east and in the west and tempers the darkness of night with a small light, completes the same course in two years; and the four other stars which are called wandering, and whatever shines in the sky, and the varieties too of crops and trees and herbs, run on their own wheels through the four seasons; and we see nothing that was not before: Circling in circles the spirit goes, and returns into its circuits. All torrents go into the sea, and the sea is not filled. Why? Because they return to their springs from the womb of the abyss. But if anyone considers the wheel and course of the Gospels, that is, of the four living creatures, which breathe, live and understand, he will see that in a short time the world was filled with the apostolic word. The wheel in a wheel, too, is either the joining of the two Testaments, which Jacob's ladder and Isaiah's tongs and the twice-sharpened sword point to, or the Gospels cohering with one another, whose course and stature reach toward heaven, and touch anything on the earth only a little, as, ever hurrying, it hastens to the heights; of which it is also said elsewhere: Holy stones roll upon the earth, from which the heavenly Jerusalem is built; I think that this same thing is signified also by what is sung in the psalm: The voice of your thunder in the wheel, and elsewhere: Which sets on fire the wheel of birth; what sense these testimonies have in their own places is not a matter for this time. That the whole body and the backs are full of eyes will be confirmed by anyone who sees that there is nothing in the Gospels that does not shine and illumine the world with its splendor, so that even the things thought small and lowly gleam with the majesty of the Holy Spirit.

1:19-21

And when the living creatures walked, the wheels too walked together beside them. And when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels too were lifted up at the same time. Wherever the spirit went, there, as the spirit went, the wheels too were lifted up together, following it; for the spirit of life was in the wheels. With those going they went, and with those standing they stood; and with those lifted up from the earth the wheels too were lifted up together, following them, because the spirit of life was in the wheels. The four living creatures followed the spirit and the cloud which was in the spirit. And again the wheels, though they followed the living creatures as they lifted themselves from the earth, were by no means following the living creatures but the spirit, so as to show their own will: Because the spirit of life was in the wheels. Three things, moreover, are indicated equally both in the living creatures and in the wheels: when they stood, when they walked, when they were lifted up — things which both the living creatures and the wheels did in common; for neither could the wheels walk while the living creatures stood, nor could the wheels lift themselves up while the living creatures walked upon the earth; but those whose preaching was one had also one rest and course and elevation. And a second time it is said: Because the spirit of life was in the wheels, so that we should by no means think of some contrivance of wheels, such as we see on carriages, wagons, coaches and chariots, but of living beings, nay rather of what is above living beings; for the animal man does not perceive the things that are of the spirit. These wheels, then, in which was the spirit of life, do all things with order and measure, and are in concord with the living creatures, following them and through them the Holy Spirit; nay rather, passing over the intermediaries, rejoicing in the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. All these things, according to the earlier understanding, the prudent reader will be able to fit to the varied interpretation.

1:22-26

And over the head of the living creatures the likeness of a firmament, as the appearance of dreadful crystal, and stretched out over their heads above. Under the firmament, moreover, their wings straight, one toward the other. Each one veiled its body with two wings, and the other was likewise veiled. And I heard the sound of the wings, as the sound of many waters, as the sound of the sublime God. When they walked, there was as it were the sound of a multitude, like the sound of a camp, and when they stood, their wings were let down. For when a voice came from above the firmament that was over their head, they stood and lowered their wings. And above the firmament that was overhanging their head, as the appearance of a sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne, and above the likeness of the throne a likeness as the appearance of a man above. (Where we put: Their wings straight, and: As the sound — or voice — of the sublime God, the Seventy translated: Their wings stretched out and flying, and: As the voice of the strong one, which in the Hebrew is called 'saddai'. And many things, both in this and in other chapters, were passed over by them, which I have refrained from setting down because of their length. As for what we have translated more plainly: One toward the other; each one veiled its body with two wings, and the other was likewise veiled, in place of which in the Hebrew is written: 'Of a woman toward her sister; a man veiled his body with two wings, and a man was likewise veiled', he put man after woman in the same person for this reason, lest we should suppose sex among heavenly beings, since in one and the same, according to the Hebrew idiom, the same is called both man and woman.) Now above the four living creatures and as many wheels is seen the likeness of the firmament, which we call heaven, having the appearance of crystal, which is most pure and is said to congeal from clean and shining waters through excessive cold, so much so that water bound by frost is also called in the Greek tongue 'crystallus' [ice]; and it was fitting that in the higher regions there should be an exceptional purity which protects all things, that is, the rational and wise powers, and the course of the four seasons, and the regions of the world, and the order of all things, and the preaching of the Gospel, which is understood in part and veiled in part. And the voice of the flying wings is heard, as the voice of many waters, which according to the Revelation of John signify peoples; and, advancing little by little, it is said to be as the voice of a camp and as the voice of the sublime God, which in Hebrew is called 'saddai', and according to the Seventy 'voice of the word', so that we may believe that all that is preached in the world is the voice of the Son of God. When the living creatures stood, their wings were let down: for they could not bear the voice of almighty God resounding in the heavens, but stood and marveled, and by their silence showed forth the power of God, who sat above the firmament; and this firmament had, for those who were below, the likeness of crystal, but to those who were above it seemed like a sapphire stone; and this likeness of sapphire was the throne of him who sat in the likeness of a man. From this we understand that the firmament and the crystal and the sapphire and the man are shown in likeness, not in reality. That the man ought to be understood as God the Father many testimonies teach, among which is this in the Gospel: A man, a certain one, planted a vineyard and let it out to husbandmen, and a little after: He sent his servants and, above all, his son, and again: A man made a marriage feast for his son — not that the Son is excluded from the kingdom, of whom Isaiah wrote: I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and John: These things, moreover, he says, Isaiah said when he saw the glory of the Son of God, but that the Son too reigns in the Father —; and all things of the Son are the Father's, who is the image of the invisible God the Father: for in Daniel too God the Father is introduced sitting, and the Son of man is brought before him to receive the kingdom; and in the Revelation of John the same things are described of the Son; and at the contest of the first martyr Stephen he is seen standing at the right hand of the Father, he of whom it is sung in the Psalms: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet. And just as in the crystal all the purest and shining things in the heavens are shown, which illumine our eyed body, so in the sapphire, that is, in the throne of God, and above the firmament, which we take as heaven, the hidden and secret and incomprehensible mysteries of God are shown, who made darkness his hiding place and is seen in the cloud and in the thick darkness: hence also it is written in Exodus: And under the feet of God there was as it were a work of sapphire brick, and like the appearance of the firmament of the clearest heaven; hence also the bride describes the beauty of the bridegroom in the Song: His belly as it were an ivory tablet upon a sapphire stone; and in the Revelation of John the first foundation is written to be of jasper, the second of sapphire; and on the breastplate of the high priest, in the row and order of the individual stones, the second row has the carbuncle and the sapphire and the jasper; of which stones we have spoken in part in the Explanations of Isaiah.

1:27-2:1a

And I saw as it were the appearance of electrum, like the look of fire, within it round about, from his loins and upward; and from his loins downward I saw as it were the appearance of fire shining round about, like the look of the bow when it is in the cloud on the day of rain: this was the look of the brightness round about. This is the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord. The likeness of the man who sat upon the likeness of the throne (the throne which had the likeness of sapphire stone) is compared from the loins and upward to electrum, and this electrum had both within and without as it were the look of fire. But from the loins and downward there was fire shining round about, to show that the things which are above the loins, where perception and reason dwell, have no need of fire or of flames but of the most precious and purest metal; whereas the things that are from the loins downward, where intercourse is, where generation is, where the incitements of the vices are, need the purgation of flames, so that, once they have been purged, they may have the likeness of the bow, which is commonly called iris, when it is in the cloud on the day of rain — for the ἴρις [rainbow], which in Holy Scripture is called the bow, and in the Revelation of John is called by the same name ἴρις, cannot appear except in rain and in a watery cloud, being of diverse and most beautiful colors that pass gradually into one another; whence the poet too says: It snatches a thousand varied colors from the light opposite; and the same poet also, following the usage of the common people: When the bow, he says, drinks, by which he signifies that the bow never appears except in a cloud and in waters —. This bow is the sign of the clemency of God and of the covenant which he made with men, so that, whenever it appears in the cloud, we may know, according to the example of antiquity, that we shall by no means perish by a flood. From this it is shown that after penalties and torments and the purgation of sins there will be mercy, at least for those who have deserved to see God reigning. Hence it is said: This was the look of the brightness round about, round about God, or the throne, or all things that are perfect; and this is the vision of the glory of the likeness of God: not that he saw the glory of the Lord, but the likeness of his glory. Now the whole vision is this: the spirit lifting up, and the great cloud, and the four living creatures, and as many wheels following the living creatures and the spirit, which were deemed worthy to be under the firmament of God; and these, after they had been lifted up and had heard a voice as of many waters and as of the word of the sublime God, and the sound of a camp and of an army, let down their wings and showed their amazement by silence; and there appeared, seated upon the likeness of sapphire, as it were the likeness of a man, who from the loins upward had the appearance of electrum and from the loins downward the appearance of fire round about; after which a surer sign of mercy is given, like the look of the bow when it is in the cloud on the day of rain. We have spoken at greater length about this vision because it is both obscure and expounded in various ways by many. In what remains, so far as can be done without loss to the sense, we shall strive for brevity because of the size of the volume.

2:1b

And I saw, and I fell upon my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking. He is not lifted up by the greatness of the visions, but from awareness of human frailty he falls down upon his face. Whence also the apostle Paul, after his ascent to heaven and to paradise and his hearing of unspeakable words, says that an angel of Satan was given to him to buffet him, lest he be exalted; and Abraham fell upon his face after he had heard the words of God. And yet, because he had fallen down not through sin but through humility, he is raised up by the Lord and is commanded to hear his words. We should know also that it is one thing to fall upon the face, another to fall backward: Abraham, after he had heard of the birth of Isaac, fell upon his face and laughed; but Eli, who had sinned, fell backward; and of Dan it is written in Genesis: Let Dan be a serpent in the path, biting the hoof of the horse, and his rider shall fall backward, awaiting the salvation of God: for since he had fallen from the horse at the bite of the serpent, he therefore awaits the coming of the Savior; and in the Gospel according to John, those who had come to seize the Lord, after he answered, 'I am', fell backward to the ground, not at all enduring the word of him who had said to Moses: Go, say to the sons of Israel: He who is has sent me to you.

2:1c

And he said to me: Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I will speak to you. Lying down, he could not hear the word of God; but he hears, with Moses: But you, stand here with me, and Daniel too records that this happened to him.

2:2-3a

And the spirit entered into me after he had spoken to me, and set me upon my feet, and I heard him speaking to me and saying. (LXX: "And the spirit came to me, and took me up, and lifted me, and set me upon my feet, and I heard him speaking to me, and he said to me.") The divine word had instructed the prophet and commanded: Stand upon your feet, but without the help of God and the coming of the Holy Spirit he could not stand; therefore the Spirit enters into him, or takes him up, and raises him, so that he may be of firm step and may be able to say: He set my feet upon a rock. And we read of no sinner standing, but to the saints it is said: Stand therefore, girded about your loins; whereas the sinner deserves to hear that word of Deuteronomy: The footstep of your foot shall not be stable. Frequently it is said to Ezekiel:

2:3b

Son of man, and to Daniel rarely; each of them, in the person of him who had said: But the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head, consoles the captive people and draws them back to repentance.

2:3c

I send you to the sons of Israel, to apostate nations which have withdrawn from me; they and their fathers have transgressed my covenant up to this day. He by no means calls them the people of God, Israel, but apostate nations, those who have withdrawn from the Lord, not only the fathers but the sons as well: lest the sons should seem liable for the sin of the fathers, but rather so that the impiety of fathers and sons alike might be equal. Moreover, as for the Seventy's translation 'irritating me' or 'turning into bitterness', it signifies that God, who is by nature kind and sweet, is changed into bitterness by our vices: for just as it is said to the saints: Taste and see that the Lord is sweet, so sinners find him bitter; whence the Apostle too refers the goodness and severity of God to the saints and to the sinners, and of the sinners who lay fallen it is written: The Lord raises up those who are dashed down, the Lord loves the righteous, the Lord looses those in fetters, while to the saints who stand he promises rewards.

2:4a

And they are sons of hard face and of untamable heart to whom I send you. (This is not found in the Seventy.) And it is a mark of great clemency for God to send to such men and not to despair of their salvation, and a mark of prophetic confidence that he is not afraid to go even to such men. Now the untamable heart and the hard face we ought to understand in accordance with what is said to the sinner: Your neck is an iron sinew, and your brow is bronze; and these men in what follows are also charged with a heart of stone, which God says he will tear out and in its place give back one of flesh, so that by its softness it may receive the precepts of God.

2:4b-5

And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God; if perhaps even they will hear, and if perhaps they will be quiet. Something similar is written in Jeremiah too: If perhaps they will hear and repent, and in the Gospel: Perhaps they will respect my son. Now God speaks these words with the disposition of one who is in doubt, so that they may show the free choice of man, lest the foreknowledge of future things make immutable, whether for evil or for good, what God knew would come to be: for it is not because he knows what is to come that we must necessarily do what he foreknew; rather, what we are going to do by our own will, he, as God, knows will come to be.

2:6a

You therefore, son of man, do not fear them, nor be afraid of their words, for they are unbelieving and subverters with you. (LXX: "And you, son of man, do not fear them, nor dread before their face, for they will rage and will gather against you round about.") Although they are hard of neck and of untamable heart, yet my precepts are stronger. And do not think yourself deceived if you are sent to those who will not hear you when you speak. Behold, I foretell to you that they will rage and gather against you and surround you, leaving you no escape; and they will do this because they are unbelieving and despise the commands of God.

2:6b

And you dwell with scorpions. Such as can strike, such as can wound both with an arched blow and with a hollow sting, so that the same stroke both opens the skin and pours in the venom. Each one receives his name according to his character: to the scribes and Pharisees it is said: Brood of vipers, and of Herod, who was a shifty turncoat: Go and tell this fox; and the false prophets in this same prophet are compared to foxes, and now, for their untamable heart, they are said to be scorpions; whence in the Gospel too we read: All who came before me were thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not hear them — and how did the lost sheep of the house of Israel hear the adversaries? —, from which it is shown that those who heard the thieves and robbers lost the name of sheep and took on other names, so that they did not perish as sheep but as vipers, foxes and scorpions.

2:7-8a

And you shall speak my words to them; perhaps they will hear and fear (or be quiet). We must therefore not cease, although those to whom we speak are wicked, from preaching the word of God in season and out of season, according to the Apostle, because it can happen both that the hard man is corrected to softness and that he who is obedient, his will changed, does not hear.

2:8b

Do not be provoking, as the house is provoking. We have said once already that for 'provocation' or 'irritation' the Seventy put 'bitterness'. What he says, then, is this: You must not imitate those whom you are sent to correct, lest like sin should also earn like punishment.

2:8c

Open your mouth and eat what I give you. 'Show yourself worthy', he says, 'of my words, and take up spiritual food', so that, just as it is said in the Gospel: He who has ears to hear, let him hear, so here too it may be said: 'He who has a mouth open to eat, let him eat'. Whence also through the psalmist the Lord speaks: Open your mouth and I will fill it, and he answered: I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit; and the apostle Paul, who had in himself the treasures of wisdom and knowledge and in whom Christ the Lord spoke, writes to the Corinthians: My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; and of the Savior Matthew records: Opening his mouth he taught the disciples.

2:9a

And I saw, and behold, a hand sent to me. For the hand 'sent' the Seventy translated 'stretched out'; it is sent and stretched out to those who obtain the benefits of the Lord, but is drawn back from those to whom he speaks through the prophet: Is the hand of the Lord shortened and drawn back? and in the psalm: Why have you turned away your hand, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom, to the end? Finally, in the passion he stretched out his wings, and took up the disciples and carried them on his shoulders, and said: All the day long I have spread out my hands to an unbelieving people, that he might gather the children of Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chicks under wings of her own, and that by the stretching out of his hands Israel might overcome Amalek.

2:9b-3:1a

In which was a rolled-up book, and he spread it out before me, and it was written within and without; there were written in it lamentations and song and woe. For 'rolled-up book' the Seventy translated 'the heading of the book', in the hand of the Lord who sits upon the throne, the hand which was sent forth and stretched out; of this book it is also said in the Psalms: In the heading of the book it is written of me — let us understand 'heading' as the beginning —. This book, rolled up and sealed, and written within and without, or before and behind, was of such difficulty that no one could, either in heaven or on earth or under the earth, open it or read it, except only the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David and of Jesse; the book which John in the Revelation said he had devoured, not whole but in its heading, that is, in its beginning. For it cannot be that human nature should devour all the treasures of this book. And he spread it out before the prophet and offered it to be read and known, the book which in Isaiah is said to be sealed to a people that does not believe — for to this day a veil has been laid upon the Old Testament for the Jews —. And it was written before and behind, concerning things to come and things past; or certainly without, in the letter of the history, and within, in the spiritual understanding, of which the psalmist also says: All the glory, he says, of the king's daughter is from within. And there were written in it, both within and without, lamentations and song and woe: lamentations over those who are called to repentance, as Samuel and the apostle Paul bewailed and mourned Saul and the Corinthians, whom they longed to save; song over those who are worthy of God's testimony and to whom the psalmist gives the command: Sing to the Lord a new song; and woe over those who are utterly despaired of and who, when they have come into the depth of sins, despise.

3:1b

Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the sons of Israel. Unless we first eat the opened scroll, we cannot teach the sons of Israel; and so David too, after he himself had obtained mercy: I will teach, he says, the unjust your ways, and the wicked shall be converted to you.

3:2-3a

And I opened my mouth, and he fed me with that scroll. 'I', he says, 'opened my mouth, because it was said to me: Open your mouth and eat'. And when the mouth was opened, the Lord bestowed food, so that the beginnings of the will may be in us and we may obtain the perfection of blessedness from the Lord: For it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy; and yet both to will and to run belong to our own free choice. For 'I opened' the Seventy translated 'he opened', so that God is understood, who himself opened the prophet's mouth and fed him.

3:3b

Your belly shall eat, and your bowels shall be filled. (LXX: "Your mouth shall eat, and your belly shall be filled".) The beginnings of reading and of the simple history are the eating of the scroll; but when by constant meditation we have stored up the book of the Lord in the treasury of memory, our belly is spiritually filled and our bowels are satisfied, so that we have, with the apostle Paul, bowels of mercy, and that belly is filled of which Jeremiah speaks: My belly, my belly, I am in pain; and the thoughts of my heart trouble me.

3:3c

And I ate it, and it became in my mouth like sweet honey. David also says: How sweet to my throat are your words, beyond honey to my mouth, and elsewhere: The judgments of the Lord are true, more to be desired than gold and very precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; and Samson found a honeycomb in the mouth of the lion, and the Lord after the resurrection ate part of a broiled fish and a honeycomb, and in Proverbs it is said of the bee, although the Hebrew copies do not have this: Go to the bee and learn how she is a worker, and makes her work chaste: whose labors kings and the unlearned use for their health; this Moses and the prophets and the evangelists and the apostles have wrought, so that whoever is a king, whose heart is in the hand of God, may enjoy sweet food, while he who is simple and, without the cunning of the serpent, has the innocence of doves, may believe with simple faith and be saved; for snares are everywhere, and often the devil transforms himself into an angel of light, and honey drips from the lips of a harlot woman, who promises sweet things so as to slip in poisons.

3:4

And he said to me: Son of man, go and enter to the house of Israel, and you shall speak my words to them. He to whom it is said: Go and enter to the house of Israel is shown not to have been with the sinful people, although he seemed to dwell within the same borders by the river Chebar — for it is written: 'And I was in the midst of the exile by the river Chebar' —: for the prophet's way of life was separate, and he was offended by the sight of the wicked. Moses also did this same thing, pitching his tabernacle far from the camp of the multitude: and when he had entered it, the pillar of fire came down and stood before the door of the tabernacle.

3:5-6

For you are not sent to a people of deep speech and of a difficult tongue, to the house of Israel; nor to many peoples of unknown speech, whose speech you cannot hear: and if I were to send you to them, they would hear you. 'Since they will not come to you, go on to them: for not indeed do the healthy have need of a physician, but those who are ill; nor can you say: I cannot speak to them because they are of another tongue, and we are barbarians to one another, nor can we hear each other's speech. Why should I speak of one people? If I were to send you to diverse nations, still my authority and power would overcome every difficulty. And would that the time were at hand when I am to send to all the nations, when I am also to give the graces of tongues, so that my apostles may preach and may bring the whole world, out of its diversity of tongues, under my yoke by one faith; more easily would those hear who are of deep and lofty speech, who have nothing of Jewish levity but walk with a grave and solid foot, and who, though their tongues are unknown, are of known faith'; whence it follows: And if I were to send you to them, they would hear you. And in fact he afterward sent, and all alike believed; whence Paul and Barnabas say to the Jews: To you indeed the word had to be preached, but because you would not receive the word, behold, we turn to the Gentiles; and of the centurion it is said: Not even in Israel have I found such faith.

3:7

But the house of Israel will not hear you, because they will not hear me. For all the house of Israel is of a brazen forehead and a hard heart. 'Do not be saddened', he says, 'if they will not hear you. For this reason they will not hear you: because they will scorn to hear me', according to what the Savior said: He who does not receive you does not receive me; in which free will is openly shown. And two causes are given why they do not hear: 'Because they are', he says, 'of perverse will, and of a brazen forehead' — or, as the Seventy rendered, 'they are contentious' —, and it is understood that, though often called to salvation, they would not hear.

3:8-10a

Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads; like adamant and like flint I have made your face. 'The house of Israel is of a brazen forehead and of impudent audacity, and so hard of heart that it is compared to scorpions. Therefore I have given you a very hard countenance and a forehead that is overcome by no shame'. From this we learn that it is at times of the grace of God to resist impudence and, when the occasion demands, to crush forehead with forehead. And this is granted lest our modesty and human shame should be terrified at the snares of rivals.

3:10b

Son of man, all my words which I speak to you, take into your heart and hear with your ears. This is the food of the scroll, and these are the words in which, according to the diversity of the hearers, we speak to men either laments or song or woe. And yet it must be noted that the words of God must first be stored in our heart, and heard and understood with great care, and so brought forth to the people.

3:11

Go, enter to the exile (or captivity), to the sons of your people. And our Lord came to the people of the Jews, the Father sending him, to preach release to the captives, and that there might be fulfilled in him what is written: Ascending on high he led captivity captive, he gave gifts among men.

3:12

And the spirit took me up, and I heard behind me a voice of great commotion: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place. God, of whom it is written: The Lord taking up the meek, himself took up the prophet too, who was not in the flesh but in the spirit and, walking in the spirit, did not fulfill the works of the flesh, for the Spirit of God was in him; for which reason, despising earthly things, he is also caught up by the spirit and hears behind him a voice of great commotion, forgetting the things that are past and stretching himself toward what is to come, so that he might leave the snares of his enemies behind his back — something of this kind we also read in Exodus, when Pharaoh and all his army were pursuing Israel, and the angel in the pillar of cloud left the front of the camp and came behind their backs and stood all night between Israel and the Egyptians, so that, the adversaries being terrified, Israel might hear: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place; and the place of the Lord is every one in whom he finds lodging, or certainly the Son is the place of the Father, just as the Father too is the place of the Son, as the Lord Savior says: I in the Father, and the Father in me; Micah too signifies this same thing: Behold, the Lord will go forth from his place, and will come down upon the high places of the earth; and the mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before the fire, and like water that is carried down a steep place: for when the Lord Savior came down and set out from the Father, the high places of the earth and the mountains were shaken, and the lower parts of the valleys were melted; the place of the glory of the Lord can also be the inaccessible light of which the Apostle speaks: Who alone has immortality, and dwells in light inaccessible —. When we turn over in our mind the past judgments of the Lord, we hear behind our back the voice of great commotion; when we meditate in our heart on the things to come, a voice is heard from what lies before us and from those things that are ahead.

3:13

And the voice of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another, and the voice of the wheels following the living creatures, and the voice of great commotion. (Whereas according to the Hebrew there is understood ἀπὸ κοινοῦ [in common, supplied from the preceding clause]: I heard behind me a voice of great commotion, and 'I heard' the voice of the wings of the living beings, and the voice of the wheels, the Seventy added: And 'I saw' the voice of the wings of the living beings, the voice of them striking one against another, and the rest, in keeping with what is read in Exodus: And all the people saw the voice of God, so that the prophet heard the voice that came behind his back, but saw the one that was before him.) But it is better and truer to have understood the voice as heard rather than seen, both that of the wings striking one another and that of the wheels, of which we spoke above, and that of the great commotion, which showed that the wrath of God was to come upon the people of Israel.

3:14a

The spirit also lifted me and took me up, and I went away bitter in the indignation of my spirit. (LXX: "And the spirit raised and received me, and I went away aloft in the rush of my spirit.") After he was raised by the spirit and taken up by it, then in indignation and in the bitterness of his own spirit he went away whither he was being borne, understanding the indignation of God and turning over in his mind what the vision signified; or else, aloft, he was borne by the very rush of his own spirit, desiring to go where the Lord commanded — but let us understand his spirit not as the Holy Spirit but as the spirit of a man, of which it is spoken in many places, and in Isaiah: By night my spirit rises to you, O God —. And the prophet is carried over, not, as some think, in spirit, but in the body itself, as we also read of Habakkuk according to Theodotion.

3:14b-15

For the hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me. And I came to the exile, to the heap of new grain, to those who dwell by the river Chebar; and I sat where they were sitting, and I remained seven days mourning in the midst of them. (LXX: "And the hand of the Lord came upon me strong. And I entered to the captivity aloft; and I went around those dwelling by the river Chebar who were there, and I sat there seven days dwelling in the midst of them.") Where we translated 'heap of new grain', Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion set down the Hebrew words themselves, 'thel abib', which the Seventy translated 'aloft, and I went around', believing it better to say something than to set down what would raise a question for the reader. But we have learned from the Hebrews that 'thel abib' signifies this: when new wheat or barley is gathered, and after famine and want, before it is threshed on the floor, it promises some hope of food; so too Israel, small and slender, dwelling on the banks of the river Chebar, as if reviving and sprung up from the earth, promised a seed-sowing of the Jewish people. And the hand of the Lord comes upon the prophet, strengthening him, so that he may receive the name of watchman and teach what he has learned. And first for seven days he moves among them, seeing all that they did, so that afterward he might know what to rebuke. And he mourns, or dwells, in the midst of them, seeing their crimes and the righteous sentence of God for the iniquity of their sins — where we said 'mourning' and in the Hebrew it is written 'masmim', Theodotion translated 'marveling', to express the stupor of the prophet as he beheld their iniquities; but the second edition of Aquila, which the Hebrews call κατὰ ἀκρίβειαν [according to exactness], translated ἠρεμάζων, that is 'resting' and 'set apart', to show that he was indeed in the midst of the captives, but separated from them in mind —.

3:16-17

And when the seven days had passed, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel, and you shall hear the word from my mouth, and you shall announce it to them from me. He who is to be a watchman and is to tell the words of God to the people ought to be still for a long time, and to grieve at the things he sees, and to have in his conscience nothing of those things which he is going to rebuke in others.

3:18-19

If, when I say to the wicked: You shall die the death, you do not announce it to him nor speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked, and he is not converted from his iniquity and from his wicked way, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but you shall deliver your soul. There are two 'wicked', or 'unjust' as the Seventy translated: one who hears nothing from the watchman and dies in his wickedness, whose blood is sought from the watchman's hands; the other, to whom the watchman announces it, and who, scorning to hear, dies by his own fault, in such a way only that the watchman is free from blame. From this we understand that the Lord threatens the wicked and says: You shall die the death for this reason, that he may turn from his wicked way and live; for the threat is not against men but against sins, nor against those who turn from their vices but against those who remain in sin. And it is a great peril to keep silent the words of God, for a threefold cause: either from fear or from sloth or from flattery; whence Isaiah too: Woe, he says, is me, wretched, because I was silent. And what follows: But you have delivered your soul, echoes that saying of the Apostle: If anyone's work burns, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire, so that it may test whether the watchman is outside the cause of the death of him who perished, or guilty of it; for the work of the teacher is the salvation of the disciple.

3:20-21

But also if the righteous, turning from his righteousness, does iniquity, I will set a stumbling block before him. He shall die because you did not announce it to him: in his sin he shall die, and his righteous deeds which he did shall not be in remembrance; but his blood I will require from your hand. But if you announce it to the righteous man that the righteous man should not sin, and he does not sin, living he shall live because you announced it to him, and you have delivered your soul. Just as we read of two wicked or unjust men: one who did not hear and perished, and the other who heard and persevered in evil, so there are two righteous: one who did not hear and perished, the other who heard and was converted to repentance and saved his soul. And it is to be noted that the righteous can fall and, if he has a teacher toward better things, may draw back his foot; and the wicked or unjust man indeed, if he is not converted, will die in his wickedness and iniquity. But the righteous, if he commits wickedness and sin, does not die at once, but a 'stumbling block' is set in his sight, or 'torment', and as Theodotion said 'infirmity', so that he may be tormented and not find a level way, and may understand that he is sick; of such the Apostle also says: Therefore many among you are infirm and many sleep; for it profits the righteous to understand his offense through the experience of torments, and to say with the psalmist: I was turned in my misery while the thorn is fastened in me. And as his iniquities do not stand in the way of the wicked if he turns from his wicked way and lives, so his old righteous deeds do not profit the righteous if he is overwhelmed by new crimes. And as for what he added: He shall die, because you did not announce it to him, it is understood that he could have lived if the watchman and teacher had taught him.

3:22

And the hand of the Lord was there upon me, and he said to me: Arise, go out into the plain, and there I will speak with you. What we translated from the Hebrew as 'there', which is not found in the Seventy, is set down with significance, and there is no doubt that it signifies the place; for above we read: And I came to the exile, to the heap of new grain, to those who dwell by the river Chebar. And rightly he who had said: I sat, is commanded to rise; and he who had entered to the exile hears: Go out, not into rugged valleys, not onto sheer crags, but into the breadth of the plain, which can contain the glory of the Lord — whence it is also said to the Corinthians: Be enlarged —. When he goes in to the captives, of whom it was said that they rage and persecute him, he needs a strong hand so that he can resist and endure the fury of his persecutors; but when he goes out into the plain, the 'hand' of the Lord does come upon him, because without his help he could not go out, but 'strong' is not added: for he goes out to see the glory of God, not to fight. And this must be observed, that the prophet, while sitting himself in the midst of the captives who were sitting, did not see the glory of the Lord.

3:23a

And I arose and went out into the plain, and behold, there the glory of the Lord was standing, like the glory which I had seen by the river Chebar. At the Lord's command he goes in and at his command he goes out, and he sat with those who were sitting, because the number of the captives could not hear him while he stood. And having gone out into the breadth of the plain, he saw the glory of the Lord standing, which before he had seen walking, and lifting itself up, and at times standing — for it was by the river of the world, 'Chobar' [Chebar], which means 'most heavy', that the glory was seen, which signifies that all the glory of this world flows past and has no stable footing; but the glory of the Lord, standing and abiding, is seen in the plain with the prophet standing, the glory which in the midst of the captives could neither stand nor be seen —.

3:23b-24

And I fell on my face. And the spirit entered into me and set me upon my feet, and spoke, and said to me: Go in and be shut up in the midst of your house. Not able to bear the standing glory of the Lord, he fell on his face, so that he might be raised up by the spirit entering into him. This spirit set him upon his feet and spoke, saying: Enter and be shut up in the midst of your house; and the sense is: 'Because you have been strengthened by the sight of the Lord's majesty, fear no one and dread no one, but return into your house — either for the needs of the body, as some think, or as a sign of the siege to come — and, just as Isaiah, barefoot and naked, announced the three years' captivity and nakedness of the people, so you too, shut up in your house, prophesy by the very deed the impending siege of the city of Jerusalem'.

3:25-26

And you, son of man, behold, bonds have been put upon you, and they shall bind you with them, and you shall not go out from their midst; and I will make your tongue cleave to your palate (or throat), and you shall be dumb and not as a man who rebukes, because it is a provoking house. That he is shut up in his house, that he is tied in bonds, that he does not go out to those among whom he dwells, but amid a multitude of captives suffers the solitude of a prison, is, as I said above, a sign of the siege, which, when Jerusalem is shut up and surrounded by the army of the Chaldeans, permits none of the inhabitants to go out; this is the pot of which Jeremiah speaks, and this prophet himself in what follows, in which the flesh of the people is consumed. But as for the prophet's tongue cleaving to his palate or throat, and his being made dumb and not having the authority of one who rebukes, the cause is plain: Because it is, he says, a provoking house; and the sense is: So great are their bitternesses and so great their contentions against God that they do not deserve to hear one who rebukes them. From this it is plain that, where there is a multitude of sins, the sinners are unworthy to be corrected by the Lord.

3:27

But when I have spoken to you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: He who hears, let him hear, and he who refrains, let him refrain, because it is a provoking house.
