And behold, at the entrance of the gate twenty-five men, and I saw in their midst Jaazaniah the son of Azur and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people. And he said to me: Son of man, these are the men who devise iniquity, and handle a most wicked counsel in this city, saying: Were not the houses built long ago? This is the cauldron, and we are the flesh. Therefore prophesy concerning them; prophesy, son of man. And the spirit of the Lord rushed upon me and said to me: Speak. Thus says the Lord: So have you spoken, house of Israel, and the thoughts of your heart I know. You have killed very many in this city, and you have filled its streets with the slain. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Your slain, whom you have laid in its midst, they are the flesh, and this is the cauldron; and I will bring you out of its midst. You have feared the sword, and the sword I will bring upon you, says the Lord God. And I will cast you out of its midst, and I will give you into the hand of enemies, and I will execute judgments upon you. By the sword you shall fall; in the borders of Israel I will judge you, and you shall know that I am the Lord. This shall not be to you for a cauldron, and you shall not be in its midst for flesh: in the borders of Israel I will judge you; and you shall know that I am the Lord. (What follows is not found in the Seventy but has been added from the Hebrew:) Because you have not walked in my precepts, and you have not done my judgments, but you have acted according to the judgments of the nations which are round about you. The prophet is taken up, according to what is written: The Lord taking up the meek, or he is lifted up from the earth and brought in to the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, so that he may come to know the mysteries of the twenty-five men who were at the entrance of the gate, and of Jaazaniah the son of Azur and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people. These, then, who were at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, despairing of salvation and, from the consciousness of their crimes, ready for destruction, and unwilling to correct their sins through repentance, say: 'Although the houses which had earlier collapsed have lately, after the first captivity, been built, yet we know that this city is like a cauldron and we are for flesh, so that in it we may be consumed and burned up together, according to what is written in Isaiah: The tempest, if it passes through, will not take us'. As they say these things, the spirit of the Lord rushed upon the prophet, and commanded him a second time to prophesy and to say: 'Since you have said these things, and the secrets of your hearts do not escape me, I will interpret to you how the city is to be reckoned a cauldron and you flesh, not according to the sense in which you spoke, but according to another which you do not fear: the city is indeed in the likeness of a cauldron, but it will not be filled with your flesh, but with that of those whom you have killed; you, however, who think that you will die in this city, I will bring out of the midst of the city and hand over into the hands of enemies, and I will execute judgments upon you, so that, when you have fallen by the sword, by no means in the city nor outside the bounds of Israel but in the borders of your own province, then too you may know that I am the Lord'. And a second time it is said: 'In the borders of Israel I will judge you, and you shall know that I am the Lord; and all these things you will suffer, because you have not walked in my precepts and have not done my judgments, but have wrought the crimes of the other nations round about'. And since what is said is plain according to the letter, setting aside for a little while the names of Jaazaniah and Azur, Pelatiah and Benaiah, which we reserve for another time, this must be said: that to this day in the Church, which is the house of God, both before the eastern gate and at the entrance, or in the way, of the gate, which signifies the Savior, through whom we enter to the Father, there are twenty-five men, referring all things to the senses — and, so far as it does not escape my memory, I have never been able to find this number in a good sense, although in Leviticus men are chosen for the priestly ministry from twenty-five years of age; for in the Hebrew it does not have this number which is given in the Seventy, but the number thirty, which is contained in the opening of this prophet and in the age of the Lord when he came to the streams of the Jordan and was baptized by John; but if in the Gospel five wise virgins and five foolish are found, let us know that this number is placed in the middle and, according to the quality of those who use it, can be applied either to the good or to the bad side —. These men, then, who refer all things to the senses, and have two princes, of whom we spoke above, are contained in the dual number, which splits unity and, in the number of the second day, is not seen by the Lord, according to the Hebrew truth — whence also into the ark of Noah the unclean are brought in two and two; but the Lord, drawing the division together into one, made both one and loosed the middle wall, condemning the enmities in his flesh; whence also he says something more august and more sublime: I and the Father are one, so that he may call us back from the Jewish duality into the union of the Christian faith; finally, when the high priesthood of the Jews had been lost, the Lord suffers by no means under one prince, but under two, Annas and Caiaphas, so that he might show the divided error of their religion —. There are many at the entrance of this gate, before the eastern house of the Lord, who by their vices are compared to the nations, and from the consciousness of their sins despair of salvation, and say: 'The city in which we dwell is a cauldron, and we are all flesh, and we shall be consumed by the Babylonian burning, whose darts are fiery', unwilling to do penance and despairing of salvation; therefore they hear that they themselves are not the flesh of the past and lost city, but those whom they have scandalized, whom they have killed; and for that reason the sword is brought upon them: so that, after they have been judged in the borders of Israel, by no means among the nations but among Christians, then they may know that he himself is the Lord, according to what is read in the Psalms: When he slew them, they sought him, so that him whom they had not perceived through benefits, they may come to know through torments.

11:13

And it came to pass, while I was prophesying, Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died; and I fell on my face, crying out with a loud voice, and I said: Alas, alas, alas, Lord God, you are making a consummation of the remnant of Israel. As the prophet prophesies, one of the two princes, Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, dies, whose name means 'a fall turning aside', and he is the son of a 'builder' or 'mason' — for οἰκοδόμος cannot be rendered into our language otherwise —; the other of the princes, Jaazaniah, is kept safe — Jaazaniah signifies 'his ear', by which 'of the soul' is understood; Azur, however, 'support' or 'help' —. He, then, who by falling had turned aside from the Lord and was of a most wicked building, rightly falls while he whom God strengthened is prophesying; but he who obeyed the precepts of God and was sustained and supported by his help rightly remains in command of the people — we read in Exodus that, when Pharaoh king of Egypt had died, the sons of Israel groaned from the works of clay, of straw and of brick, and cried out to the Lord, upon whom, while he lived, they could not call; Isaiah also, when Uzziah the leprous king had died, saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and the Seraphim standing around him, and, understanding that he had unclean lips and dwelt among a people having unclean lips, he merits that a coal be sent from the altar and purge his unclean lips; here, however, as the strength of God prophesies, the prince who had turned aside from the service of the Lord falls, so that he may be raised up by Christ: for if the Lord is the resurrection, the devil is the fall; in which it is asked how it is said of the Savior: Behold, this one is set for the fall and the resurrection of many in Israel: for the fall of those who stood most wickedly, and the resurrection of such as had fallen —. When the prophet had seen this, he fell on his face, not by the desert of one who sins but with the feeling of one who mourns, and with a loud voice, which came from the great ardor of faith, he cried out three times and said: Alas, alas, alas, Lord God, you are making a consummation of the remnant of Israel; and the sense is: 'Even the very remnant which seemed to be among the people is being destroyed in your indignation'.

11:14-16

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, your brothers, your brothers, the men your kinsmen and the whole house of Israel, all to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: Go far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given for a possession. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because I have made them far off among the nations, and because I have scattered them into the land, I will be to them for a small sanctification in the lands to which they have come. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, your brothers, your brothers and the men of your captivity and the whole house of Israel is consummated, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: You have gone far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given for an inheritance. Therefore say: Adonai the Lord says: Because I will drive them away into the nations, and I will sow them abroad into every land, and I will be to them for a little sanctification in the regions into which they shall have entered there.") First we must speak of the variety in translation. Where the Hebrew has 'men your kinsmen' — for this is what 'goolathach' means —, the Seventy translated 'men of your captivity'; then, where there follows: All to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said, in place of 'all' they put 'is consummated', because of the ambiguity of the letters and of the word: for 'chollo', which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated 'all', they rendered 'is consummated', which does not accord with the sense at all. The word of the Lord, therefore, came to Ezekiel, who had said: Alas, alas, alas, Lord God, you are making a consummation of the remnant of Israel, namely in the death of Pelatiah and of those who were killed with him: that by no means were those the remnant which the prophet supposed in Jerusalem, but those who were seen to be captives in Babylon; and the sense is: 'O son of man, your brothers, begotten of the same stock with you, your brothers, I say, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: You have gone away from the Lord, because you are captives and have handed yourselves over with Jeconiah, but to us the land of Israel has been given for an everlasting possession — say, therefore, to them that I have indeed made them far off from the land of Israel and dispersed them into the nations and ordered them to be in foreign lands, but, because they have obeyed my command, I shall be among them, even in strange and hostile places, for a little sanctification, while very many are found among them who by no means submit their necks to idolatry but are mindful of the commandments of God', as Daniel and the three youths were, and it must be believed that others were, after the likeness of such great princes as Scripture now shows. From all of which we learn that we must not insult those who by the judgment of God have been handed over to punishments, nor reproach a man converted from his sins, nor ever say to those who do penance and have gone out of the Church: You have gone far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given for a possession, because thus says the Lord: 'Although I have separated them for a little while from my Church and dispersed them among the nations, yet I will be to them for a small sanctification while they remember their sins, and those who had departed from the land of God because of their vices, may hasten, because of repentance, to return to their former seats'.

11:17-21

Therefore speak: Thus says the Lord God: I will gather you from the peoples, and I will assemble you from the lands in which you have been scattered, and I will give you the soil of Israel. And they shall enter there, and shall take away all the offenses, and all the abominations from it; and I will give them one heart (or another), and a new spirit I will bestow, in their inward parts; and I will take away the stony heart from their flesh, and I will give them a heart of flesh, that they may walk in my precepts, and keep my judgments and do them, and be to me for a people and I be to them for God. But those whose heart walks after their stumbling blocks and their abominations, their way I will set upon their own head, says the Lord God. The divine word speaks to those who were captives in the land of Babylon, and to the brothers of Ezekiel the prophet and to his kinsmen, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: You have gone far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given for a possession; and it speaks these things which follow: 'I will gather you from the peoples, and I will restore to you the land of Israel; and when you have entered, you will take away all the idols on account of which you had offended God, and I will give you one heart, of the fear and the service of God, so that you may by no means serve diverse idols, or another than the one you had before; and I will bestow a new spirit in your inward parts, according to what is written: Create a clean heart in me, and renew a holy spirit in my inward parts; and I will take away from you the stony heart — that is, a hard heart, according to what Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, says: Hard of neck and uncircumcised in heart —; and the heart of Pharaoh is hardened, so that he may not let the people of Israel go; and I will give you', he says, 'a heart of flesh, soft and tender, and one which can receive the commandments of God, so that they may be written on the fleshly tablets of the heart' — for this reason a soft heart is given and the hard heart is taken away: so that they may walk in his precepts and keep his judgments and be in the people of God, and the Lord, who before had been an adversary, may be to them for God —; 'but those who have by no means corrected their former sins by repentance, but have walked after their abominations, I will repay', he says, 'with what they deserve: let their ways be set upon their heads'. Most think that these things happened under Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and under Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the great priest, and under Ezra and Nehemiah, to the tribe of Judah and to those who returned with them, and that the inhabitants of Jerusalem who were captured under Zedekiah king of Judah, or who fled with Jeremiah into Egypt, were dispersed into all lands, so that they by no means returned to the city of Jerusalem. But the full conversion, of those who were captives and of the remnant of Israel, is understood in Christ, when the remnant was saved, and in one day three thousand believed, and again five thousand, and others, of whom James speaks to the apostle Paul: You see, brother, so many thousands of believing Jews. These are all zealous for the law. But also daily the proud inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, whose heart walks after their stumbling blocks and their abominations, earn the displeasure of God, and those who were outside, the stony heart having been taken away and a most soft heart received, return through repentance to the Church, and walk in the precepts of the Lord, and keep his judgments, and become the people of the Lord, and the Lord, whom they had previously offended, becomes God to them.

11:22-23

And the Cherubim lifted up their wings, and the wheels with them, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them; the glory of the Lord went up from the midst of the city, and stood upon the mountain which is to the east of the city. Little by little the glory of the Lord withdraws from Jerusalem: first, deserting the temple, it stands in the court or at the threshold of the house, and afterward at the entrance of the eastern gate; lastly, its wings lifted and the wheels following, it stands upon the mountain which is to the east of the city — no doubt it signifies the Mount of Olives, from which the Savior ascended to the Father; and the glory of the Lord, which had departed from the city of Jerusalem, stood upon the Mount of Olives as a sign of resurrection and of light, so that from there it might behold Jerusalem about to perish and about to burn —. And as for his saying: The glory went up from the midst of the city, in other words the Lord speaks to the disciples: Arise, let us go hence, and to the Jews: Your house will be left to you desolate; Josephus also relates that there was heard in the temple a voice of the angels and of the heavenly strength, which had previously been the city's defense: Let us go away from these seats. And, in a wondrous manner, to the present day the glory of the Lord, which deserted the temple, stands upon the Mount of Olives and, gleaming in the sign of the cross, looks upon the once Jewish temple, dissolved into embers and ashes.

11:24-25

And the spirit lifted me up, and brought me into Chaldea, to the exile, in a vision, in the spirit of God; and the vision which I had seen was taken away from me. And I spoke to the exile all the words of the Lord which he had shown me. Where we translated from the Hebrew truth: And the vision which I had seen was taken away from me, the Seventy translated: And I went up from the vision which I had seen; and both signify that the prophet was carried over to Jerusalem from Babylon not in the body but in the spirit, and, when the vision had been taken away which had led him in the spirit to Jerusalem and had shown him all the things which the preceding discourse narrated, he returned from himself, and spoke to the exile all the things which had been shown to him, namely to those of whom it is written above: I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting beside me, and the hand of the Lord God fell upon me there, and I saw. And, in a wondrous manner, while those who had come to visit him were sitting there, the prophet was beholding mystical visions, and he was absent from those who sat before him: absent in spirit, present in body. And all things happen so that those who were captives might receive consolation, in that they are to be led back into the land of Israel, and are to walk in the precepts of the Lord, and to be to him for a people, and he is to be to them for God; but those who have not been converted to repentance, but have walked after their abominations, are to receive what they have done. That in the holy Scriptures words are spoken in place of things, we have often pointed out.

12:1-2

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of a provoking house, who have eyes to see and do not see, and ears to hear and do not hear, for it is a provoking house. (Where we have rendered: You dwell in the midst of a provoking house, the Seventy put: You dwell in the midst of their iniquities; but from what follows: For it is a provoking house, we understand that the former clause too fits this little verse.) We have often shown, too, that 'bitterness' is said in place of 'provocation', so that the sense is: 'You dwell in the midst of a house that turns God to bitterness, which, by the bitterness of its vices, makes God, who is by nature sweet and merciful, bitter and cruel'; otherwise we read of God: Taste and see that gracious (or sweet) is the Lord. The prophet, then, dwells in the midst of a people provoking God to bitterness, which has eyes and does not see, ears and does not hear, not through a defect of the senses but through the obstinacy of depravity; whence the Lord also says to the Jews: If you were blind, he says, you would not have sin, censuring and condemning in them a voluntary blindness. 'Since, therefore, they have eyes to see and do not see, ears to hear and do not hear, and they despise your words, teach them through an image and a picture, and show them by bodily figures, so that they may recognize the coming captivity not only by hearing but also with their eyes'.

12:3

You therefore, son of man, make yourself vessels of exile, and you shall migrate by day before them; and you shall migrate from your place to another place in their sight, if perhaps they may look, for it is a provoking house. (LXX: "And you, son of man, make yourself vessels of captivity, and be taken captive by day before them; and be taken captive from your place to another place in their sight, that they may see, for it is a provoking house.") No one doubts that the whole content of this passage points to the future captivity of King Zedekiah of the tribe of Judah, who was taken together with Jerusalem. But since some would have the captivity of Zedekiah, which means 'righteous Lord', go before as a type of the Savior, who, descending from heavenly things to earthly, took on a human body, and would have these be the vessels of captivity, I therefore think the prudent and cautious reader must be forewarned: that we set these things down, lest we seem to pass over anything, but do not approve them; for a wicked king cannot go before as a figure of him who is the example of all piety. That Zedekiah was taken by the Babylonians and Chaldeans both Jeremiah the prophet and the history of Kings relate, and that he was led from place to place, that is, from Jerusalem to Babylon, and the rest of what Ezekiel says in what follows. But those who refer it to the Lord Jesus Christ think that his captivity and exile from place to place signify the descent from heavenly things to earthly.

12:4-6

And you shall carry out your vessels like the vessels of one going into exile by day in their sight, and you shall go out in the evening before them, as one migrating goes out. Before their eyes dig through the wall for yourself, and you shall go out through it; in their sight you shall carry on your shoulders, in the darkness you shall flee: you shall veil your face, and you shall not see the land, for I have given you as a portent to the house of Israel. (LXX: "And you shall bring forth your vessels, vessels of captivity, by day in their eyes, and you shall go out in the evening in their sight, as a captive goes out. Dig for yourself in the wall, and you shall pass through it; in their sight you shall be carried on shoulders, and you shall go out hidden: you shall cover your face, and you shall not see the land, for I have given you as a portent to the house of Israel.") The prophet is commanded to do in figure what Zedekiah is going to do in truth: 'Gather,' he says, 'your baggage — for these are the vessels of one going into exile — while they watch, and after they have seen what you are going to do, you shall go out in the evening in the likeness of one going into exile'; we read that Zedekiah fled by night, the wall having been dug under, to the deserts of the Jordan, and was there seized by the Babylonians, and that this is what the wall dug through signifies; and as for his saying: You shall carry on your shoulders, there is understood: your baggage and whatever those who flee are accustomed to carry for the comfort of the road; in the darkness you shall carry out: so that you may not be seen by anyone; you shall veil your face: either by the blindness that befell him, when his eyes were put out by Nebuchadnezzar, or so that it might not be recognized that he himself was the king and the vigilance of his guards become greater; and what follows: And you shall not see the land, signifies this: that he was led blind into Babylon and did not see it; for I have given you, he says, as a portent to the house of Israel: for both the words and the deeds of the prophets are for a sign and a figure — whence in Zechariah too they are called 'men of portent', because they portend figures; and in Hosea God says: By the hands of the prophets I have been likened —. Those, however, who want Christ to be understood in the person of Ezekiel take the vessels of captivity as the human body; and the wall dug through as that by which he broke through the bars of the underworld and, rising again, was seen by believers alone; and his being carried on shoulders as when he ascended as victor to heaven with the angelic powers; and that he goes out hidden and veils his face, so that the divine majesty may not be seen in mortal flesh; and that he does not see the land, lest that land be illumined by his eyes which does not deserve his gaze: for the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and he turns his face away from the wicked. 'And all these things,' they say, 'he is related to have done so that, through the likeness of a man, he might turn the hard hearts of the Israelite people to faith; and he is given as a portent to the house of Israel, according to what is written: Behold, this one is set for the resurrection and for the ruin of many, and for a sign that will be spoken against'.

12:7

So I did as he had commanded me: I brought out my vessels like the vessels of one migrating by day, and in the evening I dug through the wall for myself with my hand; in the darkness I went out, and I carried on my shoulders in their sight. (LXX: "And I did so according to all that he had commanded me: and I brought out vessels like vessels of captivity by day, and toward evening I dug through the wall for myself with my hand, and I went out hidden, I was taken up upon shoulders in their sight.") What he was commanded above to do, he testifies that he accomplished in deed, and it needs no interpretation, according to either sense, since it was expounded above. But this must be noted: that at one and the same time Jeremiah was prophesying in Jerusalem and Ezekiel in Babylon, and the prophecy of the former was sent to the captives, and that of the latter to those who dwelt in Jerusalem, so that the providence of the one God in different regions might be proven, and the hearers might understand that whatever befell the people came about by no means through the power of idols but by the command of the Lord.

12:8-10a

And the word of the Lord came to me in the morning, saying: Son of man, have not the house of Israel, the provoking house, said to you: What are you doing? Say to them: Thus says the Lord God. 'If the provoking house asks you: Why are you doing these things? — or, according to the Seventy, even if they do not ask, you thrust it upon them, so that they may know why you have done these things —, say to them: Thus says the Lord God.'

12:10b-16

This burden is upon the prince who is in Jerusalem, and upon all the house of Israel which is in their midst. Say: I am your portent; as I have done, so shall it be done to them: into exile and into captivity they shall go; and the prince who is in their midst shall be carried on shoulders, he shall go out in the darkness; they shall dig through the wall to lead him out: his face shall be covered, so that he may not see the land with his eyes. And I will spread my net over him, and he shall be taken in my dragnet; and I will bring him to Babylon, into the land of the Chaldeans, and he shall not see it; there he shall die. And all who are around him, his guard and his troops, I will scatter to every wind; and I will draw the sword after them. And they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have scattered them among the nations and sown them in the lands. And I will leave of them a few men from the sword and famine and pestilence, that they may tell all their crimes among the nations to which they shall enter; and they shall know that I am the Lord. First let us expound the history: 'Say,' he says, 'O son of man, to those who either ask or do not ask what you are doing, this: that this burden and vision is upon the leader who is in Jerusalem — by the leader signifying Zedekiah —. And say: I am your portent (or, as the Seventy translated: I who make portents, so that future things may be known from present ones), as I have done, so shall it be done to them, to the leader and to all who are in the leader's retinue: they shall be led captive into the Babylonian exile, and the leader who is in their midst shall be carried on the shoulders either of beasts of burden or of those who had fled with him, and he shall go out in the darkness and in the shadows of night; and his companions shall dig under the wall to lead him out: his face shall be veiled, either by the fear of one fleeing or by the injury of blindness, so that, blind, he may not see the land of Babylon. And I will spread my net over him, and he shall be taken in my dragnet — for it was with the Lord's permission that he was taken by the Babylonians, and what he suffered to be done by the enemy, he testifies that he himself did — ; and, led into Babylon, he shall not see the land of the Chaldeans, and there he shall die a captive. And all his companions and helpers and the comrades of his flight, once he has been seized, I will scatter hither and thither, nor will I allow them to get away safe, but I will draw my sword in the hands of the enemy. And when they have been scattered among the nations, let them understand that I am the Lord and that all things were done by my will. And I will leave,' he says, 'of his companions who fled with him and were able to escape, a few who escaped the sword and the famine and the pestilence, so that, when by flight or by captivity they have come to diverse regions, they may tell all their crimes, either by word or by example, on account of which they deserved such great evils; and let them understand that I myself am the Lord'. But he who tries to expound the tropology and the explanation begun concerning the Savior interprets the leader who is in the midst of Jerusalem as him who went before as a portent and a sign, in that both he himself and his companions are captives of this world, and, ascending as victor from the underworld, he was carried on the shoulders of angels, went out in the darkness, unknown to unbelievers, and, the middle wall having been destroyed, made both one; his face is covered, so that he may not look upon the land of the Jews — nor is it a wonder if the Lord has hidden his face, since to this day a veil is placed before the face of Moses for the people that does not believe —. And the Lord spread his net over him — that which the bride says of him in the Song of Songs: Behold, he is behind our wall, looking out through the windows, appearing through the nets; of whom Jeremiah too says: The Spirit of our face, Christ the Lord, was taken in our sins; and: Though he had not done sin, he was made sin for us — ; and he will be brought, he says, into Babylon, the confusion of this world, into the land of the Chaldeans, which means 'as it were demons' — or else, that he might draw back to salvation those who had been enslaved to demons and lead captive the former captivity —, and that very land of the Chaldeans, he says, he will not see, and there he will die, so that by his death he may give life to us all. And all his helpers and companions, the apostles and apostolic men, he scattered into the whole world; and he drew his sword after them, so that they might be crowned with various martyrdoms. And then they might understand, either they themselves or those who had believed through them, that he himself is the Lord, and that he had scattered them among the nations and sown them in the lands for this reason, that they might bear much fruit. And he left of them a few men, such as John the apostle and the others, delivered from sword and famine and pestilence and escaping the onslaught of persecutions, so that they might tell the crimes of the Jews and the iniquities of all the nations to which they had entered, so that, having done penance, they might know that he himself was the Lord. We have said these things leaving the judgment to the reader's discretion; for the rest, there is no doubt that it is dangerous to compare the captivity and death of a wicked king with the mystery of the Lord.

12:17-20

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Eat your bread in disturbance, and drink your water in haste and grief. And say to the people of the land: Thus says the Lord God to those who dwell in Jerusalem in the land of Israel: They shall eat their bread in anxiety, and drink their water in desolation, so that the land may be made desolate of its multitude because of the iniquity of all who dwell in it; and the cities that are now inhabited shall be desolate, and the land deserted, and you shall know that I am the Lord. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, you shall eat your bread with pain, and you shall drink your water with torment and distress. And you shall say to the people of the land: Thus says Adonai the Lord to the inhabitants of Jerusalem upon the land of Israel: They shall eat their loaves with want, and drink their water with devastation, so that the land and its fullness may be devastated; for in impiety are all who dwell in it, and their cities which are inhabited shall be in desolation, and the land shall be devastated, and you shall know that I am the Lord.") After the prophecy about the prince and his companions, which was shown under a bodily image, he comes to the people, and whatever is said to the prophet is referred through the prophet to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: that in the evil of the siege they will eat their bread in want and distress, and drink their water by no means in abundance, but with torment and tribulation. 'These things,' he says, 'O prophet, are said to you, so that you may speak to the people of your land and say: Thus says the Lord to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, which is in the land of Israel: Besieged by Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, you shall endure the evil of hunger and thirst, so that the whole land with its fullness may be destroyed', signifying the inhabitants by that which is inhabited. And lest they think this comes upon them without cause: 'Tell them,' he says, 'that because of their crimes and impieties all the cities of Judea are to be reduced to solitude, and the cultivation of the whole land is to perish, so that they may come to know as raging the God whom they would not know as merciful'. According to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], we can call the inhabitants of Jerusalem those believing in Christ who dwell in the church; and if through sins they have deserved his displeasure, let them eat bread with want and drink water with grief and distress, enduring not a lack of the food of bread or of the drink of water, but a famine of the word and teaching of God. For when, either through the fault of the princes who are to be captured and handed over to the Babylonians or through our own hardness, we have lost the word of God and have not deserved to have useful waters, then we shall take our food in pain and penury, and the land will lose the multitude of believers, and the cities, which are understood as the churches throughout the whole world, will be made desolate, and the land will be deserted, so that all may know that this is the Lord's displeasure. This indeed we can also understand of the time of persecution.

12:21-28

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, what is this proverb of yours in the land of Israel, of those saying: The days shall be put off far, and every vision shall perish? Therefore say to them: Thus says the Lord God: I will make this proverb cease, nor shall it be commonly said any longer in Israel; and speak to them that the days have drawn near, and the word of every vision. For no longer shall any vision be empty, nor divination ambiguous, in the midst of the sons of Israel; for I the Lord will speak, whatever word I speak, and it shall be done; it shall not be prolonged any more: but in your days, provoking house, I will speak the word and do it, says the Lord God. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, behold the house of Israel, of those saying: The vision that this man sees is for many days, and for distant times he prophesies; therefore say to them: Thus says the Lord God: None of my words shall be prolonged any longer; the word that I speak shall be fulfilled, says the Lord God. What we, following Symmachus, have called 'proverb', all the other translators translated 'parable', which in Hebrew is called 'masal'. (Again, where we have published: Nor will there be ambiguous divination, the Seventy rendered: Nor one divining according to favor, for which all translated 'slippery', what we have called 'ambiguous', so that we may recognize the words of the prophets that deceive their hearers.) And this is the sense of the whole chapter: above he had prophesied against the prince who was in Jerusalem, then he had announced to the people that famine and the burning of thirst were to come; and as the multitude did not believe it, an old and well-worn proverb is taken up: The threat of the prophets is put off for a long time, and every vision will perish, for in vain is it 'seen' — or, according to Symmachus, διαπνεύσει, that is, 'it will be dissolved into wind and a thin breeze' —. 'Tell them, therefore,' he says, 'that my threat is by no means put off, nor is a false and ambiguous divination put forth among the peoples, one with an uncertain end, so that it is spoken at one time and fulfilled at another; but now, while you who speak and those who hear are alive, the word that I have spoken will be fulfilled'. He signifies the impending captivity of the city of Jerusalem, and Zedekiah, with the people of Judah, about to be taken at any moment. Not only at that time, however, but to this day the unbelieving crowd and the hard hearts of mortals do not receive the prophecy of God, but all that the prophets threaten, that the Gospel proclaims, they reckon is to be put off to another time. Let us note that here 'parable', which is used by the Seventy, is taken for 'proverb', according to what we read in the psalm: And I became a parable to them, and in this same prophet: What is this parable to you among the people of Israel, of those saying: The fathers have eaten the sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge. We have touched briefly on the obvious things, so that we may linger over the more obscure.

Book Four

I would wish, Eustochium, if it could be done, to weave my explanations on Ezekiel book by book according to the prophecies proper to each, and in no way to divide in the exposition what is joined together in the prophesying, so that the course might be easier for the one dictating and for the one reading alike; and I would separate the long and immense road of the interpretation into fixed stages, so as to show, as it were by titles and indexes and, to speak more properly, by summaries, what the individual books contain. But what am I to do, since some prophecies are short and others long, so that we are often compelled by necessity both to compress several into one book and to divide one into many? Hence now too what is against the prophets and prophetesses, to the elders of the people of Israel as well, and to the land upon which the four most grievous plagues are brought, and concerning the wood of the vine, which, when it has been cut off, is useless among all the trees of the forests, and also the catalogue of the vices of Jerusalem, we wish to comprise in the fourth book; and since the narrowness of a single volume does not admit that catalogue, we reserve the other part of it for the fifth volume, forewarning the care of the most prudent reader, so that he may know what we have to explain in this book and what he has to read.

13:1-3a

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy to the prophets of Israel who prophesy; and you shall say to those who prophesy from their own heart: Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God. (This which we have set down: Who prophesy; and you shall say to those who prophesy from their own heart, the Seventy omitted, and in its place they added what is not found in the Hebrew: And you shall prophesy, and you shall say to them.) Now this speech is against the false prophets, who were deceiving the people and prophesying something else, contrary to the commandments of God. Nor should it trouble anyone that they are called prophets, for holy Scripture has this custom, that it names each one the prophet of his own prophesying and speech, just as there are called prophets of Baal and prophets of idols and prophets of confusion; whence also the apostle Paul calls a Greek poet a prophet: A certain one of them, their own prophet, said: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies, and in Hosea we read: As a raving prophet, a man bearing the spirit. But whatever was said at that time to the Israelite people is now referred to the Church, so that the holy prophets are the apostles and apostolic men, while the lying and frenzied prophets are all the heretics, whose leaders invent things from their own heart, while those who have been seduced by them acquiesce in the lies of others.

13:3b

Woe to the senseless prophets, who follow their own spirit and see nothing. (LXX: "Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart and do not see at all", leaving out that which has been set down by us: Who follow their own spirit). Since the name of prophets, according to the rule of the Scriptures, is common to the good and the bad, they differ in this, that the good prophets are said to be wise, but the bad stupid and senseless; of these the one is referred to the men of the Church, the other to all the heretics, who, abandoning the Spirit of God, follow their own spirit, because they prophesy not at all by divine inspiration but from their own heart: whence also they see nothing. But he who is wise follows not the thoughts of his own heart but the Spirit of God, according to that passage in which, earlier on, the living creatures and the wheels followed the Spirit of God; and the prophet says: After the Lord your God you shall walk, and in another place: Lead me in the right path, and again: Your Spirit, he who is good, will lead me into the land; and for the people of God the pillar of fire and the cloud was the leader in the wilderness; and Jeremiah says: I have not labored following you. But which of the heretics, who follows his own spirit, does not stumble into darkness and, blind, lead the blind into a pit? Hence, although in their mysteries, or rather their orgies, they seem to themselves to see more than the teachers of the Church, still they see nothing at all, because they have lost the sun of righteousness, and in vain they imitate those who were formerly called 'seers' and to whom it is said: You who see, go; withdraw into the land of Judah, and in Bethel you shall not prophesy; for which reason the 'vision' of Isaiah and of Obadiah is placed in the titles, and the Lord commanded the apostles: Lift up your eyes and see, and the prophet humbly entreats: Unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law.

13:4-7

Like foxes in the deserts were your prophets, Israel. You do not go up from the opposite side, nor did you set up a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord. They see vain things and divine a lie, saying: Says the Lord, when the Lord has not sent them; and they persisted in confirming the word. Have you not seen an empty vision, and spoken a lying divination, and do you say: Says the Lord, when I have not spoken? (LXX: "As foxes in the deserts are your prophets, Israel. They did not stand on the firmament, and they gathered flocks upon the house of Israel; they did not rise up, those who speak on the day of the Lord, seeing lies, divining vain things, who say: The Lord says, and the Lord did not send them; and they began to raise up the word. Have you not seen a false vision, and spoken vain divinations, ※ and you were saying: The Lord says, and I have not spoken?⁚") Let us speak first according to the Hebrew: the prophets of Israel are like foxes, daily committing thefts of domestic fowl, who dwell, according to Aquila and the Seventy, 'in the deserts', according to Symmachus and Theodotion 'in broken walls' and 'ruins'; who cannot go up from the opposite side, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel — we read that Aaron ran to meet the fire that was devouring the people of Israel, and stood in the midst, and set up a wall for the safety of the people; to Jeremiah also it is said that he should not run to meet the Lord, nor stand against his wrath by perseverance in prayer: for just as a wall is set against an enemy, and one is accustomed to meet an adversary from the opposite side and to confront one who is coming on, so the sentence of God is broken by the prayers of the saints; whence also it is said to Moses: Let me go, and I will blot out this people: for in the one to whom it is said: Let me go, it is shown that he has the power of holding back —. These cannot stand in battle on the day of the Lord, so as to fight for the people with prayers and to resist the sentence of God with supplications. Since, therefore, they behold vain things and divine a lie and say that they have been sent by the Lord, when they have not been sent by him, and persist in their errors and desire to make their own word firm, they are convicted that all the things they preach are empty, since they say that their own lie is the word of the Lord. Moreover, according to the Seventy the sense here is this: all the heretics, because of their deceitfulness and wickedness, are like foxes, of whom the Savior speaks: Foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky nests; and of Herod it is written: Tell this fox; and of these same foxes, which deceive the little and simple ones and lay waste the vineyard of Christ, Solomon speaks: Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards; and in the psalm it is sung concerning those who are tripped up by their deceitfulness: They will go into the lower parts of the earth, they will be handed over into the hands of the sword, they will be the portions of foxes. These prophets, who are like foxes, did not stand on the firmament; nor did they deserve to hear with Peter: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; nor are they like Moses, to whom it was said: But you, stand here with me, nor like him who says: He set my feet upon a rock, but they are tossed about by every wind of doctrine; nor did they stand on the firmament of which we read in Psalm 18 (19): The heavens tell the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands. These gathered all sorts of irrational people, who on account of their excessive innocence are like cattle, against the house of God; hence it is now said: And they gathered flocks upon the house of Israel; nor did they themselves rise up, nor could they raise up others, but whatever they have done and are doing is full of lies. And what follows: And they began to raise up the word, signifies this: that they wish indeed to rise up and to lift themselves to the heights, but cannot fulfill what they desire; and it is said to them: Have you not seen a false vision, and spoken vain divinations? — and what follows: And you were saying: The Lord says, and I have not spoken, is not found in the Seventy —.

13:8-9

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have spoken vain things and seen a lie, therefore behold, I am against you, says the Lord God; and my hand shall be upon the prophets who see vain things and divine a lie: in the council of my people they shall not be, and in the writing of the house of Israel they shall not be written, nor shall they enter into the land of Israel, and you shall know that I am the Lord God. (LXX: "Therefore say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Since your words are lies and your divinations vain, therefore behold, I am over you, says the Lord God; and I will stretch out my hand upon the prophets who see a lie and who speak vain things: in the discipline of my people they shall not be, nor shall they be written in the writing of the house of Israel, and into the land of Israel they shall not enter, and they shall know that I am Adonai the Lord.") Under the person of the prophets, the speech is against the heretics who speak vain things and see a lie, and persist in making their own doctrine firm: that the Lord himself comes against them and rises up and stretches out his hand over them to strike, and does not draw it back to spare; and he threatens that they will not be in the council of the people of the Lord, nor in his Church but in the synagogue of the devil, nor will they be written in the house of Israel — of whom it is said in another place: Let them be written upon the earth: not into the land of Israel, which is the land of the living, of which it is now said: Nor shall they enter into the land of Israel, but into the land of the dead and the shadow of death — so that, after they have suffered these things, separated from the assembly of the people of God, they may understand that he himself is the Lord. Where we have rendered: In the council of my people they shall not be, the Seventy translated: In the discipline (or in the correction) of my people they shall not be: for the correction of adversaries is one thing, that of sons another; whence also Jeremiah: Correct, he says, us, O Lord, but in judgment, and not in fury, so that you may by no means make us few. Pour out your fury upon the nations which have not known you, and upon the kingdoms which have not called upon your name.

13:10-16

Because they have deceived my people, saying: Peace, peace, and there is no peace; and he himself was building a wall, but they were daubing it with mud without straw. Say to those who daub without tempering that it will fall; for there will be a flooding shower, and I will give very great stones rushing down from above, and a wind of tempest scattering it. For behold, the wall has fallen; will it not be said to you: Where is the daubing with which you daubed? Therefore thus says the Lord God: And I will make the spirit of tempests burst forth in my indignation, and there will be a flooding shower in my fury, and great stones of wrath in consummation; and I will destroy the wall which you daubed without due mixture, and I will level it with the earth, and its foundation will be uncovered, and it will fall and be consumed in its midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord. And I will fulfill my indignation on the wall and on those who daub it without due mixture, and I will say to you: There is no wall, and there are none who daub it; the prophets of Israel who prophesy to Jerusalem, and see for her a vision of peace, and there is no peace, says the Lord God. (LXX: "Because they deceived my people, saying: Peace, peace, and there was no peace; and this one builds a wall, and these daub it with folly. Say to those who daub with folly: It will fall; there will be a flooding rain, and I will give great stones into their joints and they will fall, and a spirit carrying away, and it will be broken apart. And behold, the wall has fallen; and will they not say to you: Where is your daubing with which you daubed? Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: And I will make a spirit carrying away break forth in my fury, and there will be a flooding rain in my wrath, and I will bring great stones in fury unto consummation; and I will dig under the wall which you daubed, and it will fall, and I will set it upon the earth, and its foundations will be uncovered, and it will fall, and you will be consumed with rebukes, and you will know that I am the Lord. And I will fulfill my fury upon the wall and upon those who daub it it will fall, and I said to you: There is no wall, nor those who daub it; the prophets of Israel who prophesy over Jerusalem, and who see peace for her, and there is no peace for them, says the Lord God.") The prophets of Israel, who will not be in the council of the people of God, nor be written in the writing of the house of Israel, nor enter the land of promise, will suffer these things because they deceived my people, wrongfully announcing to them peace and prosperity instead of the rigor of penitence and conversion, according to that which is said elsewhere: Peace, peace: and where is peace? God, then, was building for them μεταφορικῶς [metaphorically], through the commandments of the law and the utterances and threats of the holy prophets, an enclosure — for this is what the Hebrew word 'his' signifies — so as to keep from them every incursion of beasts and every hostile assault, as long as, converted to God, they were girded by this as by a bulwark and a most solid wall —; but the false prophets promised them peace not once but often: for this is what the repeated word of peace signifies. And that very wall, which in what follows is called 'cir', the false prophets were daubing 'without due mixture' — as Symmachus translated, that is, 'with pure mud', which had no straw and could not supply any strength; but as the Seventy and Theodotion have it, they daub it 'with folly'; while Aquila translated the Hebrew word 'thaphel' by ἀνάλῳ, which means 'without salt', passing from one metaphor to another metaphor, so that, just as food without salt has no flavor, so also mud without the straw by which it is made firm and bound together can provide no strength to the wall —. 'Say,' he says, 'to those who promise them vain things and pledge empty help, that this wall, this enclosure, will fall, and I will send a most violent shower, that is, most savage enemies — and he means the Babylonians and Chaldeans —, and these same enemies as stones of hail rushing down from above', all by μεταφορὰν [metaphor], so that a sudden whirlwind may overturn and undermine the unstable enclosure; and that afterward it may be said to them — that is, to the false prophets —: 'Where is the daubing with which you daubed? and where is the help you promised?'. But whatever we have said of the false prophets can be referred also to the heretics: that all their fabrications are dissolved by the wrath of God, and the building of the worst dogmas, which does not have the seasoning of the Holy Spirit, collapses and slides down to its foundations and to dust, and the enclosure itself is leveled with the earth and falls, and both the prophets who were promising and the people to whom it was promised are consumed in its midst, so that, after he has fulfilled his indignation and has said to them: There is no such wall — that is, 'you have no defense' — and there are none who daub it, but all things are vain and come to nothing, then you will know by deed that I am the Lord. And so that we may know who those are who daub the wall, there follows: The prophets of Israel — that is, the false prophets — who prophesy to Jerusalem, and see for her a vision of peace; these are the cause of sin and ruin and foolish security: For there will be no peace, says the Lord, because the Lord did not send them nor did he speak to them. That which the Seventy translated: And upon their joints, is not found in the Hebrew; and it signifies the joints of the stones in a wall, or the supports of timber by which walls are strengthened. Also that which we read above: He himself was building (or builds) a wall, many refer to the people of Israel, which was promising itself vain help, either from the Egyptians or from peace.

13:17-23

And you, son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart, and prophesy over them, and say: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand, and make pillows under the head of every age to catch souls; and when they caught the souls of my people, they made their souls alive. And they profaned me before my people for a handful of barley and a fragment of bread, to kill souls which do not die, and to make alive souls which do not live, lying to my people who believe lies. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against your cushions, with which you catch flying souls, and I will tear them from your arms, and I will let go the souls which you catch, souls to fly, and I will tear your pillows, and I will free my people from your hand, and they shall no longer be in your hands for plunder; and you shall know that I am the Lord. Because you made the heart of the righteous grieve falsely, whom I did not sadden, and strengthened the hands of the wicked, so that he should not turn back from his evil way and live, therefore you shall not see vain things, and you shall divine divinations no more, and I will rescue my people from your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord. (LXX: "And you, son of man, make your face firm upon the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart, and prophesy over them, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to those who sew pillows under every elbow of the hand, and make veils over every head of every age to pervert souls; the souls of my people have been overturned, and they were saving souls. And they defiled me before my people for a handful of barley and a fragment of bread, to slay souls which ought not to die, and to save souls which ought not to live, while they speak vain words to a people that listens. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am over your pillows, upon which you have gathered souls, and I will tear them from your arms, and I will let go the souls which you pervert, their souls into dispersion, and I will tear your veils, and I will free my people from your hands, and they shall no longer be in your hands for gathering; and you shall know that I am the Lord. Because you were perverting the soul of the righteous unjustly, and I was not perverting him, and you were strengthening the hands of the unjust, so that he should not be converted at all from his most evil way and live, therefore you shall see lies no more, and you shall by no means divine divinations any longer, and I will free my people from your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord.") Above, the divine word was directed to the prophets, who were daubing the wall with mud, because it had no straw and could give no strength to the wall or enclosure; now he is ordered to set his face, or to direct it, or, as the Seventy translated, to make it firm, against the daughters of the people, the prophetesses. And just as other, false prophets were inspired against the prophets by a diabolical spirit, to overturn the commandments of God, so against the prophetesses — such as were Deborah and Huldah and, in the Acts of the Apostles, the four prophesying daughters of Philip the evangelist — other women of the same sex were inspired by a demonic spirit, such as were Prisca and Maximilla, to overturn the faith of the truth by the prophesying of a lie. These, the Hebrews say, were trained in magic arts through necromancies and a pythonic spirit, such as was she who seemed to have raised up the soul of Samuel, and, in the Acts of the Apostles, she whose divination brought much income to her masters, out of whom the unclean spirit was cast at the command of the apostle Paul. But we say this: that some heretics, by the falsity of their dogmas, preach virtue — of whom were Pythagoras, and Zeno, from whom come the Stoics, the Brahmans of the Indians and the Gymnosophists of the Ethiopians, who because of the continence of their diet win the admiration of the nations — and rightly are they said to daub a wall and to promise some strength —, but because they lack the seasoning of Christ, their labor is vain and their building will perish: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain; others, however, teachers of pleasures and of lust, are said to sew cushions and to place them under every elbow of the hand: the Epicureans and the Pyrrhonists, and among us Jovinian and Eunomius, who say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. The prophet, then, is ordered to set, or to make firm, his face against the daughters of his people. And first we must say what the face 'set' or 'directed' and 'made firm' means: namely that which is written of the Lord: The face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth. As indeed wax melts before the face of the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God; according to which sense it is said in this same prophet: Son of man, make your face firm upon Theman and Darom and Nageb, and again: The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make your face firm upon Jerusalem, and a little after: The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make your face firm upon the Ammonites, and again: Make your countenance firm upon Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and again: Son of man, make your face firm upon Gog and Magog, and in another place: I will make my face firm upon that man, and I will put him into the desert and into dissipation, and I will take him away from the midst of the people, and you shall know that I am the Lord. Woe, then, to these heresies and to these doctrines, which, promising rest, deceive every age and sex, to catch the souls of the wretched and to defile me before my people, while I am believed to love pleasure; and this not for a corus and a hemicorus of barley, as we read in Hosea, but for a handful of barley, on which brute animals feed, and a fragment of bread: not a whole loaf, nor the solid testimonies of the Scriptures, but those which have been broken and cut short and diminished by heretical depravity, so as to deceive all the holy and drag them to death, while they strive to make sinners alive with vain promises. Therefore the clement and merciful God does not slay the prophetesses themselves, but will tear their cushions, which like nets catch flying souls, so that, after these have been torn, the souls may have free power of flying; and he will rend the veils, or pillows, on which the ruling part of the soul was reclining and with which the heads of the deceived were covered; since the apostle teaches that the heads of men are not to be veiled, but that the glory of the Lord is to be contemplated with unveiled face: 'For you,' he says, 'were breaking the spirits of those who serve God with false terrors, and were keeping the wicked shut in with fraudulent promises, lest by doing penance they should recover the life which they had lost; therefore you shall by no means see vain visions, nor will I call your lies prophecies, but divinations, of which it is written: There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel, so that I may rescue my people from your hands, and you may know by deed that I am the Lord, who have freed the lost'.

14:1-11

And men, elders of Israel, came to me and sat before me. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, these men have set uncleannesses in their hearts, and have set up the stumbling block of their iniquity against their face; shall I, being asked, answer them? Therefore speak to them, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: A man, a man of the house of Israel who sets his uncleannesses in his heart, and sets up the stumbling block of his iniquity against his face, and comes to the prophet inquiring of me through him, I the Lord will answer him according to the multitude of his uncleannesses, that the house of Israel may be caught in their heart, in which they have withdrawn from me in all their idols. Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Turn and withdraw from your idols, and turn away your faces from all your defilements. For a man, a man of the house of Israel and of the proselytes, whoever is a stranger in Israel, if he is estranged from me and sets his idols in his heart, and sets up the stumbling block of his iniquity against his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire of me through him, I the Lord will answer him by myself; and I will set my face upon that man, and I will make him an example and a proverb, and I will destroy him from the midst of my people, and you shall know that I am the Lord. And the prophet, when he errs and speaks a word, I the Lord have deceived that prophet, and I will stretch out my hand upon him, and I will blot him out from the midst of my people Israel. And they shall bear their iniquity: as the iniquity of the one inquiring, so shall the iniquity of the prophet be, that the house of Israel may no longer stray from me, nor be polluted in all their transgressions, but may be to me for a people, and I may be to them for God, says the Lord of hosts. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, these men have set their thoughts in their hearts, and have set the torment of their iniquities before their face; shall I, answering, answer them? Therefore speak to them and say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: A man, a man of the house of Israel who sets his thoughts in his heart, and sets the torment of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire of him in me, I the Lord will answer him in those things by which his mind is held, so as to turn away the house of Israel according to their hearts, which have been estranged from me in their thoughts. Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Turn and withdraw from your inventions and from all your impieties, and turn your faces. For a man, a man of the house of Israel and of the strangers who sojourn in Israel, who is estranged from me and sets his thoughts in his heart, and sets the torment of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire of him in me, I the Lord will answer him in that by which he is held; and I will make my face firm upon that man, and I will make him a desert and an extermination, and I will take him away from the midst of my people, and you shall know that I am the Lord. And the prophet, if he errs and speaks a word, I the Lord have made that prophet err, and I will stretch out my hand upon him, and I will exterminate him from the midst of my people Israel. And they shall receive their iniquity: according to the iniquity of the one inquiring, the iniquity of the prophet also shall likewise be, that the house of Israel may by no means stray from me, and that they may not be polluted any more in all their offenses, and they shall be to me for a people, and I will be to them for God, says Adonai the Lord.") After he had spoken to the prophets who prophesied out of their own heart and daubed the wall without tempering, and to the prophetesses who sewed cushions and put them under every elbow of the hand, and made veils, and covered the heads of every age — by which the teaching of perverse doctrines is shown —, there came to the prophet not all the old men, lest all should seem to err, but certain of the elders of Israel, and they sat before the prophet, meanwhile deferring in silence the reason for which they had come; and at once the word of God came to the prophet, indicating why they were present — for it is not in the nature of man, however holy, to know the secrets of the heart; hence it is said of the Savior alone: But Jesus, seeing their thoughts and why do you think evil things in your hearts —. And the sense is: 'Son of man, these men who sit before you have set their uncleannesses in their hearts — or thoughts, and, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, idols —, and they have set the stumbling block — that is, the ruin and torment — of their iniquity against their face, and so they have come to inquire after the word of the Lord. Ought I to answer men of this sort, who come to me with their former thoughts, not abandoning the crimes of their impiety even at this time, but believing in idols and deceitful divinations, and having the ruin and torment of iniquity against their face, while they despair of better things and are ready for punishment, and so desire to learn my words through you? Since, therefore, they have come to you with a perverse heart, you answer not in your own person — lest the authority of the one answering be slight —, but by my command, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God'. Now the meaning of the whole passage, to comprehend a broad explanation in a brief discourse, is this: 'A man, a man not of the other nations — whose error can have pardon —, but of the house of Israel, who comes to the prophet to inquire with his former vices — of which we have spoken above —, I will answer him according to his heart and his uncleannesses, so that he may hear according to what he wishes and believes: for he who asks not in a spirit of learning but of testing does not deserve correction. For they have withdrawn from me and have followed idols; and this is a brief threat, so that they may withdraw from idols and perverse thoughts and turn to me, abandoning their former crimes'; for he who asks deceitfully does not deserve to hear the truth, but is to be caught by his own heart, just as the scribes and Pharisees, questioning the Lord, or rather testing him, hear: Why do you test me?, and again: Neither will I tell you by what power I do these things; but whoever is such a man and asks in this way, God sets his face upon him, or makes it firm, so that by the severity of his countenance the hardness of the brow may be softened and he may be for an example and a proverb, or for a solitude and a destruction, so that, when he has been destroyed out of the people of God, the rest may know that he himself is the Lord, who knows the secrets of the heart and understands the perversity of the mind, and considers not the words of those who speak but their hearts. And what follows also seems to raise a question: The prophet, when he errs and speaks a word, I the Lord have deceived that prophet; let us not think that this is said of a true prophet, but of a false prophet, who is called a prophet συνωνυμῶς [by a shared name]. And it can be resolved from that passage of the Scriptures where Ahab king of Israel, going to battle, will not listen to Micaiah the prophet, but acquiesces in the counsels of the false prophets, and Micaiah says that he saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and that a spirit of error offered itself of its own accord to deceive the king; the devil too, in the book of Job, going around the earth, is said to stand in the sight of God and to receive power from the Lord, first over Job's substance, then over his body; and Balaam the soothsayer also is sent by the Lord to deceive Balak the son of Beor. All this, however, is said so that it may not be reckoned to the strength of the false prophets that the people is deceived and would rather hear a lie than lend its ear to the truth, but that it is of the wrath of God that a perverse and unbelieving people listens to false prophets rather than to prophets. Then he stretches out his hand upon him — the prophet is understood — and he is blotted out from the midst of his people, so that he may bear his iniquity, because for like error the punishment too is alike, so that both he who asks and he who is asked may bear their iniquity, and the house of Israel, that of those who wish to hear the words of God, may by no means be mocked by perverse prophesyings, but may be the people of God, and may itself deserve to have the Lord as God. With what he said: I the Lord have deceived him, the words of Solomon agree, who, discoursing of God, says: And he will mock the mockers, and that testimony: If they walk perversely toward me, I too will walk against them in perverse fury. And what is said a second time: A man, a man of the sons of Israel and of the strangers who are joined to them, shows, according to the Apostle, a twofold man in us: the outer and the inner — for many, having the bodily face of a man, take on the images of various beasts, whose destruction the prophet desires when he prays: Lord, in your city you will destroy their image; those of whom it is written: Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts of burden, and became like them, are not men who are men, but men who are beasts of burden; again, those who hear in the Gospel: Serpents, brood of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come?, are not men who are men, but men who are serpents as well; and those of whom it is written: Foxes have holes, and the birds of heaven nests, and of Herod: Tell this fox, are not men who are men, but men who are foxes —; but those who possess both words 'man', if they err, are corrected by punishments for this reason, that they may understand that he himself is the Lord. Moreover, what we have set down according to the Seventy: A man who is estranged from me and sets his thoughts in his heart, and the torment (or punishment) of his iniquity before his face, agrees with that testimony which is written in Isaiah: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled; for each one kindles for himself the blazing of flames and prepares punishments for himself, while he is unwilling to correct his errors by repentance, but remains in errors that deserve the burning of flames.

14:12-23

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, when a land sins against me so as to transgress, transgressing, I will stretch out my hand upon it, and I will break the staff of its bread, and I will send famine into it and kill from it man and beasts; and if these three men are in its midst, Noah and Daniel and Job, they by their righteousness shall deliver their own souls, says the Lord of hosts. But if I also bring most evil beasts upon the land to lay it waste, and it becomes impassable because there is no one passing through on account of the beasts, if these three men are in it, as I live, says the Lord, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone shall be delivered, and the land shall be made desolate. Or if I bring a sword upon that land, and say to the sword: Pass through the land, and I kill from it man and beast, and these three men are in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they shall not deliver sons or daughters, but they alone shall be delivered. But if I also send pestilence upon that land, and pour out my indignation upon it in blood, to take away from it man and beast, and Noah and Daniel and Job are in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they shall not deliver son and daughter, but they by their righteousness shall deliver their own souls. For thus says the Lord God: But if I also send my four most evil judgments, sword and famine and evil beasts and pestilence, against Jerusalem, to kill from it man and cattle, yet there shall be left in it a deliverance of those who bring out sons and daughters: behold, they shall come out to you, and you shall see their way and their inventions, and you shall be consoled over the evil which I brought upon Jerusalem, in all that I have brought in upon it. And they shall console you, when you see their way and their inventions, and you shall know that not in vain have I done all that I did in it, says the Lord God. Four plagues are brought upon the 'transgressing' land — or, as the Seventy translated, the 'sinning' land —: famine, beasts, sword, pestilence; and if these are brought one at a time, piece by piece, upon individual regions, and these three men, Noah and Daniel and Job, whose righteousness is proclaimed by the voices of the Scriptures, pray for the sinning land, not only will they be unable to preserve it, but not even their own sons and daughters, if these have committed the works of the sinning land; they will be able to deliver themselves alone. — It is asked, since Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, Moses too and the other patriarchs and prophets, were righteous, why mention is made of these alone; which is easily resolved: for Noah could not put off the flood impending over the world, because all the earth had polluted the ways of the Lord, but he had his sons preserved, who perhaps were of the same virtue, and also for the sake of a seedbed of the human race; Daniel too softened by no weeping the captivity impending over the people of the Jews; and Job as well, not on account of sins but for the sake of testing, delivered neither his house nor his sons. Others, however, say that because these three men alone beheld both prosperity and adversity and prosperity again, they are for that reason named together, and that this is secretly signified: that, just as they saw both good things and evil and again joyful things, so also the people of Israel, which had first enjoyed good things and afterward bore the yoke of captivity, if it does penance, returns to its former happiness. — But if Noah and Daniel and Job, gathered together and placed in one place, cannot withdraw the sinning land, that is, those who dwell in the land, from the wrath of God, what is to be said of those who think that sinful sons can be delivered from the fires of Gehenna by the merit and virtues of their parents? Hence neither will a martyr father be able to deliver a transgressing son, nor will a mother of holy life give the rewards of chastity to an unchaste daughter; and on the contrary the vices of parents will not harm their children, but: The soul that sins, it shall die. Lot, dwelling in Sodom but a stranger both in spirit and in flesh, did not deliver his wife, who had looked back behind her, but only his daughters, who perhaps had not sinned; and Josiah, a holy man, not only did not save a sinful people by his virtues, but he himself also died in its sins. But if at times the Lord promises his mercy to their posterity on account of Abraham and David, it must be noted that he does not spare those who persevere in crimes, but those who do penance, so that the conduct of the sons assists the merits of the fathers. 'Since,' he says, 'these things are so, and the prayer of such great men does not save a sinning land from single plagues, thus says the Lord: Because Jerusalem has sinned abominably, I will bring four plagues upon it at once: the sword by which it is slaughtered by its enemies, and famine which it endures under siege, and beasts by which those who flee are devoured in deserts and forests, and pestilence, which always follows famine and want — for which the common edition translated 'death' —. And these things,' he says, 'I will bring upon it, so that neither men remain in it nor beasts; and yet, in my clemency, while the four plagues impend at once and lay everything waste, I will leave in it some who bring out their sons and daughters, and let them come here as captives — that is, to Babylon and to Chaldea —; and when you see them and have looked closely at their works, then you will understand that they were justly taken captive and that my sentence was just, and your captivity will have consolation, while you understand that I delivered them from sword and famine and beasts and pestilence for this reason: that from their perversity you may learn that Jerusalem was deservedly overthrown and the temple burned and the people led captive, except those whom sword, famine, beasts and pestilence consumed'. These things were said of that Jerusalem upon which, while Ezekiel was prophesying among the Chaldeans, captivity was drawing near.
