But upon our land too, to which it is said: You are earth, and into earth you shall go, and upon our Jerusalem, each and every one of the believers, if they despise the commandments of God and deserve to be called transgressors, famine will be brought: Not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God; the sword too will be brought, of which we read: They shall be delivered into the hands of the sword, they shall be the portions of foxes, and to Mary: A sword shall pierce through your own soul also; beasts too will be brought, to which the righteous man asks not to be handed over: Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses to you; and pestilence will be brought — for which the Seventy translated 'death' —, of which it is written: The death of sinners is very evil, and: The soul that sins, it shall die, and: So bitter is death. From all of which neither the teaching of spiritual parents — whom we understand to be teachers — nor princes will be able to deliver us, unless the sons give their assent and assist the parents' entreaties by their own efforts; for the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the iniquity of the wicked shall abide in him: Each shall die for his own sin, and shall be saved by his own righteousness; and in vain do the Jews say: Abraham is our father, since they do not have the works of Abraham; but if there is confidence in anyone, let us trust in the Lord alone: Cursed, for, is every man who puts his hope in man, however holy they may be, however much they may be prophets; we read: Do not trust in men, and again: It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in princes, not in the princes of the world only but in the princes of the churches, who will deliver only their own souls, if they are righteous, but the sons and daughters whom they have begotten in the Church they will not be able to save, if these are negligent; and yet the Apostle says: If anyone's work is burned up, he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire. And the hand is stretched out over the transgressing land so that the staff, or strength, of bread may be broken; and that hand, stretched out, threatens plagues, since he who stretches it out and lifts it up does not wish to strike sinners, but by its stretching out to terrify them and to preserve them once terrified.

15:1-8

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, what will become of the wood of the vine, out of all the woods of the groves that are among the trees of the forests? Is wood taken from it to make a work, or will a peg be fashioned from it, so that any vessel may hang from it? Behold, it has been given to the fire for food; the fire has consumed both its parts, and its middle has been reduced to ashes; will it be useful for a work? Even when it was whole it was not fit for a work; how much more, when the fire has devoured it and burnt it up, will no work be made of it! Therefore thus says the Lord God: As the wood of the vine among the trees of the forests, which I have given to the fire to devour, so will I give up the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will set my face against them: they will go out from the fire, and the fire will consume them, and you will know that I am the Lord, when I have set my face against them and have made the land pathless and desolate, because they have proved transgressors, says the Lord God. (Where we translated: The fire has consumed both its parts, and its middle has been reduced to ashes, the Seventy translated: The fire consumes its yearly cleansing, and lets it go to the end. Again, where we said: When I have set my face against them, they rendered: When I have set firm. 'Transgression', too, they translated as 'offense'.) By various similitudes, then, which the Greeks call parables, the overthrow of the city of Jerusalem is foretold; and just as above, in the frying pan in which the flesh of the people was fried, and in the brick on which the siegeworks and mounds and the engines of rams and of mantlets were drawn, the siege and famine of that same city were described, and as we shall read later in this same prophet — in Jeremiah too it is written that the 'pot' which is kindled from the face of the north signifies the city of Jerusalem; and the forest of Nageb and Theman and Darom [three Hebrew words for the south], cut down, foretells this very thing —, so in the present passage the same Jerusalem is compared to a vineyard and a fruitful vine — of which it is written in another place: I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true; how have you been turned into bitterness, O alien vine?, and in Isaiah: I planted, he says, a vine 'sorec', which means 'chosen' and 'beautiful'; and in the Psalms we read: You brought a vine out of Egypt, you cast out the nations and planted it; you were the guide of its way before it; and we learn it more plainly when Scripture says: But the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel —. As long as this vine bears fruit, among all the trees of the woodlands nothing is more precious than it; but if it ceases to have grapes, it is useful for nothing except to be given to the fire with its root and its layered shoots. The other trees of the forests — to say nothing of the fruit-bearing trees, of which Scripture here makes no mention —, though they have no fruit, once cut down provide a great deal of usefulness and serve both all of agriculture and the making of arms, while they are thinned into shields and shaved into spear-shafts; they close doorways, they hold things as cupboards, as chests and coffers, and they furnish all the equipment of a house. But the vine, once it has ceased to bear grapes, is so useless that not even a peg can be made from it on which something might hang; and when you have cut off its shoots, the fire first seizes both their parts, then the flame consumes them; and it is of no use whatever once it has been reduced to ashes, seeing that even when it is whole it offers no usefulness without its fruit. Now the ambiguity of the Hebrew word 'sene', which is written with three letters, 'sin' and 'nun' and 'iod', is this: if it is read 'sene' it means 'two', if 'sane', 'years'; hence it came about that for its two extremities, which we translated 'both its parts', the Seventy translated 'its yearly cleansing', whereas Aquila said 'its two last parts', Symmachus and Theodotion 'its two extremities'; and the sequence is this: 'As a fruitless vine is given to the fire to no use, so Jerusalem too, or rather its inhabitants, will be given up to the flames, so that they go out from the fire and the fire consumes them, that is: even if they escape from the city, outside they will be consumed by the enemy's sword, and those who remain, crushed by the very weight of their miseries, will recognize that I am the Lord, when I have set, or set firm, my face against them and have given them up to everlasting desolation: for they proved not sinners like the other nations, but transgressors' — for it is one thing to neglect what you do not know, and another to despise what you have worshiped —. According to the spiritual understanding, we can understand the vineyard and Jerusalem as the multitude of believers, which, if it has been negligent and has lost the cultivation of its former religion, and has not borne the fruits of the virtues nor made wine that gladdens the heart of man, will be given up to everlasting flames and reckoned as nothing: for the servant who knows the will of his master, and does not do it, will be beaten with many blows. The Lord too says something of the kind in the Gospel according to John: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch that abides in me and does not bear fruit, the Father will take it away; and every one that bears fruit he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit; but if the Savior is the vine and we the branches and God the Father the husbandman, as long as we keep God's commandments we are continually cultivated, and our cultivation is a cleansing: for it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy; and if, bearing fruit, we are cleansed by the Father so that we may bear more abundant fruit, it is shown that all our effort, by God's help, reaches its end and yields the fruit of fullness; but the branch that has not borne fruit will be taken away by the Father, and once it has been taken away, what the Father does with it Scripture does not say, unless perhaps separation from the body of Christ is everlasting punishment and destruction. What we have understood of the vineyard and the vine, the Savior teaches under another figure in the Gospel: Salt is good; but if the salt has lost its savor, it is useful for nothing except to be thrown out and trodden underfoot by men; and the eye, which gives light to the whole body, if it has been blinded, hears from the Lord: If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be? For in comparison with the transgressor, and with him who has denied the God he first confessed, lighter is the punishment of those who never had knowledge of God. The trees of the woodlands or forests, however, according to the variety of believers, have some usefulness in a great house, in which there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and earthenware, some for honor, and some for dishonor.

16:1-3a

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make known to Jerusalem her abominations, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God to Jerusalem. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, bear witness to Jerusalem of her iniquities, and you shall say to her: Thus says Adonai the Lord.") Where the compass of the individual prophecies was brief, we set down whole passages, adding at once beneath them what seemed right to us; here, however, because a long discourse is directed to Jerusalem by one who bears witness to her and teaches her the sins she has committed, and the prophecy extends to nearly two hundred lines, namely up to that place in which it is written: When I have been appeased toward you in all that you have done, says the Lord God, we must set out the whole prophecy in parts, and fit the due explanations to the parts we have set out. Under the person of a harlot woman, who was first joined in union with a husband, there is woven together the birth and upbringing and youth and marriage and adultery and divorce and recall again of Jerusalem, so that both the clemency and the judgment of the husband and the crimes of the adulteress and harlot may be recognized, when after all the punishments he raises up for her an everlasting covenant, that she may remember her iniquity and be confounded, and it may no longer be hers to open her mouth because of her confusion, when he has been appeased toward her in all that she had done; and it greatly profits sinners to know what they have done: whence the penitent too says: For I know my iniquity, and my sin is ever against me. Now Jerusalem can be understood in four ways: either this one which was set on fire by the Babylonian and the Roman flame, or the heavenly one of the firstborn, or the Church, which means 'vision of peace', or the souls of individuals who by faith behold God. And what many think should be interpreted of the heavenly Jerusalem the Church does not accept, lest we be compelled to take all that is woven together in the present prophecy as referring to the fall and torments of the heavenly powers, and to their restoration to their former state.

16:3b

Your root and your generation from the land of Canaan, your father an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. Great is the faith, great the boldness of the prophets, that one man should charge a whole city with ignoble birth; admirable is Daniel who, to an elder who was sinning and joining murder to adultery, dared as a boy to say: Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you; great too is Isaiah, who cries out to the princes and to the people of the Jews: Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; give ear to the words of the Lord, people of Gomorrah; but no less is Ezekiel, who speaks confidently to the whole city: Your root and your generation from the land of Canaan, your father an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. Although Stephen too, the first martyr of the Gospel, spoke thus to the raging people: Stiff of neck, and uncircumcised in heart, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit, and although we can take the root of Jerusalem and her generation, the land of Canaan, in the sense that the people was called in Egypt and dwelt there a long time — for Ham, the father of Canaan, was the founder of the Egyptian nation —, yet, according to the likeness of their crimes, let us say that the root of Jerusalem is the land of Egypt; whence also her father is called 'amorrhaeus' [Amorite], which means διαδούμενος, that is, 'celebrated by much talk', and her mother 'chethaea' [Hittite], that is, ἐξιστῶσα, 'she who' either 'is herself mad' or 'drives others into madness': Everyone, indeed, who commits sin is born of the devil, whence also in the whole world the name of this ancient father is notorious, and it turns many into madness. And Jerusalem is commanded, whether according to the letter or according to the spirit, to leave her ancient father, and it is said to her: Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house; and the king will desire your beauty, and it is promised her, if after sin she is willing to return to her true father: I will restore you as you were when you were born. Such is the nobility of the city of Jerusalem, which, descending from the stock of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, had God as her father, and yet, because she sinned and left her true parent, deserves to hear: Your root and your generation from the land of Canaan, your father an Amorite and your mother a Hittite! If she heard this, what will become of us, who, called out of the filth of the nations, lost every stain in the washing of the Savior, if we defile the garment of Christ and do not have the wedding garment at the banquet? Surely this: that, with hands and feet bound, we be handed over to everlasting fires, in which there is weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth.

16:4-5

And when you were born, on the day of your birth, your navel was not cut, and you were not washed in water for salvation, nor salted with salt, nor wrapped in swaddling cloths. No eye spared you, to do for you one of these things, having pity on you, but you were cast out upon the face of the earth in the abjection of your soul on the day on which you were born. (LXX: "And your generation: on the day on which you were born, they did not bind your breasts, and you were not washed in water for salvation, nor salted with salt, and you were not wrapped in swaddling cloths. Nor did your eye spare you, that I should do for you one of all these things, and that it should suffer anything over you, and you were cast out upon the face of the field for the depravity of your soul on the day on which you were born.") Let us discuss each point in the order of the reading. When Jerusalem was born of an Amorite father and a Hittite mother and poured forth from the womb, her navel was not cut, the navel by which fetuses are nourished in the belly, like trees and shrubs which are nourished through their roots by the hidden moisture of the earth — and just as the seed-bed of men is signified in the loins, so the genitals of women, by a decent expression, according to the custom of the Scriptures, are called the navel, on the testimony of Job who, under the figure of the dragon, speaks of the devil: His strength is in his loins, and his might in the navel of his belly; for this dragon, the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan and deceived the whole world, has his strength against men in the loins, against women in the navel —, and this signifies of Jerusalem that she did not at once receive the Law, nor were the beginnings of her shameful birth cut away from her, but she first lived a Gentile life; for which the Seventy translated: On the day on which you were born, they did not bind your breasts, since Holy Scripture has this custom, that for the heart it names the little breast, or the breast, and the breasts, as it sees fit for each place — the priests, in whom there ought to be doctrine, and from whose mouth they seek the Law, receive the little breast; John reclines upon the breast of the Lord, to draw the streams of wisdom from the richest fountain; the virgin's two breasts in the Song of Songs are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows are removed; a careful mother, as soon as her baby girl is born, binds her breasts, so that they may refrain from tender swelling and keep their virginal beauty, but when she has come to the age of puberty, it is said of her: Will a bride forget her adornment, or a virgin her breast-band? —. There follows: And you were not washed in water for salvation; the bloody bodies of infants are usually washed as soon as they are sent forth from the womb; so too the spiritual birth needs the saving washing: For no one is clean from filth, not even if his life has been of one day, and in the Psalms we read: In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me; the second birth undoes the first birth, for it is written: Unless one is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God; and there are many washings which the pagans, in their mysteries, and the heretics promise, who all wash but do not wash for salvation; therefore it is added: And you were not washed in water for salvation, which indeed can be understood not only of heretics but also of churchmen who do not receive saving baptism with full faith, of whom it must be said that they received the water but did not receive the Spirit — just as that Simon the magician, who wished to buy the grace of God with money, was indeed baptized in water but was by no means baptized for salvation —. Thirdly it is said: Nor salted with salt; the tender bodies of infants, while they still keep the warmth of the womb and with their first wail bear witness to the beginnings of a toilsome life, are usually touched with salt by the midwives, so that they may be drier and be firmed; but Jerusalem, born of evil parents, obtained no savor, no care; to those, however, who are reborn in Christ it is said: You are the salt of the earth, and they are commanded by the Apostle: Let your speech always be seasoned with salt in grace — whence also in common speech the wise are called 'salty' and the foolish 'unsalted', and in Leviticus it is enacted by law: Every sacrifice of yours shall be salted with salt, the salt of the covenant of the Lord shall not cease from your sacrifices: in all your gifts you shall offer salt; he who has been seasoned with this salt and by its admixture has dried up all stench and harmful moisture will no longer say: My scars have putrefied and become corrupt before the face of my foolishness. I know that I have read in a certain volume about the Lord Savior that he himself is the heavenly salt, and has seasoned with his savor not only earthly and infernal things but heavenly ones too, and that what is written is fulfilled: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will —. Fourth is: Nor wrapped in swaddling cloths; the Savior too was wrapped in the swaddling cloths of infancy, and everyone who is born needs the protection of God through the wrappings of swaddling cloths. It is natural, where at least the care of the parents is not lacking, for newborn infants first to have the navel cut, then to be washed with water to wash off the blood, thirdly for the moisture of the little bodies to be dried by the application of salt, fourthly for the tender bodies of infants to be wrapped in swaddling cloths, for a twofold reason: both so that the body may be dried by the salt, the body being kept and held tight by the cloths so that it does not run off, and so that the most tender limbs may not easily become misshapen — whence also the bodies of the barbarians are straighter than Roman bodies: for up to the second and third year they are always wrapped in swaddling cloths —; but not so Jerusalem, whose navel was not cut off, nor were her breasts bound, nor was she washed with water for salvation, nor salted with salt, nor wrapped and bound in the swaddling cloths of infancy. But why she deserved none of these things, the following Scripture testifies: No eye spared you, to do for you one of these things, having pity on you, for which the Seventy put: Your eye did not spare you, that I should do for you one of all these things, and the twofold edition must have a twofold understanding; the former signifies this: No eye spared you, to do for you one of these things, having pity on you, and the sense is: 'No one had pity on you, since God was offended; no one's heart was moved over you, so as to do for you at least one of the four things above, since you did not deserve to receive them all together'; in the other it is said: Your eye did not spare you, that I should do for you one of all these things, and it has this sense: 'You acted so, and were so born in sins, and in sins your mother conceived you, that not even you yourself had pity on yourself. And since you behaved so as to be cruel against yourself through evil works, what could I do for you, who did not deserve to receive even one of the things above? Since, then, none of these things which are usually done for infants was done in you, and this not without cause nor without judgment but through your own fault and sin, since not even you yourself had pity on yourself, therefore: You were cast out on the face of the earth (or of the field), and cast out because of the depravity of your soul on the day on which you were born' — let us pray that we be not cast out through depravity of soul onto the face of the field, in which wide and spacious is the way that leads to death, in which the cavalry of the Chaldeans runs riot —. And at the same time it must be considered that no one, on the day on which he is born, can commit anything depraved, except at the time of the washing, when a wise generation is taken up by the faith of the believer.

16:6-7

But passing by you I saw you trampled in your blood, and I said to you, when you were in your blood: Live. I said, I say, to you: In your blood live. I made you multiplied like the sprout of the field, and you went in and came to womanly finery, your breasts swelled and your hair sprouted; and you were naked and full of confusion. (LXX: "And I passed by you and saw you mixed in your blood, and I said to you: From your blood, life; be multiplied. Like the growth of the field I made you, and you were multiplied and were magnified; and you entered into the cities of cities, your breasts were raised and your hair sprang up; but you were naked, full of disgrace.") 'After you were cast out on the face of the field, or upon the face of the earth, because of the depravity of your soul, you no longer deserved my help. Nevertheless: Passing by you I saw you trampled (or mixed) in your blood, that is, guilty of deadly crimes, and I summoned you, granting repentance, and I said to you: Although you are in blood, yet live, converted. And so great was the abundance of all things in you, that you had the likeness of a most fertile field — and the blessing of Jacob with which his father blessed him, saying: Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed —, and that you entered the inner chambers of the Lord — and said with the bride: The king has brought me into his chamber —, and came to womanly finery'; for which the Seventy translated: And you entered into the cities of cities, so that, just as one speaks of the Song of 'Songs' and of an age of 'ages', so cities are called cities of 'cities', of which it is said in the Gospel: 'Have authority over ten (or over five) cities, so that you are called not only a city but a metropolis city', according to what is written in Isaiah: Faithful Zion, mother of cities; moreover, what Symmachus translated: And you came to the adornment of women, or Theodotion: And you entered to the adornment of adornments, for which we, following the Hebrew sense, said: And you came to womanly finery, shows the time of puberty, when girls are called 'marriageable' and can be joined in the embraces of husbands. Then there follows: Your breasts swelled and your hair sprouted: the maturity of young girls is decently indicated, when the breasts swell, or are raised, and the hair sprouts. And although she was ready for marriage and had beauty of body, she did not have the covering of garments nor was she protected by the help of God; if anyone does not have the garment of Christ, he is naked; if anyone is not clothed with the bowels of mercy, of goodness, of humility, of modesty, of meekness, of patience, he lies upon the face of the earth, and his beauty is disfigured by confusion and nakedness.

16:8a

And I passed by you and saw you; and behold, your time, the time of lovers. And I spread my cloak over you, and covered your disgrace. (LXX: "And I passed by you and saw you; and behold, your time, the time of those turning aside. And I spread my wings over you, and covered your disgrace.") What great clemency! It had not been enough to have seen her once trampled in blood and to have called her to repentance, but when she sins again he visits her and, because she was naked and full of confusion, he comes again and visits; and behold, her time, the time 'of lovers' — or according to the Seventy 'of those turning aside', and according to the second translation of Aquila, συναλλαγῆς, namely 'of betrothal' and 'of the time of the nuptials', but according to the first edition of the same and Theodotion μαστῶν, which means 'of breasts', for which Symmachus rendered ἀγαπῆς, which signifies 'love' —; that, then, was the time when women can be joined and sustain marital intercourse. Nevertheless the merciful God spread his wings, took them up, and carried them on his shoulders — according to what is written in the Gospel: How often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not —, or he spread a 'cloak' in place of 'wings' — for this is what πτερυγίῳ [wing; also the skirt of a garment] means, with which Ruth too was covered as she slept at the feet of Boaz; and on the border, that is, the πτερυγίῳ, of our garment we are commanded to fasten ὑακίνθινας [hyacinth-blue] fringes —; and he did these things to cover the disgrace of Jerusalem — indicating by this name the genital body of women; for indeed, according to the Apostle, we surround the uncomely parts of our body with greater honor, whence also the psalmist sings: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; and because Ham did not cover these in his father, he is marked with an everlasting curse —. What we have said of Jerusalem, let us refer to our soul, which, as long as it is set in infancy, is without sin; but when the time of its age has come, there are many lovers — of demons and of heretics and of perverse dogmas — who desire to turn aside to it; they are repelled by the protection of the Lord, so that it may receive not the satellites of the devil but the ministers of the Savior. For 'of those turning aside', 'love' and 'of breasts', the Hebrew has 'dodim', which, according to the peculiar character of their language, signifies all the things translated above. The time 'of love' and 'of breasts', or 'of the lovers of God', can be understood as Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, when the Lord promised them that his people would be freed after the Egyptian servitude.

16:8b

And I swore to you, and entered into a pact with you, says the Lord God. (LXX: "And I swore to you, and entered into a covenant with you, says Adonai the Lord.") 'Because I spread my cloak, or my wings, over you and covered your confusion, therefore I swore to you and entered into a pact, or covenant, with you, so that you might be joined to me rather than to the others who wished to turn aside to you' — according to that: The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek; for an oath is the end of every dispute, and: As I live, says the Lord, 'I would rather have the repentance of the sinner than his death' —. At the time of the nuptials, then, Israel received the oath of God in place of every dowry gift — and because David had said of himself: Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness, who swore to the Lord, vowed a vow to the God of Jacob, the Lord himself also swears to him, as Scripture says: The Lord has sworn truth to David, and will not frustrate him.

16:8c-9

And you became mine. And I washed you with water, and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil. 'Because I spread my wings and covered your disgrace and swore to you and entered into a pact with you, therefore you have become my possession, so that you, who were another's when you were seen unclean, began to be mine when I confirmed my pact with you by an oath', or, according to the custom of the prophets: 'You became mine', he says, 'stands for: you were joined to me in marriage; and I washed you', he says, 'with the water of saving baptism': Unless, indeed, one is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God; and elsewhere we read: He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire, of which baptism Isaiah too speaks, saying: The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. And when he has washed, and cleansed her of the blood — the blood from which, by the touch of his fringe, he also healed the αἱμορροοῦσαν [woman with a flow of blood] who for twelve years had been running with gore —, it is not enough to wash with water and cleanse from blood, unless he also anoints with oil, according to which the Samaritan, which means 'guardian', first soothed the wounds of the half-dead man by pouring in oil, then checked them with the sharpness of wine; but our Lord was anointed with another oil, which would not soothe the pain of wounds but grant gladness, as the Holy Spirit says to him: Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation above your fellows. The opposing powers too have the smoothness of a counterfeit oil, promising sweet things through the heretics: things which are turned into bitterness, and which the prophet detests, recalling: But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head. But if from anointing the anointed one, that is, Christ, is so named, see how far Jerusalem had advanced, that she too, anointed with spiritual oil, received the name of Christ, according to what we read in the Psalms of Abraham: Do not touch my christs, and do no evil among my prophets.

16:10a

And I clothed you in parti-colored garments. (LXX: "And I dressed you in varied garments.") In the ceremonies of the Law, so that, occupied in the study of them, you would forsake idols. These are the varied garments with which Joseph was clothed, and his brothers could not sell him until they had first stripped him of the variety of his tunic; and of the bride it is said in Psalm 44 (45): The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety; this is the garment of which the Apostle too speaks: Having put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the Creator. Do we want to know what the varied garments are? Let the same Apostle teach us, writing to believers: Put on therefore the bowels of mercy, of goodness, of humility, of meekness, of patience — what is more beautiful than this variety? —, of which Job too spoke: Who gave women the wisdom of weaving or the skill of variety?, and the high priest, once a year, when he burned incense for the people and entered the Holy of Holies, used varied vestments. Certainly, if riches, and not holiness and diversity of virtues, made the variety of garments, Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar would be written to have had these garments, and not Joseph, who under a sojourning and shepherd father could not have parti-colored and royal garments.

16:10b

And I shod you with violet. (LXX: "And I shod you with hyacinth.") Aquila and Symmachus translated 'violet', the Seventy and Theodotion 'hyacinthine', for which in the Hebrew is written 'thas'. And beautifully, because the discourse is directed to Jerusalem and, under the person of a woman, all her adornment is set out, ὑακίνθινα [hyacinth-colored] or ἰάνθινα [violet] shoes are spoken of, which do not suit the person of men — indeed, those who are to keep the Passover are commanded, without any variety of color, to have their loins girded and their feet shod; these are the shoes of which the Apostle writes: Feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace; Philo, the most eloquent man among the Jews, compares the ὑάκινθον [hyacinth] in the vestments of the high priest to the air, by which he thinks the higher and heavenly things are signified —. Nor is Jerusalem shod with hyacinthine shoes until she has been washed with water — whence also the apostles, whom the Lord had earlier commanded to shake off the dust of their feet, have their feet washed by the Savior; and the bride says in the Song of Songs: I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?; and the divine word testifies to Moses and Joshua that they should loose the latchet of their shoe, because the place in which they stand is holy —; but when the feet have been washed and purged of all filth, they are shod with ὑακίνθινις or ἰάνθινις — both of which are of an ἀέριον [air-like] and κυανέου [dark blue] color — so that they may be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, and hasten to the heavenly kingdoms.

16:10c

And I girded you with fine linen. Jerusalem is not only clothed in parti-colored garments and shod with ὑακίνθινις, but is also girded with fine linen, from which the finest threads are woven in the vestment of the high priest; and the wife in Proverbs, who wove two cloaks for her husband, of the present age and of the future, is said to have made garments for herself of fine linen and purple. With this fine linen the reins are girded whenever the rich incitements of lust are to be thinned, and nothing of gross moisture is left in them, and we fulfill the precept of the Apostle, who says: Stand therefore with your loins girded in truth — as though he said in other words 'with fine linen' —. And the Lord says to the apostles: Let your loins be girded, and lamps in your hands: for unless we bind up the flowing humors of the loins, we cannot have lamps in our hands; whence God also says to Job: Gird up your loins like a man. And those who are to eat the lamb, with feet shod, holding a staff, standing in the truth of the Gospel and prepared for the blood of Christ, are said to have their loins girded; with this belt, which mortifies the loins, Elijah too and John the Baptist are girded; of these the penitent too groans tearfully, saying: For my loins are filled with illusions.

10 d. And I clothed you with fine stuffs. (LXX: "And I surrounded you with trichaptum.") For which Aquila put 'flowery' or 'palpable', Symmachus 'garment', Theodotion the Hebrew word itself, 'messe'; and when I was diligently inquiring what the word 'trichaptum', which the Seventy translated, meant, and could find from none of the Greeks either the usage or the ἐτυμολογίαν [etymology] of the word, at last I learned that it was coined by the Seventy — for new names must be fixed to new things —, because the garment was of such fineness that it was believed to have the thinness of hairs and of the hair of the head; whence I too, wishing to express the thinness of the garment, translated 'subtilibus' [fine stuffs] for 'trichapto', because it was woven with fine warp and weft. And fittingly, to those whom he had rebuked, saying: The heart of this people has grown fat, and Jacob ate and drank and was filled and grew fat, and the beloved kicked and forsook God his maker, fineness of garments is now granted; for in the book of Wisdom too, which by some is ascribed to Solomon, the spirit of wisdom is called only-begotten and manifold, fine and mobile; and the manna, of which it is written: Man ate the bread of angels, is said to have been very fine, in the likeness of hoarfrost and of coriander seed. We can, according to the interpretation of the second edition of Aquila, who translated 'flowery', understand the 'garment' through a μεταφορὰν [metaphor] as the fertility of the land of Judea, or as the beauty of divine worship.

16:11a

And I adorned you with adornment. Here he sets down the adornments in general, which in what follows he enumerates one by one: bracelets and torque, earrings and crown, and the rest, which adornments he bestowed on Jerusalem, and in Isaiah it is said that by her own fault she lost them all: for it is written: Because the daughters of Jerusalem were lifted up (that is, were proud) and walked with lofty neck, and the rest: instead of a girdle they were girded with ropes, and instead of the adornment of the head disfigured with baldness, and instead of beautiful and soft clothes surrounded with the roughness of sackcloth.

16:11b

And I put bracelets on your hands. (LXX: "And I surrounded your hands with bracelets.") When God gives us good works, he puts bracelets around our hands. Whence also he says that he was likened in the hands of the prophets, and we frequently read that the word came in the hand of Haggai or Jeremiah and the others; in Job too the lip of the dragon is pierced with a bracelet, and all his venomous hissings, which are understood in perverse dogmas, are pierced by the ring of good works.

16:11c

And a torque around your neck. For 'torque', which we translated following the second edition of Aquila and Symmachus, the Seventy and Theodotion translated κάθεμα [pendant] — which is written not only here but also in Isaiah: The Lord will take away the glory of their garment, and the little lamprey-chains and the clusters and the rings, and the κάθεμα —; and I think that by κάθεμα they meant a necklace of various gems descending onto the breast of women, which itself too is a most beautiful adornment of women.

16:12a

And I gave an earring over the mouth (or your nostrils). The Hebrew word 'nezem', except for Symmachus, who translated ἐπιρρίνιον [nose-ring], all translated 'earring', not that earrings are put in the nostrils — they are called 'inaures' [earrings] from the fact that they hang from the ears [aures] —, but that a ring, made in the likeness of earrings, is called by the same word; and to this day, among the other adornments of women, golden rings are wont to hang from the forehead over the mouth and to overhang the nostrils. These we receive according to mystical understanding when with the Apostle we can say: We are the good odor of Christ in those who are being saved, and in those who perish: to some an odor of death unto death, to others an odor of life unto life; when we live and it can be said of us: The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, but we the living, then God smells the odor of our sacrifice of good fragrance, and we have the golden ring of divine senses and dogmas in our nostrils; but when we are dead and wallow in the mire and in the filth of lusts, we have in our nostrils that earring of which Solomon wrote: As golden earrings in the nostrils of a swine, so is beauty to an ill-mannered woman.

16:12b

And rings for your ears. (LXX: "And little wheels upon your ears.") He who stops his ears so as not to hear the judgment of blood, and hedges them with thorns so as not to become a partaker with the envious and the detractors — of whom it is written: Do not mingle with detractors; for their destruction will come suddenly, and who knows the ruin of both? —, namely both of him who detracts and of him who gladly listens, this man has rings and little wheels in his ears — not the wheels which follow the Cherubim: for that belongs to the evangelical powers, but little wheels, in the diminutive —, which befit human frailty. Therefore it is also said to God: The voice of your thunder in the wheel: for in those who pass over earthly things and touch the earth with scarcely the slightest footprints — of whom it is written: Holy stones are rolled upon the earth —, the voice of the Lord's thunder and of lofty dogmas resounds; but those who are led by human errors and have no solid footing but are carried about by every wind of doctrine and, cast out of the paradise of firmness, dwell in the region of Naid [Nod], which means 'fluctuation', deserve to bear the sentence of a lying tongue, which sets on fire the wheel of our birth.

16:12c

And a crown of beauty on your head. (LXX: "And a crown of boasting upon your head.") We translated 'beauty' following Symmachus, for the elegance of the sense; otherwise both in the Hebrew, 'thopherth', and in the other translators, καύχησις, it is called 'boasting'. The other adornments belong to individual members; the adornment of the head is the dignity of the whole body; and he calls crown the diadem of women, by which the abundance of the hair is bound and adorned. Do we want to know what the crown of beauty on the head of Jerusalem is? Let us unroll Exodus, in which it is written: And he made a plate of gold, and wrote on it letters formed with the seal of the sanctification of the Lord, and put it upon the head of Aaron; 'the sign of the Lord's holiness' is the name of almighty God, which is written with four Hebrew letters and among them is called 'ineffable', since his name cannot be spoken — whose majesty even paganism is not ignorant of, and the altar of the Athenians bears witness, 'To the Unknown God', whence also the Apostle: What you, he says, worship as unknown, this we proclaim to you —. This I think is the crown of which he also speaks thus in the Psalms: The light of your countenance is sealed upon us, O Lord, and the Apostle says: I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the righteous judge will render to me, and in another place to believers: My joy and my crown: for the glory of fathers is their sons; and in Solomon it is written: Old age is a crown of glory, namely of those who have destroyed the things that belong to little ones and, after the age of the perfect man, have come to old age and to the name of fathers, to whom John writes after the children and the young men, who can say: When I was a little one, I spoke as a little one, I understood as a little one, I thought as a little one; when I became a man, I destroyed the things that belong to a little one.

16:13a

And you were adorned with gold and silver. We have often said that gold pertains to the mind, silver to speech. And may the Lord grant us that we may deserve to receive the divine sense and wisdom, and to bring forth with grace of eloquence what we conceive in the mind, and by no means to make idols of these, as the heretics do, of whom it is written: I gave them silver and gold; but they made Baal of the silver and gold. And this, according to the spiritual understanding, is the more fitting for the adornment of women; otherwise silver, the cheaper material, is the adornment of country women and of poor women and maidservants, which does not befit Jerusalem, who is said to have advanced to be queen.

16:13b

And you were clothed with fine linen and many-threaded stuff and many colors. (LXX: "And your cloaks of fine linen and trichapta and variegated things.") The Hebrew word 'mesi' Theodotion here too set down as it stands, as above, Aquila ἄνθινον [flowered], Symmachus 'polymitum' [many-threaded], and we, what above we called 'subtile' [fine], here, following Symmachus, called 'polymitum'; the Seventy translated 'trichapta', keeping their former interpretation, so as to show garments fine like hairs. Now the whole adornment of women is described: that she is washed, that she is cleansed, that she is anointed with oil, and is clothed in parti-colored garments, is shod with ὑακίνθινις, is girded with fine linen, is clothed with trichapta or fine stuffs, receives bracelets, and the golden torque, rings hanging over the mouth, and little wheels in the ears, a diadem on the head, is decorated with gold and silver — although silver is the cheaper material —, and after all this there is added: You were clothed with fine linen and many-threaded stuff and variegated colors — or, as the Seventy translated, 'with cloak and mantles', for this is what περιβόλαια signifies —, so that she was not only adorned in the care of her body and had all the necklaces of women, but the husband's diligence was also solicitous for her bedding and her couch, so that, when he had completed these things, he might come to the delights of foods, and would not allow anything to be lacking to her even in these. All of which, following the explanation above, we have fitted to the spiritual understanding: that she is covered with fine linen and fine stuffs, so that the delicate limbs of the wife may not be weighed down by the heavy burden of mantles, but may display usefulness and beauty alike.

16:13c

Fine flour and honey and oil you ate, and you became beautiful greatly, exceedingly. After the clothing he takes care of food, that Jerusalem may eat fine flour and honey and oil, either separately, as many reckon, or, by a mixture of the three, a sweeter bread, the bread which came down from heaven; and under three names, as some think, it indicates the mystery of the Trinity, not that there is one substance and another, but that by the diverse names of fine flour and honey and oil the one sweetness of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is shown. And this is to be noted, that in many sacrifices fine flour is offered, the marrow of the wheat and the purest, of which it is written: And he satisfied them with the fat of wheat, not of barley nor of meal, which is offered only when a husband is moved by a spirit of jealousy. In the volume of Judges we read of 'Debboram' [Deborah], which means 'bee', whose prophecy is the sweetest honey, and this is referred to the Holy Spirit, who among the Hebrews is called by a feminine name: in the Gospel of the Hebrews too, which the Nazarenes read, the Savior is introduced speaking: Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took hold of me; moreover the fine flour, which is made from wheat, is referred to the Lord, who says of himself: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit; and the oil, which sustains and refreshes the limbs of the weary, and is the nourishment of light, and with which the light of the lamp is kindled continually in the tabernacle of God, is said to befit the Father; and all these grant one grace to believers, as the Apostle says: There are divisions of graces, but one Spirit; and divisions of ministries, but one Lord; and divisions of operations, but one and the same God. He who has eaten such food, and has been fed and nourished with this sweetest and most delightful bread and the splendor of shining oil, will be turned into beauty and become most beautiful: not once, but repeated: 'exceedingly, exceedingly'; for the doubled adverb gives the speech this weight, that nothing further could be added to the greatness of the beauty.

13 d. And you advanced to a kingdom. — This is not found in the Seventy, who perhaps, translating the Scriptures at Alexandria from the Hebrew truth into the Greek language, feared to publish it, lest they seem to offend the king of Egypt by recording that a kingdom was owed to Jerusalem by God; although the learned prove that only the five books of Moses were translated by them. — After manifold adornment, then, after the crown, after the abundance of gold and silver, after the most beautiful garments and mantles, after incredible beauty, she advances to be queen, because she is the city of the great king, of whom it is written: O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son; and in the Revelation of John Jerusalem is described as a bride adorned and arrayed for her husband; in the Psalms also it is said of her: The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety. But all that we say of Jerusalem, lest we dwell on each detail and the size of the books bring weariness to the readers, let us refer to the Church; for if Jerusalem, according to the Apostle, is our mother, and our mother is the Church, consequently Jerusalem is the Church, the mother of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.

16:14

And your name went forth among the nations because of your fairness; for you were perfect in my beauty, which I set upon you, says the Lord God. (LXX: "And your name went out among the nations in your fairness; which was made complete in loveliness, which I set upon you, says the Lord God.") Symmachus translated this passage more clearly: And your name went forth among the nations; which was perfect because of my dignity, which I had set upon you, says the Lord God. And the sense is: 'By my benefits and my incredible bounty you came to the title of queen, so that the talk of all the nations spoke of you, and you were perfect, not by your own merits and virtues but by my liberality': Unless, indeed, the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it. Unless the Lord guards the city, he has watched in vain who guards it; for he who plants and he who waters is nothing, unless the Lord gives the increase, because: It is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy, so that, when we have done all things, we may say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do; not that the free choice of man is taken away by the beneficence of God, but that this very freedom ought to have the Lord as its helper.

16:15

And having confidence in your loveliness you fornicated in your name, and you laid out your fornication to everyone passing by, to become his. Great is the peril of trusting not in the clemency of God but in one's own beauty; and the more exalted anyone has been, the more he ought to fear lest he fall and fornicate in his own name. For the adverse powers despise ordinary foods and desire foreign nourishment; whence it is said of the devil: His foods are choice; he does not want to deceive just anyone: it is King Saul, who was chosen by the Lord, and Judas the apostle that he hastens to trip up. Let us not, therefore, trust in our own loveliness, nor think the liberality of God to be our own virtue, but rather let us hear: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day may bring forth, and in another place: Brothers, if a man is overtaken in any sin, you who are spiritual, perfect such a one in a spirit of meekness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted; and let us not lay out, or pour out, our fornication to everyone passing by, so as to become not God's, in whom we believe, but his by whom we are defiled: he who receives all vices, and takes into his bosom the passing spirit of diverse sins, and spreads his feet for everyone passing by, he pours out his fornication, and begins to endure the dominion of him whose host he has become.

16:16

And taking some of your garments you made for yourself high places sewn together here and there; and you fornicated upon them, as has not been done nor will be. (LXX: "And you took some of your garments and made yourself idols sewn together; and you fornicated upon them, and you will not enter nor shall it be.") Symmachus translated this passage thus: And when you had taken some of your clothes, you made yourself many-colored high places; and you fornicated in them, things not done nor to be. For 'sewn together' and 'variegated' and 'high places' or 'idols', Aquila and Theodotion translated ἐμβολίσματα, which signifies 'diverse rags sewn together here and there' and 'an idol made like a plaster', as it were 'a πολύρραφον [much-stitched] garment'. 'I clothed you', he says, 'in variegated garments, and you were dressed in fine linen and many-threaded stuff and the variety of many forms; but you took your garments, with which you were gifted by my bounty, and made for yourself idols, or high places, which in Hebrew are called 'bamoth', a thing which never was done before nor will be done, that what you had received for adornment you should turn to the injury of the giver'. This can be understood of Jerusalem according to the letter thus: that she assigned all the precepts of the Law and her riches and the abundance of all things to idols, which no other nation has done or will do; for all the nations which from the beginning served idols are not guilty of so great a crime. But our Jerusalem, which means 'vision of peace', is torn by the heretics, when, plucking one testimony of the Scriptures or another from their proper places, they try to sew them onto places to which they cannot be fitted; to whom, as we read, it was also said above in this same prophet: Woe to those who sew pillows under every elbow of the hand, and make a covering over the head of every age, and the Lord, forbidding this to be done, says in the Gospel: No one puts a patch of rough cloth on an old garment; otherwise it takes away from its fullness, and a worse tear is made. Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins; such are the Nazarenes, who try to fit the observance of the old Law to the grace of the Gospel, and all the heretics who strive to sew a testimony that fits one sense in its own place onto another, whereas the Lord's tunic, woven from the top throughout, cannot be torn, but, woven by the Holy Spirit, admits no tearing. But what is said according to the Seventy: And you will not enter nor will it be, signifies this: 'When you have made for yourself idols of perverse dogmas which you take for high places, and have fornicated upon them, believing in the things which you yourself have fashioned, you will not be able to enter the temple of God, and your images will have no substance nor will they exist forever', as the Apostle says: We know, indeed, that an idol is nothing in the world.

16:17

And you took the vessels of your beauty, from my gold and from my silver which I gave you, and you made yourself male images, and you fornicated with them. According to the letter, the Lord commanded in the Law that there be made censers, bowls, a lampstand, the ark of the Covenant: all either of gold or gilded, and others of silver, all of which Jerusalem melted down and turned into idols of Bel or Baal, Chemosh, Ashtaroth and Milcom. According to the spiritual understanding, we make idols of the gold and silver of the holy Scriptures when we corrupt the grace of sense and eloquence by heretical depravity, and set our mouth in heaven, and our tongue passes through the earth; and male images is the name given to those in which every heresy fornicates, from the fact that each one thinks that what he worships and holds, which he has fashioned, is most robust and cannot be overthrown by any assault; these are the images which we have fashioned from our own heart and which are to be destroyed in the heavenly Jerusalem, of which the prophet foretells: O Lord, in your city you will scatter their image; for whoever is a man and has lost the name of God, it is said of him: Nevertheless man walks in an image; nevertheless he is disquieted in vain; but let us have one husband and venerate one image, which is the image of the invisible and almighty God.

16:18a

And you took your many-colored garments, and covered them. 'The male images' is understood, so that she turned all the finery she had received for use into blasphemy. And we do this whenever we surround heretical depravity with prudence, temperance, fortitude, righteousness and all the virtues and, under their pretext, deceive all the simple, so that, seeing the honey of the virtues, they do not beware of the poisons of the vices.

16:18b-19a

And my oil and my perfume you set before them. And my bread (or, as the Seventy translated, my loaves which I gave you), fine flour, honey and oil with which I nourished you, you set in their sight for an odor of sweetness. The oil of which we spoke above, and the perfume or incense of which the psalmist cries out: Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight, and the loaves of proposition which we are commanded to offer to God, the fine flour too, the purest sense of the Scriptures, and the honey which Jonathan tasted, and his eyes were opened and he was strengthened, wretched Jerusalem set in the sight of the idols — or before the male images —, that they might be for an odor of sweetness to them, things which by their nature are sweet and most delightful but, when they are offered to idols and false doctrines, are turned into bitterness.

Book Five

So that the number of the books may not be confused, and the order of the volumes, separated from one another by long stretches of time, may not be corrupted, I have set little prefaces before the individual books, so that from the front of the title the reader may at once recognize which book he has to read and what prophecy is to be explained by us. In like manner, then, in the preceding volume, that is, the fourth, I discussed, as well as I could and in brief discourse, the part of the prophecy against Jerusalem whose beginning is this: Your root and your generation from the land of Canaan, up to the place where it is written: The fine flour and oil and honey with which I nourished you, you set in their sight for an odor of sweetness. Now the remaining part of the same prophecy, together with the rest that follows, is dedicated to the fifth volume and to your name, Eustochium; in it you will find nothing from the art of rhetoric, nothing from the arrangement and elegance of words, but the care of a simple and skillful diligence, so that this, and this alone, may be my praise: if through me you understand the sayings of the prophet.

16:19b-22

And it came to pass, says the Lord God. And you took your sons and your daughters whom you bore to me, and you sacrificed them to them to be devoured — is your fornication a small thing, that you sacrificed my sons? —, you gave them up, consecrating them to them. And after all your abominations and fornications, you did not remember the days of your youth, when you were naked and full of shame, trampled in your blood. (LXX: "And it came to pass, says Adonai the Lord. And you took your sons and your daughters whom you bore, and you sacrificed them to them for consumption, as though you had committed little fornication, and you killed your sons and gave them up when you offered them to them. This over and above all your fornication and your abominations; and you did not remember the day of your infancy, when you were naked and disgraced, you lived mingled in your blood.") That Jerusalem sacrificed her sons and daughters to idols — the sons and daughters of whom it is written: Sons I have begotten and exalted, but they have despised me — holy Scripture records: They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons, and again: They poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan. Now according to the Hebrew he calls them 'his own' — for he himself had said of them: Israel is my firstborn son — or, according to the Seventy, 'yours', those whom you begot of fornication. And in that place where we have put: And you gave them up, consecrating them to them, for which the Seventy translated: And you gave them up for appeasing (or for expiating), Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion put: You carried them across and led them through, by which the heathens, through fire, either carry their sons across while they are little or compel them, when grown, to pass through. 'Although you have done these things so, you did not remember your infancy, when I took you up, spattered with blood, and washed you, and — after the many things which the prophetic discourse has related — joined you to myself'. Our Jerusalem too, if she has been tripped up by heretical deceit, takes her sons who are stronger in faith and her daughters who do not have such great strength of faith — or certainly the sons who know every mystical thing, the daughters who follow the simple history — and hands them over to demons to be devoured, and while she kills them she believes that she is giving life and appeasing the images, which are glutted with their slaughter. And what is said according to the Seventy: This is over and above all your fornication and your abominations, signifies that the teaching of the heretics is worse than all sins and fornications, for it makes the sons of God sons of demons, nay rather it kills those whom she had either begotten for God with much labor or had made her own sons, those whom she begot in fornication.

16:23-26

And it happened after all your wickedness, woe, woe to you, says the Lord God, and you built yourself a brothel, and you made yourself a place of prostitution in all the streets; at every head of the way you built the sign of your prostitution, and you made your beauty abominable, and you parted your feet to every passer-by, and you multiplied your fornications. And you committed fornication with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, of great flesh, and you multiplied your fornication to provoke me. (LXX: "And it came to pass after all your wickednesses, ※ woe, woe to you, ⁚ says Adonai the Lord, and you built yourself a dwelling of fornication, and you made yourself prostitution in every street, and at the beginning of every way you built your fornications, and you corrupted your beauty, and you spread your legs to every passer-by, and you multiplied your fornication. And you committed fornication with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, who are of great flesh, and you committed fornication manifoldly to provoke me to anger.") This, which is said a second time: Woe, woe to you, the common edition does not have, but it was added from the translation of Theodotion; and again, where we said: And you built yourself a brothel, for which the Seventy translated: And you built yourself a dwelling of fornication, Symmachus and Theodotion translated πορνεῖον [brothel], while Aquila, wishing to express the ἐτυμολογίαν [etymology] of the Hebrew word 'gob', put βόθυνον, which we could call 'a pit', to signify a den of vice and a dug-out, dark cave in which the lust of prostitutes has its haunt; and what follows: And you made yourself a place of prostitution in all the streets, for which the Seventy said ἔκθεμα [a thing set out for show], has in the Hebrew 'rama', and Aquila as well as Symmachus and Theodotion translated it 'high place' or 'lofty'; and then in what follows it is also written: At every head of the way you built the sign of your prostitution — for 'sign' and 'fornication' the Hebrew again has 'rama', which we have translated either 'place of prostitution' or 'sign', since among the Hebrews it is a single word —, and this is set up, or is made rather high, so that the place of fornication may be seen from afar by those who wish to fornicate and there may be no need to search for it. What we have said once, and again and again, let it suffice to have said for good: that under the person of a woman who commits fornication after her husband's many benefits, the fornication of Jerusalem is described: how she withdrew from God and was joined to idols and was not content with hidden fornication, but built herself a brothel and in every way set up a sign for passers-by — that they might come to the harlot and sate their lust, not so much their own as hers who spread her legs to every passer-by —, and disfigured the greatness of her beauty by the greatness of her fornication; and among other things she prostrated herself to the Egyptians too, her neighbors, out of love for great flesh, and, to display every kind of foulness, was disfigured by a manifold kind of filth. Now no one doubts that Palestine is a neighbor of Egypt, since the Lord says to Abraham: I will give you all the land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates, so that on one side it has the Egyptians, on the other the Assyrians, with whom too she is said further on to have committed fornication; and the fornication of Jerusalem with the Egyptians is the imitation of their idolatry. To our Jerusalem too, whether the Church or the souls of believers, if they have been negligent and have lain open to all vices, a twofold word of cursing is addressed, so that they hear: Woe, woe to you, says the Lord God, according to what is written in the Revelation of John: Woe upon all the inhabitants of the earth. For if a holy man says: I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were, why should not the sinner be said to be an inhabitant of the earth? Now he builds himself a brothel who sins with complete brazenness of brow, according to what is written: The sinner, when he has come into the depth of impiety, despises. And he raises a very high place in all the streets: For wide and spacious is the way that leads to death. And he builds at every head of the way, so as to leave no kind of sin untried, but, imitating the harlot of Proverbs, openly in the streets and at the corners of the streets he invites the foolish young men passing by to his embraces, and defiles the beauty of the soul which he received as a gift from God the creator. And all his ways are full of foulness, and to all the thoughts that supply the incitements of vices he opens his heart and spreads his legs, and he commits fornication with the Egyptians his neighbors, whose examples he follows, namely the heathens, who glory in their foulnesses, and he is so wicked as to surpass even them in foulness. And all this he does to provoke God to anger. Now the Egyptians are said to be of great flesh, either because of the greatness of their foulness or because of the deformity of their sins: hence the holy man is said to be of little flesh, which in him decreases daily and is thinned away by the virtues, so that it is no longer called flesh but spirit; and he says in the psalm: My soul has thirsted for you, O God, how manifoldly my flesh for you (or, as some copies have, how my flesh has been consumed), in a desert land, pathless and waterless, so in the holy place I have appeared to you; for this reason the Corinthian fornicator too is handed over: For the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved; of this flesh it is written: All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass; the grass has withered and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord abides forever, of which the Apostle also spoke: Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, and in Genesis God says: My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh, and to believers it is said: Those who are in the flesh cannot appease God. But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit; but the flesh of the saints is another, of which it is written: All flesh shall see the salvation of God.

16:27

Behold, I will stretch out my hand over you, and I will take away your justification, and I will give you up in the souls of those who hate you, of the Palestinian daughters, who blush at your wicked way. (LXX: "But if I stretch out my hand over you, and I will take away your ordinances, and I will give you into the souls of those who hate you, of the daughters of the foreigners, who made you turn aside from your way." And what follows: Ἠσέβησας, that is: You acted impiously, is fitted according to the Seventy to the following section, according to the others it is the end of the preceding one.) Now the Lord stretches out his hand over Jerusalem, to correct her in her sinning and to take away her ordinances, which, as long as she kept the precepts of God, were called the ordinances of the Lord, but when she worshiped idols and exchanged religion for impiety, are called her ordinances — which is to be understood not only of the law and the ceremonies, but also of the sabbaths and the feast days and the new moons: for when he gives the law he says: My sabbaths and: My feast days, but when they withdrew from God, it is said to them: Your new moons and sabbaths and the great day I will not receive; your fasting and rest and your solemnities my soul has hated; which is written of the people as well: for those who were formerly called the people of God, after they withdrew from the Lord, it is said of them to Moses: Your people have sinned, whom you led out of the land of Egypt —. What is here called the stretching out of the hand is elsewhere called lifting up or visitation: for when God does not rebuke the sinner, he draws back his hand, but if he sins and begins to sicken in the law of God, a visitation is sent to him, according to what is sung in the Psalms: If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and in this prophet it is written: The land, if it sins against me so as to commit an offense, I will stretch out my hand over it, and I will break the staff of its bread, and the rest; in which we ask what difference there is between the stretching out of the hand and the sending of it: for the devil says to the Lord: Send your hand, and touch all that he has; unless he blesses you to your face, and it seems to me that the hand is sent for the testing of those to whom it is sent, but stretched out for the punishment of those who deserve torments; and not only the stretching out and the sending, but also the spreading out of the hand of God is spoken of, as Isaiah proclaims in the person of the Lord: All day long I have spread out my hands to a people unbelieving and contradicting; the saints too are related to lift up their hands, as Scripture says: The lifting up of my hands an evening sacrifice. Now since the ordinances of God have been taken away from the people of the Jews, let us ask them what observance of the law they have: victims they cannot offer, since the temple has been taken away and overthrown, nor can the stoning of adulteresses and of the other crimes, granted by the law, be carried out, nor the rest of the land in the year of remission, and the other things of this kind; and she is given into the souls of those who hate her, of the Palestinian daughters, when she is handed over to the Palestinians, whom the Seventy indiscriminately call 'foreigners', by which we may understand the cities or towns of Palestine. Our Jerusalem too, if we pass over the ceremonies of God, and his hand has been stretched out over us, and, the observance of the whole law having been taken away, she will be handed over to the daughters of Palestine and not to the sons; for we are not handed over first to the heavier punishments but, according to the quality of our sins, to the lesser ones, so that, chastised in the smaller, we may escape the greater torments of tortures. 'Philistim', that is 'Palaestini' [Palestinians], with the first part of the letters changed, means 'falling by the cup — or by the making —', by which it is signified that we are to be handed over to the adverse powers, which have drunk from the cup of Babylon and have fallen, and whose works are perverse; and so great will be the chastisement and disgrace of wretched Jerusalem that even the adverse powers themselves blush at the greatness of our sins. What we have translated, following Symmachus, 'wicked', Theodotion put as the Hebrew word itself, 'zemma'. And since the ceremonies of God have been taken away from the people of the Jews, the giving of the law passes over to us together with the priesthood, as Scripture says: Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them, and in another place: Set me a law, O Lord, in your way.

16:28-29

And you committed fornication with the sons of the Assyrians, because you had not yet been filled; and after you committed fornication, not even so were you satisfied. And you multiplied your fornication in the land of Canaan with the Chaldeans, and not even so were you satisfied. (LXX: "And you acted impiously, and you committed fornication with the sons of Assyria, and not even so were you satisfied; and you committed fornication, and you were not filled. And you multiplied your covenants toward the land of Canaan of the Chaldeans, and not even in these were you filled.") Above it was written that Jerusalem committed fornication with the sons of Egypt her neighbors, who are of great flesh; here the other neighborhood, that of the Assyrians, is indicated; and therefore they are handed over to both nations: because they venerated the images of both, and, entering Chaldea, which is the land of Canaan, they took on in exchange the errors of those to whose rule they were subject. According to tropology we often pass from some sins to others; and when we have not done penance for our former crimes, we add offense to offenses and are sated by no error, but as with a long rope and the strap of a heifer's yoke we drag along our sins and our covenant, or we multiply fornication in the land of 'Chanaan' [Canaan], which means 'as it were a tossing', with the Chaldeans, who themselves also sound to us 'as it were demons'; and we always have our footprints in the sand and can never say: He has set my feet upon a rock; and we are subjected to the depravities of the heretics, who have the likeness of demons, or to the demons themselves, of whom Paul writes: Our fight is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of these darknesses, against the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places.

16:30-31

In what shall I cleanse your heart, says the Lord God, when you do all these works of a harlot and wanton woman? For you have built your brothel at the head of every way, and you have made your high place in every street; nor have you become like a harlot who increases her price by disdain. (LXX: "What shall I do to your heart, says Adonai the Lord, when you have done all these works of a fornicating and shameless woman? ÷ and you committed fornication threefold in your daughters ⁚ when you built your brothel at the beginning of every way, and made your base in every street; and you were not like a harlot gathering wages.") And what the Seventy said: And you committed fornication threefold in your daughters, is not found in the Hebrew, nor did any of the other translators put it. Now God says all these things to Jerusalem Ἐπαπορητικῶς [as one at a loss], because he cannot find the remedy by which he might heal her, sick and half dead, according to what Isaiah writes: What is there that I ought to have done further for my vineyard, and have not done for it?, and Hosea: What shall I do to you, Ephraim? What shall I do to you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud, and like the dew passing away early. 'For your idolatry was committed not in secret but with full license, so that at all the beginnings of the ways and at the crossroads you set up altars, and made your base, or your high place, of which we spoke above, in every street; nor did you imitate the cunning harlots, who are accustomed to increase the price of lust by difficulty and thereby provoke their lovers the more to madness — according to the Seventy: You were not like a harlot gathering wages —, but you gave what you ought to have received, so that not even in this, that you committed fornication and followed demons, were you protected by their help, but, oppressed by various captivities, you felt your calamities'. Which indeed can also be referred to every Christian soul that, having deserted the worship of God, has given itself up to vices and luxury and, having followed the worldly life, has not fared happily even in it, but has both lost the riches of religion and not received the riches of the world, nor was there any difficulty in debauching her, but she thrust herself upon your lovers. There is also another, spiritual fornication, when, deserting the Church, we are joined to heretics and build our brothel at the head of every way, the ways of which the divine word commands: Stand in the ways and seek the everlasting paths of the Lord, and see which is the good way, and walk in it, namely the books of Moses, of Joshua, of Judges and of Kings, and Isaiah and Jeremiah and the other prophets. He builds his brothel at all the beginnings of the ways who, for the perversity of his doctrine, wickedly abuses the testimonies of the Scriptures and says: 'Thus says Isaiah': 'Thus said Hosea': 'Thus spoke Moses' and: 'Thus Daniel'; and fittingly he places his brothel not in the middle of the ways nor at the ends of the ways, but at the beginning: for if he had come to the knowledge and the depths of the divine books, he could not go astray. His high place too, or base, he makes in every street, giving himself up to the wantonness and vices of heathens and impious men, even among the heretics themselves, when she has been defiled by them, having no favor but lying open to contempt, because she easily lost her former chastity of faith. And this which, as we said above, is not found in the Hebrew: You committed fornication threefold in your daughters, is said either to Jerusalem according to the letter: that she committed fornication in every way in her towns and villages, and no corner or street remained where she did not set up the signs of idolatry; or to the Church and to the believers who were deceived: who did not heed that word of the Apostle: May the God of peace himself sanctify you in all things, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole without complaint at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but committed fornication in every way, both in body and in spirit and in soul. We read in Proverbs: But you, describe them threefold, that you may answer words of truth which are proposed to you, and we are commanded to understand the utterances of truth, that is, the holy Scriptures, threefold: first, according to the letter; second, in a middle way, through tropology; third, more loftily, so that we may know all mystical things. According to the letter is this: Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day, and: Do not murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer; in the middle way and according to tropology, when we withdraw from the letter and climb a little to higher things, as the Apostle says: It is written: You shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain, and immediately there follows: Is it for oxen that God cares? Or did he speak surely for our sake?; but the last, that is, the third, sublime and sacred understanding, according to that word of the same Apostle: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife. This mystery is great; but I speak in Christ and in the Church. Now the daughters of the fornicating Church are the souls of those who first believed and afterwards were deceived into heresy, whose guilt is referred back to the mother.

16:32-34

But as an adulterous woman who brings in strangers over her husband.
