To all harlots wages are given, but you have given wages to all your lovers, and you made gifts to them that they might come in to you from every side to commit fornication with you. And it has happened in you contrary to the custom of women in your fornications, and after you there will be no fornication; for in that you gave wages and did not receive wages, the contrary has happened in you. (LXX: "An adulterous woman ÷ like you ⁚ receiving wages from her husband. To all who committed fornication with her she gave wages, and you gave wages to all your lovers, and you loaded them that they might come to you round about in your fornication. And there happened in you a perverse thing against women in your fornication, and after you they have not committed fornication; in that you gave wages and wages were not given to you, there also happened in you a perverse thing.") This which is written in the Seventy: Like you, is not found in the Hebrew; and it disturbs the order of the reading, and raises no small question: what woman, and like whom she is, since Jerusalem herself is said to be the adulterous woman. Jerusalem, then, took the abundance of all things with which she had been endowed by her husband's liberality, and gave it to strangers, namely to demons and idols, according to what is written in Hosea: And this I did not know, that I gave her wheat and wine and oil, and multiplied silver for her; but she made silver and golden Baalim, whence, angered, he at once adds: Therefore I will turn back, and take away my wheat in its season and my wine in its season; and I will take away my garments and my linens, so that I may no longer cover her disgrace; and now I will uncover her disgrace in the sight of her lovers, and no one shall rescue her from my hand. And whereas all fornicating women are accustomed to receive wages from their lovers, Jerusalem did the contrary, giving rather than receiving; and to show the lavishness of her wages: She loaded them, he says, that they might come to her round about, lest there be any neighbor who was not mingled in her disgrace. And indeed Jerusalem surpassed the other harlots in this too, that she not only gave her own things, which she had acquired by labor in the practice of foulness, but also bestowed her marriage gifts on her lovers and debauchers. And so great was the adulteress's exposure to every magnitude of foulness that she is ranked above not only present but also future harlots; hence we too translated according to Symmachus: 'And after you there will be no fornication; for in comparison with you every fornication from now on will be reckoned lighter'. Whatever we have said of Jerusalem, refer also to the Church and to the souls of believers, who give their marriage gifts — namely gold in understanding and silver in speech and the garments by which our foulness and disgrace are veiled — to their lovers, either to the contrary powers or to the teachers of perverse doctrines, when they assert that luxury does no harm, and that indiscriminate lust, according to the genitals of the body, demands intercourse by natural law, that all foods are to be used without distinction, since they were made for this, to be eaten, that prudence is necessary only in so far as it profits oneself, and that righteousness has no place, for if it prevailed one would have to beg, and other things of this kind; receiving which, wretched Jerusalem, in whom there ought to have been a vision of peace, turned the sharpness of her intellect and the charm of her eloquence to foulness; and for her lovers she went forth against her husband adorned with those ornaments with which she had been adorned by her husband, to the abuse of the good. And what follows: And you made gifts to them that they might come in to you from every side to commit fornication with you, signifies every kind of sin, so that she is not content with one offense, but endures a hunger for sinning and, against the laws of nature, defiled in all her members, is polluted even to the crown of her head.

16:35-43

Therefore, harlot, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Because your bronze has been poured out, and your disgrace has been uncovered in your fornication over your lovers, and over the idols of your abominations in the blood of your sons whom you gave to them, behold, I will gather all your lovers with whom you mingled, and all whom you loved, together with all whom you hated; and I will gather them against you from every side, and I will lay bare your disgrace before them, and they will see all your foulness. And I will judge you with the judgments of adulteresses and of those who shed blood, and I will give you into the blood of fury and jealousy. And I will give you into their hands, and they will destroy your brothel, and they will demolish your place of prostitution, and they will strip you of your garments, and they will take away the vessels of your beauty; and they will leave you naked, and full of disgrace. And they will bring a multitude upon you, and they will stone you with stones, and they will cut you down with their swords. And they will burn your houses with fire, and they will execute judgments upon you in the eyes of very many women; and you will cease to commit fornication, and you will no longer give wages. And my indignation will rest in you, and my jealousy will be taken away from you; and I will be quiet, and will be angry no more. Because you did not remember the days of your youth, and provoked me in all these things, therefore I too have given your ways upon your head, says the Lord God, and I have not done according to your crimes in all your abominations. (LXX: "Therefore, harlot, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Because you poured out your bronze, and your disgrace will be uncovered in your fornication to all your lovers, and into all the thoughts of your iniquities and in the blood of your sons whom you gave to them, therefore behold, I will gather against you all your lovers with whom you mingled, and all whom you loved together with all whom you hated; and I will gather them against you round about, and I will uncover your wickednesses to them, and all will see your disgrace. And I will take vengeance on you with the vengeance of adulteresses and of those who shed blood, and I will set you in the blood of fury and jealousy. And I will deliver you into their hands, and they will dig under your brothel, and they will destroy your base, and they will strip you of your garments, and they will take away the vessels of your glorying; and they will leave you naked, and full of disgrace. And they will bring a multitude upon you, and they will stone you with stones and cut you down with their swords. And they will set fire to your houses, and they will execute vengeances upon you before very many women; and I will turn you away from fornication, and you will no longer give wages. And I will send my fury upon you, and my jealousy will be taken away from you; and I will rest, and I will no longer be anxious. Because you did not remember the day of your infancy, and you grieved me in all these things, I too, behold, will give your ways upon your head, says Adonai the Lord, and thus you have done iniquity above all your iniquities.") Let us first lay the foundations of the history. 'Because you have done these things and those which the preceding discourse has set out, therefore hear, harlot, what you have done and what you are going to suffer: You poured out your bronze, which you had received from me, and gave to your lovers the wages which you ought to have received, and you killed your sons, so that, in offering them to idols, you have proved to be not only an adulteress but also a parricide. Therefore I will gather against you all your lovers with whom you committed fornication, both those whom you loved and those whom you hated, and I will strip you by the law of adulteresses, so that all may see your foulness and the genitals for whose sake they were formerly carried away by the madness of love'. Now all these things, through the μεταφορὰν [metaphor] of an adulterous and murderous woman who not only committed fornication against her husband but also killed her sons, are said to Jerusalem: both that all the nations are to be gathered against her, whose idols she worshiped and into whose worship she turned all the gifts of God, and that the temple of Baal is to be destroyed, and the altars of the whole city overthrown by fire, and nothing is to remain in her; and that, just as all are accustomed to throw stones at an adulteress and to slaughter a harlot, so that she is killed by the wounds of each one, in such a way that all women see the punishment of the fornicatress, so Jerusalem is to be abandoned in the sight of the other cities round about and of all the nations; and that this is done so that she may cease to commit fornication and may no longer give wages to her lovers, and so that the indignation of God may rest and he may not be angry with her whom he has ceased to love; from which we perceive that it is a great mark of displeasure to be in no way an object of God's care, but for a man to be left to his crimes and sins. My jealousy, he says, will be taken away from you; and I will be quiet, and will be angry no more, as with one estranged, who has withdrawn from me and whom I have handed over to everlasting nakedness — but if Jerusalem suffered this because she committed fornication with idols, what do we think she will suffer when she has slaughtered the Son of God? —. 'And all these things', he says, 'you have done, forgetful of former benefits, and you have provoked me to anger, or grieved me, whom you ought to have provoked to joy by good works. Therefore I too have rendered your works upon your head. And although I overthrew you, O adulteress, yet I will exercise less of my anger on you than you deserved'; so that in this too the divine clemency may be shown, that the sins are greater than the punishments. According to tropology, every soul has received spiritual money from God, according to that passage of the Gospel which is told in the parables of the five, the two and the one talents, and of the ten servants receiving a mina each, who, when they have acted negligently, will become debtors of fifty denarii and of five hundred; and for this reason, in the presence of the lovers, whom we understand to be the demons and the contrary powers, the disgrace of Jerusalem is uncovered, either on the day of judgment or in the time of penance, when they are rebuked; and at first, indeed, God almighty alone discerns hidden things, as the word of the Gospel says: And the Father who sees in secret, and in another place: God searching hearts and reins, and in the volume of Kings: You alone know the hearts of all men; but when there has been fulfilled: There is nothing hidden that will not be made manifest and covered that will not be revealed, and in another place: Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts, and then each one will have praise from God, and when the time of rebuke has come, then that word of Hosea is fulfilled: Now their thoughts have surrounded them, and in another place: Their thoughts among themselves accusing or else defending, on the day when God judges the secrets of men, and again: Behold the man, and his works before his face. And those who formerly committed fornication with her will see all her foulness, and God will give her into the blood of fury and jealousy; for the fury of a husband against an adulterous wife is full, and can be redeemed by no price. The blood of the sons, moreover, can be understood thus, that we call the sons of Jerusalem λογισμούς καλούς, that is, 'good thoughts', which have been implanted in men by God, and which the adulteress killed when she turned aside to evil works. It also profits Jerusalem that her brothel should be dug under and every seedbed of fornication destroyed: for when this has been done, she will no longer give wages, and the indignation of God will rest, and he will in no way be jealous over her, being secure about her chastity; that is, according to those who take what is said in a good sense. Others, however, as we said above, refer it to the contrary sense, so that it belongs to God's great anger not to be angry with them, once he has despised the fornicatress and despaired of her salvation; but if the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament should, according to the edition of the Seventy, find fault in this place with what is said: And you grieved me in all these things, on the ground that God not only admits anger but is also subject to grief and sadness, let us ask them how they accept this, which is certainly a command of the good God: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed in the day of redemption; for whatever they say in defense of that testimony, we shall apply in satisfaction of the present passage.

16:44-45a

Behold, everyone who speaks a common proverb will take it up against you, saying: As the mother, so also her daughter. You are the daughter of your mother, who cast off her husband and her sons; and you are the sister of your sisters, who cast off their husbands and their sons. (LXX: "These are all the things which they said against you in a parable, saying: As the mother, also the daughter. You are the daughter of your mother, who leaves her husband and her sons, and sisters of your sisters, who left their husbands and their sons.") After the κατάλογον [catalogue] of the vices and of the chastisement of Jerusalem, by which she is drawn back to salvation, there is also applied a proverb worn by the common speech of the people, or, as the Seventy translated, a 'parable': Such as the mother, such also the daughter. Now the mother of Jerusalem, as is written both above and in what follows, is called 'chethaea' [Hittite], and it means 'raving' or 'turning into madness', by which are shown the incitements of this world, which lead the captive soul to destruction and separate her from her husband — there is no doubt that by him the word of God and doctrine are meant —; and she is the sister of her sisters, who, as we shall read a little later, are called Sodom and Samaria, of whom the one signifies the life and luxury of the Gentiles, the other the snares of the heretics. Furthermore, what is read in the Seventy: Sisters of your sisters, who repulsed their husbands and their sons, makes no sense — for what other sisters did Sodom and Samaria have, who are the sisters of Jerusalem? And this too must be asked, what husbands Sodom and Samaria sent away and what sons they cast off —, unless perhaps we can say this: that the feet of those who go astray always waver, and theirs are not the solid footsteps that properly belong to the truth, but they run hither and thither and are carried about by every wind of doctrine, while they pass from falsehood to another falsehood and, when they have realized that they toiled in vain over the first, cross over to the second and the third.

16:45b-47

Your mother a Hittite, and your father an Amorite. And your greater sister is Samaria, she — and her daughters — who dwells at your left hand; but your sister lesser than you, who dwells at your right hand, is Sodom and her daughters. But you have not walked in their ways, nor done a little less according to their crimes; you have done things almost more wicked than they in all your ways. (LXX: "Your mother a Hittite, and your father an Amorite. Your elder sister is Samaria, she — and her daughters — who dwells on your left; and your sister younger than you, who dwells on your right, is Sodom and her daughters. And not even so did you walk in their ways, nor did you act a little less according to her iniquities; and you surpassed them in all your ways.") Above he had said: Your father an Amorite and your mother a Hittite; here, with the order and the number changed: Your mother a Hittite and your father an Amorite. For when crimes have advanced, they are split into parts, and, unity forsaken, they advance into a crowd and a multitude, which cannot climb to the mountains with Jesus. Now that Samaria and Sodom are the sisters of Jerusalem, of whom one is on the left and the other on the right, you will confirm even according to the bodily understanding, if you look toward the east from the temple of Jerusalem; and Samaria is called greater because she sinned first and was led into captivity by the Assyrians, and Sodom lesser and younger, which is referred to the crowd of the Gentiles; otherwise, at that time Sodom did not exist, for before we read of Jerusalem in the Scriptures, it had been destroyed by divine fire together with Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim. And Jerusalem, in the middle between the two sisters, which by another name is called Judah, was led by the Chaldeans into Babylon, and Jerusalem sinned far more wickedly than Samaria and Sodom, worshiping in the temple the idol of Jealousy and afterwards killing the Son of God. Furthermore, according to tropology, Samaria and Sodom, that is, the heretics and the heathens, often commit lighter things than those who are reckoned to be Jerusalem, that is, the churchmen; hence it is said to the Corinthians, who believed indeed in Christ but were weighed down by evil works: Fornication is actually heard of among you; and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father's wife, and the rest. The heretics who nevertheless accept the Old Testament are accustomed to understand three natures from this passage: spiritual, animal and earthly, and they refer the spiritual to Jerusalem, the animal to Samaria, the earthly to Sodom; let us briefly ask them how three natures, spiritual, animal and earthly, which are certainly different from one another, are said to have one mother and one father — which does not agree with their fiction —, and how the animal and the earthly nature, according to this same prophet, are restored to their ancient state, that is, to the spiritual — which is itself also contrary to their reasonings —. Now that Samaria is to be understood of the heresies is proved both in the prophet Hosea and in many other places, and especially by that testimony: Woe to those who despise Zion and who trust in the mountain of Samaria; they have gathered as a vintage the chiefs of the nations; for all heretics despise 'Sion' [Zion], which means 'watchtower' and is referred to the Church, and they trust in the mountain of Samaria, namely in the pride of perverse doctrines which they think sublime, and through these frauds of preaching they gather as a vintage and lay waste the chiefs of the nations, so that, by the marvel of their doctrines, they draw all the powerful among the Gentiles into heretical error.

16:48-51

As I live, says the Lord God, Sodom your sister, she and her daughters, has not done as you and your daughters have done. Behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, fullness of bread and abundance, and the idleness of her and of her daughters, and they did not stretch out a hand to the needy and the poor; and they were lifted up and committed abominations before me, and I took them away as you saw. And Samaria did not commit half of your sins; but you have surpassed her by your crimes, and you have justified your sisters in all your abominations which you have wrought. (LXX: "As I live, says Adonai the Lord, if Sodom your sister has done, she and her daughters, as you and your daughters have done. Nevertheless the iniquity of Sodom your sister was pride in fullness of breads and in abundance. She abounded in delights, she and her daughters ÷ this she had, she and her daughters ⁚ and she did not take hold of the hand of the poor and needy; and they gloried magnificently and committed iniquities in my sight, and I took them away as you saw. And Samaria did not commit half of your sins; and you multiplied your iniquities beyond them, and you justified your sisters in all your iniquities which you have wrought.") What the Seventy put: This she had, she and her daughters, is not found in the Hebrew. In the Old Testament the oath of God is: As I live, says the Lord God, but in the New: Amen, amen I say to you; but if this is common with others: The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob; he is not the God of the dead, but of the living, and in another place: I will please the Lord in the land of the living, we ask by what reason God claims a common word as properly his own; but just as a good tree is spoken of, and a good man, and a good shepherd, and a good servant — yet no one is absolutely good but the one God —, so, although the angels and the other powers, and also the patriarchs and prophets and apostles, are living, in comparison with God almighty they are called dead: Who is the man who shall live and not see death?; hence the apostle Paul too says of God: Who alone, he says, has immortality, and dwells in light inaccessible, and of the fountain of the living: Our life, he says, is hidden with Christ in God. He therefore who swears and says: As I live, says the Lord, in describing the crimes of Sodom and her daughters, set first pride, which is properly the devil's, and the first sin; hence the same Apostle: Lest, puffed up, he says, with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil, on account of which he fell from heaven: For he had said: I will make strength and wisdom of understanding, I will take away the boundaries of the nations and lay waste their strength and shake the inhabited cities, and I will seize the whole world with my hand like a nest, and like broken eggs I will carry it off, and: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble; we read also in another place: Why is earth and ashes proud?; and the Gospel relates the pride of the Pharisee overcome by the humility of the publican; whose seedbed is fullness of bread and abundance of all things and idleness, or, as the Seventy translated, an opulence of delights and luxury; that rich man in the Gospel, clothed in purple, is related to have had no other crime except that, abounding in wealth and riches, he had broken out into such pride that he did not stretch out his hand to the needy and poor Lazarus, and so forgot his own condition that he did not give to the wretched man even what was to be thrown away; for which reason it is also written in another place: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. Pride, fullness, abundance of all things, idleness and delights: this is the sin of Sodom, and on account of it there follows forgetfulness of God, which thinks present goods everlasting and that it will never lack necessities; for which reason it is also commanded in the law: Take heed lest, eating and drinking and being filled, having built very fine houses, and having sheep and oxen, silver and gold, you forget the Lord your God, and in another place it is written of Israel: He ate and drank, and was filled and grew fat, and the beloved kicked; knowing which, Solomon too, the wisest of all, prays in Proverbs: Grant me what is necessary and what suffices, lest, being filled, I become a liar and say: Who will see me? or, being made poor, I steal and forswear the name of God. And what follows: And you have justified your sisters in all your abominations which you have wrought, does not declare Sodom and Samaria simply righteous, but by comparison with those who are worse, just as the publican too, of whom we spoke above, is called righteous not absolutely but by comparison with one worse. And yet, though Sodom and Samaria are such, they have not sinned even half, in comparison with Jerusalem: The servant, for, who knows the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes, and: The mighty will mightily suffer torments. Furthermore, as to the fact that for 'delights' the Hebrew contains 'idleness', it should be known that it belongs to this sense: every soul of the idle man is in desires; that is, something must always be being done, lest the field of our breast, when the hand ceases, be overrun by the brambles of evil thoughts.

16:52a

Therefore you too, bear your shame, you who have surpassed your sisters by your sins, acting more wickedly than they; for they have been justified by you. (LXX: "And you, endure your torment, in that you corrupted your sisters in your sins, by which you acted iniquitously beyond them, and you justified them beyond yourself.") The second plank after shipwreck is, when you have sinned, to blush, and not to fall under that reproach which is spoken against Jerusalem: The face of a harlot has become yours; you do not know how to blush. Now he bears his torment who is tortured by his own conscience, and in this world endures torture of his own will, so that he may not endure eternal torments; and we corrupt our brothers or sisters by our sins when through our sins they are provoked to greater crimes — let what I say be made clearer thus: imagine someone set on the summit of the priesthood not living well and disfiguring his dignity by his works: is not the lay brother corrupted by the imitation of his vices? —; for he too who has scandalized one of the least is cast headlong into the deep with a millstone tied to his neck. The sisters of Jerusalem too, Sodom and Samaria, are justified, not because they are righteous in themselves, but, as we said, in comparison with one who is worse.

16:52b

Therefore you too, be ashamed and bear your disgrace, you who have justified your sisters. (LXX: "And you, be ashamed and take up your disgrace, because you have justified your sisters.") Shame is followed by disgrace, disgrace by chastisement, chastisement by consolation, consolation by salvation, according to that word of the Apostle: Tribulation works patience, patience proof, proof hope. And hope does not put to shame — no doubt with respect to the future, since in the present it has blotted out its sins through shame —; something of the same kind is sounded by that word of the Gospel too: There is a shame that leads to death, and there is a shame that leads to life; the Holy Spirit too exhorts sinners in the Psalms: Let all my enemies be put to shame and be afraid; let them be turned back, and be put to shame very swiftly; it is written also in another place: Tell your sins first, that you may be justified, and again: The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech. It is no wonder, then, if Jerusalem is called to shame and disgrace, she who sinned to such a degree that she justified her sisters, and to whom it is said thereafter: Both you and your daughters, return to your ancient state.

16:53-54

And I will turn them, restoring them, with the turning of Sodom with her daughters, and with the turning of Samaria and of her daughters; and I will turn your return in the midst of them, that you may bear your disgrace, and you will be ashamed in all that you have done, consoling them. (LXX: "And I will turn their turnings with the turning of Sodom and of her daughters, and I will turn the turning of Samaria and of her daughters; and I will turn your turning in the midst of them, that you may bear your torment, and have disgrace from all that you have done to provoke me to anger.") Great is the progress of Jerusalem, that, after the shame and disgrace brought upon her by the judgment of God, which she willingly accepted and bore, saying: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, restoration to her ancient state should be promised her. But yet, since by comparison with her crimes Sodom and Samaria were justified, of whom one is on the right and the other on the left, first the 'turning', or 'captivity', of Sodom is restored, as Aquila translated, second the 'captivity' of Samaria, as the same Aquila and Symmachus translated, and last of all Jerusalem is restored, which had been weighed down by greater iniquity and had shown her sinful sisters to be righteous in comparison with herself. For who doubts that among three sinners, nay rather impious men — the Gentile, the heretic, the churchman — he is worthy of much greater punishments who has been of greater dignity? : For the mighty, as we said, will mightily suffer torments; but he who has been least is worthy of mercy, and: The servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes. Hence Peter too: It is time, he says, for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord; and in this same prophet it is commanded to those who hold axes: Begin from my holy ones, so that Jerusalem last of all, after her sisters have first been turned back and restored to their former state, may bear her disgrace and be ashamed and blush over the things in which she had sinned and in all things console her sisters, while she endures heavier things; or certainly she is ashamed and blushes for this reason, that she provoked God to anger. From which it is plain that anger is not natural to God, but that God, most clement and most gentle, is provoked to anger by our vices, as the Apostle says: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God calls you to penance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you treasure up wrath for yourself, which the Lord does not have by nature; whence it is also written in another place: You sent forth your wrath, and it devoured them like stubble — for what is joined and united in one body cannot be sent, but only what is outside the body, for example a lance, a javelin, an arrow, a sword —; we read in the Gospel that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for the land that has not received the apostles.

16:55

And your sister Sodom and her daughters will return to their antiquity, and Samaria and her daughters will return to their antiquity, and you and your daughters, return to your antiquity. (LXX: "And your sister Sodom and her daughters will be restored as they had been from the beginning, and Samaria and her daughters will be restored as they were from the beginning, and you and your daughters will be restored as you were from the start.") The Jews, among the other fables and endless genealogies and ravings which they invent, dream this too: that at the coming of their Christ, whom we know to be Antichrist, and in the kingdom of a thousand years, Sodom is to be restored to its ancient state, so that it will be like the paradise of God and like the land of Egypt, and that Samaria will receive its former happiness, so that they will return from the Assyrians to the land of Judea — for we read that the ten tribes were taken captive by Pul and Shalmaneser and Tiglath-pileser, kings of the Assyrians, and are captives there to this day —; that Jerusalem too is then to be built, and all her daughters, namely the cities and villages and fortresses that are to be under her power, will flourish as they flourished before, and Jerusalem herself is to be built of gold and silver and precious stones, of which Isaiah too is said to prophesy: I will establish your judges as before and your counselors as from the beginning, and after this you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful mother of cities, Zion, and our Revelation to speak, and David to sing: Deal kindly, O Lord, in your good will with Zion, and let the walls of Jerusalem be built, and in another place: The cities of Judea shall be built, and they shall dwell and abide there, and their seed shall be directed forever. But we, leaving the perfect knowledge of these things to the judgment of God, nay rather clearly confessing that after the second coming of the Lord Savior there will be nothing lowly, nothing earthly, but the heavenly kingdoms which are first promised in the Gospel, say this: that in the state of the Church all things have been fulfilled and are fulfilled daily. Sodom returns to its ancient state when the soul, formerly Gentile and impious, restored to its own nature, understands the Creator. Samaria receives her ancient blessedness, the error of the heretics despised, and joined to Christian doctrine and faith. And when they have returned, Jerusalem too, 'vision of peace', which is interpreted as the Church, will return to her former state — of which it is written: His place has been made in peace, and: Jerusalem, which is built as a city whose sharing thereof is in the selfsame, and in the Apostle: But the Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother, and in the same: You have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and thousands of angels in throngs —, and she will return with her daughters, who are scattered over the whole world; of which we have treated more fully in the explanations of Isaiah.

16:56-58

But Sodom your sister was not heard in your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was uncovered, as at this time, to the reproach of the daughters of Syria, and of all the Palestinian daughters round about you, who surround you on every side. Your crime and your disgrace you have borne, says the Lord God. (LXX: "If Sodom your sister had not been for hearing in your mouth in the days of your pride, before your wickednesses were uncovered, as now is the case with the daughters of Syria, and if this had not been, what would have been done to you, and to all round about you, the daughters of the foreigners who surround you on every side? Your impieties and your iniquities, you, bear them.") Symmachus translated this passage thus: Because Sodom your sister was not in hearing through your mouth in the day of your pride, before your disgrace was uncovered, as in the time of the reproach of the daughters of Syria, and of all the Palestinian daughters who are round about you, who surround you on every side. Your crime and your wickedness you will bear; Theodotion in this way: And Sodom your sister was not in the hearing of your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was uncovered, as the time of the reproach of the daughters of Syria, and of all the daughters of the foreigners round about her, who abhor you on every side. Your fornication and your abominations you have borne, says Adonai the Lord; our translation agrees with the edition of Aquila. All these I have set down so that from the comparison of them all we may be able to find a trace of some sense; and meanwhile, without prejudice to others, the order of the reading seems to us to be rendered thus: 'In the days of your pride, when you were sinning, you did not remember the overthrow of Sodom your sister, before your wickedness lay open, which at this time has been uncovered to such a degree that you became a reproach to all the cities of Syria and Palestine which are round about you; since, therefore, you surpassed your sister in crime, and were not frightened by her example so as not to suffer like things and to hold back your foot, but now your disgrace has been uncovered, hear the sentence of God: either 'bear' — according to the Seventy —, or 'you have borne' — according to Aquila and Theodotion, or 'you are going to bear' — according to Symmachus — your crime and disgrace, so that, after you have endured the punishment for sacrilege, you may obtain pardon, not from your covenant but from my clemency'. 'Syria' in the Hebrew tongue is called 'aram', which means 'loftiness'; and according to the explanation of that passage of the prophet Isaiah in which Aram and Ephraim conspire against Judah and Jerusalem, the subtle wisdom of the heathens, which promises itself the loftiness of knowledge, in all the wickedness of the heretics, attacks Judah, in which is the true confession, and cannot prevail; here too the same arrogance of Syria, that is, of the philosophers, together with the daughters of the foreigners, in whom is shown the manifold error of the diverse doctrines among the nations, mocks Jerusalem and holds in reproach her by whose vices it has been surpassed.

16:59-63

For thus says the Lord God: And I will do to you as you despised the oath, so as to make void the covenant. And I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will raise up for you an everlasting covenant. And you will remember your ways, and you will be ashamed when you receive your sisters with you, the greater with your lesser ones; and I will give them to you as daughters, but not by your covenant. And I will raise up for you my covenant with you, and you will know that I am the Lord, that you may remember and be ashamed, and that it may no longer be yours to open your mouth because of your shame, when I have been appeased toward you in all that you have done, says the Lord God. (LXX: "Thus says Adonai the Lord: And I will do in you as you have done, as you despised these things, so as to transgress my testament. And I will remember my testament which I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will raise up for you an everlasting testament. And you will remember your way, and you will be despised when you receive your sisters greater than you together with your younger ones; and I will give them to you for proving, and not by your testament. And I will raise up my testament with you, and you will know that I am the Lord, and you may remember and be ashamed, and it may no longer be yours to open your mouth before the face of your disgrace, when I have been propitiated toward you according to all that you have done, says the Lord God.") 'For this reason I said to you: Your crime and your disgrace, you, bear them (or you have borne or you are going to bear), : that you may receive what you deserve, because you despised my oath and made void my covenant. But when there has been fulfilled: I will kill and I will make alive, I will strike and I will heal, then I will remember my covenant which I once had with you. And I will raise up for you a covenant, by no means that of the law, which has passed away, but the everlasting covenant of the Gospel, so that, when you have remembered your ways and received your sisters, greater or lesser, Samaria and Sodom and their companions, I may grant them to you as daughters — or for proving: For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest to each —, not from your merit, but from my mercy; and then you may know that I am the Lord, and remember my benefits and be ashamed, and say with the Apostle: I who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God'. And that it may no longer be yours to open your mouth because of your shame: for it belongs to the saints to open the mouth — according to the Apostle, who says: My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians —, and to the Lord Savior — who, opening his mouth, taught them, and who says in the psalm too: I will open my mouth in parables —; but to the sinner it is said: You have sinned, be still, and: Why do you take up my testament through your mouth?, and: Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner; and the holy man deserves to hear: Open your mouth and I will fill it. From this we understand that even when, through the mercy of the Lord, we have received back our former glory, nay rather have received the everlasting covenant of the Gospel, after the Lord has been appeased toward us in all that we have done, we keep the memory of past sin and always close our mouth, because we have been saved not by our works but by the grace of God.

17:1-6

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, propound a riddle and tell a parable to the house of Israel, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: A great eagle with great wings, long in the extent of its limbs, full of feathers and of variety, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar; it plucked off the top of its foliage and carried it over into the land of Canaan; in a city of merchants it set it. And it took of the seed of the land and set it in the ground for seed, that it might make firm its root upon many waters; on the surface it set it. And when it had sprouted, it grew into a broader vine of low stature, its branches looking toward it, and its roots were under it; so it became a vine, and bore fruit in vine-shoots and sent out offshoots. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, narrate a narration and speak a parable to the house of Israel, and you shall say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: A great eagle with great wings, of long extent, full of talons, which has the leading to enter into Lebanon, and it took the choice parts of the cedar; it plucked off the tops of the tenderness and brought them into the land of Canaan; in a walled city it set it. And it took of the seed of the land and gave it in a plain as a planting upon many waters, that it might be looked upon, and it set it, and it sprang up and became a weak vine and small in size, so that only its branches appeared under it, and its roots were beneath it; and it became a vine, and made offshoots and stretched out its branches.") When it is said to the prophet: Propound a riddle, tell a parable (or, as the Seventy translated: Narrate a narration and speak a parable), it is shown that what is said is obscure; for no one doubts that both a riddle and a parable put forward one thing in the words and hold another in the sense: for the Savior too spoke to the people in parables, which he explained privately to the apostles; therefore we must understand the riddle and the parable in just this way, as a riddle and a parable. Now in the present prophecy of Ezekiel two eagles are set forth; of the first we must speak now, of the other we shall treat in what follows. And meanwhile let us gather the simple history. A great eagle with great wings, long in the extent of its limbs, full of feathers and of variety (or, as the Seventy rendered, full of talons) is Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, of whom Hosea also speaks: As an eagle over the house of the Lord. He, ruling over many nations and hedged about by a countless army, came upon the house of God — no doubt it means the temple — or, as Scripture now says, to Lebanon, of which Zechariah speaks: Open your gates, O Lebanon; and let fire devour your cedars. Howl, fir tree, for the cedar has fallen, since the magnificent have been laid waste; and often the temple, which was renowned and lofty, is called Lebanon in the holy Scriptures. And it took the marrow of the cedar, and plucked off the top of its foliage and carried it over into the land of Canaan; in a city of merchants it set it (for 'merchants', or 'commerce', the Seventy translated 'walled'); and it indicates Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar captured together with his mother and the princes of the people and all the wealth of Jerusalem and the vessels of the temple, and carried over to Babylon, which is in the land of Canaan, and there he grew old; of whose line afterward, as the writing of Matthew the evangelist testifies, our Lord and Savior was born, through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. In his place he took of the seed of the same land, that is, of the royal stock, Mattaniah, the paternal uncle of Jeconiah, whose name he changed, and he called him Zedekiah and set him as king in Jerusalem, and put him over many peoples. And yet he set him on the surface, and did not make his power firm with a deep root of rule, but set him so that he might be looked upon and be under Babylonian power, or: Of low stature, its branches looking toward it, so that he would indeed rule over the peoples of the Jews, but would look to the authority of the Babylonian who gave the orders: for this is what Scripture says: Of low stature, its branches looking toward it — understand: toward the eagle — which the Seventy rendered more plainly: And it sprang up — what had been planted — and became a weak and small vine, so that only its branches appeared, and he would seem indeed to have a kingdom, but his kingdom itself, low and weak, would be ruled by the will of the Babylonian prince. So much for the present passage for now; let us join the rest to it as well.

17:7-10

And there was another great eagle with great wings and many feathers; and behold, this vine, as if sending its roots to it, stretched out its vine-shoots to it, that it might water it from the beds of its growth. In good land upon many waters he planted it, that it may make foliage and bear fruit, and become a great vine. Say: Thus says the Lord God: Shall it then prosper? Will he not pull up its roots and strip off its fruit, and dry up all the vine-shoots of its growth, and it will wither? And not with a great arm nor with many peoples, so as to pull it up by the roots. Behold, it is planted; shall it then prosper? Will it not, when the burning wind touches it, be dried up, and wither in the beds of its growth? (LXX: "And there was another great eagle with great wings, with very many talons; and behold, this vine was entwined toward it, and its roots toward it, and it stretched out its branches toward it, that it might water it with the clod of its planting. In a good plain upon much water it was fattened, that it might make sprouts and bring forth fruit, and become a great vine. Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Shall it be guided aright? Will not the roots of its tenderness and its fruit rot, and all that has sprung from it wither? And not with a great arm nor with a numerous people, so as to pull it up from its roots. And behold, it is fattened; shall it be guided aright? Will it not, as soon as the burning wind touches it, wither, and be dried up with dryness? With the clod of its growth it will wither.") The second eagle, that is, the other one, itself also great, full of feathers and of many talons, because of its rapacity and its devastation of very many nations, is Pharaoh king of Egypt. And behold, this vine — understand: King Zedekiah, who had been set up in Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar — began, it says, to send its offshoots to it, that is, to direct envoys to the king of the Egyptians and to ask him for help against the king to whom he was subject — for this is what Scripture now says: That it might water it from the beds of its growth —. It had been planted in good land by Nebuchadnezzar, that it might make foliage and bring forth fruit and grow into a broader vine; therefore the prophet is commanded to speak to the vine which had been planted by Nebuchadnezzar and had sent its branches to the Egyptian eagle: 'Shall it prosper because it has attempted to do this, and will not all its offshoots and vine-shoots at once be dried up? And not,' it says, 'with a great arm nor with a numerous people'; for Zedekiah, fleeing and left destitute of the help of the Egyptian king, was caught by the leaders of Nebuchadnezzar in the deserts of Jericho, and all his companions were scattered here and there, as is written in the volume of Kings and in Παραλιπομήνῳ [Chronicles] and in Jeremiah.

17:11-18

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say to the provoking house: Do you not know what these things signify? Say: Behold, the king of Babylon comes to Jerusalem, and he will take its king and its princes, and lead them to himself into Babylon; and he will take of the seed of the kingdom, and strike a covenant with him, and receive an oath from him; but he will also take away the mighty of the land, that the kingdom may be lowly and not lift itself up, but keep his compact and observe it. But he, withdrawing from him, sent messengers to Egypt, that it might give him horses and a numerous people; shall he prosper or obtain safety who has done these things? And shall he who has broken the compact escape? As I live, says the Lord God, surely in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he made void and whose compact, which he had with him, he broke, in the midst of Babylon he shall die. And not with a great army nor with a numerous people will Pharaoh make war against him, in the casting up of a mound and the building of ramparts, to kill many souls. For he had despised the oath so as to break the covenant, and behold, he gave his hand; and when he has done all these things, he shall not escape. This is the riddle and this is the parable: that under two eagles and a vine Scripture was showing two kings, of Babylon and of Egypt, and King Zedekiah, who, against his oath, abandoning his friendship with Nebuchadnezzar, transferred himself to the Egyptian king: And he will strike, it says, a covenant with him, and receive an oath from him, that he may keep his compact and observe it. He who has dissolved, it says, the compact, shall he escape? From this we learn that faith must be kept even among enemies, and that one must consider not to whom but by whom you have sworn; for far more faithful is he found who, on account of the name of God, trusted you and was deceived, than you who, under pretext of the divine majesty, plotted snares against your enemy, nay rather, by now your friend. Surely, it says, in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he made void and whose compact, which he had with him, he broke, in the midst of Babylon he shall die; for we read that Zedekiah was captured, led to Riblah, and there, after his sons had been killed, blinded, and, shut in a cage like a wild beast, carried over to Babylon — whence also Scripture, though it seems to be contrary to itself, is nevertheless most true in both: it had been said to Zedekiah: And you shall enter Babylon and: You shall not see it: for he entered, because he was led to Babylon, and he did not see it, because he had been blinded —. But what follows: And not with a great army nor with a numerous people will Pharaoh make war against him, in the casting up of a mound and the building of ramparts, to kill many souls, is understood in two ways: either the Egyptian king, coming against Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, will not be able to give battle nor with a small army resist so great a multitude; or Zedekiah himself will be conquered by Pharaoh, from whom he hoped for help, not that Pharaoh conquered him — or that Scripture anywhere attests this —, but that Nebuchadnezzar's conquest was brought about on the occasion given by the king of Egypt; and that not he who was besieging seemed to conquer Jerusalem, but he in whom Zedekiah had hoped in vain. Behold, it says, he gave his hand to the king of Egypt, and handed himself over, and committed the sacrilege of perjury against God: 'Will it,' it says, 'profit him?'. And when he has done all these things, he shall not escape.

17:19-21

Therefore thus says the Lord God: As I live, surely the oath that he despised and the covenant that he transgressed I will lay upon his head, and I will spread my net over him and he shall be caught in my dragnet, and I will bring him into Babylon, and I will judge him there in the transgression by which he despised me. And all his fugitives with the whole column shall fall by the sword; and the rest shall be scattered to every wind, and you shall know that I the Lord have spoken. It is a worldly maxim: Deceit or valor, who would ask, in an enemy?, which those who say that enemies are to be deceived by fraud are wont to set against us; yet even if we were to assent to it, Zedekiah did much worse: for he did not deceive an enemy, but a friend to whom he had been bound by a covenant of the Lord. Therefore, so long as you do not swear and do not enter into a compact under the name of God, it belongs to prudence and courage either to deceive or to overcome the adversary in whatever way you can; but when you have bound yourself by an oath, he who trusted you is by no means an adversary but a friend, and he was deceived under pretext of an oath, that is, of the invocation of God. That is why Scripture now says: The oath that he despised and the covenant that he transgressed I will lay upon his head; and lest we should think that the oath and the covenant and the compact belonged to the king of Babylon or to Zedekiah who had made it, there follows: In the transgression by which he despised me. So he who scorns an oath despises him by whom he swore, and does wrong to him in whose name the adversary trusted; for which reason: I will spread, it says, my net over him and he shall be caught in my dragnet, and I will bring him into Babylon, and I will judge him there. Whatever, then, Nebuchadnezzar did against Zedekiah, he did not do by his own strength, but by the wrath of God, in whose name perjury had been committed. According to anagogy — although the interpretation may seem forced — this must be known: that, just as the other living creatures are customarily referred both to a good and to a bad sense, so also is the eagle. Of the lion it is said in a good sense: A lion's whelp is Judah; in the contrary sense: Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, and that in the psalm: He lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den. He lies in wait to seize the poor. In a good sense it is said of the eagle that the righteous man, having become rich, may make himself wings like an eagle, that he may be able to return to the house of his superior, and in Isaiah it is written that the righteous may put forth feathers like eagles, may run and not grow weary, may walk and not hunger; but rightly he who had said: I will do strength and wisdom of understanding, I will remove the boundaries of the nations and plunder their strength, and I will shake the cities that are inhabited, and I will grasp the whole world in my hand like a nest and like broken eggs, is now described in the person of an eagle: in that he by no means wishes to strip from Lebanon — which means 'whiteness' and is referred to incense — the small and low shrubs, but the tops of the cedars, and of the princes and the royal stock, according to that saying of Habakkuk: His food is choice. And he makes a covenant with those whom he has captured, that they may bow their necks to the Babylonian king and fulfill what the Apostle says: Whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme, and in another place: Whom I have delivered, he says, to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved. We ought not, then, if perhaps on account of some sin we are cast out of the congregation of the brethren and out of the house of God, to struggle against it, but to bear with an even mind the sentence brought against us and to say with the prophet: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, and so on. And it often happens that, being subject to one, we go over to another who promises us his help and does not make us abide in the former sentence; which must be avoided by every means, lest our vine-shoots be dried up and our sprouts wither, and we be believed to act against the compact of God.

17:22-24

Thus says the Lord: And I myself will take of the marrow of the lofty cedar, and will set it; from the top of its branches I will strip off a tender shoot, and I will plant it upon a high and eminent mountain. On the lofty mountain of Israel I will plant it, and it will break forth into a sprout and bear fruit, and it will become a great cedar, and all birds will dwell under it, every winged creature nesting under the shade of its foliage. And all the trees of the region shall know that I the Lord have brought low the lofty tree and raised up the low tree, and dried up the green tree and made the dry tree flourish: I the Lord have spoken and have done it. (LXX: "For thus says Adonai the Lord: And I will take away of the choice parts of the cedar from the top ※ and I will give from the head of its branches ⁚, from their heart I will take away, and I will plant upon a high mountain; and I will hang it on the lofty mountain of Israel, and I will plant, and it will bring forth a sprout and bear fruit and will become a great cedar, and every bird will rest under it, and every winged creature will rest under its shade ÷ and its branches will be restored ⁚. And all the trees of the field shall know that I am the Lord who bring low the lofty tree and exalt the low tree, and make the green tree dry and make the dry tree sprout: I the Lord have spoken and I do it.") What is read in the Seventy: And I will give from the head of its branches, has been added from the edition of Theodotion; and again what follows: And its branches will be restored, must be marked with an obelus, because it is not found in the Hebrew. The real Nebuchadnezzar takes of the marrow of the lofty cedar, from the top of its branches, for this purpose: That the kingdom may be lowly and not lift itself up; but the Lord God, the Father almighty, who spoke to Ezekiel, takes from the royal stock and from the line of David: And plants it upon a high and eminent mountain; he it is who speaks in the psalm: But I have been set up as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain. For the prince had failed from Judah and the leader from Israel, until he should come for whom it is reserved: And he shall be the expectation of the nations. He broke forth into a sprout and bore fruit, and surpassed all the cedars by his loftiness, so that all the birds of heaven dwell under him, and all winged creatures are protected by his shade — he of whom Habakkuk says: Horns in his hands: there his strength is hidden, and who desires to gather, like a hen, the chicks under his wings —, so that all the trees of the region may know that he himself is the Lord; τροπικῶς [figuratively] speaking of believers: he who brought low Israel, once a lofty tree, and exalted the lowly people of the Gentiles; who dried up the green tree of the Jews, flowering and sprouting in the Law and the Prophets, and made the dry tree of the nations flourish, so that what he had always spoken he might fulfill in deed; the same thing is signified also by the words of Simeon in the Gospel, saying: Behold, this one is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many, and by the grain of mustard seed which, though it is the smallest of all seeds, once it has grown is a dwelling place for birds. Some interpret it otherwise, referring the lofty tree brought low and the low tree exalted to the passion of the Lord Savior: Who, though he was in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and after the resurrection the very tree was afterward raised on high which, at first green, was dried up in death and afterward, reviving, recovered its former greenness. Others, in Jewish fashion, refer both to Israel: that at the first coming it was brought low and dried up, and at the second it will be restored to its former state, when that is fulfilled which the apostle Paul says: When the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved.

Book Six

I used to think that, once the serpent had been run through the middle, the seedlings of the young hydra would not come back to life, and that, as in the fables of the poets, once Scylla was dead, the Scyllaean dogs, which never cease barking, would by no means rage against me; and that, the heretics having been struck by the hand of God so that if it can be, even the elect of God should not be tempted— yet heresy itself does not die, for it has left behind against us whelps that are heirs of its hatreds, who, feigning what is ours, do not abandon the poisons of their ancient mother and of beguiling Ulysses, and smear only their lips round with honey, and, in the words of the Scriptures, have softened their words beyond oil, while they themselves are darts, and fiery darts, which must be both repelled and extinguished with the shield of faith. I have said these things, daughter Eustochium, so that you may help me with your prayers as I labor at the prophetic work and resist the heretics, and so that the Lord may unfold the sixth volume of explanations on Ezekiel by my mouth but with his own sense, and that by the grace of the same Spirit, by which the things we read written were revealed to the prophets, they may be revealed to us also as we discuss them, so that we may be able to say: I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit.

18:1-2

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What is it that you turn a parable into this proverb among you in the land of Israel, saying: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge? (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ÷ Son of man, ⁚ what is the parable among the sons of Israel, of those who say: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge?") What the Seventy said, Son of man, is not found in the Hebrew. Now divine Scripture warns that what was said in Exodus, I am the Lord your God; a jealous God, who render the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation for those who hate me, and show mercy to thousands for those who love me and keep my precepts, and again, The Lord descended in a cloud and stood beside Moses, and Moses called on the name of the Lord, and the Lord passed before his face, and he called on him, saying: Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of much mercy and true, and keeping righteousness and mercy to thousands, taking away iniquities and injustices and sins, and he will not cleanse the guilty, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons and upon the sons of the sons to the third and fourth generation, ought to be taken thus, as a parable and a proverb, so that it sounds one thing in the words and holds another in the sense; which we also said above on the parable of the two eagles. Hence the Lord in Psalm 77 (78): I will open, he says, my mouth in parables, I will utter propositions from the beginning; and in the Gospel he sets forth the parable of the sowing, and of the darnel, and of the mustard seed, which, though it is the least of all seeds, rises up into a great tree, in such a way that he presents one thing in the words and holds another in the sense; and we, up to the present day, think that the two testimonies of Exodus which we set down above are not a parable, but set out a simple statement. And although we would not dare to say anything, nor would the earthen vessel speak against the potter, 'why have you made me thus or thus', yet we suffered a hidden stumbling block, because it seemed an injustice on God's part that one should sin and another pay for the sins. For if he renders the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one should sin and another be punished; but from what follows, for those who hate me, the stumbling block of the threat, or of the precept, is resolved: for they are not punished to the third and fourth generation because their fathers transgressed, since it is rather the fathers, who were the sinners, who ought to have been punished, but because they proved to be imitators of their fathers and hated God, by an inherited evil, the impiety growing from the root into the branches as well. At this place the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament are accustomed to say against the Creator: How good and righteous is the God of the Law and the Prophets, who, resting and silent at the sins of the fathers, repays those who have not sinned; nay rather, how great is the cruelty in him, that he should extend his wrath even to the third and fourth generation! To them we shall reply that even in this the clemency of God the Creator is shown: for it is not a mark of ferocity and severity to hold back wrath until the third and fourth generation, but a sign of mercy to defer the punishment of sin; for when he says, The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of much compassion, and adds, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons and the sons of the sons, he indicates this: that he is of such great mercy that he does not punish at once but defers the sentence of punishment. But if the vengeance on sinners is deferred to the third and fourth generation, what more will he do with the righteous and the holy? There follows: And keeping righteousness and mercy to many thousands for those who keep his commandments and do his precepts. It is written in Proverbs: As a sour grape is harmful to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who practice it; from which it is clear that it is not the teeth of others that ache and are set on edge, but the teeth of those who have eaten the sour grape. And this is the sense of this passage: just as, if anyone should wish to say, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge, it is ridiculous and has no logical consequence, so it is unjust and perverse that the fathers should sin and the sons and grandsons be tormented. There are those who expound what is written in Exodus, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, in such a way as to refer the statement to the human soul, saying that the father in us is the light prick of the senses and the incitements of the vices; the son, if the thought has conceived the sin; the grandson, if you carry out in deed what you have thought and conceived; and the great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, if you not only do what is evil and wicked but glory in your crimes, according to what is written: The impious man, when he has come into the depth of evils, despises. God therefore by no means punishes the first and second goads of thoughts, which the Greeks call προπαθείας [pre-passions, the first movements of the mind], without which no human being can exist, but only if someone has resolved to do what he has thought, or has been unwilling to correct by repentance the very things he has done; whence it is written: No human being is without sin, not even if his life be of a single day. But the years of his life are numbered; and in another place: Who will boast that he has a chaste heart?; and again: The stars too are not clean in his sight, and against his angels he has devised something perverse. But if that sublime nature is not free of sin, what is to be said of human beings who, surrounded by fragile flesh, must say with the Apostle: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?, and that word, that when we have done all things we must say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done, and: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it has kept watch in vain? Now in proof of this point, that the first impulse of thoughts, or rather the slight prompting of the mind, is by no means punished by God, but only if you complete in deed what you have conceived in the mind, that passage of Genesis must be brought forward: Ham sinned in mocking his father's nakedness, and the sentence was received not by him who laughed but by his son Canaan: Cursed, he says, be Canaan; a servant he shall be to his brothers. For what righteousness is there in this, that the father should have sinned and the sentence be pronounced against the son? Likewise what the Apostle sets down in the opposite direction, that the woman is saved if her son remains in faith and holiness and chastity, would seem not to have the righteousness of a sentence, namely that if the sons and grandsons are good, the parents are saved; for how many parents are holy and have wicked sons, and, on the contrary, how many are sinners and beget holy sons? Therefore all that we said above is to be taken according to this sense: that the sins of parents and begetters are punished in the branches, not in the root. Let it suffice for the present to have said this about the proverb, or the parable: that the Law and the Prophets, that is, Exodus and Ezekiel, or rather God himself, who spoke both here and there, should by no means seem to disagree in their statements, or to correct here what he had said badly there. But if anyone can find either a better sense or another one, which removes the stumbling block of testimonies contrary to one another, it is rather his opinion that is to be accepted.

18:3-4

As I live, says the Lord, if this parable shall be any longer to you as a proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sins, it shall die. (LXX: "As I live, says the Lord Adonai, if it shall be any longer that this parable is spoken in Israel; for all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sins, it shall die.") What As I live, says the Lord means, and parable or proverb, we have said more fully above; it will by no means be spoken in Israel, but among those who do not have the knowledge of God and cannot discern the truth. All, he says, souls are mine, according to creation, not according to merit, as Moses was called a man of God, of whom it is written, A prayer of Moses, the man of God, and Elijah, who said to the captain of fifty soldiers, And if I am a man of God, let fire come down upon you and upon the fifty men; but the man of sin and son of iniquity is not called a man of God, just as those are called servants and attendants of God of whom it cannot be said, Everyone who commits sin is the servant of sin, and again, For by whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also a servant. Just as the sins of the sons do not harm the fathers, so the sins of the fathers do not overflow onto the sons, but the soul that sins, it shall die: not by the abolition of its substance, but out of the fellowship of him who says, I am the life, and who says elsewhere, Everyone who lives and believes in me shall not die for ever, and, Amen, amen I say to you, whoever keeps my word shall not see death for ever; for our life indeed is hidden with Christ in God, the life by which we shall live when Christ, our life, appears in glory, and that which is written will be fulfilled: Amen, amen I say to you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but passes from death to life. But what is said by Balaam, Let my soul die the death of the righteous, has this sense: that he desires to die to the world and to sin, and to live with the souls of the righteous, whose life is Christ, and who can sing, I will please the Lord in the land of the living; he is not indeed the God of the dead, but of the living; and if Balaam, translated into our language, means 'a vain people', which is most true, it is clear that the formerly vain people of the nations desired to have fellowship with the souls of the righteous Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who are called εὐθεῖς, that is, 'upright' and 'righteous'; whence also the book of Genesis received its name from their designation.

18:5-9

And a man, if he is righteous and does judgment and righteousness, does not eat on the mountains and does not lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, and does not violate his neighbor's wife, and does not approach a menstruous woman, and does not grieve a man, returns the pledge to the debtor, seizes nothing by force, gives his bread to the hungry, and covers the naked with a garment, and does not lend at usury, and does not take more, turns his hand away from iniquity, does true judgment between man and man, walks in my precepts, and keeps my judgments so as to do truth: this man is righteous and shall live with life, says the Lord God. (LXX: "But a man who is righteous, who does judgment and righteousness, does not eat upon the mountains and does not lift up his eyes to the thoughts of the house of Israel, and does not defile his neighbor's wife, and does not approach a woman flowing with blood, and does not oppress a man, returns the pledge owed, and does not seize plunder, gives his bread to the hungry, and covers the naked with a garment, and does not give his money at usury, and does not take more, turns his hand away from iniquity, will do righteous judgment between a man and his neighbor, and walks in my precepts, keeps my justifications so as to do them: this man is righteous, he shall live with life, says Adonai the Lord.") 'Do you wish', he says, 'to know that what was said, I will render the sins of the fathers to the third and fourth generation, does not mean what most people suppose, and is not like this saying, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge? Hear what I am about to add: if a father is righteous, who has done these things and has not done those, and has a very wicked son who, abandoning his father's virtues, gives himself over to crimes, will not the one live with life because he is righteous, and the other die by death because he has committed all the things by avoiding which his father was made righteous?' Let us look at the catalogue of the father's virtues, which seem to me to be divided into seventeen parts; of which the first is: to have done judgment; the second, similar to this: to have joined righteousness to judgment; the third: not to have eaten on the mountains; the fourth: not to have lifted the eyes to the idols — or, as the Seventy translated, the thoughts — of the house of Israel; the fifth: not to have violated his neighbor's wife; the sixth: to have avoided the embraces of a menstruous wife; the seventh: not to have grieved a man — or, as the Seventy rendered it, oppressed through power —; the eighth: to have returned the pledge to the debtor; the ninth: to have seized nothing by force — or, according to the Seventy, not to have seized plunder —; the tenth: to have given his bread to the hungry; the eleventh: to have covered the naked with a garment; the twelfth: not to have given money at usury; the thirteenth: to have taken nothing more from what you have given; the fourteenth: to have turned his hand away from iniquity; the fifteenth, which seems similar to the first but is different in part: to have done true judgment between man and man — or, his neighbor —; the sixteenth: to have walked in the precepts of the Lord; the seventeenth: to have kept his judgments and justifications. What each of these means we shall say in what follows. ·i· If, he says, a man is righteous and does judgment. It is written in Proverbs: The thoughts of the righteous are judgments. He who possesses this virtue, so as to do nothing without reason and judgment, can say that prophetic word, The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves; and when he has judged all things rightly, so as not to accept the person of the poor in judgment, he will fulfill the precept of the Lord, As the lesser, so also shall you judge the greater, saying boldly, My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times, and again, I have chosen the way of truth, I have not forgotten your judgments, and in the same psalm, I have known that your judgments are righteousness; and he will advance to such great blessedness that he understands the judgments of the Lord, which are a great deep, and says with the Apostle, O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and his ways unsearchable!, and recalls in prayer, For your judgments are delightful. ·ii· After judgment follows 'righteousness', and he who has it will clearly possess Christ, who, according to the Apostle, was made for us righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that he does true righteousness and does not regard persons in judgment, but knows that, in his judgment of others, he must be judged on his own righteousness. ·iii· The third is: He does not eat on the mountains, which the Jews think pertains to the sin of idolatry; for we read frequently in the books of Kings and of Chronicles: Nevertheless he did not depart from the high places; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the heights, Scripture signifying this: that on mountains and in groves they sacrificed victims to idols and kindled incense. We, however, say that he eats on the mountains who says with the Pharisee: I give you thanks, God, that I am not like this tax collector. I fast twice in the sabbath, I give tithes of all my substance, and so on; but on the contrary the tax collector, hearing him who had said, Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, struck his breast with his hand, that is, the treasury of the worst thoughts, and did not dare to raise his eyes to heaven. But that too which is said elsewhere, Do not seek things greater than you, and do not search out things stronger than you, convicts all heretics of eating on the mountains of pride, and of despising the simplicity of the Church, and of not knowing that it is written of them: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. ·iiii· In the fourth place is set: And does not lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, for which the Seventy translated 'thoughts'. Now idols, that is, images which they have fashioned from their own heart, all heretics make, and to them they lift up the eyes of the heart, since they have supposed their falsehood and lie to be the truth. And those are called images of the house of Israel which are found in the Church and, by occasion of knowledge falsely so called, seduce all the simple, as they bring the dogmas of the philosophers into the house of Israel, that is, of those who behold God with the mind. ·v· In the fifth place is set: And does not violate his neighbor's wife (or defile), which plainly forbids adultery; but from the fact that it says 'his neighbor's', unless every human being is understood as a neighbor, the precept would seem to be that we abstain from the wives of friends, but freely pollute the spouses of enemies and strangers. Every human being, therefore, is to be taken as the neighbor of every human being, according to the Gospel parable set forth by the Savior about a certain man who, going down to Jericho, was wounded by robbers, when the Pharisee asks, 'who was his neighbor?', teaching that he is the neighbor who has done good. According to the mystical understanding, the wife of the holy man can be understood as wisdom, as Solomon says: Love her and she will embrace you, cherish her and she will guard you; and he desires to defile her who finds fault with the good words of others and, kindled by the torches of envy, violates holy things, corrupts chaste things, defiles pure things. ·vi· The sixth is: And does not approach a menstruous woman. Each month the heavy and sluggish bodies of women are relieved by the outflow of unclean blood, and if at that time a man has intercourse with a woman, the fetuses conceived are said to contract a defect of the seed, so that lepers and elephantiacs are born from this conception, and corrupted gore makes bodies, foul in either sex, degenerate through the smallness or the enormity of their limbs. Men are therefore commanded, not only with respect to other men's women but also with their own, to whom they are seen to be joined by law, Scripture saying, Increase and multiply and fill the earth, to know fixed times for intercourse, when they must come together and when they must abstain from their wives; which indeed both the Apostle and Ecclesiastes express: A time to embrace and a time to be far from embraces.
