Let the wife therefore beware lest, overcome by the desire for intercourse, she conceal it from her husband, and the husband lest he do violence to his wife, thinking that the pleasure of marriage ought to be subject to him at every time; whence Paul too: That each one, he says, may know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and chastity. It is finely said in the little maxims of Sextus the Pythagorean: An adulterer is the too ardent lover of his own wife; a book which a certain man, translating it into the Latin language, wished to adorn with the name of the martyr Sixtus, not considering that in the whole volume, which he pointlessly divided into two parts, the name of Christ and of the apostles is entirely passed over in silence; nor is it surprising if he turned a pagan philosopher into a martyr and bishop of the city of Rome, since he also changed the first book of Eusebius of Caesarea in defense of Origen to the name of the martyr Pamphilus, so that with such a eulogist he might more easily commend the most impious books Περὶ Ἀρχῶν [On First Principles] to Roman ears. ·vii· There follows in the seventh place: And does not grieve a man (or, as the Seventy translated, does not oppress through power). I do not know who is free of this vice and sin; for the Egyptians too oppressed the Hebrews through power, whence Habakkuk also complains that the impious oppresses the righteous. And would that this were said only of those who are outside, and not of those who are within! For the princes of the churches too are accustomed to oppress the people through pride, of whom it is written: They have made you prince: do not be lifted up; be among them as one of them, and the Savior commanded: Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be the least of all. But what is said according to the Hebrew, And does not grieve a man, agrees with the apostolic testimony, Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, who dwells in you; and in the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes are accustomed to read, it is placed among the greatest crimes: he who has grieved his brother's spirit. But if the sadness of another kills the one who causes the grief, what must be said of iniquity and a tyrannical mind, when that saying fits, Why do earth and ashes glory?, so that a man, forgetful of his condition, how he is full of phlegm, bile and dung, and shortly to be ploughed through by worms, sets his mouth in heaven, and his tongue passes through even to the earth, and he says with the true Nebuchadnezzar, I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne and I will be like the Most High? ·viii· The eighth is: If he returns the pledge to the debtor; not to every debtor, otherwise for many the occasion of receiving back their pledges would become a means to riches, but to that debtor of whom it is written in the Law that he is poor and has put up his own garment, and ought to receive back his covering before sunset, lest, tormented by cold, he cry out to the Lord, who is the avenger of his injury. But if, according to what follows, we ought to give bread to the hungry and cover the naked with a garment, how much more to return what is his own, provided the debtor's poverty is beyond doubt? We can also return the pledge to the debtor when, to one to whom we are joined in love and who owes us mutual charity, we return his pledge, retaining with us nothing further of his debt. ·viiii· The ninth place is held by: Seizes nothing by force (or, according to the Seventy, does not seize plunder). The Apostle too speaks of plunderers, that among the other sinners one must not even eat with such men; and every plunder is mixed with violence, for unless force has been applied, plunder does not succeed. But there is also a holy violence and a desirable plunder, of which the Gospel writes: From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent tear it away; of which Jude the brother of James also speaks: And some indeed seize from the fire; but have mercy on others who are judged. On the contrary, the adverse powers hasten to seize their prey to the destruction of those whom they seize, which Jacob too signifies when he says: An evil beast has devoured him, an evil beast has seized Joseph. Hence also the sheep of the Lord which follow him are not seized from his hands, and he himself says: What the Father has given me is greater than all, and no one can seize it from the hand of the Father; from which is seen the one power, might and substance of the Father and the Son: for if no one can seize from the Son's hand what the Father has given, and these same things are in the Father's hand and are not seized from him, it is clearly proved that all things are common to the Father and the Son, and that the Father holds in the Son's hand, just as the things that are the Son's are held in the Father's hand. ·x· The tenth is: Gives his bread to the hungry; by which we are taught that alms are to be given not to the sated but to the hungry, and that bread is to be given not to those who belch with fullness but to those who are tormented by emptiness. In bread, moreover, every food is contained, and 'his' is said significantly, lest we turn into an act of mercy bread acquired from plunder and usury and the misfortune of others: for the redemption indeed of a man's soul is his own riches; which we see many doing who oppress their clients and the poor and the farmers through power, or commit thefts against them, to say nothing of the violence of soldiers and judges, so that out of much they bestow a little on the poor and glory in their crimes; and the deacon reads out publicly in the churches the names of the offerers, 'She offers so much, he has promised so much'; and they are pleased with themselves at the applause of the people, while their conscience torments them; and we give the wretches occasion to rejoice over what they bestow and not to mourn over what they have seized. But it is better for us to understand that the bread of righteousness is he who said, I am the bread who came down from heaven, and whom we pray in prayer to be granted to us: Our substantial bread (or that is to come) give us, so that him whom we shall afterwards receive always, we may deserve to receive daily in the present age. This bread the righteous man gives to the hungry, of whom it is written, Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled, because he who is righteous makes the common bread of all his own, the bread which had failed in Judea, as the prophet says: I will take away from them the strength (or the staff) of bread. What we are saying, provided that we are Christ's, or rather what the prophet records, is the bread of believers and of the hungry, which is by no means to be given to those who have eaten and drunk and been sated and, grown fat, have kicked, of whom it is said, Woe to you who are sated now, for you will hunger, lest they vomit it up, as Solomon says: For he will vomit it up and will defile your good words; which the Savior says in other words: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine. ·xi· The eleventh place is held by: And has covered the naked with a garment, a saying which, according to the explanation of the preceding little verse, must be expounded in two ways: that we both give covering to the naked, as the Savior says, I was naked, and you covered me, and give to those who are naked of faith and virtues the garment of Christ, of whom it is written, For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. Naked of this garment was he who, not having a wedding garment, was thrown out of the banquet. Of this nakedness the Lord also speaks to Jerusalem: You moreover were naked and full of confusion. ·xii· The twelfth number is held by: And does not lend at usury (or, as the Seventy translated, does not give his money at usury). In the Hebrew usury on all kinds of goods is forbidden, in the Seventy only on money, according to what is also written in Psalm 14 (15), Who has not given his money at usury, and as it is said, To your brother you shall not lend at interest, but to a foreigner you shall lend at interest. But see the progress: at the beginning of the Law interest is removed only from brothers; in the prophet usury is forbidden from all, as Ezekiel says, He has not given his money at usury; and further, in the Gospel there is an increase of virtue, as the Lord commands, 'Lend to those from whom you do not hope to receive back'. ·xiii· There follows in the thirteenth place: And does not take more. Some think that usury applies only to money; foreseeing this, divine Scripture removes the surplus on everything, so that you may not receive back more than you gave. In the country it is customary for 'usury', or, as the divine word calls it, 'abundance', to be exacted on grain and millet, wine and oil, and other kinds of goods; for example, that in winter we give ten modii and at harvest receive back fifteen, that is, more by half. He who thinks himself most just will take a fourth part more; and they are accustomed to argue and say: 'I gave one modius, which, when sown, made ten modii. Is it not just that I should receive half a modius more of what is mine, when he, by my generosity, has nine and a half from what is mine?' Do not err, says the Apostle: God is not mocked. For let the merciful moneylender answer us briefly whether he gave to one who had or to one who did not have. If to one who had, he certainly ought not to have given; but he gave as if to one who did not have: why then does he exact more as if from one who has? Others, in return for money lent at interest, are accustomed to accept little gifts of various kinds, and do not understand that whatever it is is called 'usury' and 'surplus' if they have received more than what they gave. ·xiiii· The fourteenth step: From iniquity, he says, he turns away his hand, so that he flees iniquity in every work. For iniquity is committed not only with the hand but with the other members too, as Solomon says, Remove iniquitous lips far from you, and in the Psalms, They have spoken iniquity on high; the foot too runs to iniquity, and the eye, if it covets another man's wife; nor would he be an imitator of him of whom it is said, He did no iniquity and no deceit was found in his mouth. Hence also we are commanded to make friends for ourselves from the unrighteous mammon, who may receive us into the eternal tabernacles. ·xv· The fifteenth is: Does true judgment between man and man (or his neighbor), which seems to mean the same as the first, where it is written, If he is righteous and does judgment; but it adds the 'truth' of the judgment which he does between man and man, or his neighbor: it is seen to have an ἐπίτασιν [intensification] of the virtues. Hence also at the opening of Proverbs, after many precepts, the 'correction' of judgment is added: To know, it says, wisdom and discipline, and to understand the words of prudence, to receive the subtleties of words, and to know true righteousness, and after all things to correct judgment. For this reason the Apostle too rebukes those who are established in the Church, because they have lawsuits among themselves, and the least and despised one is chosen, who according to the Gospel is first, to judge between man and man, he who has put away the things of a child and has attained to the perfect man; and yet he needs a greater discernment to be able to attain to the 'truth' of judgment. ·xvi· There follows in the sixteenth place: Walks in my precepts, ·xvii· and in the seventeenth: Judgments (or my justifications) he keeps, so as to do them, and keeps them once done; each of which has a manifold understanding, if we wish to go over all the commandments of the Law, in which there are said to be precepts of the Lord and in which justifications. Psalm 118 (119) is full of precepts and justifications, and in part Psalm 18 (19), in which it is written, The righteousnesses of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts and the precept of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes; in this the question is raised how God said in this same prophet, I gave them justifications not good, in which they should not live in them; and the answer is easy, and fuller in what follows: that the Jews, following the killing letter, do not live, and the Christians, understanding the life-giving spirit, do live. It would be long, if we wished to prove by testimonies where there are said to be precepts of the Lord and where justifications, and in what differences or obscurities they are each wrapped. Hence too in the present place it is added: This man is righteous, he shall live with life, says the Lord God; he who has done these things and has not done those will by no means be punished for the offenses of his father, but will live by his own virtues.

18:10-13

But if he begets a son who is a robber, shedding blood, and does one of these things (or, as the Seventy translated, and does sins, does not walk in the way of his righteous father), and who does not do all these things, but eats on the mountains, and pollutes his neighbor's wife, grieves the needy and the poor (or oppresses), seizes plunder, does not return the pledge, and lifts up his eyes to idols, commits abomination, gives at usury and takes more: shall he live? He shall not live; since he has done all these detestable things, he shall die by death, his blood shall be upon him. For 'robber' in the Hebrew is written 'pharis', which the second edition of Aquila translated 'sinner', Symmachus 'transgressor', the Seventy and Theodotion 'pestilent'. Just as a pestilence creates diseases and is wont to lay waste far and wide the regions on which it has settled, so the pestilent man ravages everything. And let us speak first according to the history, so that you may know that the iniquities of the fathers do not overflow onto the sons. If the righteous man does what the preceding discourse wove together in order, he shall live with life; but if he begets a son who departs from the service of the Lord and exchanges his father's virtues for vices, so that he does what the father did not do and does not do what the father wrought, will he be able to live? Certainly he will not live, but will be guilty of his own blood. Further, according to the spiritual understanding, if a righteous man of the Church has preached the evangelical faith, and his son and disciple has been deceived by heretical error, the son will be called pestilent, of whom it is written also in Psalm 1, And has not sat in the chair of pestilence, and in Proverbs, The bold and insolent and proud man is called pestilent. He has shed the blood of the deceived and doubles all sins upon himself, eating on the mountains of pride and polluting his neighbor's church, grieving the needy and the poor in the knowledge of the Scriptures, oppressing and supplanting them, seizing as plunder those whom he has seduced from the Church, not returning the pledge which he had received from his teacher so as to fulfill what is written, Freely you have received, freely give, and lifting up his eyes to the idols and images which he has fashioned from his own heart, and committing all abominations, and giving money at usury, so as to increase the teacher's error by the diligence of the disciples, and demanding back from those to whom he gave more than he had given: certainly he will not be able to live, but will die in his own blood.

18:14-18

But if he begets a son who, seeing all the sins of his father which he did, fears and does not do likewise, does not eat upon the mountains and does not lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, and does not violate his neighbor's wife, and does not grieve a man, does not retain the pledge, and does not seize plunder, gives his bread to the hungry, and covers the naked with a garment, turns his hand away from injury to the poor, does not take usury and surplus, does my judgments, walks in my precepts: this man shall not die in the iniquity of his father, but shall live with life. His father, because he practiced calumny and did violence to his brother, and wrought evil in the midst of his people, has died in his iniquity. 'And do not wonder', he says, 'if the son of a righteous man, turning aside to vices and sins, dies by death, since, on the contrary, the son of a sinner and impious man, if he sees the perversity of his father's ways and turns himself so as not to do evil things and to do good things, is not held guilty of his father's crimes'. This can be taken also of us, to whom it is said in the Psalms, Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and the father's house; and the king will desire your beauty, and who have been born of the stock of the nations: that we should leave behind the crimes of our parents and do judgment and righteousness and live in it. He therefore repeats what we have treated more broadly above, and so we run through everything briefly, wishing to pass on to the things that are more obscure and new.

18:19-20

And you say: Why has the son not borne the iniquity of the father? Clearly because the son has wrought judgment and righteousness, has kept all my precepts, and has done them: he shall live with life. The soul that sins, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the impiety of the impious shall be upon him. He solves the question which the hearer could raise as an objection: 'You are accustomed', he says, 'to say: Why has the righteous son not borne the iniquity of the father?'; to which he himself replied: 'Clearly because the son has done well and has not committed his father's offenses'. And it is just that, as the sinner dies in his crime, so the righteous man should live in his virtues; and that the soul that sins should die, and he who keeps the precepts of God should live.

18:21-22a

But if the impious man repents of all his sins which he has wrought, and keeps all my precepts, and does judgment and righteousness, he shall live with life and shall not die. Of all his iniquities which he has wrought I will not be mindful. 'To such a degree', he says, 'do the sins of the fathers not overflow onto the sons, nor does a criminal father weigh down a righteous son, nor are some punished for the crimes of others, that one and the same man who was formerly impious and a sinner, if afterwards he repents and, turned to better things, blots out his former sins, is not judged by the oldness of his sin, but is received into my flock by the renewal of virtue'. And at the same time it must be considered what kind of impious man and sinner he receives as a penitent: 'If from all his sins', he says, 'which he has wrought he turns himself away, and keeps all the precepts of the Lord, so, namely, that he abandons all crimes and follows all virtues; if he does all good things and forsakes all evil things, I too will forget all his iniquities which he has wrought'.

18:22b

In his righteousness which he has wrought he shall live. 'He shall live not so much by my righteousness as by his own, although it belongs to my righteousness to render good things to the good and evil things to the evil'.

18:23

Is the death of the impious man of my will, says the Lord God, and not that he should turn from his ways and live? Therefore it is of the Lord's will that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth; and wherever the sentence of God seems severe and ferocious, he condemns not men but sins.

18:24

But if the righteous man turns himself away from his righteousness, and does iniquity according to all the abominations which the impious man is accustomed to work, shall he live? All his righteousnesses which he had done shall not be remembered; in the transgression by which he transgressed and in his sin which he sinned, in it he shall die. Just as old offenses do not weigh down the righteous man who was formerly a sinner, so former righteousnesses do not help the sinner who was formerly righteous; each one is judged in that in which he is found.

18:25

And you have said: The way of the Lord is not equitable. Hear, house of Israel: Is my way not equitable, and are not rather your ways crooked? He gives the reasons why the sentence of the Lord is just: 'Do you think me unjust', he says, 'in rendering the sins of the fathers to the sons, so that while some eat the sour grape, the teeth of others are set on edge? Behold, each one dies in his own sin and is given life in his own righteousness; in both cases, not the things past but the things present. Rather it is your sentence that is unjust, you who think that the parable is not a parable, but take it as though it were the truth of history, that the crimes of some are punished in others'.

18:26

For when the righteous man turns himself away from his righteousness and does iniquity, he shall die in them: in the iniquity which he has wrought he shall die. This can be understood thus: the people of Israel, formerly righteous, turned itself away from its righteousness, because it abandoned the author of righteousness, and did iniquity by denying the Son of God; in the sin and crime which it wrought it will die, not in many but in one, killing the heir so that it lost the inheritance.

18:27-28

And when the impious man turns himself away from his impiety which he has wrought, and does judgment and righteousness, he has given life to his own soul; for, considering, he has turned himself away from all his iniquities which he has wrought; he shall live with life, and shall not die. 'On the contrary', he says, 'the people of the nations, not having the knowledge of God, and impious, if it turns itself away from its impiety which it formerly wrought in idolatry, and does the things which were commanded to Israel in the Law, has itself, formerly dead, given life to its own soul; and seeing that it had perished in the iniquities which it wrought, it will believe in him who says, 'I am the way and the life and the truth'; it shall live with life, and shall not die'.

18:29

And the sons of Israel say: The way of the Lord is not equitable. Are my ways not equitable, house of Israel, and are not rather your ways crooked? To this day Israel blasphemes God: why has he abandoned his people and taken up the multitude of the nations? The Lord rebukes them because their ways are crooked, while the sentence of the Lord is just: having despised or destroyed the former tenants, he sends other farmers into his vineyard; understanding which, in the parable of the Gospel, the Jews said: This shall not be.

18:30a

Therefore I will judge each one of you according to his ways, house of Israel, says the Lord God. Whether those who are judged are from the multitude of the Gentiles or from the people of Israel, there is no respect of persons with God, but each one will be crowned by his own faith, and condemned by impiety and unbelief.

18:30b-31a

Turn, and repent of all your iniquities, and iniquity shall not be a ruin to you. Cast away from you all your transgressions by which you have transgressed. This word is properly directed to Israel, that they should repent and abandon their iniquities, or transgressions, by which they transgressed against God. But it can also be understood of both peoples, so that both Israel and the crowd of the nations, abandoning their vices, may turn to him who is able to heal their bruises.

18:31b

'And make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit, so that, abandoning the oldness of the letter, you may live in the newness of the spirit'. The new heart of Israel is to believe in him whom it had formerly denied; the new heart of the nations is to abandon idols and, having despised the cult of the dead, to believe in him who is the God of the living.

18:31c

And why will you die, house of Israel? It is better, as we said above, to take this exhortation, in which it is written, Turn, and repent, as addressed to the person of the Jews, whom he does not wish to die and to whom he is now speaking: 'Why will you die, house of Israel, you who have as fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — of whom it is written, The God of the living and not of the dead —? Why will you die by your own fault, you who ought to live by the merit of your fathers and by my mercy?'

18:32

For I do not want the death of the dying sinner, says the Lord God; return and live. 'I do not want you to die', he says, 'whom I begot in salvation: for sons indeed I have begotten and exalted, but they have despised me; return therefore and live'. Return is not said except to those who were formerly with God and afterwards deserted his company. And live through repentance, you who are dead through sin. Therefore Israel, because it does not return to its former state, must be believed to be dead.

19:1-9

And you, take up a lament over the princes of Israel, and you shall say: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions, in the midst of young lions rear her whelps? And she brought out one of her young lions, he became a lion, and he learned to catch prey and to devour man. And the nations heard of him, and not without wounds of their own they caught him, and they brought him in chains into the land of Egypt. And when she had seen that she was weakened and her expectation had perished, she took one of her young lions, she made him a lion. He went about among the lions and became a lion, he learned to catch prey and to devour men; he learned to make widows, and to bring their cities into a desert, and the land and its fullness was made desolate by the sound of his roaring. And the nations gathered against him from every side, from the provinces, and they spread their net over him; in their wounds he was caught. And they put him into a cage, in chains, and they brought him to the king of Babylon; and they put him into prison, so that his voice should no longer be heard upon the mountains of Israel. (LXX: "And you, take a lamentation over the prince of Israel, and you shall say: Why has your mother become a whelp in the midst of lions, in the midst of lions she multiplied her whelps? And one of her whelps sprang forth, he became a lion, and he learned to seize spoils, he devoured men. And the nations heard against him, in their corruption he was caught, and they brought him in a muzzle into the land of Egypt. And she saw that he had been taken away from her and that her substance had perished, and she took another of her whelps, she made him a lion. And he went about in the midst of the lions, he became a lion, and he learned to seize spoils, he devoured men; and he fed in his boldness, and he brought their cities to a desert, and he laid waste the land and its fullness by the sound of his roaring. And he set nations against him round about from the regions, and they spread their nets over him, in their corruption he was caught. And they put him in a muzzle and in a cage, he came to the king of Babylon; and they brought him into prison, so that his voice should not be heard any longer upon the mountains of Israel.") I know that I have read in this place a manifold explanation, and one entangled in such great obscurities that it did not so much open up the reading as wrap it up, since it refers everything that is written to the opposing powers and describes lions and wars in the heavenly Jerusalem, how one of them was captured and another was in turn set up in his place; and it sets out many testimonies that the devil and his companions are customarily called lions, such as that saying of the apostle Peter: Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion and seeks how he may enter, and that of the Psalms: Do not hand over to the beasts the souls that confess to you; certainly, when it comes to the history, it says that Johanan the son of Kareah was led into Egypt (how he, fleeing with a few men, is to be called a lion, I am unable to know), and that the other lion is Zedekiah, who was himself also led into Babylon. But we, leaving explanations of this kind to the judgment of the reader, say that, with the captivity close at hand, the prophet is not so much foretelling things to come as narrating things past. For after the sixth year of King Zedekiah — since immediately in what follows we read: And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth of the month — a lament is taken up over the princes — or the prince — of Israel, and it is said: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions? The lament, then, is over the princes, namely all who were begotten of the stock of Josiah. Jerusalem, the mother of the princes, is called a lioness, who bore and reared young lions, and brought out one of her young lions and made him a lion, signifying Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, whom Pharaoh Neco led into Egypt, and in his place he set up Jehoiakim; and when he had died, Jeconiah his son, having been made king, was led to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar together with his mother and the nobles of the city; of him is born Shealtiel, the father of Zerubbabel, who received his name from the fact that he was born in Babylon. And it is plain that under the μεταφορᾷ [metaphor] of the lioness, of the young lions and of the lion, and again of another lion, those things are described which had already been done at the time when the prophet was saying these things. For after Jerusalem had brought out Jehoahaz the son of Josiah from the royal stock and made him king, he proved so cruel in a short time that he is related, tropologically, to have caught prey and devoured men. When the Egyptian had come against him, he caught him not without wounds — or in a pit, as is properly contained in the Hebrew, so as to preserve the tropological capture of lions, which are always caught in pits — and he brought him in a muzzle, or in chains, into the land of Egypt, and there he died. When his mother Jerusalem, who had borne him, who had reared him, who had set him in the kingship, had seen that her expectation had perished, she took from among the other kings Jeconiah, the son of Jehoiakim, and set him up as king. He too, having imitated the cruelty of his predecessor, is described under the ferocity of a lion, in that he devoured men, made many widows, brought cities to a desert, and at the sound of his roaring the whole province was terrified, so that the nations gathered against him and spread their net and caught him in a pit and put him in a cage and in chains — not that this was done to Jeconiah: for he gave himself up to the king of Babylonia and was carried off into Chaldea; but so that the metaphor of the lion may be preserved, which is caught in pits and bound with chains and kept in cages —. Otherwise, according to the history, we read this of Zedekiah, who was set up as king of Jerusalem after Jeconiah — and this is what gave occasion for most people to understand Zedekiah rather than Jeconiah, because chains are read of, and cages, and a prison is named —; he was, then, kept in prison and not put to death, and was only removed from the kingship. But the history relates that Zedekiah was led blind into Babylon and there immediately killed.

19:10-14

Your mother is like a vine in your blood, planted upon the water; its fruits and its leaves grew from many waters; and it had solid rods for the scepters of rulers, and its stature was exalted into leaves, and it saw its height in the multitude of its shoots. And it was plucked up in wrath, and cast down to the ground, and the burning wind dried up its fruits; the rods of its strength withered and were dried up, fire devoured it. And now it is transplanted into the desert, in a land impassable and thirsty. And fire went out from the rod of its branches, which devoured its fruit; and there was not in it a strong rod, a scepter of rulers. It is a lament, and it shall be for a lament. (LXX: "Your mother is like a vine, like a flower on pomegranates, planted in water; its fruit and its sprout came from much water; and it had a rod of strength for a tribe of leaders, and it was exalted in its greatness in the midst of its offshoots, and it saw its greatness in the multitude of its shoots. And broken in fury, it was cast to the ground, and the burning wind dried up its choice parts; they were avenged, and the rod of its strength was dried up, fire consumed it. And now they have planted it in the desert, in a land without water. And fire went out from the rod of its choice ones, and devoured it, and there was not in it a rod of strength. A tribe is in a parable of lamentation, and it shall be for a lament.") One thing is said in different words; and just as in the earlier passages we read that Jerusalem was compared to a beautiful woman, and again to a lioness who reared lions in her lair, so now she is compared to a vine-stock or a most beautiful vine planted upon many waters; and that therefore its shoots, nourished by the moisture, grew so much that one shoot, which Scripture calls a most solid or most strong rod, advanced 'into the scepters of rulers' — for which the Seventy rendered 'into a tribe of leaders' — so, namely, that kings should be made from it. And the vine itself was of such beauty that the splendor of its greenness was made equal to the flowers of the pomegranate, which is what is said in the Hebrew, like a vine in your blood, the redness of its flowers being compared to blood. The vine, then, was exalted and raised up; because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, it was plucked up in the fury of the Lord and cast down to the ground, so that the elegant metaphor of the vine-stock might preserve the ruins of Jerusalem; for however beautiful a vine may be and however far it stretches out with long runners, unless you raise up stakes and reeds, joined to the earth it dries up from the heat, especially if the burning wind, which the Greeks call καύσωνα [the scorching wind], has dried up its fruits, so that it withers and is burned as though by the blazing heat of fire. But as for what has been added in the Seventy, And they were avenged, in place of what is written in the Hebrew, They withered, what coherence it can have I am unable to know. That vine, then, of such abundance and of such fruits and of such beauty, how is it now carried over into the desert, in a land impassable and thirsty? And it signifies the land of Babylon, to which they were carried over, or Egypt, where they fled for refuge, or the land of Judea itself, in which a few poor people remained, over whom Gedaliah was set to gather and rule the remnant of the people; against him there rose up, from the royal stock and from the rod of the branches of the vine, Ishmael, who killed him at Mizpah and devoured all the fruit of the vine; and from then on there was not in that vine a strong rod and a scepter of rulers: for none of the kings remained to govern the people, but with Johanan, the son of Kareah, they fled to Egypt. Therefore it is a lament and a parable of lamentation, so that the royal line may be lamented, which will thenceforth cease in Judea until he should come for whom it is reserved: And he was the expectation of the nations. From this it is plain that both the earlier reading, in which it is said: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions?, and this one, in which it is written: Your mother is like a vine in your blood, planted upon water, pertain to Jerusalem, which lost her lions and her shoots, and there did not remain in her a rod that might rise up into a tribe or into the scepters of rulers. For it begins from a lament and ends in a lament: Take up a lament over the princes of Israel, that is, at the beginning, and now at the end: It is a lament; and the royal stock is to be attended by the lamentation and lament of the parable. Moreover, according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], what others refer to the heavenly Jerusalem — so as to say that from it very many fell down into this valley of tears, and that kings ceased to be, and that the once most beautiful vine was dried up by the burning wind, so that none of its green shoots remained in it, the vine which Jeremiah afterwards laments under the figure of the city — we understand of the Church — because in the last time, iniquity having been multiplied, the love of many grows cold, so that if it can be, even the elect of God are tested, and her princes are caught in the nets of the devil, who is not content with the capture of one king but hastens daily to capture kings and princes, according to what is written: His foods are choice —. The shoots of the Church too, which formerly were equaled to flowers and to the redness of blood, are afterwards dried up by the burning wind; and this exposition the parable of the Gospel also sounds forth, in which, when the sun had risen, the things that had sprouted were scorched and suddenly dried up, so that scarcely one of the shoots remains to rise up into a rod and become a worthy prince of the people, which Isaiah says in other words: I will bring famine and thirst upon the land, and not a famine of bread and a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God. Hence we must lament and wail over the princes of Israel, through whose vice and pride Judea was deserted, and Jerusalem was captured.

20:1

And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth, on the tenth of the month, there came men of the elders of Israel to inquire of the Lord, and they sat before me. Eleven months and five days after the previous vision, the word again comes to the prophet, after some of the elders of the house of Israel had come to inquire of the Lord and had sat before him. That it was the custom of the people of Israel to seek from the Lord through the prophets whatever they desired to know, many examples testify: Saul, looking for the asses, goes to Samuel and received advice from the servant boy to offer the prophet the fourth part of a shekel; when the son of Jeroboam fell ill, his wife is sent to Shiloh to the prophet Ahijah, bringing little gifts, loaves and cakes, grapes and a small jar of honey, to learn about her son's sickness; David too, a prophet, inquires of another prophet, Nathan, whether he ought to build a temple to the Lord; and Ahab asks whether he should go up to Ramoth-gilead or not; in Isaiah also and in the volume of Kings the things that were to come upon Sennacherib are announced. Nor is it surprising if in the Old Testament the prophets announce to individuals the things that are to come, since we read that Agabus prophesied the things that were to come upon Paul; for it is written in Deuteronomy: The nations which the Lord is about to destroy in your sight, these will listen to dreams and divinations; but to you the Lord your God has not granted it so: for it belongs to the nations to resort to Chaldeans, soothsayers, haruspices, diviners, lot-casters, the oracles of demons, by which their error is mocked. Hence now too the elders of Israel approach the prophet in order to inquire of the Lord through him, and yet they are silent about their question, while he who was to be questioned knew what they were asking, so that in this too there might be a miracle: to know why they had come and to answer the things that a silent speech held within their mind.

20:2-3

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Have you come to inquire of me? As I live, I will not answer you, says the Lord God. To the saints and to those who ask fitting things a promise is given: 'While you are still speaking I will say: Behold, I am here'; but to sinners, such as the elders of Israel were, whose crimes the prophet describes in what follows, no answer is given, but a rebuke for their sins, and he adds an oath: As I live, so that the sentence of the one who refuses may be the firmer. What the Seventy said: If I answer you, Symmachus translated more plainly: I will not answer you.

20:4a

If you judge them, if you judge, son of man. (LXX: "If I avenge them with vengeance, son of man.") 'They indeed came to inquire, wishing to learn the future concerning the things about which they are in doubt. But you, son of man, judge them, so that there may be no prophet's answer, but the sentence of one who judges, for the iniquities which they have committed, and they have followed the crimes of their fathers'; or certainly: If I avenge them with vengeance, so that the sense is: 'They are covered with such great iniquity that they are not worthy even of correction and reproof', according to what is said in the prophet: I will no longer visit your daughters and your daughters-in-law, when they have committed adultery. Hence sinners too, who have come into the depth of sin, are let go to do the desires of their heart.

20:4b-5a

Show them the abominations of their fathers. And you shall say to them. (LXX: "Testify to them the iniquities of their fathers, and you shall say to them.") If the sins of the fathers do not overflow onto the sons, how is it that the abominations and iniquities of the fathers are now set before the elders? For this reason, evidently: that they may be shown to act like their parents and, by a hereditary evil, to drag a very long rope of sins, so that they may dread the punishments of those whose vices they imitate.

20:5b-6

Thus says the Lord God: On the day when I chose Israel, and lifted up my hand for the stock of the house of Jacob, and appeared to them in the land of Egypt, and lifted up my hand for them, saying: I am the Lord your God. On that day I lifted up my hand for them, to lead them out of the land of Egypt into the land which I had provided for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is excellent among all lands. (LXX: "Thus says the Lord God: From the day on which I chose the house of Israel, and became known to the seed of the house of Jacob, and was known to them in the land of Egypt, and took them up, saying: I am the Lord your God. On that day I took hold of them with my hand, saying, to lead them out of the land of Egypt into the land which I prepared for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, it is a honeycomb beyond all lands.") For what the Seventy said: It is a honeycomb beyond all lands, for which we translated: It is excellent among all lands, the first edition of Aquila put 'firm support', the second 'renowned', Symmachus 'region', Theodotion 'strength', namely because this land is the foundation of all lands, because in it are the religion of God and the temple and the ceremonies and the knowledge of God; and so far was the people of Israel, settled in Egypt, from knowing God, that Moses, sent to them: If they ask, he says, me: Who sent you?, what shall I say to them? Say, he says, to them: He who is, sent me. In Egypt, then, he became known to the people and to the seed of the house of Jacob, when he lifted up his hand for them against the Egyptians, and said: I am the Lord your God, and he chose them to lead them out of the land of Egypt to a land flowing with milk and honey; for they were not yet able to take solid food, but like little children and sucklings they needed the honey and milk of infancy. According to the letter, however, that the land of Judea is renowned and more fertile than all lands, no one will be able to doubt who has considered the whole land from Rhinocorura as far as Mount Taurus and the river Euphrates, and the power of its cities and the pleasantness of its regions, namely Palestine and Phoenicia, Arabia, Coele-Syria, Cilicia, and the other regions which the Lord promised to Israel if he had kept the precepts of God; and that he did not receive them was the fault of his unbelief. For even in Palestine itself and the province of Judea very many nations remained which were not driven out; for the guarantor is not to blame if the one to whom the promise is made has made himself unworthy of the pledge, especially since the one who promises sets out a choice: If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling, the sword shall devour you. They are chosen, then, according to the present, and it does not follow that one who is chosen cannot be tempted or perish, since both Saul, chosen as king, and Judas, chosen as apostle, afterward fell by their own fault. The lifting up of the hand, or its stretching out, shows the posture of one who strikes: that he might strike the Egyptians for them and free the people of Israel from Egypt.

20:7

And he said to them: Let each one cast away the offenses of his eyes, and do not be defiled with the idols of Egypt: I am the Lord your God. (LXX: "And he said to them: Let each one cast away the abominations of his eyes, and let him not be defiled with the inventions of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.") For 'offenses', which in Hebrew are called 'seccuse', Symmachus translated 'nauseating things', the second edition of Aquila 'cuttings-off', so as to signify that bleariness must be cast away from the eyes, and a kind of nausea which not only hinders the sight but also produces vomiting in those who look at it; 'gelule' too is a Hebrew word, which the Seventy translated 'inventions', the first edition of Aquila 'defilements', the second, and Symmachus and Theodotion, 'idols', whom we too have followed for the present. He commanded them, as they were first going out of Egypt, to forget the idols which they had served for a long time; to cast them away from their eyes, so as not to hold them worthy even of a glance, and no longer to give consent to the things by which they had long been defiled. I, he says, am the Lord your God, not the portents of Egypt, not the fabrications of various monsters. But we too, when we go out of Egypt, are commanded to cast away the offenses of our eyes, namely so that we may not take delight in the things in which we formerly took delight in the world, lest we be defiled with the images of Egypt, that is, with the inventions of the philosophers and of the heretics, which are rightly called idols. Let us also turn our eyes away from the spectacles, or rather the offenses, of Egypt: of the arena, the circus, the theaters, and all the things that defile the purity of the soul and enter the mind through the senses; and what is written is fulfilled: Death will come in through your windows.

20:8a

And they provoked me. (LXX: "And they withdrew from me.") Or, as Symmachus translated: They did not consent to me; and as soon as they are called, they withdraw from God, so that there is no interval between the calling and the withdrawal. And this is to be noted, that no one withdraws from God except one who was formerly with him; hence the dragon too in the book of Job is called ἀποστάτης, a transgressor and one who withdraws.

20:8b

And they would not listen; each one did not cast away the abominations of his eyes, nor did they abandon the idols of Egypt. (LXX: "And they would not listen to me; they did not cast away the abominations of their eyes, and did not abandon the inventions of Egypt.") 'For this reason', he says, 'they provoked me and withdrew from me: because they would not listen, while man's free will is preserved, and they did all the things which I commanded in the law that they should not do, at once despairing of salvation and muttering against Moses, and distrusting the promises of God'. There follows:

20:8c

And I said that I would pour out my indignation upon them, and fulfill my wrath on them in the midst of the land of Egypt. 'As soon as I commanded them to leave or cast away the offenses of their eyes and by no means to be defiled with the idols of Egypt, they provoked me and would not listen to what I said, but on the contrary did what I had commanded should not be done. Therefore I had decreed to pour out on them my fury and my indignation and to fulfill my wrath, which I had conceived in my mind, in the midst of Egypt, upon those who had not yet gone out of Egypt'. For there follows: I therefore cast them out of the land of Egypt and led them down into the desert, from which it is shown that they had not yet gone out of the land of Egypt when he wished to pour out his indignation and fulfill his wrath upon them and to strike them in the midst of the land of Egypt.

20:9

And I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations in whose midst they were, and among whom I appeared to them, to lead them out of the land of Egypt. 'What I was thinking of doing on account of justice I did not do on account of the greatness of my clemency, lest my name be defiled and I should seem not to have been able to fulfill what I had promised to Israel. I spared my name, then, lest the nations among whom I became known to them in the land of Egypt should have occasion to blaspheme'. Up to this point the prophet describes what he promised them while they were settled in the land of Egypt, and how they at once gave offense, and what the Lord thought of doing against them and yet did not do; what follows he spoke to them after they had gone out of Egypt.

20:10-14

I therefore cast them out of the land of Egypt, and led them out into the desert. And I gave them my precepts, and showed them my judgments, which a man should do and live in them. Moreover I also gave them my sabbaths, that it might be a sign between me and them, and that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them. And the house of Israel provoked me in the desert: they did not walk in my precepts, and they cast away my judgments, which, if a man does them, he shall live in them, and they violated my sabbaths exceedingly. I said therefore that I would pour out my fury upon them in the desert and consume them. And I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out in their sight. These things are said to those who were led out of Egypt into the desert, so that, freed from the vices of the Egyptians, they might more easily fulfill the precepts of God in the wilderness and do his judgments and keep the sabbaths, which were given as a sign between the one who gave them and those to whom they were given, as Scripture says: The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the children of Israel and you shall say to them: See that you keep my sabbaths, for it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you; and keep the sabbath, for it is holy to you: whoever violates it shall surely die; everyone who does work on it, that soul shall be put to death from the midst of its people. So the sabbath and circumcision were given as a sign of the true sabbath and the true circumcision: that we may know that we must rest from earthly works in the perfect and true sabbath, and that we should circumcise not the foreskin but the heart. Hence, working for six days, we rest on the seventh day, so that day and night we may do nothing else than recognize that all that we live is owed to the Lord, and, as the week comes round again, consecrate ourselves wholly to his name, so that through the sanctification of the day we may remember the Lord who sanctifies us. These precepts and ordinances and the observance of the sabbath the Lord gave in the desert, so that doing them they might live in them, not that they should pass from them to greater things, as is promised in the Gospel; and these they violated, not once nor a little but exceedingly, so that the ἐπίτασις [intensification] of the violation might be shown. He said, therefore, and decreed in his mind, that he would pour out his fury upon them in the desert and consume them, when he spoke to Moses: Let me alone, and, angered with fury against them, I will destroy them; but he would not do it, sparing the Egyptians and the other nations, lest they be scandalized, and them as well, on whom he had mercy, awaiting the repentance of those who would turn back. And it is to be noted that, when he was speaking to them while they were settled in Egypt, after the offense: I acted, he says, for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations, but now he says: I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out in their sight; for then they were still in their midst, not yet having gone out, but now, after they have gone out, it is said: From which I cast them out in their sight.

20:15-17

I therefore lifted up my hand over them into the desert, not to bring them into the land which I gave them, flowing with milk and honey, the foremost of all lands; because they cast away my judgments, and did not walk in my precepts, and violated my sabbaths, for their heart went after idols. And my eye spared them, so that I did not kill them; nor did I consume them in the desert. (LXX: "And I lifted up my hand over them in the desert, so as not at all to bring them into the land which I gave them, a land flowing with milk and honey, it is a honeycomb beyond every land; because they rejected my ordinances, and did not walk in my precepts, and violated my sabbaths, and they walk after the thoughts of their hearts. And my eye spared them, so that I did not wipe them out; and I did not kill them to consumption in the desert.") 'I had indeed decreed to pour out all my fury upon them and to wipe them out and consume them, but I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned among the nations — namely the Amalekites and the rest, which fought against them in the wilderness —, so that I would by no means bring them into the land which I promised them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the foremost of all lands — or a honeycomb —'. The cause of the punishment and of this sentence is: Because they cast away my judgments, and did not walk in my precepts, and violated the sabbaths; and the cause of that cause is this: that they did not do these things because their heart followed the idols of Egypt. 'But my eye', he says, 'spared them, so that I did not kill them and wipe them out: so that I did not consume them altogether'; in which it is asked how he spared those whose corpses lay in the wilderness and, except for Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, no one entered the land of promise. From this we understand that they live, and are not reserved for eternal punishments, nor blotted out of the book of the living, nor consumed before the face of the Lord; for if, because they were not brought into the land of promise, they must be believed to have perished, then Moses too perished, who only saw the land of promise and did not enter it, of whom the Lord speaks in the book of Joshua: Moses my servant is dead, and in Malachi: Remember the law of Moses my servant, and in Jeremiah God speaks of him as of his friend and most intimate: If Moses and Samuel should stand in my sight? Otherwise we must also believe that the prayers of Moses were heard, when, interceding for the people, he says: If you forgive them their sin, forgive; but if you will not, blot me too out of your book. And that the sentence of the Lord against sons and servants is not perdition but correction, let us hear the testimonies of the Scriptures: Son, do not be saddened at the discipline of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked by him: for whom the Lord loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives, and in another place: When he slew them, then they sought him, and in the song of Deuteronomy: I will kill and I will make alive. We can also say this according to the letter: that he did not wipe them out nor consume them along with their stock and offspring, but, when the fathers had been killed, he spared the sons, whom he brought into the land of promise.

20:18-20

But he said to their sons in the wilderness: In the precepts (or statutes) of your fathers do not walk, and neither with their idols nor keep their judgments (or be defiled by thoughts). I am the Lord your God: walk in my precepts, and keep my judgments and do them, and sanctify my sabbaths, that it may be a sign between me and you, and that it may be known (or that you may know) that I am the Lord your God. After the slaying of the fathers who fell in the wilderness, he gives precepts to the sons, in whose salvation he had mercy on the fathers: 'And the eye of the Lord', he says, 'spared them, so as not to kill them altogether and wipe them out, but to preserve the fathers in the sons'; and he testifies to them the same things that he also spoke to the fathers: that, after they have walked in his precepts and kept his judgments and observed the sanctification of the sabbath, which was given as a sign, they may then know that he is the Lord their God. By the precepts and statutes of the fathers and their judgments he signifies ingrained error, so that they may not imitate the sins of those whose torments they behold.

20:21-22

And the sons exasperated me; they did not walk in my precepts, and did not keep my judgments to do them, which, when a man has done them, he shall live in them, and they violated my sabbaths; and I threatened to pour out my fury upon them, and to fulfill my wrath on them in the desert. But I turned back my hand and acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out in their eyes. 'But the sons too', he says, 'followed the crimes of their parents and did all that those had done; hence they too deserved a like sentence; but they were preserved by the same greatness of my mercy as their fathers too, and for the same reasons for which I also had mercy on the fathers, so that I, the one and the same Creator of both, might soften my wrath with a like patience'. We run through the plain things so as to pass on to the more obscure.

20:23-26

Again I lifted up my hand against them in the wilderness, to scatter them among the nations and winnow them into the lands, because they had not done my judgments, and had rejected my precepts, and had violated my sabbaths, and their eyes had been after the idols (or thoughts) of their fathers. Therefore I too gave them precepts not good, and judgments in which they shall not live; and I defiled them in their gifts, when they offered (or made pass over) everything that opens the womb, for their transgressions (for which the Seventy translated that I might destroy them. And what they passed over:), and they shall know that I am the Lord. Where in the Old Testament the Lord lifted up his hand against the sons of those who fell in the wilderness, wishing to scatter them among the nations, Scripture does not say, but from what he relates here we must believe that it happened; or else this signifies that, after they had entered the land of promise, at various times on account of many sins they were handed over to diverse nations and kings, and at that time the precepts of the Lord and the judgments, which were good by their nature and in which believers could live, were made not good for them, since in captivity they were by no means able to keep the precepts of the law and do what the divine word commanded; nor did he say: I gave them 'evil' precepts, but 'not good' — for it does not at once follow that what is not good is evil, as the Apostle too teaches: that it is good for a man not to touch a wife or a woman, but, because of incontinence, for each one to possess his own vessel in sanctification and chastity; and if he does this, it is neither good nor evil —; so God gave them, scattered among the nations, precepts not good — that is, he gave them up to their own thoughts and desires —, so that they did what is not fitting; and he defiled them in their gifts, like a priest separating the lepers from the people and declaring them to be defiled, while they offer to idols what they ought to offer to God; and they make everything that opens the womb, that is, the firstborn, pass through the fire to Baal, so that, after they have been abandoned by God and handed over to the worship of idols, they may then understand that he is the Lord whom by their own fault they roused to anger. Symmachus translated this passage more plainly, putting the future for the past: Therefore I too will give them precepts not good, and judgments on account of which they shall not live, and I will defile them on account of their gifts; because they consecrate and make pass over what opens the womb, that I may destroy them, and they may know that I am the Lord; and the sense is: 'Because I saw that the sons were equaling the crimes of their fathers and doing the same things for which those had offended God, I wished to divide them among the nations, and scatter them through the whole world, and give them precepts not good, and judgments in which they would not live, so as to defile them in their gifts, because they were consecrating all the firstborn to idols, and to destroy them forever, and that they might know that I am the Lord'. He shows that he did not give the precepts not good to those who were staying in the desert, but that to those whom he wished to scatter among the nations and make strangers throughout the whole world he had thought of giving what he did not give, so that there, by their own fault, they would make the good precepts of God not good, while they present to idols what God had commanded to be presented to himself. This too can be said: that before the offense they received only the Decalogue, but after the idolatry and blasphemy the manifold ceremonies of the law, so that they would rather offer to God the victims which they were offering to demons, and, by comparison with sacrilege, what was not good in itself would become lighter: by no means evil, because they were offered to God, and yet not good, because they had offended the author of good.

20:27-29

Wherefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Still in this too your fathers blasphemed me, when they had spurned me with contempt, and I had brought them into the land over which I lifted up my hand to give it to them; they saw every high hill and every leafy tree, and they sacrificed their victims there, and there they gave the provocation of their offering, and there they set their odor of sweetness and poured out their libations. And I said to them: What is the high place to which you go in? And its name was called 'high place' to this day. (LXX: "Therefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and you shall say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Even to this your fathers provoked me to anger in their transgressions by which they fell away against me, and I brought them into the land over which I lifted up my hand to hand it over to them; and they saw every high hill and every leafy tree, and they sacrificed there to their gods and set the fury of their gifts, and set there the odor of their fragrance, and poured out there their libations. And I said to them: What is ἀβανὰ [abana, a transliteration], that you go in there? And they called its name ἀβανὰ to this present day.") 'I wished', he says, 'to scatter them among all the nations when they sinned in the wilderness and to give them precepts not good, so that they would sacrifice to idols what they ought to have offered to me, and consecrate to them all their firstborn through fire, so that I might kill them and wipe them out'. — When he says 'I wished', he shows that he did not do what he wished. And what follows: They shall know that I am the Lord, is not found in the Seventy; for it did not seem to them consistent that after the slaying they should know that he is the Lord —. 'But you, son of man, speak again to them, that is, to the elders of the house of Israel who came to inquire of you: Your fathers, from whose stock you are descended, blasphemed me in this too and held me for nothing: after I had brought them into the land, which they possessed by my strength, which I had given them to possess, they turned it to provoking me; for when they had seen every high hill and leafy tree, they sacrificed on the mountains and in the groves and in the woodlands, and sacrificed victims to idols, and poured out offerings; and when I saw this, I said to them: What is 'bama' — for this means 'high place' —, or why do you go into such a place, which you have chosen for yourselves on all the hills, so that to this day places of this kind are called 'bamoth' and the ancient error keeps its former name?'. For 'bama', which we rendered as 'high place', an error has prevailed in the edition of the Seventy, so that ἀβανὰ is written, which means nothing in the Hebrew language; 'bama', if you divide its two syllables into two words, can mean 'in what', but that sense does not fit the present passage; but wherever it is written in the books of Kings and Chronicles: Still the people burned incense and sacrificed on the high place, 'bama' in the singular and 'bamoth' in the plural mean 'high places'.

20:30-31

Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: You are defiled in the way of your fathers, and you commit fornication after their stumbling-blocks, and in the offering of your gifts, when you make your sons pass through the fire, you are defiled with all your idols to this day; and shall I answer you, house of Israel? As I live, says the Lord God, I will not answer you. 'You imitate the vices of your fathers and walk by the same ways, so that like offenses deserve a like punishment too; and you have advanced so far in crimes that you consecrate your sons to demons through fire, nor is it enough to have done this once, but even at present you do the same things; not that the elders in captivity do these things, but that those who were staying in Jerusalem and over whom captivity was hanging do not cease to do all these things. And when you are bound by such great outrages, do you seek', he says, 'my answer? As I live, says the Lord, and I swear by my own self, I will not answer you'. And what follows:

20:32-33

Nor shall the thought of your mind come to pass, of you who say: We will be like the nations and like the families of the earth, to worship wood and stones. As I live, says the Lord God, with a strong hand and with an outstretched arm and with fury poured out I will reign over you, has this sense: 'Do not think that your thoughts, by which you blaspheme against me, can be fulfilled; for you say: We do not wish to be under the Lord nor to be called his people, but, as all the nations in the whole world are, and each people lives by its own will, so as to worship wood and stones and serve idols, we too will be one nation out of many'. To which God replies, and swears by himself, and says: 'I will not leave you nor despise you, as negligent masters are accustomed to despise runaway slaves, but I will drag you back to my rule, and with arm outstretched and striking I will reduce you to your former servitude and reign over you, so that, whether you will or not, you may have me as king, and may feel as an angry king him whose clemency you neglected'.

20:34

And I will lead you out from the peoples, and gather you from the lands in which you are scattered; with a mighty hand, and an outstretched arm, and with fury poured out I will reign over you. 'I will not suffer you', he says, 'to be among the nations nor to be held in eternal captivity, but I will lead you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands into which hostile necessity has scattered you here and there to be slaves; and I will do these things not to destroy you and wipe you out, but to be your king'. From this we understand that even what the heretics call the cruelty of the Creator sounds of clemency, since he is angry and rages and pours out all his fury for this purpose: to draw back to his kingdom those who had chosen the tyranny of demons, and that to be its slaves.

20:35-38

And I will bring you into the desert of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face. As I contended in judgment against your fathers in the desert of the land of Egypt, so will I judge you, says the Lord, and I will subject you to my scepter, and bring you into the bonds of the covenant. And I will pick out from you the transgressors and the ungodly, and I will lead them out of the land of their sojourning, and they shall not enter the land of Israel, and you shall know that I am the Lord. 'I will do', he says, 'to you who are in Babylon and now serve idols what I did to your fathers in Egypt: I will lead you out into the desert of the peoples and there enter into judgment with you face to face, as I contended in judgment against them when they went out of Egypt; and after I have judged you, I will subject you to my scepter and rule, and enter into a covenant with you, and bring you into your land in the bonds of love, so that, bound by my love, you may by no means be able to depart from me. But the transgressors and the ungodly, who in hardness of heart persevere in evil works, I will pick out from you, not to possess them but to cast them away; and I will indeed lead them out of the land of their sojourning, so that, once led out, they may not enter the land of Israel but perish in diverse regions, and that, by the distinction of the good and the evil, you may know that I am the Lord who do all things with judgment'. The discourse hastens on to what remains, and we run briefly through each point, so as to offer readers only the sense.

20:39

And you, house of Israel, thus says the Lord God: Walk each of you after your idols, and serve them. But if in this too you do not listen to me, and pollute my holy name any more with your gifts and with your idols. (LXX: "And you, house of Israel, thus says Adonai the Lord: Let each one take away his inventions; and after this, if you listen to me, and do not pollute my holy name any more with your gifts and with your pursuits.") Symmachus translated this passage more plainly: Each of you, go and serve your idols, since you would not listen to me. But my holy name do not pollute any more through your gifts and images. But on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there all the house of Israel shall serve me. Symmachus' translation has this meaning: 'Since you do not wish to serve me, go, serve idols and tread in the footsteps of your images; for you do not wish to listen to me: by no means sacrifice victims to me, nor burn incense, nor be called my people — for my worshipers will by no means serve me in groves and shrines and the places of idols, as you do, but on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel —'. The Seventy, for their part, unfold a sense of their own: 'Abandon your former thoughts, and take away the evil sins of your inventions; and if after this you listen to me and do not pollute my name with your gifts and images, then on my holy mountain you shall offer me victims and serve me, all the house of Israel'. Aquila, however, agreeing in part with Symmachus, disagrees in part: Go, he says, after your idols and serve them, since you are unworthy of my rule, nor does your worship delight me; but if in this too you by no means listen to me, but pollute my holy name, while you pretend to offer to me what you offer to idols, and do such blasphemy to my name that, being worshipers of idols, you say that you are mine, know this: that on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, there all the house of Israel shall serve me, not you who serve idols, but all the house of Israel which is afterward to believe.

20:40-42a

On my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there all the house of Israel shall serve me: all, I say, in the land in which they shall please me; and there I will require your firstfruits and the beginning of your tithes in all your sanctifications. In an odor of sweetness I will receive you, when I have led you out from the peoples and gathered you from the lands into which you were scattered, and I shall be sanctified in you in the eyes of the nations. And you shall know that I am the Lord. Of this mountain, on which all the house of Israel is to serve God, Isaiah and Micah sang with one voice: In the last days the mountain of the house shall be manifest on the summit of the mountains and shall be raised above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways and we will walk in his paths; for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and again Isaiah: Go up onto a high mountain, he says, you who proclaim to Zion; lift up and exalt your voice, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem. This mountain, Zion, we understand either as the Church, which means 'watchtower' and is set on the height of holy doctrines, or as the Lord Savior himself, in whom the firstfruits and the tithes and all worship are turned into an odor of sweetness, so that all the nations round about, seeing that the people of the Lord has been saved, may glorify God, and those who have been saved may know that he is the Lord.

20:42b

When I bring you into the land of Israel, into the land for which I lifted up my hand to give it to your fathers. 'Then you shall know that I am the Lord, when I bring you', he says, 'into the land of Israel, for which I lifted up my hand to bring your fathers into it, which they lost by their own fault and which you have received back not so much by your own merit as by my clemency'.

20:43-44

And you shall remember your ways and all your crimes, with which you were defiled in them; and you shall be displeasing to yourselves in your own sight in all your wickednesses which you have done. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways nor according to your most wicked crimes, house of Israel, says the Lord God. We cannot remember our crimes and vices unless we have been brought into the land of Israel and, set there, say with the Apostle: I who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. And you shall be displeasing, he says, to yourselves in your own sight in all your wickednesses which you have done (or, as Symmachus translated: And you shall seem little to yourselves because of all your wickednesses which you have wrought), so that, after they have been exalted, they may believe themselves to be lowly, because: The Lord gives grace to the humble, and in another place it is written: Before crushing the heart of a man is exalted, and before height it is humbled: for crushing follows pride, and exaltation follows humility. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you: and we came to know the Lord Savior the more at that time when he did good to us and suffered for our sins and bore our iniquities and grieved for us, not for any merit of those who are saved but for his name's sake; otherwise our ways and most wicked crimes deserved not mercy but punishment. But whatever we have said of the people of Israel, which, freed from Egypt, committed many things in the wilderness and offended God, and afterward, brought into the land of promise, venerated idols and worshiped wood and stones, and afterward was preserved by the clemency of God, let us refer to those who have been freed from the Egypt of this world by the high hand of the Lord and, brought into the wilderness of vices, sighed again for Egypt and did the things for which they ought to have been punished, but nonetheless, through repentance, not by their own merit but by the clemency of the Lord, have been preserved.

Book Seven

Long ago, as boys, we read: Nothing is so easy that it does not become difficult when you do it unwillingly. I confess that I promised an explanation of Ezekiel a long time ago, and that I have not been able to fulfill it because of my being occupied with those who come here from the whole world, since there is no hour and no moment in which we do not meet crowds of brothers, and we exchange the solitude of the monastery for a throng of guests, so much so that either we must shut the door, or abandon the study of the Scriptures, through which the doors are to be opened. And so it is that, by the gainful, or rather stolen, labors of the nights, which with winter approaching have begun to be longer, we try to dictate these things, such as they are, by a little lamp, and to work off the weariness of a seething mind by interpretation. Nor do we boast, as some perhaps suspect, of our receiving the brothers, but we simply confess the causes of our delays, especially since the flight of the westerners and the crowding of the holy places display, in the nakedness and wounds of the needy, the fury of the barbarians; and we cannot see them without tears and groaning: that that once-great power and ignorance of riches should have come to such want that it lacks roof and food and clothing! And yet the hard and cruel hearts of some are by no means softened, while they shake out their rags and little bundles, seeking gold in captivity. To this difficulty of dictating is added the fact that, since our eyes are dimmed with old age and suffer something of what blessed Isaac suffered, we are by no means able by the light of night to reread the volumes of the Hebrews, which even in the brightness of the sun and of the day are blinded to us by the smallness of the letters. Moreover, the commentaries of the Greeks too we know only through the voice of the brothers; and no one doubts that food ground by another's teeth causes nausea in those who eat it. Therefore I beseech you, daughter Eustochium, to receive after intervals these things which we hammer out with the stylus of secretaries and for the correcting of which we scarcely have time, that is, the seventh book on Ezekiel; and, as I have already said before, if the brevity or the length of the books should be unequal among themselves, to impute it to the brevity and length of the visions, or rather of the ὑποθέσεων [subjects, themes], since we neither wish to separate what is joined nor to compress what is discordant into one heap.

20:45-49

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against the way of the south, and drip toward the southwest, and prophesy to the forest of the southern field. And you shall say to the southern forest: Hear the word of the Lord: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and I will burn up in you all green wood and all dry wood; the flame of the kindling shall not be extinguished, and every face shall be burned in it from the south to the north: and all flesh shall see that I the Lord have kindled it, and it shall not be extinguished. And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God; they say of me: Does not this man speak in parables? (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make firm your face upon Theman, and look toward Darom, prophesy upon the forest, the leader Nageb. And you shall say to the forest Nageb: Hear the speech of the Lord: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour in you all green wood and all dry wood; the kindled flame shall not be extinguished, and every face shall burn in it from the midday to the north: and all flesh shall know that I the Lord have kindled it; it shall not be extinguished.
