And put into it the divisions, every good cut, the leg and the shoulder, taken from choice cattle, with the flesh separated from the bones; and burn the bones beneath them. It has boiled, it has boiled, and its bones have been boiled out in the midst of it. Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: O city of bloods, cauldron in which there is rust in it, and the rust has not gone out of it. By its parts it has brought it out; the lot has not fallen upon it, because its blood is in the midst of it; upon a most smooth rock I have set it; I did not pour it out upon the ground, so that it should be covered with earth: that fury might go up to the avenging of vengeance, I have set her blood upon the most clear rock, so that it should not be covered. Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Woe to the city of bloods, and I will make the firebrand great and I will multiply the wood and I will kindle the fire, that the flesh may waste away and the broth be diminished, and the bones be burned up and it stand upon its coals. It has been kindled that it may be burned out, and its bronze be roasted, and its uncleanness be burned up in its midst, and its rust fail. The rust shall be humbled, and its abundant rust shall not go out of it; its rust shall be put to confusion. Your uncleanness is 'zemma', because you were defiled, and you have not been cleansed of your uncleanness. And what will it be if you are not cleansed any more, until I fulfil my fury upon you? I the Lord have spoken; and it will come, and I will do it: I will not delay, nor have mercy, nor be entreated. According to your ways and according to your devices I will judge you, says Adonai the Lord." — Most of these were added from Theodotion, and so was the Hebrew word 'zemma', for which we translated 'execrable uncleanness'; and this too was added by them, which is not found in the Hebrew and must be marked beforehand with an obelus: ÷ Therefore I judge you according to your blood, and according to your thoughts I will judge you, unclean and notorious and excessive in provoking. ⁚) Let us speak, then, about each point. In the ninth year of the captivity of King Jehoiakim — for he began to prophesy in the fifth —, and in the tenth month of the same ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month, the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel the prophet, who was placed in the regions of Babylon, and said to him: 'Son of man, write down for yourself this same day, and know that today the king of Babylon has begun, in the region of Judea, to besiege Jerusalem and to wall it in with an army; and describe the siege itself by a parable and a proverb — which in the present place signifies a metaphor and transference — : Set on,' he says, 'a bronze pot, that is, a cauldron, and put water into it, and cut into pieces the whole body of the fattest animals, the thigh as well as the leg and the shoulder, and carefully separate the flesh from the bones and, once the flesh has been put into the cauldron, set, or arrange, the bones beneath the cauldron, and make piles and heaps of bones, so that the cooking of the cauldron may boil up not once but again and again, and the flesh may be boiled through within, and the bones beneath may be burned up by the fire. But do you wish, prophet, to know what this cauldron is, or what the flesh or the bones are? Speak these things, says the Lord: Woe to the city of bloods, that is, Jerusalem, to the cauldron whose rust, that is, malice, is excessive, and although fire has been put beneath it, yet its rust has not gone out of it; for even when captured and tortured they persevered in their former crime. Consume it part by part and one by one, so that no one remains to be saved. The lot has not fallen upon it, so that some should perish and others be saved, but a common destruction has come upon all; for its blood, that is, its murders and the slaughter of sons, is in the midst of it. This blood she poured out upon the most clear rock, so that it would be visible to all and not be covered with earth or with dust, so, namely, that my indignation might not pass by, but vengeance might hasten upon blood lying wholly in the open — for it is the way of nature that, if blood is poured out on the earth, the soil drinks up the moisture of the blood, or it is gradually covered with earth and dust; but when blood has been poured out upon a most clear rock which has no hollow, it slides and spreads over a wide space. And this indicates that she committed murders not hidden but public, according to what is said to Cain: The blood of your brother cries to me —. Therefore say to the city of blood — of bloods not of one but of many —: Behold, I will make a great pyre in you, or I will bring a firebrand, which the common people call a titio [the everyday word for a firebrand], and I will set alight in you not only the soft and tender flesh but the hardest bones as well, and nothing shall remain in you that is not burned up by the fire. And when both the flesh and the bones have been consumed and burned, set the empty cauldron itself upon the live coals, so that its bronze too may melt and be consumed and, the bronze being consumed, its rust too may perish; that is, when the city has been burned up by the fire, its malice may perish utterly with the city. But what does it profit to have done what was commanded? Not even by fire could the rust and malice of the cauldron and of the city be taken away, and there remains in it a wicked and execrable uncleanness — for this is what 'zemma' signifies. And he makes an apostrophe to the cauldron itself, that is, to the city itself — : I wished to cleanse you, and you were not cleansed of your filth, nor will you be able to be cleansed any more until I fulfil my indignation upon you. I the Lord have spoken, and my sentence cannot pass away. The siege of the city has already come; I will do what I have threatened, and I will not pass over — as I have often done — your crimes, and I will spare no longer, nor will I be appeased toward you even if you multiply your prayers, but I will repay you your ways and your devices; indeed, I will judge you according to your works and your thoughts, so that in this too I may show my clemency' — like a physician who does not spare rotten flesh, so that the healthy limbs may be saved: he does not spare in order to spare, he is cruel in order to have mercy, and he considers not the pain of the patient but the healing of the wound, according to that saying of the Gospel, preferring that one member should perish rather than that the whole body be killed —. It must also be noted how, from the beginning of the prophecy up to the present day when Jerusalem began to be besieged, the captivity comes in order. First the sword is called forth; then two ways are set out, Ammon and Jerusalem, and of these the lot falls for Nebuchadnezzar on the right-hand one; silver, bronze, tin, lead and iron are melted together in the city; the land too is not rained upon, but is overgrown with briers; afterwards, under the name of the two sisters Oholah and Oholibah, the sins of Samaria and Jerusalem are narrated, how the one has been captured and the other is to be captured; finally, in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, it is shown to Ezekiel, placed in captivity, and to those who were with him and had surrendered themselves with King Jeconiah, on what day the city began to be besieged, and the likeness of the cauldron is set forth so that, just as the flesh and the bones, heaped into the cauldron, are burned up by the fire, so the whole city is to perish together with its citizens, and none of those who were besieged is to remain without being consumed by famine, sword, pestilence, and the remaining part is to be led captive into Babylon. This same prophecy, however, can also pertain to the time of the Lord's passion, on account of which Jerusalem was surrounded by an army and her sons were slain and, when Titus the son of Vespasian besieged it, no one escaped to safety, and the temple suddenly, and, after fifty years, under Hadrian, the city was consumed by an everlasting fire. As for the present captivity, when Ezekiel was beholding these things in Babylon, and which Jeremiah sets at the beginning of his volume: What do you see, Jeremiah? And answering he said: A pot set alight, and its face from the face of the north, there are those who, according to tropology, transfer this whole passage to the consummation of the world, and who temper the ninth number, which in the holy Scriptures is the number of punishments and sorrows and always follows righteousness, by the clemency of the tenth month and the tenth day. For punishments are applied to the sick for this reason: that health may follow pain. The world, therefore, which is set in the evil one, is set alight by divine fire on the day of judgment; and the city of bloods is set upon coals of fire, so that what is written in Isaiah may be fulfilled: You have coals of fire, sit upon them: these will be a help to you. And this is difficult: how, when the coals and the bones are consumed — the bones of which even the Pharisees are full, to whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who are like whitewashed tombs, which within are full of filth and of the bones of the dead —, it is now said that the rust and filth of the world have not been consumed, but that even after the severity of judgment malice remains; this is easily resolved if we understand that saying of the Apostle: God has shut up all things under sin, that he may have mercy on all; for the creation was subjected to vanity. And the blood that has been poured out is set in the open sight of the whole creation, so that the crimes of all may be laid bare. But we can also take the most clear rock to be the Lord Savior, the rock which followed the people of Israel into the wilderness, of which it is written: They drank, moreover, from the rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ, because in him all things are revealed and what is written is fulfilled: Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed. And the Lord says that he will not have mercy, nor pass over the sins of the world, nor spare the impious nor be appeased, so that the ways of the impious may perish, according to what is set at the end of the first psalm: And the way of the impious will perish.

24:15-27

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, behold, I am taking from you the desirable thing of your eyes with a stroke, and you shall not mourn nor weep, nor shall your tears flow. Groan in silence; you shall not make the mourning for the dead; let your crown be bound about you, and your shoes shall be on your feet, and you shall not veil your face with a mantle, nor eat the food of mourners. So I spoke to the people in the morning, and my wife died in the evening; and in the morning I did as he had commanded me. And the people said to me: Why do you not show us what these things mean that you are doing? And I said to them: The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Speak to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your dominion and the desirable thing of your eyes, and that over which your soul trembles. And your sons and daughters, whom you have left behind, shall fall by the sword. And you shall do as I have done: you shall not veil your faces with a mantle, and you shall not eat the food of mourners; you shall have crowns on your heads and shoes on your feet; you shall not mourn nor weep, but you shall waste away in your iniquities, and each shall groan to his brother. And Ezekiel shall be a portent to you: according to all that he has done you shall do, when this comes, and you shall know that I am the Lord God. And you, son of man, behold, on the day when I take from them their strength, and the joy of their dignity, and the desire of their eyes, on which their souls rest, their sons and their daughters; on that day, when one fleeing comes to you to announce it to you, on that day, I say, your mouth shall be opened with him who fled; and you shall speak and be silent no longer, and you shall be a portent to them, and you shall know that I am the Lord. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, behold, I will take away from you the desirable things of your eyes in battle array (or in preparation); you shall not mourn nor weep, nor shall tears come to you. The groaning of the blood of the reins is mourning; your hair shall be bound up upon you and your shoes on your feet, nor shall you be comforted by their lips, and you shall not eat the bread of men. And I spoke to the people in the morning as he had commanded me, and my wife died in the evening; and in the morning I did as it was commanded me. And the people said to me: Will you not announce to us what these things are that you are doing? And I said to them: The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say to the house of Israel: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I will defile my holy things, the pride of your strength, the desirable thing of your eyes, and the things which your souls spare. Your sons and your daughters, whom you have left behind, shall fall by the sword. And you shall do as I have done: you shall not be comforted by their mouth, and you shall not eat the bread of men, and your locks shall be upon your heads and your shoes on your feet; you shall not mourn nor weep, and you shall be consumed in your iniquities, and each shall comfort his brother. And Ezekiel shall be a portent to you: according to all that I have done you shall do, and when these things come, you shall know that I am Adonai the Lord. And you, son of man, will it not be on the day when I take away from them their strength, the exaltation of their glorying, the desirable things of their eyes, and the elation of their soul, their sons and their daughters; on that day he who has been saved will come to you, to announce it in your ears? On that day your mouth shall be opened to him who has fled; and you shall speak, and by no means be silent any longer, and you shall be a portent to them, and they shall know that I am the Lord.") Above, by the kindling of the pot and the cauldron, he had shown the siege of the city; now the prophetic word testifies that it has been captured and destroyed, and that the whole people has been either slain by the sword or led into captivity. And first, according to our custom, let us lay the foundations of the history. 'Son of man,' he says, 'behold, I will take away from the sight of your eyes whatever is desirable to you, and I will take it away 'with a stroke' — or, as the Seventy rendered, 'in preparation' —, so that, namely, you may prepare yourself not to do the things that are customarily done in mourning. You shall not mourn nor weep, nor shall flowing tears show the grief of your heart, but if perhaps you are overcome by excessive sorrow, keep your groaning silent, such as does not burst out into words'. You shall not make the mourning for the dead (or, as the Seventy rendered: The groaning of the blood of the reins is mourning): by this he shows that his wife is going to die; for there follows immediately: And my wife died in the evening, which properly pertains to the union of the reins: nothing is more lovable to a man than a good wife, who is provided for a man by God, and to whom he is joined by the law of the Lord, and with whom he becomes one body. And what follows: Let your crown be bound about you, and your shoes shall be on your feet, signifies this: 'You shall have the hair which is shorn in mourning, and on your feet the shoes which mourners are accustomed to cast off' — whence David too, fleeing from his son Absalom and repenting over the murder of Uriah, walks with bare feet —. The Hebrews say: up to this day the Babylonian teachers, keeping the precepts of the law, bind the Decalogue, written on little parchments, around their heads, and these are the things that are commanded to hang before the eyes and on the forehead, so that they may always see what has been commanded; and because Ezekiel was a priest, he ought by no means to lay aside the crown of glorying, but to have it bound on his head. This is what they said. But let us, following the Seventy, understand by 'crown' the head of hair, although their translation too has by no means expressed the force of the Hebrew word. Nor shall you veil your face, he says, with a mantle, nor take the food of mourners: things which are customarily done in mourning, that people cover the face and receive from those who console them what the Greeks call περίδειπνα [funeral meals]. 'I spoke,' he says, 'to the people the things the Lord had commanded me, and in the evening my wife died, the desirable thing of my eyes and the mourning of the loins and of the blood. And immediately, on the next day, in the morning, I did all the things that had been commanded me; and the people asked me why I had acted against the custom of all; and to those seeking the reasons for such great endurance I replied: The word of the Lord which came to me, that I should speak to the people of Israel, commanded these things: Behold, I (that is: now already) will profane my sanctuary, so that the temple may be burned and lie open to all foreigners and profane persons, the temple in which you had your pride, that is, your confidence and hope and the desire of your salvation, and at whose siege your souls were in dread; your sons too and your daughters, whom famine and pestilence had left remaining to you, I will consume with the sword, so that whatever I have done, you too may do'. When custom is observed in mourning, the grief is moderate; but when so great a necessity of evils presses upon men that it is greater than all lamentation, each one, anxious about his own death, does not groan over the miseries of others, even though they are his nearest. 'You shall do nothing,' he says, 'of what is customarily done in mourning, but, when the city and the temple have been set on fire, you will be stunned at the magnitude of the evils; you will not cut your hair nor walk with bare feet, you will not mourn nor veil your faces with a mantle nor receive food from those who console you, but you will waste away, and you will be consumed in your iniquities, and you will scarcely have free groaning, lest you offend the pride of the victors if you are seen to weep publicly; so that Ezekiel the prophet may be a portent to you, and all that he did not do at the death of his wife, you may not do at the overthrow of the city and the temple'. And yet more plainly: 'O son of man,' he says, 'at the time when I take away from them their strength — the confidence of the temple, as we have said —, and the joy of dignity and that in which they had their only hope, and the desire in which their souls rested, and besides their sons and their daughters — understood from the above: — I take away, at that time,' he says, 'when one fleeing from Jerusalem, or one who has escaped, comes to you, saying that the city has been overthrown, then you, who before had been silent and had no free groaning, and were of such great endurance that at the death of your wife and in the pain of your loins you did not shed a tear, will open your mouth and speak, not to him who has come but with him, so that whatever you had foretold was to come, he may announce as now accomplished; and you will no longer be silent, but you will rebuke them and say that all these things have befallen them deservedly, so that you may be a portent to them', according to what is written in Zechariah, that the prophets are men who portend, and the Lord says elsewhere: In the hands of the prophets I have been likened. Let this be said according to the history. Let us come to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], if only it does not seem forced to the prudence of a cautious reader. No one doubts that the son of man is said to be the Lord Savior, who at the last hour, that is, at the evening of this world, lost his former wife, and did not weep for her nor veil his face with a mantle nor receive any consolation from men, and who foretold in the morning the things to come which were fulfilled in the evening, and again in the morning, at his second coming, proved accomplished what he had foretold was to come: that the sanctuary of the Jews, and what they had held desirable in their eyes and that over which their souls trembled, had been profaned, and that their sons too and their daughters had fallen by the Roman sword. But what is said: You shall have a crown on your heads, and shoes shall be on your feet, we shall refer to this part: that they ought by no means to mourn nor to take up the signs of mourning, after they have received the truth in place of the shadow and certain of them have become Nazirites, and each one will be comforted over his brother, so that Ezekiel, whom God the Father strengthened, may be a portent to them, foretelling things to come; and that, after Jerusalem has been overthrown and the temple burned, and the whole world has heard this, and the dispersion of Israel, which inhabits the ends of the earth, then the words of the Lord, fulfilled in deed, may have freedom, and, his sanctuary having been profaned and the law fulfilled or destroyed according to the letter that kills, the glory of the Gospel may be laid open, and Israel may know that he himself is Lord and God, who foretold in the morning that these things would come, and proved by his coming that they were fulfilled in the evening and at the consummation of the world.

Book Eight

What profit our dictation on the prophets may bring to others is a matter for the judgment of God, and for the conscience of those who, setting aside declamations and applause and the arrangement of words, desire to know what the prophets' speech either narrates as past, or rebukes as present, or foretells as yet to come. For ourselves, meanwhile, it is first of all a profit; for while we do this and think of nothing else, we take up our explanations as if by stealth, and make up for the miseries of the days by study through the nights; the mind is fed and forgets the calamities of the world, which, set now at its very end, groans and travails, until he who restrains is taken out of the way, and the feet of the statue, once of iron, are broken through the fragility of the toes of clay. The world is falling, and the stiff neck does not bend; riches perish, and avarice by no means ceases; men hasten to gather what will in turn be seized by others; tears have dried up, all compassion has been taken away; many are those who ask, few those who give. Nor do we blush, while we display our poverty in a cheap little cloak, to brood over the wealth of Croesus, and to guard in our treasuries the hunger and death of very many, after the manner of that rich man clothed in purple, who, granting that he did nothing else (for Scripture does not attest his robberies and iniquities), yet his cruelty and pride have no measure: to Lazarus, lying before his doors and half-dead, he did not order even those things to be given which are thrown to the dogs. How many Lazaruses lie now, and how many men's purple robes are kept covered under garments of various colors, men who do not turn even to their own use the things they keep only to perish! Let these words, Eustochium, virgin of Christ, be what the mouth has spoken out of the abundance of the heart, and let us have said them a little more freely than befits our lowliness. But the eighth book on Ezekiel, which contains the rebuke of the Ammonites and of the other nations and the prophecy of things to come, will have this beginning.

25:1-7

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set (or make firm) your face against the Ammonites and you shall prophesy concerning them, and you shall say to the Ammonites: Hear the word of the Lord God. Thus says the Lord God: Because you said: Well done, well done, over my sanctuary (or because you rejoiced over my sanctuary) because it was profaned, and over the land of Israel because it was made desolate, and over the house of Judah because they were led into captivity, therefore I will hand you over to the sons of the east (or Cedem) as an inheritance; they shall set up their sheepfolds in you, and they shall pitch their tents in you; they themselves shall eat your fruits, and they themselves shall drink milk (or your richness). And I will make Rabbath a dwelling for camels (or the city of Ammon pastures for camels), and the Ammonites a lair for cattle, and you shall know that I am the Lord. For thus says the Lord God: Because you clapped with the hand, and struck (or stamped) with the foot, and rejoiced with all your feeling (or mocked from your soul) over the land of Israel, therefore behold, I will stretch out my hand over you, and I will hand you over for plunder to the nations, and I will slay you from among the peoples, and destroy from the lands, and crush, and you shall know that I am the Lord. When Jerusalem had been taken or besieged, after the one who had been able to escape came to Babylon and announced that the city was at any moment to be taken, or had been overthrown together with the temple, the prophetic discourse, according to the custom of all the prophets, turns against the other nations round about, which had mocked at the ruin of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple; and first against the Ammonites, who had a capital named Rabbath, which today is called Philadelphia after the king of Egypt Ptolemy, surnamed Philadelphus, who held Arabia together with Judea: 'Son' he says 'of man, set (or make firm) your face against the Ammonites, who were begotten of the stock of Lot, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God — for these are not the words of the prophet but of the Lord. Concerning the making firm of the face we have discussed more fully in this same prophet —: Because you said: Well done, well done, or, you mocked and rejoiced, because my temple and sanctuary was profaned by the entry of enemies, and over the land of Israel, because it was made desolate, and especially over the house of Judah, of the two tribes, which have now been led into captivity, therefore I too will hand you over to the sons of Cedem', whom we have translated 'eastern' — and no one doubts that the Midianites and the whole vast expanse of the desert lie next to the land of Arabia, who have herds of camels and multitudes of sheep and goats and live on this wealth —; which, as history relates in the book of Judges, also befell the land of Israel, when the Midianites came and grazed bare all their regions as far as Gaza. Μεταφορικῶς [metaphorically], then, Scripture signifies by way of the Midianites, the Ishmaelites and the Agarenes — who are now called Saracens, falsely taking to themselves the name of Sarah, so that, of course, they may seem to have been born of the free woman and mistress —; and it is said of King Nebuchadnezzar and all his army that he will come and take the city of Rabbath, which is called by this name either properly or because of its size — for 'Rabbath' means 'greatest' —; and so that we may not doubt that Nebuchadnezzar overthrew Arabia after Jerusalem was taken, Scripture testifies above: And you, son of man, set for yourself two ways, Ammon and Jerusalem, and the sword of the king of Babylon shall come, and again: At the head of the way of the city he shall cast. You shall set a way so that the sword may come to Rabbath of the Ammonites, and to Judah in most fortified Jerusalem, and again: Thus says the Lord God to the Ammonites and to their reproach. 'So the sons of Cedem will come and set up their sheepfolds like shepherds, and pitch tents; they themselves will lay waste your fruits and drink the milk and the richness of the land, once the flocks of camels and of all peoples have been let in, so that the Ammonites may be a lair for cattle', and by the compulsion of their misfortunes they may understand that he himself is the Lord, who both foretold the things to come and commanded that they should happen. Nor was it enough for the Ammonites to mock and say 'Well done, well done' over the temple and sanctuary of the Lord, which had been profaned by the entry of various nations; but so great was the wantonness of their mocking that the whole people together clattered with hands and feet and shouted with all the passion of the heart, because the land of Israel was desolate. Therefore not through angels nor through other ministries, but the Lord himself, stretching out his hand to strike, will hand it over for plunder — not at all to camels and flocks of sheep but, more plainly, to the nations — so that it may be utterly uprooted from the number of the peoples, and perish, and be brought to nothing; and after it has been crushed, then it may understand that he himself is the Lord, who judges all things and has power over all lands. According to tropology we can understand the Ammonites — who were begotten of the seed of Lot in a cave, and begotten in drunkenness and incest — as all the heretics, of whom the apostle John also says: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us; these have sprung from 'inclination' — for this is what 'Lot' is rendered in our language —, because: All have turned aside, together they have become useless; there is none who does good, there is not even one. Against these the prophet's face is set, or made firm, so that it may crush them by its severity, and it says to them: 'Because you mocked my Church in the time of persecution, and because my sanctuary had been profaned through various vices, whether by the vice of those who served me or by the cruelty of the enemies who persecuted my own, and because the land of Israel too, the senses that see God, was desolate of the choir of virtues, and because the sons of the house of Judah — the house that confesses the Lord, in which is the true faith and right confession — were led into captivity and ceased to serve the Lord, therefore you, who are all mockery, will be handed over to the sons of the east, who have set out from the true light, and you will be handed over as an inheritance, so that you too may learn to confess the Lord'. And by metaphor it is said that the sons of the east set their sheepfolds over them and pitch tents and drink milk and eat fruits, and that the city once of pride becomes a dwelling for camels, which, having laid down the burden of sins, can enter through the eye of a needle, and a lair for cattle, which are ruled by the good shepherd, so that, when they have done this, mingled with and handed over to the shepherds of the east, they may understand that he himself is the Lord. And again he reproaches them for having mocked with excessive passion of heart at the ruins of the people of God, and for having thought the land of Israel utterly deserted, for which they deserve the hand of the avenging God, so that those who had exceeded the measure of exultation and joy over the ruin of the house of Judah are not handed over to the sons of the east at all, but become a plunder for all the nations, and are slain from among the peoples, and perish, and are crushed, and are to be believed to belong not at all to the stock of Abraham but to all the nations; and then, by the greatness of their misfortunes and by their own crushing and the slaughter of their people, they may know that he himself is the Lord. What we have understood generally of the Church can be understood of each one of the saints, at whose ruin the men of the world rejoice, and the adverse powers too, if they have lost a chastity of long standing, since the wicked think it a consolation for their own crimes if they have many partners in crimes and in punishment; and no one does this unless he is a son of Ammon, that is, a son of the people, who was begotten in declination.

25:8-11

Thus says the Lord God: Because Moab and Seir said: Behold, the house of Judah is like all the nations, therefore behold, I will open the shoulder of Moab, from its cities, I say, and from its borders, the glorious places of the land, Bethiesimoth and Beelmeon and Cariathaim, to the sons of the east together with the Ammonites; and I will give it as an inheritance, so that there may be no more remembrance of the Ammonites among the nations. And upon Moab I will execute judgments, and they shall know that I am the Lord. (LXX: "Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because Moab ※ and Seir ⁚ said: Behold, the house of Judah is like all the nations, therefore behold, I will loosen the shoulder of Moab from the cities of its promontories, the chosen land, the house of Bethiesimuth above the spring of the maritime city, the sons of the east over the Ammonites; I have given it to him as an inheritance, so that there may be no remembrance of the Ammonites among the nations. And upon Moab I will execute vengeances, and they shall know that I am the Lord." What we have translated 'and Seir' is not found in the Seventy but has been added from Theodotion.) In this place, however, the Hebrews tell a ridiculous tale: after the city was opened and the temple unbarred, and the sons of Ammon and Moab and Seir had entered the temple and seen the Cherubim protecting the mercy seat, they said: 'As all the nations worship images, so Judah too has idols of its religion'; and for this reason, they say, the Lord was angered and handed them over to captivity. We, however, say this: that these too mocked the house of Judah when it was taken by the Chaldeans, thinking that, as there had been no help from God among the other nations, so too the kingdom of Judah and Jerusalem, bereft of God's protection, had lain open to the power of Babylon. Therefore, not a long time afterward but at the present moment, the Lord threatens that he will loosen, or open, the shoulder of Moab — that is, its strength and might — from its cities, so that the Babylonian conqueror may enter in to them too, and the cities in Moab may cease to be, and in its borders and boundaries the glorious cities may be destroyed whose names he sets down: 'Bethiesimoth and Beelmeon and Cariathaim', for which the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated 'the house of Bethiesimuth', although this word signifies 'a deserted village', while 'Beelmeon' too is to this day a very large village in Moab, which they rendered 'above the spring', and 'Cariathaim' 'a maritime city'; and it too is handed over, together with the Ammonites, to the sons of the east, namely the Babylonians, according to the sense which we have expounded against the Ammonites. 'And I will give,' he says, 'Moab as an inheritance, so that, as there is no more remembrance of the Ammonites among the nations, so also upon Moab I will execute vengeances and judgments, and they may know that I am the Lord, who handed Judah over for sin and stand forth as avenger against the Ammonites and against Moab'. But to this day 'Moab', which means 'from the father', and 'Seir', which is rendered 'hairy' and 'shaggy', looks down on and despises the house of Judah, in which is the true confession, and thinks that it can be overthrown as easily as the fortifications of the other cities are overthrown. Hence the Lord threatens that he will open, or loosen, all the strength of the Moabites, so that they may cease to have cities and may no longer trust in the dialectical art, but that all its boundaries, which he calls promontories because of the dashing of the waves, may be destroyed, and that the glorious and chosen lands — 'Bethiesimoth', which means 'house of solitude' and 'deserted', and 'Beelmeon', which is likewise rendered 'having a spring' or 'above the spring', and 'Cariathaim', which the Seventy translated 'a maritime city' — may perish; for although they have the strength of fighters, and the glorious go forth to battle with the art of fighting, and advance hedged about and fortified on every side, yet their glorious land is not a house of habitation but a house of solitude; and though they think that they have a spring of knowledge and a maritime city that can withstand all the storms of the world, promising themselves endurance and strength, yet they will be turned to this end, that they too may be handed over to the sons of the east of the true light in Christ, just as the Ammonites were handed over, who trusted in their heretical multitude. And let us consider the benefit, and the clemency of God in the very threat: that they are handed over together with the Ammonites to the sons of the east as an inheritance, and that no heresy at all may be named among the nations, but that, judgments and vengeances having been executed upon Moab for its arrogance, they may know by the outcome of things that it is the Lord who orders all things. Now to prove that in the present place Moab is to be understood of the pride of the philosophers, of whom it is said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the understanding I will reject, a few examples from the prophet must be unfolded: Amos says: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Moab and for four I will not turn away from him, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes — for truly, whatever there is in the world of perverse doctrines, whatever pertains to earthly knowledge and is thought to be robust, this is overthrown by the dialectical art and, like a fire, dissolved into ashes and embers, so that what was thought to be strongest is proved to be worth nothing —; Isaiah too rebukes the pride of Moab, saying: We have heard the insolence of Moab, he is exceedingly insolent; I have taken away his pride; Jeremiah also, prophesying against all the nations, speaks specifically to Moab: Because you trusted in your fortifications, and a little after: You had confidence in your glory, and again: How do you say: We are strong?, and then: Near is the day of Moab, that it should come, and its malice is exceedingly swift, and more plainly: Say: How has the glorious staff been broken, the rod of magnificence?, and again: The horn of Moab is broken; and these things are said so that, under the name of Moab, the foolish pride of the world that lifts itself up to heaven may be crushed.

25:12-14

Thus says the Lord God: Because Idumaea took vengeance, to avenge itself on the sons of Judah, and sinned in transgressing and sought vengeance on them, therefore thus says the Lord God: I will stretch out my hand over the Idumaeans, and I will take away from it man and beast, and I will make it desert from the south, and those who are in Dedan shall fall by the sword. And I will lay my vengeance on Idumaea by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall do in Edom according to my anger and my fury, and they shall know my indignation, says the Lord God. (LXX: "Thus says the Lord Adonai: Because Idumaea acted so that they avenged a vengeance on the house of Judah, and they kept the memory of evil and avenged themselves with vengeance, therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: I will stretch out my hand over Idumaea, and I will slay from it man and beast, and I will make it desert, and those fleeing from Theman shall fall by the sword. And I will lay my vengeance on Idumaea in the hand of my people Israel, and they shall do in Idumaea according to my anger and my fury, and they shall know my vengeance, says Adonai the Lord.") Above he had set out two: Because Moab and Seir said, and afterwards, keeping silent about Seir, he spoke against Moab only; now he returns to the πρόβλημα [problem, the question set] he had begun: what Seir, that is, Idumaea, did — that Esau and Seir and Edom and Idumaea and Duma are called one nation, no one who has knowledge of the Scriptures will doubt; and, to say nothing of the other prophets — Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, who prophesied against Idumaea and Duma and Edom — the prophet Obadiah directs his whole prophecy against this nation; we expounded him long ago as best we could —. So Seir is rebuked, who, because he was shaggy, received the name of hairy, and bloody Edom, who for the cooking of red lentils lost his birthright and took his name from the dish; Esau too they interpret as 'made'; and this must be known, that in the Hebrew Idumaea is never written, but always Edom, which the Greek translation expressed as Idumaea. So Idumaea did not speak, as Moab did, but took vengeance on the sons of Judah, and sinned, or kept the memory of the former pain, so as to take vengeance on those by whom he had been supplanted in the womb. Therefore not through angels nor through anyone else, but the Lord himself, stretching out his hand over Idumaea, took away from it man and beast, and reduced its cities to desert, that is, 'Theman', which we rendered 'south', from which, and from the other city, Dedan, the slain will fall by the sword; 'and when they have avenged themselves on Judah, I will lay vengeance on the Idumaeans by the hand, or in the hand, of my people Israel, so that they may be crushed by those on whom they exercised vengeance, who will do in Edom, or Idumaea, according to my anger and fury, so as to fulfil my indignation, and so that, through the hands of my people Israel, my anger may rage against the hostile nation, and they may understand that, against the unjust vengeance of Idumaea, my vengeance was just,' says Adonai the Lord. According to tropology, this seems to me the sense: Idumaea is called 'earthly' and 'fleshly', which rises up against the spirit so that we do not do the things that are of the spirit, and hastens to draw to itself the soul placed in the middle, and wishes to repay vengeance on the sons of Judah, to whom it had formerly been subject, and remembers the old pain, that it was not in its own power, and therefore seeks vengeance on those who, withdrawing from the flesh, followed the spirit; therefore this Lord, being the avenger of the sons of Judah, stretches out his hand over Idumaea and takes away from it man and beast — whatever it seems to have either of reason or of simple faith — so as to reduce it to solitude, and of 'Theman', which means 'failing', and 'Dedan', which itself signifies 'kinship', he slew all with the sword which he placed in the hand of his people Israel, so that Edom may be overthrown, and feel the anger and fury of the Lord, and understand that his vengeance has served to this end: that it should serve the house of Judah. This is what the Apostle too argues about, writing: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated; and he loves Jacob because he supplants and overcomes what is fleshly and earthly, and deserves to receive its blessings; for first we live according to the flesh and afterwards according to the spirit. First the vices, then the virtues by which the vices are undermined, because the heart of man is set on malice from boyhood, and mature age condemns the errors of youth; hence David too: The offenses, he says, of my youth and my ignorances do not remember. And yet it must be known that Jacob receives the first blessing, Esau the second, and at the last it is said of him: You shall be the servant of your brother, so that, after the flesh has been made subject to the spirit and joined to it, it may cease to be flesh, and Idumaea may pass over into Judea.

25:15-17

Thus says the Lord God: Because the Philistines acted in vengeance, and avenged themselves with their whole soul, slaying, and fulfilling old enmities, therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will stretch out my hand over the Philistines, and I will slay the slayers, and destroy the remnants of the maritime region; and I will execute great vengeances on them, rebuking in fury, and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have laid my vengeance on them. (LXX: "Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Because the foreigners acted in vengeance, and stirred up retribution, mocking from the soul, so as to destroy for ever, therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I will stretch out my hand over the foreigners, and I will destroy (or slay) the Cretans, and destroy the remnants of the shore; and I will execute great vengeances on them in the retribution of fury, and they shall know that I am Adonai the Lord, when I have laid my vengeance on them.") After the Ammonites, Moab and Seir — who are the Edomites, and who through Lot and Esau are joined by kinship to the people of Israel and the house of Judah — he comes to the Philisthiim — whom the Seventy translated 'allophylos', that is, 'foreigners', not by the general name of all the nations that are not of the race of the Jews, but by the special name of their own nation, which is now called Palaestina, the letter 'phe' having been changed into 'pi' according to the custom of the Greeks, just as among us, in place of the Hebrew 'phascha', the Greek and Latin 'pascha' is celebrated —. 'Philisthiim' they interpret as 'falling by the cup'; they too were made drunk from the golden cup of Babylon, and they rage, and mock with their whole soul, remembering their old enmities against Israel, by which they were divided from the people of God; and whereas the Lord says: Vengeance to me, I will repay, the Lord says: They themselves avenge themselves, slaying and fulfilling ancient hatreds; on account of which they will feel the hand of the Lord stretched out over them, who will slay the 'slayers' — for which the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated 'Cretans', whereas Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion rendered either the Hebrew word itself, 'chorethim', or 'slayers' and 'slaying', not only in the present place but also in Zephaniah, where these things are said against the Philistines: Gaza shall be plundered, and Ashkelon given to destruction, and Ashdod and Ekron shall be uprooted. Woe to the inhabitants of the cord of the sea, neighbors of the Cretans! The word of the Lord is upon you, Canaan, land of the foreigners; and I will destroy you from habitation. And Crete shall be pasture for shepherds and a fold for sheep. For there too, whereas the Seventy rendered 'Crete', the other translators translated ὄλεθρον, that is, 'slaying' or 'destruction', about which we said what seemed right to us in the above-mentioned prophet, God granting it; hence too, of David's two legions, one of which was called 'Phelethi' and the other 'Cerethim', the latter, because they slew and cut throats, received the name 'Chorethim', that is, 'of the slayers' —; and the Lord destroys all the remnants of the maritime region, which is beaten by salt waves, and will execute vengeances, not small but great, in fury, so that his fury may have mercy as its end and, after he has executed vengeances, rebuking with fury, then the Philistines may know that he himself is the Lord.

26:1-6

And it came to pass in the eleventh year, on the first (or one) of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, because Tyre (or Sor) has said of Jerusalem: Aha, the gates of the peoples (or nations) are broken, she is turned to me, I shall be filled, she is laid waste (or she who was full is laid waste); therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and I will make many nations come up to you, as the surging sea comes up; and they shall break down the walls of Tyre and destroy her towers, and I will scrape (or winnow) her dust from her, and I will make her a most clear (or most gleaming) rock. There shall be a drying of dragnets in the midst of the sea, for I have spoken, says the Lord God; and she shall be for plunder to the nations. Her daughters also who are in the field (or in the plain) shall be slain by the sword, and they shall know that I am the Lord. The order of the prophecy is woven together in sequence. He had spoken against the Ammonites and Moab and Seir, who are themselves the Edomites, and the Philistines who are on the coast; and he keeps the same boundary along the cord of the sea: for after the Palestinians comes the region of Phoenicia, whose metropolis is the city 'Tyre', which in the Hebrew and Syrian tongue is called 'Sor': 'And because, when Jerusalem was taken, she too rejoiced and insulted her and said: The gates of the peoples are broken; I have a most secure harbor, and now that she is overthrown, the whole multitude that was ruled by her will has turned to me; and because she is laid waste, therefore I shall be filled; or, she who was full before will be reduced to a wilderness: you have said these things, then, and have insulted the ruins of Jerusalem, which was overthrown by the judgment of God because of her sins; therefore, not through messengers nor through any others, but I myself will be against you, O Tyre, and like the waves of the sea I will make the Babylonians come up against you with very many nations, by whose assault your walls and towers will be destroyed, so far that they fall right down to the ground and its dust is scraped away or winnowed into various parts; and she will be so humbled that she is compared to a most gleaming rock, and so great will be the desolation in the city, once most thronged, that the dragnets of fishermen will be spread out and dried in its midst; for I the Lord have spoken, whose words cannot be void, and I will hand her over for plunder to the nations; her daughters also who are in the field, or in the plain, that is, on the coast of Phoenicia, cities and towns, villages and forts, will be slain by the sword — μεταφορικῶς [metaphorically]: because he called them daughters, he speaks of a slaying by the sword —, so that by the outcome of events they may know that I am the Lord, who commanded these things to happen'. According to tropology, since the Hebrew name 'Sor' is rendered 'distress', every soul that is seized by passions can be called 'Sor'; when it sees Jerusalem, in which were the temple and the vision of peace, overthrown by the judgment of God for her vices and sins, it exults and thinks that the dominion of the once famous city is to be transferred to itself. This is understood both of contrary doctrines and of the men of the world: for when they see that a holy man has slipped through negligence, they rejoice and exult, as if the ruin of others were their own resurrection. Therefore the Lord threatens that he himself will fight against men of this kind, and will make very many nations come up against them like the waves of the sea, which destroy in them whatever seems most fortified and firm, and that he will so overthrow all their arguments that they are reduced to dust; that he will also make the dragnets and nets with which they formerly fished for the deceived multitude cease, and have them spread out and dried on the ground of the deserted city, so that in their place other fishermen may come in, whom the Lord sent to fish; and also that her daughters, who were formerly kept as if in a chamber and, being mystic and more secret doctrines, were not readily entrusted to anyone, will come forth and be dragged out into public and cut down by the Church's blade, so that then they may understand that he is the Lord, who both abandoned Jerusalem for a little while on account of her sins and destroyed the fortifications of Tyre on account of her insulting and her rejoicing.

26:7-14

For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring to Tyre (or to you, Sor) Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the north, king of kings, with horses and chariots and horsemen and a company and a great people. Your daughters who are in the field he shall slay with the sword, and he shall surround you with siegeworks, and heap up a mound round about, and raise the shield against you, and he shall direct mantlets and rams (or lances) against your walls, and destroy your towers with his weaponry. By the flood of his horses their dust shall cover you; at the sound of horsemen and wheels and chariots your walls shall be shaken, when he has entered your gates as through the entry of a city laid waste (or as one entering a city from the plain). With the hoofs of his horses he shall trample all your streets, your people he shall cut down with the sword, and your noble statues shall fall to the ground (or he shall bring down the substance of your strength to the ground). They shall lay waste (or he shall lay waste) your riches, they shall plunder your merchandise (or he shall despoil your substance), and they shall destroy (or he shall destroy) your walls, and your splendid (or desirable) houses they shall overthrow (or he shall overthrow), and your stones and your timber or your dust they shall put in the midst of the waters (or he shall cast into the midst of the sea). And I will make the multitude of your singers cease (or he shall destroy the multitude of your musicians), and the sound of your lyres (or the voice of your instruments) shall be heard no more, and I will make you a most clear (or a most gleaming) rock; you shall be a drying of dragnets, nor shall you be built any more, for I have spoken, says the Lord God. As is my custom, I have joined both editions, and where they differ I have coupled them side by side, looking to the brevity of the volumes. So what he had said: I will make many nations come up to you as the surging sea comes up, and Tyre shall be for plunder to the nations, he now sets out more plainly: that the Lord will bring Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the north, the king of kings, with horses and chariots and with a boundless multitude of troops, who will first overthrow the cities and forts on the coast that are subject to Tyre, and afterwards cause Tyre to be besieged, and wall her in with his army and mound and siegeworks, and assail her walls with mantlets and rams, and destroy them; and so great will be the multitude of his horsemen that, by the dust of the cavalry and the noise of the howling army and the rattle of wheels and the neighing of horses, the foundations of the city will be shaken; and so he will enter the city, its walls torn down, like one entering securely from the plain; and so great will be the security of the conquering army that the hoofs of horses will trample the streets of Tyre, and all the people will fall in the midst of the city, and the once noble statues, or all her substance, will fall to the ground, and nothing of her former riches will be preserved in the captured city; but along with the walls the noble houses too will be destroyed, and so great will be the savagery of the victors that the timber and stones left over from the fire will be thrown into the midst of the sea; and either Nebuchadnezzar or the Lord himself will make cease all the gladness of the city with which it once resounded in songs and psalteries, and, overthrown right down to the ground, it will be a drying of dragnets. But what follows: Nor shall you be built any more, seems to raise a question: how has she not been built, when today we see her as the most noble and most beautiful city of Phoenicia? — whence some will have it that Tyre is to suffer these things in the last time, and is not to be built afterwards —; but how will they be able to keep to the person of Nebuchadnezzar — especially since we read in what follows that Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre and did not receive the wages of his labor, and that Egypt was therefore handed over to him, because he had served the sentence of God in the siege of Tyre —? Those who contradict this history say that they have read the Greek histories and those of the Phoenicians, and especially of Nicolaus of Damascus, and others of the barbarians, and have found nothing about a siege of the city of Tyre by the Chaldeans; whereas we can prove that many things are said in the Scriptures to have been done which are not found in Greek volumes, and that we ought not to acquiesce in the authority of those whose faithlessness and lies we detest. So what is said: Nor shall you be built any more, can be taken thus: that she will by no means any longer be queen of the peoples, nor have her own dominion as she had under Hiram and the other kings, but will be in servitude either under the Chaldeans or the Macedonians or the Ptolemies and, last of all, the Roman kings. But it is doubtful to no one that, according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who comes from the north, is understood as the devil, who, though he is a most harsh wind and a left-hand one, is called by the name 'right-hand', claiming for himself the dignity of the name; and he is the king of kings and of all the kingdoms which he showed to the Lord, when he said to him: All these have been handed over to me, and I will give them to you if you fall down and worship me. He has horses and chariots, of which it is written: A horse is deceitful for safety, and: All who mount horses have fallen asleep, and in another place: Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea. He slays the daughters of Tyre, souls placed in distress and in a kind of prison of sins, in the field and the widest plain, and surrounds Tyre with his siegeworks, so as to hold her shut in, so that no one from her can escape the dominion of the Babylonian king; he destroys her walls and overthrows her towers, and whatever she may have had in the way of doctrines trembles violently at the flood of his horses and the sound of his horsemen and the clatter of wheels and chariots; and he will enter her gates with no one preventing him, and the hoofs of his horses will trample the streets of the city — for wide and spacious is the way that leads to death —, and he will cast down to the ground all her substance — or the noble statues, by which they had fashioned for themselves images of falsehood, of which it is written: Lord, in your city you will scatter their image —; and, the walls destroyed, the noble houses too will be overthrown which she had prepared for herself and in which she exulted; and she will come to such desolation that they throw into the deep her stones and timber, with which she had built her walls and constructed her masonry, and her songs and music, by which she trusted in herself in the wisdom of this world, and all the sound of lyres will be heard no more; and her fishing will cease, and she will be brought so low that she is a drying of dragnets and is not built any more, because, handed over to Nebuchadnezzar at the sentence of the Lord, she has been utterly overthrown, in accord with what the Apostle also says: Whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme. The passages are difficult, and the prudent and diligent reader ought to pardon my labor; or if he can find something better, I too shall pass over to his opinion, provided he knows that he will receive from others the pardon he grants to me.

26:15-18

Thus says the Lord God to Tyre: Shall not the isles be shaken at the sound of your fall and the groaning of your slain, when they have been killed in your midst? And all the princes of the sea shall come down from their seats, and shall take off their spoils, and cast away their varied garments; and they shall be clothed with astonishment, they shall sit on the ground, and, dumbfounded at your sudden fall, they shall marvel. And taking up a lamentation over you, they shall say to you: How you have perished, you who dwell in the sea, renowned city, who were strong in the sea with your inhabitants, whom all shall dread! Now the ships shall be astonished in the day of your terror, and the isles in the sea shall be troubled, because no one goes out from you. (LXX: "For thus says the Lord God to Sor: Shall not the isles be shaken at the voice of your fall, when your wounded groan, when the sword has been drawn in your midst? And all the princes of the sea shall come down from their seats, and shall take off their crowns, and shall be stripped of their varied garments; they shall go mad with frenzy, they shall sit on the ground, and they shall dread their own destruction, and shall groan over you. And they shall take up a lamentation over you, and shall say to you: How you have perished and been scattered in the sea, praised city, who were strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, who gave her fear to all her inhabitants! And the isles shall dread in the day of your fall, and the isles in the sea shall be troubled at your going out.") First let us lay open the very words of the history, disclosing the sense of what is said by a very brief μεταφράσει [paraphrase]. 'Thus says Adonai the Lord to Tyre, which is called 'Sor': In the day of your fall, when you have collapsed under Nebuchadnezzar's assault, and at the groaning of the wounded or slain who have been killed in your midst, shall not the isles be shaken? And all the kings will come down from their seats or thrones, and the princes of the sea who rule over various isles, and they will take the diadems off their heads, laying aside all the glory of reigning, and will cast from them their most precious garments, gleaming with incredible variety; and by the greatness of their astonishment they will be turned to madness and, cast down in humility, will sit on the ground; and when they see that you have collapsed, they will dread like things for themselves, and will think that no good thing on earth is lasting; rather, on the contrary, they will take up a lamentation over you and recite a tearful song, saying: How you have perished, you who dwell in the sea, renowned city (or praised)' — for we read in Greek and Latin and barbarian histories that Tyre was an island and had no approach from the land, but that afterwards mounds were thrown up by Nebuchadnezzar king of the Chaldeans or, as some affirm, by Alexander king of the Macedonians, and the place was prepared by siege and with mantlets and rams, and from an island a peninsula was made —; 'you, then, O Sor, O Tyre, who were once the strongest among all the isles, or praised by the voice of all among the cities, together with your inhabitants whom all feared, how suddenly you have collapsed! Now the isles will be astonished or terrified over you, and — as it stands better in the Hebrew — the ships, in the day of your terror and fall, and the isles in the sea will be troubled — hence it is more consistent to read 'ships' above, so that 'isles' is not set down a second time —, because no one goes out from you — or, as the Seventy translated, in the day of your going in —, when you have been led away captive'. Let these meanwhile be laid as a kind of foundation of the history; now we shall strive to set the spiritual roof upon it. Imagine someone who, having long kept his chastity, flourished in many virtues, and afterwards collapsed into some grave and mortal sin: will not all the isles be moved at the sound of his fall and of his slain virtues, those, namely, who are beaten by the salt and bitter waves of this world? And all who seemed to be princes in the brine of this world will come down from the throne of their pride and, cast down in humility, will take off from their heads the diadems they seemed to possess through good works, and will cast away the garments varied with a diversity of virtues, and will be clothed with astonishment, or through the greatness of their fear will seem in some way insane, and will sit on the ground, and, stunned at his sudden fall, will marvel, so much so that all take up wailing and lamentation over him who has collapsed, and say: How you have perished, you who were formerly safe; how you have collapsed, you who had stood so long, who in the sea of this world were thought renowned among all, who were strong in the opinion of all; and your inhabitants, that is, your most strong thoughts that resisted all the fiery darts of the devil, which formerly were a terror to all adversaries, have been turned to astonishment! And the ships too, namely all the saints, who cross the waves of this world, are stunned when they see that you have fallen, in the day of your terror and fall; and the isles will be troubled, lest they too suffer like things — for the falls of others are examples for the righteous, since we all dwell in this world in a weak and feeble state and with wavering step, and our victory is never certain and secure, when those who had stood before go out from you, or at your going out, in your end and consummation —. For we are judged not by things past but by things present; and we must beware and always fear lest the storm of a single hour overthrow old glory and solid firmness.

26:19-21

For thus says the Lord God: When I make you a desolate city like the cities that are not inhabited, and bring up the deep upon you, and many waters cover you, and I drag you down with those who go down into the pit (or to those who go down into the ditch) to the everlasting people, and set you in the uttermost land (or in the depth of the lands) like the ancient wastes, with those who are led down into the pit (or go down into the ditch), so that you are not inhabited, and I give glory in the land of the living (or so that you do not rise again in the land of the living), I will reduce you to nothing (or I will give you to destruction), and you shall not be, and when sought you shall not be found any more forever, says the Lord God. Join what has been said with what preceded. 'When I make you, O Tyre, a city desolate forever, as are other cities that are not inhabited at all, and bring up the deep upon you, and many waters, or boundless multitudes of enemies, cover you — or certainly, because he is speaking to an island and to a city set on an island, he τροπικῶς [figuratively] compares the throng of adversaries to the waves of the deep —, and drag you down, with those who go down into the pit or into the ditch, to those who are in hell — of whom we also read in the Psalms: They shall go into the lower parts of the earth and shall be delivered into the hands of the sword, they shall be portions for foxes —, to the everlasting people, where there is weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth, and set you in the uttermost land, in which the ancient dragon has been placed, and like the ancient wastes and deserts, where there is no remembrance of good things but punishments are everlasting, and do not cause you to be raised up in the land of the living — of which it is written: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land, and in another place: I will please the Lord in the region of the living —, then you will be reduced to nothing, or you will perish forever, and you shall be no more', according to what is written in another psalm: Spare me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and shall be no more: not that he who is in everlasting punishments ceases to be, but that he who does not live to God is said in the holy Scriptures not to subsist. Hence Esther too, speaking against idols: Do not hand over, she says, your scepter to those who are not: surely those to whom she begs that it not be handed over existed, but they were not, to God, since they had ceased to be to the virtues and to the living God. And this is to be noted: that Tyre is sought by him who came to seek and to save what had perished, and who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep on the mountains, seeks the one straying sheep — the woman too who had lost one drachma seeks and finds it, and calls together her neighbors to share her joy —; but if Tyre, when sought, is not found, the fault is not the seeker's but his who has fled the hand of the good shepherd. 'And no more', he says, 'shall you be forever' — or, as is written in the Hebrew 'lolam' and in the Greek αἰών [age], it signifies 'one age', according to that passage of Isaiah, who says that after seventy years Tyre is to be restored to her whole state; and they say that 'one age', that is, the span of a human lifetime, is reckoned at the number of seventy years, as the psalmist says: The days of our years in them are seventy years; but if in the strong, eighty years; whatever is beyond is toil and pain —. This we have said briefly about Tyre μεταφραστικῶς [by way of paraphrase]; it can also be referred to those who, set in the distress of this world, are led down to the underworld and are covered by the deeps and waves of punishments, and are dragged to the lower parts of the earth, and are joined to those who are in the ancient wilderness, and are led down into the pit or the everlasting ditch, so that they are no longer inhabited by the Holy Spirit; of whom it is written: The ungodly, when he has fallen into the depth of evils, despises; and henceforth they will not be in the land of the living, but will perish, and be reduced to nothing, and cease to be to God. These testimonies are made use of by those who say that the punishments of the ungodly, and not of sinners, are perpetual: of the ungodly who, sought by God, were not found, and have ceased to be forever, because by their own fault they lost him who says: I am the life.

27:1-3a

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: You therefore, son of man, take up a lamentation over Tyre, and you shall say to Tyre, which dwells at the entrance of the sea, the trade of the peoples to many islands (or from many islands): Thus says the Lord God. If I should wish to comprehend the whole prophecy against Tyre, or over the lamentation of Tyre, in a single discourse, I shall both make it long and obscure the reader's understanding, since he cannot hold everything in mind at once, especially the places in which the edition of the Seventy differs from the Hebrew in this passage, that is, what they have added or what they have taken away. Therefore we shall be content with our own translation, and wherever they disagree we shall attach theirs alongside, leaving the perfect knowledge of all things to God, and we shall briefly point out what seems right to us in each point. He who is lamented is still a concern to the one by whom he is lamented; hence Samuel too wept and lamented over Saul, and the Apostle Paul laments and mourns over those who have committed fornication and have not done penance, and Jeremiah writes lamentations over the overthrow of Jerusalem in four alphabets. Tyre, then, or Sor, according to the letter, dwells at the entrance of the sea, either because it was formerly an island or because it receives ships coming from the deep into a most safe harbor, and it is the trade of the peoples to many islands, or from many islands, which indeed continues to this day, so that the commerce of almost all nations is carried on in it. But following the interpretation we have begun, let us refer whatever is said of Tyre to the συνοχὴν, that is, the 'straits', of this world, which is set in the evil one and is hemmed in and battered by various disturbances as if by waves — of traders of this sort it is told also in the Psalms in mystical language: Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business in many waters, these have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep —.

27:3b-4a

O Tyre, you have said: I am of perfect beauty (or you have said: I have surrounded myself with beauty), and set in the heart of the sea. The first charge against Tyre is that, if she seems to have anything good, she thinks it not God's but her own, and reckons all the beauty that came to her from various regions to be the work of her own diligence and strength; for she said: I am of perfect beauty, or: I have surrounded myself with beauty, although she is set in the heart, that is, in the middle, of the sea, and is tossed about like an island, and is shattered by the surge and the dashing of the waves. That the heart of the sea signifies its middle, that prophetic saying also shows: Therefore we will not fear when the earth is troubled, and the mountains are carried into the heart of the sea. Their waters roared and were troubled; and our Lord too is said to have descended into the heart of the earth, that is, into its middle, and to the underworld. But true and perfect beauty is in no human being except in the body of Christ, which is interpreted as the Church, and which is gathered together from the virtues of many saints; hence he himself also speaks to the bride: You are all beautiful, my nearest, and there is no blemish in you.

27:4b-5

Your neighbors, who built you, have filled up your beauty; with firs from Sanir they constructed you, with all the planking of the sea; they took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you. (In place of which, intending I know not what, the Seventy translated thus: Beelim your sons surrounded you with beauty; cedar from Sanir was built for you; they took thin boards of cypress from Lebanon to make masts of fir for you; for the word 'Beelim' is not found at all in this place among the Hebrews, but in place of 'Beelim' is written 'gebulaich', which means 'your borders'; in what they said, 'your sons', too, they were deceived by the ambiguity of the word and the similarity of the writing, since the same letters, with a different pronunciation, are read as 'of masons' and 'of sons', 'bonaich' and 'benaich'.) 'O Tyre, then, you who said in pride: I am of perfect beauty (or: I have surrounded myself with beauty), although you are set in the middle of the sea, hear how much has been bestowed on you by the bounty of God: your neighbors and those who border on you, who are not from distant but from nearby regions, they themselves have filled up your beauty; and you think yours what is another's!' And he speaks as if to a ship, τροπικῶς [figuratively] signifying the beauty of the city and its abundance of all things, so that, after he has described all its equipment — mast, yards, oars, sails, prow, keel, ropes, coverings, hides, and the other things which the use of the best-fitted ships requires — he may then announce that a storm and the south wind, by which the greatest waves will be stirred up, will come upon it, and that it will be subjected to shipwreck — by which he signifies the overthrow of the Tyrian city by king Nebuchadnezzar, or, as many think, by Alexander king of the Macedonians, who is related to have besieged and taken that very city in six months, after he had defeated Darius in Lycia —. According to the mystical understandings, the planking of the Tyrian ship, with which it is fitted and joined together, is cut from firs or cedars from Sanir, and its mast is raised from a cedar or cypress from Lebanon: from firs because of their lightness and the joints of the boards, which hold and bite into one another more gently, or from cedars because it is a wood that does not rot; and they are said to be 'from Sanir', which means 'way of the lamp' or, as we judge more truly, 'tooth of the watches', because all the prosperity and illumination of the ship came from the true light; Sanir, moreover, according to the letter, is the very mountain that is also Hermon, which others call Sarion — read the history —; it means 'whiteness' or 'whitening', which itself also pertains to grace coming from elsewhere.

27:6

Oaks from Bashan they hewed into your oars, your benches they made for you of Indian ivory, and cabins from the islands of Italy. (LXX: "From Bashan they made your oars, your temples they made for you of ivory, forest houses from the islands of Chetthiim.") How great the beauty of the ship and of its equipment, that it should have oars of cedar — not from just anywhere but from Bashan —, and benches of ivory, and cabins — or storerooms in which the most precious merchandise is laid up — from the islands of 'Chetthiim' — which we have rendered as 'Italy' —, from that region which is nearer to Greece, understanding by it all the parts of the western islands! Let us say, then, according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], that the oars of the Tyrian ship are made from Bashan — of which it is also written in the Psalms: The Lord said: From Bashan I will turn back, I will turn back from the depth of the sea; Basan in our language means 'ignominy' —; those, then, who were in the depth of the sea and in the ignominy of sins, the Lord turns back, and turns them into oars, so that, sailing with the apostles, they may reach the land and the shores; and benches are made of ivory when they have mortified their bodies, or have devoted the use of their teeth to the praises of God; and cabins or storerooms from the islands of 'Chetthiim', which, according to the ἐτυμολογιὰν [etymology] of the Hebrew language, is rendered 'struck', so that it has been not so much killed as tested by the blows of the devil. We can speak of the 'of ivory, and forest houses' 'from the islands of Chetthiim' as those which the heretics try to construct not in the house of God but in the Tyrian ship, they themselves having their own ivory of speech, and building temples of the tongue contrary to the temple of God, and forest houses, the dwellings of beasts, whereas Scripture says that groves and woods and sacred groves are not to be planted in the house of God.

27:7

Embroidered byssus from Egypt was woven for you into a sail, to be set on the mast; hyacinth and purple from the islands of Elishah became your covering. (LXX: "Byssus with embroidery from Egypt was made for you into a spread to surround you with glory, and to cover you with hyacinth and purple from the islands of Elisee, and they became your coverings.") Because Tyre had said: I am of perfect beauty (or: I myself have surrounded myself with beauty), she is convicted as to what she has received from each region, according to that word of Scripture: What do you have that you have not received? But if you have received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it? So it is described what each province sends, according to that line of Vergil: India sends ivory, the soft Sabaeans their incense, But the hardy Chalybes iron, and Pontus the rank castoreum, and the rest. Byssus grows most of all in Egypt, and from it was woven the sail of the Tyrian ship, which is hung on the mast; and its covering, which in the heat of the sun and in calm weather affords shade to sailors and passengers, is made of hyacinth and purple, which come from the islands of Elishah, so he calls the islands of the Ionian Sea. Further, according to the Seventy, coverings of byssus are woven for the spread and for the repose of the Tyrian ship, so that, covered with these, it may be more glorious, and, surrounded with them, may have a more beautiful garment. Now we have often pointed out that byssus is referred to the earth because it springs from the earth, and hyacinth to the air, purple to the sea, from which it is made, with the twice-dyed scarlet added, of which the vestments of the high priest are woven, because it signifies the four elements: earth, fire, air and waters, of which all things consist; and these Tyre takes to herself, so as not to use God's creatures with thanks, but to say: I am of perfect beauty (or: I myself have surrounded myself with beauty).

27:8-9

The inhabitants of Sidon and the Aradians were your rowers; your wise men, O Tyre, became your pilots. The elders of Byblus and its prudent men provided sailors for the service of your varied equipment. All the ships of the sea and their sailors were among the people of your trade. (LXX: "Your princes who dwelt in Sidon and the Aradians were your rowers; your wise men, Sor, who were in you, these were your pilots. The elders of Byblus and its wise men were in you: these strengthened your counsel. And all the ships of the sea and their rowers became yours toward the west of the west.")
