He had said above: Your neighbors, who built you, have filled up your beauty; before he comes to those who dwell far off, he describes the help of the nearest provinces: 'Your inhabitants,' he says, 'or the princes of Sidon and of Aradus, which is a neighboring island, are your rowers; your wise men, O Tyre, have become your pilots' — for piloting belongs properly to the wise, as Scripture says: Those who have no piloting fall like leaves —. 'The old men or elders of Byblus and its prudent men provided sailors for the service, or strengthened the counsel of Tyre, and provided varied equipment; and all the ships of the sea and their sailors were among the people of the Tyrian trade, or toward the west of the west'. So much meanwhile according to the letter; but according to the mystical understandings, since 'Sidonians' means 'hunters', and 'Aradians' 'those who put down', we say that Tyre, the glorious and most proud city, which is afterwards to be shattered when the wind blows, has citizens or princes who are hunters — of whom it is written: Our soul has been snatched like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; for where we read 'of the hunters', in the Hebrew is written 'of the Sidonians' —; these hunt: they draw unwary souls, set on high, down to earthly things, and they become rowers to lead them to shipwreck; but the wise men of Tyre, who are taken in the bad sense, in which the sons of darkness are wiser than the sons of light, they themselves steer what has been made ready for Tyre for shipwreck; the elders of Byblus and its prudent men provided sailors to Tyre for the service, or strengthened its counsel — sacred history relates that very many elders were rejected by the Lord, and younger ones chosen, as a type of the Synagogue and the Church: the elder Cain is cast off, and the younger Abel is chosen; Ishmael, the son of Abraham, is estranged from his father, and Isaac the younger received the inheritance; of the sons of Isaac too, the elder Esau is a hunter and roams in the woodlands, the younger Jacob dwells simply at home, whence it is written also in Malachi: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated; and certainly, according to the Apostle, while set in their mother's womb they had done nothing good or bad, nor had they merit or offense, that the one should be chosen and the other cast off, except that, in a type, as we have said, of the Synagogue and the Church, the elder is rejected and the younger taken up —. All, he says, the ships of the sea and their sailors were among the people of the Tyrian trade (or toward the west of the west — just as 'Song of Songs' and 'age of ages' and 'work of works' are said, so that a song is greater than the other songs, and an age longer than the other ages, and a work more useful than the other works, so 'west of the west' is said in order to signify the greatness of the western regions —), and fittingly the ships of the sea and their sailors and rowers, who are in aid of the Tyrian ship, do not go to the east, nor to the rising of the light, where the sun of righteousness rises, but to the 'west of the west', where the light sets and whence is the beginning of darkness.

27:10

Persians and Lydians and Libyans were in your army; your men of war hung up shield and helmet in you for your adornment (or hung up targes and helmets in you, they gave you your glory). That the Persians were most brave, whose king Cyrus, as is foretold by the prophecy of Isaiah, having overthrown Astyages king of the Medes, captured Babylon, both sacred and secular history relate; that the Lydians too were reckoned at that time among the most robust nations, whose king Croesus was captured by the same Cyrus, Xenophon writes most fully; and that Libyans came against Jerusalem with the Troglodytes and Ethiopians, we read in the volume of Chronicles; because in those times they were most flourishing and fighters famous in battle, they are recorded to have been defenders of the Tyrian city, and to have hung up shields and helmets on the battlements of the walls to terrify enemies. But the spiritual understanding sounds thus: that the 'Persians', who mean 'tempting' or 'tempted', and the 'Lydians', whom we understand as 'begotten', and the 'Libyans', who in the Hebrew language are called 'phut' and are rendered 'os' [mouth] — from 'ore' [mouth], not from 'osse' [bone] —, strive in vain to defend Tyre, since they are overcome by temptation and serve generation and lust, and only multiply empty words, not having the helmet of salvation nor the shield of faith, but only put forward glory and the din of words for its adornment.

27:11

The sons of the Aradians with your army were upon your walls round about; but the Pygmies too, who were in your towers, hung their quivers on your walls all around; they completed your beauty. (LXX: "The sons of the Aradians and your strength were upon your walls round about; guards were in your towers; they hung their quivers upon your battlements all around; they perfected your beauty.") The word 'gamadim' the first edition of Aquila translated 'Pygmies', Symmachus 'Medes', the Seventy 'guards', Theodotion 'gomadim', the Hebrew word itself; we see to this day the island of Aradus, which is entirely a city, and has opposite it the town of Antaradus, and is near to Tyre, and lies out off the Phoenician shore of the mainland. These are in the army of the Tyrian city and are the guards of its towers, and they hang their quivers all around and complete its beauty, so as to show that they are archers; or they are pygmies, that is, warriors and most ready for wars, ἀπὸ τῆς πυγμῆς, which in the Greek language is rendered 'into combat'. But if the Aradians mean 'those who put down', everyone who puts forward the knowledge falsely so called, and has in the quiver of his breast the fiery darts of the devil, with which he wounds and sets on fire the hearts of the deceived, is to be called an Aradian: for he desires to put down those who strive to climb to the heights, and he completes the beauty of Tyre, of which it is also written in Proverbs: Let not the desire of beauty deceive you, nor be captured by your eyes, and again: Like earrings in the nostrils of a pig, so is beauty to a woman of bad character.

27:12

The Carthaginians were your traders, by reason of the multitude of all riches; with silver, iron, tin and lead they filled your fairs. Not only in the present place, but also in Isaiah, where it is written: Howl, ships of Carthage, the other translators rendered the Hebrew word as 'Tharsis'; and that these are a colony of the Tyrians no one doubts; they themselves, from the regions of the west, filled the fairs of Tyre with silver, iron, tin and lead. 'Tharsis' in our language sounds 'exploration of joy'; but we ought not to understand the explorers here in a good sense, such as Moses had sent to explore the land of promise, but in the contrary sense, such as the Apostle too says that he avoids: Because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who came in to explore our liberty which we have in Christ, and of whom Joseph speaks: You are explorers; you have come to examine the tracks of the land, and his brothers, understanding that it is no small crime to explore other people's things through ambush, answered: Your servants are not explorers. These, then, multiply the fairs of Tyre not with gold nor with precious stone, but with silver, iron, tin and lead, having the charm of eloquence and weapons for assault, and in the tin the likeness of eloquence, which counterfeits silver, and in the lead the heaviest impiety, according to Zechariah, in whom a woman sits upon a talent of lead, and the Egyptians were sunk into the deep like lead. The discussion of the individual metals would be long, but we must strive for brevity.

27:13-14

Greece, Tubal and Meshech, they were your dealers; they brought slaves and vessels of bronze to your people. From the house of Togarmah they brought horses and horsemen and mules to your market. (LXX: "All Greece and the parts adjacent to it, they were your traders in the souls of men, and they gave vessels of bronze as your merchandise. From the house of Togarmah they gave horses and horsemen and mules as your fairs.") 'The Ionians,' he says, '— who in Hebrew are called Iauan —, and Tubal — that is, the eastern Iberians, or the Spaniards from the regions of the west, who are called by this name from the river Iberus —, and Meshech — whom we understand as the Cappadocians, whose metropolis, which was later called Caesarea by Augustus Caesar, is to this day called Mazaca in their own language —, these made the precious commerce of Tyre, bringing slaves and bronze vessels from Corinth to Tyre, and from the house of Togarmah, that is, from Phrygia, horses and horsemen and mules, of which that province once had the greatest abundance'. The Hebrews say that 'Greece', that is, 'Iauan', means 'is and is not', which refers properly to secular 'wisdom', in which, if they find something rightly, it is called 'is', if in the contrary sense, 'is not'. For they too, by the good of nature, discourse much on duties, on continence, on despising riches — which the Stoics properly claim for themselves —, and they seem to gain the souls of the men whom they have deceived; and they have bronze vessels, with which they counterfeit the likeness of gold, which they press upon the peoples of Tyre so as to trip them up with the opinion of false doctrine; from the house too of 'Thogorma', which means 'pilgrim' and 'stranger', horses will be brought to its market and fairs, and horsemen and mules, of which it is written: A horse is a deceitful thing for safety, and in another place: All who mounted horses have slumbered, and in the Psalms: Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding; for which reason Doeg too, the accuser and slayer of the priests, was also the overseer of many; and that these are from the house of the stranger and pilgrim, who do not eat the flesh of the lamb, of whom it is written: The stranger and the hireling shall not eat of it, so that all the fairs of Tyre are filled with these wares.

27:15a

The sons of Dadan were your traders. In place of which, intending I know not what, the Seventy translated 'the sons of the Rhodians', unless perhaps by the deceptive similarity of the first letter, so that instead of 'Dadan' they read 'Radan', which itself is also the largest of the Cyclades, and was once a most powerful city in the Ionian Sea and glorious in naval combat, and, because of its very safe harbor, the resort of all merchants. And since 'Rhodians' is rendered in our language 'seeing judgment', it is now said tropologically of those who discern the truth of judgment and do not themselves do it, as the Apostle says: Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, every one who judges; for in that in which you judge another, you condemn yourself, for you do the same things which you judge. But it is better to take 'Dadan' as the name of another place, as it is found in the Hebrew and among the other translators.

27:15b-16

Many islands were the trade of your hand: they exchanged teeth of ivory and of ebony at your price. The Syrian was your trader because of the multitude of your works: drop, purple and checkered cloths and byssus and silk and chodchod they set out in your market. (LXX: "From the islands they multiplied your trade: elephants' teeth, and to those who were brought in you paid your wages. Men were your trade from the multitude of your market: in aphec, stacte, and many-threaded cloths from Tharsis, and ramoth and chodchod they gave as your fairs.") The edition of the Seventy differs much from the Hebrew in the present place; therefore a few things must be said according to each, lest, occupied with the wares of Tyre, we pass too slowly to the remaining prophecies. The sons of Dadan, the traders of Tyre, multiplied its trade from many islands, so that they gave elephants' teeth to those who came to its commerce, and had men in the fairs because of the multitude of the trade. They had, moreover, 'in aphec' — which was added in the Seventy from the edition of Theodotion, for which Symmachus rendered 'polymita' [many-threaded cloths] —, 'stacte' too — for which all the others translated 'purple', which in Hebrew is called 'argaman' —, and 'varieties from Tharsis' — for which in the Hebrew 'bus' is said, which has been translated by all as 'byssus'. But Tharsis is not found at all in the present place —. And 'ramoth', they say, and 'chodchod' they gave as your fairs — which is found so in the Hebrew, except that for 'ramoth' Aquila translated 'silks' or 'fine stuffs'; but 'chodchod' all the translators rendered just as it is set down in the Hebrew —'. Therefore, according to the Seventy, the sons of the Rhodians, traders of Tyre, multiplied its trade from very many islands; according to the Hebrew, after the sons of Dadan, its traders, islands too of various nations increased its merchandise, bringing teeth of ivory from India and ebony wood — which, being of a black color, are most precious —, and exchanged them for other wares of Tyre. 'The Syrian' too was a trader of Tyre, for which in the Hebrew is set down 'aram', in whose place the Seventy translated 'men', reading 'adam' for 'aram', deceived, as above, by the similarity of the letters 'res' and 'daleth' [r and d]. And to this day there remains in the Syrians an inborn ardor for trade: they run about through the whole world out of desire for gain, and they have such a madness for trading that, now that the Roman world has been seized, they seek riches amid swords and the slaughter of the wretched, and flee poverty through dangers; men of this kind are the traders of Tyre who deal in many-threaded cloths, purple and checkered cloths, and who set out byssus too, and silk and chodchod, in the market for her. For 'purple', which all translated, the Seventy rendered 'stacte', that is, 'drop'; but what 'chodchod' signifies I have not been able to find up to the present — the Hebrews say that all the most precious wares are signified by this name, or that it is a certain kind of precious wares which the Roman tongue does not express, or that it is the common term of those who sell trinkets —. But from many islands, to pass to the ἀναγωγὴν, which are beaten by the salty and bitter waves of this age, the traders of Dadan bring teeth of ivory, promising the whiteness of eloquence, of which it is written: From the ivory houses, from which the daughters of kings delighted you in your honor; but they are not white, nor do they imitate the bride of whom it is said: Who is this who comes up made white, leaning upon her kinsman?, but are of ebony, of a black color, who cannot change their blackness, as Jeremiah says: If the Ethiopian will change his skin and the leopard his mottling. 'The Syrian' too, that is, 'aram', who means 'lofty' and swells with pride, is a trader of Tyre, and in the multitude of the Tyrian works he brings in the knowledge falsely so called, promising many varieties and 'stacte' of the best odor, and purple of royal dignity, and checkered cloths from the dialectical art, and byssus, for which the Seventy translated 'Tharsis', given over to the works of the earth, and silk, for which in the Hebrew is written 'ramoth', which means 'vision of death' — for all earthly works hasten to destruction —, and 'chodchod', whatever it is that is understood by it, setting them out in the fairs of Tyre. 'Dadan', moreover, judging from those wares which are said to be brought by its traders and islands, is to be understood either as the region of India, or, as some suppose, as that of the Edomites and of the vast desert, and it sounds 'kinship', so that we may recognize in the heretics a likeness of the divine doctrines.

27:17

Judah and the land of Israel, they were your dealers in first wheat; balsam and honey and oil and resin they set out in your fairs. (LXX: "Judah and the sons of Israel, these were your traders in the commerce of grain and in ointments; first honey and oil and resin they gave in your fairs.") The Hebrew word 'phanag' Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated just as it is set down among the Hebrews; for it the Seventy rendered 'ointments', we 'balsam'. It is told, moreover, with what supplies the land of Judea, which is now called Palestine, abounds: grain, balsam, honey and oil and resin, which are brought by Judah and Israel to the fairs of Tyre. And since the letter is plain, according to the spiritual sense we say: the land of confession and the understanding of one who sees God, which refers to the Church, ought not to bring to Tyre the first wheat, which, falling into the earth, is multiplied and is taken for the word of God: for not by bread alone does man live, but by every word of God; then balsam, which grows in the vineyards of En-gedi, or ointment, of which it is written: Like the ointment on the head, which runs down onto the beard, the beard of Aaron; and honey, of which Solomon also speaks: Finding honey, eat as much as is enough; for if you eat more, you will vomit it up, since through excessive surfeit honey turns into wormwood; oil too, from which the lamp is lit in the tabernacle of God, lest that prophetic word be applied to us: You were selling oil in Egypt; for if it is in Egypt and in Tyre, it will be turned into its contrary, and it will be said of it: But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head; and resin too is gentle, suited to bodies, and is taken for medicine, whence it is written in Jeremiah also: Is there no resin in Gilead; or is there no physician there? Why has the healing of the daughter of my people not gone up?; this resin Jacob too had, and he sent it to his son Joseph with honey and terebinth, nuts, incense and stacte; the Ishmaelites too, who bought Joseph from the land of Israel, were carrying these things to Egypt: incense and resin from Gilead and stacte. And that we may know more clearly what it is to bring grain, balsam, honey and oil and resin to the market of Tyre, let us hear the words of the Lord, who says: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine; to the Canaanite woman also, who was praying for her daughter, saying: My daughter is badly troubled by a demon, the Lord answered: It is not right to take the children's bread and give it to dogs. But because she had gone out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon and was drawing near to the land of Israel, she therefore obtained what she had asked.

27:18

The Damascene was your trader in the multitude of your works, in the abundance of various riches, in rich wine, in wool of the best color. (LXX: "Damascus was your trader in the multitude of your works, out of the multitude of all your strength: wine from Chelbon and wool from Miletus.") For 'rich wine', which Symmachus translated, both in Aquila and Theodotion and in the Hebrew itself it has 'wine from Chelbon'; and again, where we have put 'wool of the best color' or 'shining', Aquila and Theodotion translated 'in wool of Soor'. It signifies, moreover, that among the other trades of Tyre, very rich wine and choice wool were brought to its fairs from Damascus, which we see to this day. But if 'Damascus' means 'drinking blood', and it is a true tradition of the Hebrews that the field in which Abel was killed by the fratricide Cain was in Damascus, whence the place too is marked with this name — rightly, too, Paul, after the killing of Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, went to Damascus to lead believers in Christ bound to Jerusalem, and, by the mercy of God, who makes the seeing and the blind, he lost the eyes of the flesh so as to receive those of the mind, and the scales of the dragon fell from his eyes, through which he had lost the light of truth, so that he went to the street which is called 'Straight', and found 'Ananias', who in our language means 'obedient' —, from this land, then, to which it was said: Cursed is the earth which opened its mouth and drank the blood of your brother, the fairs of Tyre are gathered, and rich wine or shining wool, for which 'Chelbon' means 'milky', and for 'wool of the best color', 'wool from Miletus' — or 'Soor': 'Miletus' is not found in the Hebrew, but because choice wool is brought from there, those who translated understood 'Miletus' for 'Soor' —; from which it is to be perceived that Tyre feeds on the milk of infancy, and has no garments of its own, but from elsewhere: gathered from various provinces. That 'Damascus' means 'blood of sackcloth' and 'blood of a kiss' does not suit the present place; for Hebrew names are frequently interpreted variously, according to the diversity of accents and the change of letters and vowels, especially those which have their own properties among them.

27:19

Dan and Greece and Mozel set out wrought iron in your fairs; stacte and calamus were in your trade. (LXX: "※ Dan and Iauan and Mozel in your fairs ⁚" — which in their edition were added from Theodotion —; "iron made by workmanship and a wheel is in your mixture.") From the name of the patriarch Dan both the tribe and the place in which the tribe dwelt received their name, where today is Paneas, which was formerly called Caesarea Philippi, whence the river Jordan too obtained its name: 'Ior', that is, stream, 'Dan', which flows from Lebanon; 'Iauan', moreover, sounds 'Greece', which means, as we have said, 'is and is not'; for 'Mozel' too Symmachus translated 'bringing', so that the sense is: 'Dan and Greece brought wrought iron into your fairs, and the rest'; but Aquila for 'Mozel' put 'from Uzal', from which regions we must believe that iron and stacte and calamus were carried to the fairs of Tyre. And let us say that Greece, that is, Iauan, has wrought iron, most ready for wars and constructed by the dialectical art, boasting that it brings forth all things by judgment and reason, and that it promises a vocal sound, which is interpreted in the calamus, and stacte of the best odor; or wrought iron, and a wheel which revolves in the composition of words and has the course of speech.

27:20

Dadan were your dealers in carpets for sitting. (LXX: "Dedan were your traders with choice beasts for chariots.") The Hebrew and the Seventy differ much in the present place, except for the name of the region, which is close: 'Dedan' and 'Dadan'. For there is an infinite distance between 'carpets for sitting' and 'choice beasts for chariots'; nor is there any doubt that four-horse teams, chariots and horses are taken in the bad sense if they are earthly; otherwise, of heavenly ones, Elijah too is carried off in a chariot, and is called by Elisha: Father, father, charioteer and chariot of Israel, and the eyes of Gehazi are opened, so that he sees chariots on the mountain and horses without riders, prepared for the Lord's seat; but in the carpets the beauty of words is shown, on which the dealers of Dedan ride and rest, in a composed sitting, coming to the fairs of Tyre.

27:21

Arabia and all the princes of Kedar, they were the traders of your hand; with lambs and rams and kids they came to you. For 'lambs, rams and kids' the Seventy translated 'camels and rams and lambs'. Arabia and the princes of Kedar — which today is the region of the Saracens —, as has been shown most fully in the discourse of Jeremiah which is written against Kedar, abound in these animals, namely lambs and rams and kids — and it multiplies the fairs of Tyre by this importation —, and it is also a region most fertile in camels, because of the breadth of the desert's pastures and the mildness of the air, in which this animal delights. 'Arabia', moreover, means 'evening', and 'Cedar' 'darkness', of which it is also said in the Psalms: I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; these regions bring to Tyre camels weighed down with the heaviest burdens of sins, or lambs and rams and kids, which they sacrifice on their altars, which they have feigned out of an iniquitous, rebellious heart. But in this same prophet too, in the vision of the shepherds, we read of rams troubling the purest waters and thrusting at the sheep with their flanks and fighting with their horns; of kids too, which are accustomed to stand at the left; and of lambs, which counterfeit the lamb of whom it is written: Behold the lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world. But in the good sense: Isaiah writes that camels from 'Madian' — which means 'judgment of the Lord' — come to Jerusalem, and Ephah, and the rams of Nebaioth, and Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense — the last two of which are also offered to the Lord by the Magi —; and these camels, having laid down the burden of sins, can enter the strait and narrow way which leads to life.

27:22

The sellers of Sheba and Rema, they were your traders, with all the first spices and with most precious stone and gold, which they set out in your market. In the Psalms, where it is written: The kings of the Arabians and of Saba will offer gifts to you, in the Hebrew it has: The kings of Saba and Saba will offer gifts to you, of which one 'Saba' is written with the letter 'sen', the other with 'samech', which is like our letter. Since, then, 'Saba' means 'conversion', this must be said: that in the present place it signifies not 'conversion' but 'aversion', from which gifts are brought to Tyre, with all spices and the best odors and precious stone and gold, all of which are set out in the fairs of Tyre; for they too counterfeit the best odor, and the precious stone with which they strive to build the churches of their perversity, and the gold which they promise in meaning, and all things are perverse — for they receive nothing freely nor give freely, but trade in everything, whereas the kings of the Arabians and of Sheba offer gifts to Christ freely —; these are they who do all things for the sake of shameful gain, and they have received these gifts from him who says in the Gospel: All these have been delivered to me, and these, if you fall down, I will give you. 'Rema', or, according to the Seventy, 'Regma', I have not been able to find in any other place of the Scriptures, nor what region it is, or what it signifies, except, what is clear, also from the fact that it is joined to Saba, that it is a region neighboring this province.

27:23-24a

Aran and Chenne and Eden were traders, Saba, Assur, Chelmad your sellers. They were your traders in many ways, in wrappings of hyacinth and of many-threaded cloths and of precious treasures, which were wrapped and bound with ropes. (LXX: "Charran and Channa and Edne, these were traders, Saba, Assur and Chalmad your dealers, bringing trade ※ in Machalim and in Galima ⁚ hyacinth, and ※ polymita ⁚ choice treasures bound with ropes.") These too are nations containing the names of various places. What was added in the Seventy from Theodotion: In Machalim and in Galima, Symmachus translated: In precious wrappings; 'polymita' too, for which Theodotion translated 'varied', we added from Aquila and Symmachus — the garments of the traders were so precious that they were carried in wrappings and bound with ropes of hyacinth —; 'Aran', or, as the Seventy said, 'Charran', sounds in our language 'holes'; 'Chenne', 'preparation'; 'Eden', 'delights', for which among the Seventy is 'Edne', which is not found in the Hebrew; what it sounds we do not know, and we ought not to seek the ἐτυμολογιὰν of a fictitious name. In the trade of Tyre, then, through the fleshly senses, which are indicated in the holes, is the whole preparation of the men of the world, who think it the only delights if they increase the commerce of the Tyrian city. Of 'Saba' we have spoken above; 'Assur' means 'directing'; 'Chelmad', or, as is contained in some copies, 'Cherma', is rendered 'vineyards'; no doubt those of the Sodomites, who come into the market of Tyre so that they may direct crooked things, or rather may rebuke with punishments and correct what had been perverted, according to that which is said in the Psalms: That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger. And they have manifold equipment, distinguished with incredible variety, which is bound in wrappings of hyacinth; or their treasures, which they have treasured up for themselves on earth, are bound with ropes, according to what is written: Each one is bound with the ropes of his own sins, and they did not have a free trade, but bound everything with the chains of sins. The wrappings of hyacinth, because of the similarity of the color, I shall refer to the powers of the air, which lavish their treasures on the fairs of the world.

27:24b-25a

They also had cedars in your trades. The ships of the sea (or, as is contained in the Hebrew: Tharsis) were your princes in your trade. For 'cedars' the Seventy translated 'cypresses'. And since we have spoken of both above, it is superfluous to increase the reader's weariness.

27:25b

And she was filled and glorified (or weighed down) exceedingly in the heart of the sea. 'Nothing,' he says, 'was lacking to you that pertains to the riches of the islands; yet that glorification was a weighing down of the possessor, since you cannot bear riches with moderation, although poverty too is often a temptation' — whence Solomon too asks only for necessities, and detests riches and poverty alike, lest pride creep in in the one, and in the other impatience and lying.

27:26a

Your rowers brought you into many waters. Above we read that the rowers of the Tyrian city were the 'Sidonians' and the 'Aradians', of whom the one mean 'hunters', the others 'those who put down': for they hunt the souls of those whom they lead by their own will amid the waves of this age, and they do not lift them up to the heights but sink them into the depths; nor do they imitate those who, sailing until the morning watch, broke the raging waves of the sea and were found worthy to receive the Lord Savior, and at once, with such a passenger and companion, reached the harbor of rest. Of which it is written more fully in the Gospel.

27:26b

The south wind has shattered you in the heart of the sea. All the riches of Tyre perish when the 'south wind' blows, which more expressively is called in Hebrew 'cadim', and is rendered in Greek καύσων, which we can translate as 'burning wind'; of which the holy man also said: By day the sun will not burn you, nor the moon by night. By this wind Jacob had been burned, and yet not shattered, when he says: I was burned by day by the heat and by the frost of night; those too who were hired from the first hour bore the heat and burning of the whole day, and yet they receive the denarius, because they were burned and not shattered; whence the bride too says in the Song: I am black and beautiful, because there has looked down on me (or, as is better contained in the Hebrew, there has discolored me) the sun.

27:27a

Your riches and your treasures and your manifold equipment. Many read thus: In the heart of the sea are your riches and your treasures and your manifold equipment, so that all the riches of Tyre and all its substance are set in the heart of the sea and are overwhelmed by the waves of the world, and its inhabitants have nothing stable and lasting, that Gospel word being fulfilled: Fool, this night they will take your soul from you; and what you have prepared, whose will it be?, and that apostolic one: Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and many snares, and are dragged down into the depth. The history is plain; and therefore we fit short little comments to almost each little verse. For our discourse is already hastening to the end of the book.

27:27b

Your sailors (or rowers) and your pilots, who held your equipment and were over your people; and your men of war who were in you, with all your multitude which is in your midst, will fall in the heart of the sea on the day of your ruin. The rowers, or sailors, of the Tyrian city — we read that they are the Sidonians and the Aradians, of whom we have already spoken, and, according to the edition of the Seventy, the counselors of 'Byblus', which in Hebrew is called 'gebal' —, its men of war too — Persians, Lydians and Libyans —, will all fall and be shown to be of no account, when Tyre has fallen and all its glory has had the end of ruin; but the multitude — which the Seventy translated 'mixture' —, apart from the princes, signifies the common people, who, without titles of dignity, will be crushed by a like judgment. And the prophecy is mixed between the city and the ship, so that from the one you may understand the other; and yet both pertain to the consummation of the age and to shipwreck.

27:28-32a

At the sound of the cry of your pilots the fleets will be troubled, and they will come down from their ships, all who held the oar (or the sailors and all the pilots of the sea), and the passengers and the prow-men will stand on the land, and they will wail over you with a loud voice and cry out bitterly, and they will cast dust upon their heads and be sprinkled with ash (or will strew ash for themselves). But what follows, ※ And they will shave baldness over you, and gird themselves with sackcloth, and weep for you in bitterness of soul with most bitter weeping, and take up over you a mournful song, and lament you ⁚, is not found in the Seventy, but was added from the edition of Theodotion. When Tyre has fallen, its pilots will be troubled and will come down from the fleets, and the rowers and passengers and prow-men — or the sailors and all the pilots of the sea —, tossed by the waves, will at last stand with a firm step; they will wail with a loud voice over her whom they formerly enriched with their wares, and will mark the bitterness of their mind with a cry; dust too — or earth — they will cast upon their heads, doing penance for earthly works, and they are sprinkled with ash, either of the heifer according to the law, so that they may be purified, or at least they will strew ash under themselves — according to what is said to Jerusalem: Sprinkle earth upon your head, and strew ash under you, and make lament, and in the Gospel it is written: If these signs had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have done penance in sackcloth and ash, and the psalmist says: I have eaten ash like bread —; and they will shave the head over Tyre and make baldness, which is customarily done in mourning, at the time when the greatness of grief has shut out all gladness — but the hairs of the apostles were numbered, because they had consecrated their hair to the Lord after the manner of the Nazirites; and Samson, as long as he had his locks, possessed strength; when his hair was taken away, he was captured by the foreigners —; and when it is said: And they will gird themselves with sackcloth, the old lust of the loins is condemned, so that those who had lived in delights may afterwards, doing penance, live in austerity and hardness — the Ninevites had sackcloth; and again it is said to Jerusalem: Lament to me like a bride girded with sackcloth over the husband of her virginity —. And they will weep for you, he says, in bitterness of soul with most bitter weeping — for it is better to go into the house of mourning than into the house of feasting —, so that they may lament Tyre and redouble the mournful song; which the following Scripture adds. But that we may know that there is profit for those who lament her as she falls, and who formerly dwelt in the heart of the sea and in its midst, let the example of the prophet teach us, who himself too is commanded to lament Tyre, so that, when the time of penance has been completed, she may be restored to her ancient state, and, having taken up the harp, may sound forth to the Lord: read Isaiah. Some, ridiculously — but still, what we have read must be told — interpret the 'pilots' as the bishops of the heretics, the 'counselors' as the presbyters, the 'prow-men' as the archdeacons, the 'rowers' and 'sailors' as the deacons, and they refer the 'passengers' to the whole people — if they had added the 'shipmaster' as the devil, they would have completed the tragedy —, who will all wail together and weep most bitterly and do penance after they have perceived the shipwreck of their ship and have stood on land, and have lost all the beauty of the knowledge falsely so called, and in place of joy and gladness have marked their penance with grief in bitterness of heart.

27:32b-36

Who is like Tyre, which has become dumb (or has fallen silent) in the midst of the sea? — which is not found in the Seventy —. You who, in the going out of your trades (or what reward you found), from the sea filled many peoples, in the multitude of your riches and of peoples enriched many kings; now you have been crushed by the sea (or in the sea), your wealth is in the depths of the waters (or your trade); and all your multitude which was in your midst have fallen. All the inhabitants of the islands were astonished (or were crushed) over you, and all their kings, struck by the storm (or turned to madness), changed their countenances (or wept); the traders of the nations (or of the peoples) hissed over you: you have been brought to nothing (or you have become perdition), and you will be no more for ever (or in perpetuity). The pilots, rowers, prow-men and passengers will recall these things in the lament of Tyre: what other of the cities has so fallen silent that it had no confidence to speak, and heard that Gospel word: Be silent and be dumb, and that from the Psalms: But to the sinner God said: Why do you declare my righteousnesses, and take my covenant in your mouth?. 'With how great wares, O Tyre, have you been enriched? And what have you sought with so much labor, that by day and by night you should gather what was to perish by shipwreck? You did indeed fill many peoples and enriched kings with your wealth — of whom it is written: The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ —; but now you have been crushed in the sea and in the depths of the waters' — according to what is written of Pharaoh: The chariots of Pharaoh and his strength he cast into the sea, who sank into the depth like a stone and could say: I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm sank me —. 'All the islands, or the inhabitants of the islands, which are beaten by the waves of this age, will be astonished over you, and their kings, struck by the storm, will perceive their own destruction, and, imitating the voice of the serpent, will hiss and say: You have been brought to nothing (or you have become perdition) — so that you had not the nature of perdition, but the will —, and you will not be' — if he had spoken up to this point, a great question would arise: how it should not be, when we now see it built up; but from what follows: 'for ever', he shows the time of one age, which, according to the age of man, is reckoned in a cycle of seventy years —, or 'you will not be to God' — as the Apostle says: Who called the things that were not, and Isaiah the prophet: Behold, all your adversaries will be confounded and will blush; for they will be as though they were not, and Esther, according to the Seventy translators: Do not hand over your scepter to those who are not, and in the Psalms: Spare me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and be no more; in what sense these testimonies are to be taken we have said above —. All these things, moreover, we can refer to the person of the heretics, who, in the crushing and shipwreck of Tyre, will perceive their error, and, set in the midst of the sea, will long to free their souls, and will lament the riches wrongly gathered, with which they had enriched many kings, namely their patriarchs, and the ignoble common people, whose wealth will collapse in the midst of the sea; the inhabitants too of all the islands — if, however, we wish to refer what has been said to the good sense — will be astonished over the crushing of Tyre, and the kings of all the islands either will themselves, as if struck by a storm, change their countenances, or at least will show the grief of their heart with weeping and tears, and will testify to the greatness of their stupor with wonder and hissing, at how she has been brought to nothing and has perished who promised salvation to many nations; and she will be no more, not at all for a fixed time — so that we should interpret αἰῶνα as 'in the age' —, but in perpetuity, because the same word signifies both.

Book Nine

It would have been fitting, daughter Eustochium, for me to take in the prophecy of Tyre and of the prince of Tyre in a single volume, and by no means to separate by the order of the books those that are joined as much by their places as by the prophecy. But because the things that are said are many and exceed the measure of length, the explanation has therefore been deferred to the ninth book; and we believe that through your prayers and those of all the saints it will reach its end, so that we may also discuss what is written in Ezekiel against Pharaoh and all Egypt. These too, by their own length, must be divided by us into a tenth book, so that the measure of the volumes in relation to one another may be kept, and the labor of the one dictating, of the one writing and of the one reading, being divided, may draw breath in its parts.

28:1-10

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been lifted up, and you have said: I am God, and I have sat in the chair of God in the heart of the sea; though you are a man and not God, and you have set your heart as the heart of God. Behold, you are wiser than Daniel, no secret is hidden from you; in your wisdom and your understanding you have made strength for yourself, and you have acquired gold and silver in your treasuries; in the multitude of your wisdom, in your trading you have multiplied strength for yourself, and your heart has been lifted up in your might. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been lifted up as the heart of God, therefore behold, I will bring upon you strangers, the mightiest of the nations; and they will bare their swords against the beauty of your wisdom, and they will defile your comeliness. They will slay you and drag you down, and you will die in the destruction of the slain in the heart of the sea. Will you indeed speak, saying: I am God, before those who slay you, though you are a man and not God in the hand of those who kill you? By the death of the uncircumcised you will die in the hand of strangers, for I have spoken, says the Lord God. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been exalted, and you have said: I am God, I have dwelt in the dwelling of God in the heart of the sea; but you are a man and not God, and you have set your heart as the heart of God. Are you wiser than Daniel? The wise have not instructed you with their discipline: did you by your erudition or your understanding make strength for yourself, and make gold and silver in your treasuries, or by your great erudition and your trading did you multiply your strength? Your heart has been raised up in your strength. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have set your heart as the heart of God, on account of this behold, I will bring upon you strangers, pestilent ones from the nations; and they will unsheathe their swords against you, upon the beauty of your learning, and they will humble your beauty in perdition. And they will bring you down and lay you low, and you will die the death of the wounded in the heart of the sea. Will you indeed, speaking, say: I am God, in the sight of those who slay you? But you are a man and not God in the multitude of those who wound you. By the deaths of the uncircumcised you will die in the hands of strangers, for I have spoken, says Adonai the Lord.") Wherever, according to the Seventy, 'Lord, Lord' is set down twice, the first name is the tetragrammaton, which belongs properly to God and is called 'ineffable', the second is the common one, which is often found among men as well. Now just as, under the figure of a ship, first the riches of the city of Tyre and then its ruin and lament were described, so the prophetic word is addressed first to the prince of Tyre, that he was raised up through pride and did not use well the wealth that he had, then comes mourning and lamentation over the great goods from which he came to such great evils. First things, then, must be said first. It is written in Isaiah of the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, that he made himself equal to the power of God and was lifted up into such arrogance that he dared to say: I will ascend above the stars of heaven, and I will be like the Most High — and, cast headlong from his throne, he deserved to hear: How has Lucifer fallen, who rose in the morning? —, and of Pharaoh in this same prophet: The rivers are mine, and I made them, and of the prince of Tyre, that with lifted-up heart he said arrogantly: I am God and I sit in the chair of God (or I have dwelt in the dwelling-place of God), though he is a man and not God; and these words, although they seem to exceed the strength of human frailty and to be the words not so much of men as of raving demons, we must nevertheless take as ὑπερβολὴν [hyperbole, exaggeration]: that they swelled up to such a degree and did not know their own measure that, lifted up by the prosperity of the world and the power of their kingdom, while they think present goods to be everlasting, they did not know that they were men and claimed eternal rule for themselves; although under the type of princes and kings and of individual cities or provinces the adverse powers are shown — of whom the apostle Paul also writes: Our fight is not against flesh and blood, but against the princes and powers and rulers of this darkness and the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places, and in another place: We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this world, nor of the princes of this age, who are being destroyed, and, again discussing wisdom, he says: Which none of the princes of this world knew: for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory; in the prophecy of Daniel too one reads plainly: The prince of the Israelite people Michael, and the prince of Greece, and the prince of the Persians; and Moses writes more openly in the song of Deuteronomy: When the Most High was dividing the nations, was scattering the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God (or, as it stands better in the Hebrew, according to the number of the sons of Israel); and the Lord's portion became his people, Jacob, the cord of his inheritance Israel; nor shall we wonder that on the contrary side the worst kings go before as a type of the transgressing princes, since we teach that the best kings, David and Solomon and Josiah, and the patriarchs and prophets went before in figure of the Lord Savior —. Therefore let us discuss what is written according to both understandings, that of proud kings and equally that of apostate princes: 'Though you are', he says, 'in the midst of the sea, and are held in the narrow confines of an island, and, I will say more, though you are a man and surrounded by the frailty of human flesh, lifted up by the swelling of your heart you have supposed that you dwell on the throne of God, in the heavens; and at the same time, because you boast of wisdom, so much so that the men of your kingdom challenged Solomon with riddles: are you then wiser than Daniel, who by the grace of God overcame all the magi and soothsayers and is now the wisest in Babylon?' Or it is to be understood thus: 'Even if you are wiser than Daniel, who by the confession of all is the wisest, and by the greatness of your riches and power desire to make yourself equal to the power of God, nevertheless you will be taken by your adversaries and, your city lost, you will be pierced with many wounds, and you will no longer say: I am God; taught by your destruction that you are a man, not God'. But if we wish to say that the prince of Tyre is that same power to whom the city itself, or province, was entrusted by God, let us take up that testimony: I said: You are gods, and all sons of the Most High. But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes; for provinces were handed over to them to rule, as to judges, by the Emperor; and they, forgetting that their honor depended on the command of another, such as Heraclianus lately was in Africa, rose up with a tyrant's mind against their king and Lord, so that, scattered through the whole world, under the names of idolatry, they took to themselves the names of gods and, puffed up with pride, fell into the judgment and the snare of the devil, of which the Savior also spoke in the Gospel: I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven.

28:11-19

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, raise a lament over the king of Tyre, and you shall say to him: Thus says the Lord God: You, the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in comeliness; you were in the delights of the paradise of God, every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz and jasper, chrysolite and onyx and beryl, sapphire and carbuncle and emerald; gold, the work of your comeliness, and your openings were prepared on the day on which you were formed. You, a Cherub stretched out and protecting; and I set you on the holy mountain of God; you walked in the midst of the fiery stones, perfect in your ways from the day of your formation, until iniquity was found in you. In the multitude of your trading your inner parts were filled with iniquity, and you sinned. And I cast you out from the mountain of God, and I destroyed you, O protecting Cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was lifted up in your comeliness; you lost wisdom in your beauty: I cast you down to the earth, I set you before the face of kings that they might behold you. In the multitude of your iniquities and the iniquity of your trading you have polluted your sanctification; I will therefore bring forth a fire from your midst which shall devour you, and I will make you ashes upon the earth in the sight of all who see you. All who see you among the nations will be astonished over you; you have been made nothing, and you shall not be for ever. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lament over the prince of Tyre, and say to him: Thus says the Lord God: You are the seal of likeness full of wisdom, and a crown of comeliness; you were in the delights of the paradise of God, you were surrounded with every good stone: with sardius and topaz and emerald and carbuncle and sapphire and jasper and silver and gold and ligure and agate and amethyst and chrysolite and beryl and onyx, and with gold you filled your treasuries, and your granaries in you they prepared from the day on which you were formed, with the Cherub anointed by God and dwelling in the tabernacle, and I set you on the holy mountain of God: you were in the midst of the fiery stones, you were unblemished in your days from the day on which you were created, until iniquities were found in you. From the multitude of your trading you filled your storerooms with iniquity, and you sinned. And you were wounded from the mountain of God, and the overshadowing Cherub led you out from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was raised up in your comeliness; your discipline was corrupted with your comeliness: because of the multitude of your sins and iniquities I cast you down to the earth, in the sight of kings I set you, that you might be put to shame. Because of the multitude of your sins and the iniquities of your trading I have defiled your holy things; and I will bring out fire from your midst, it will devour you, and I will make you ashes upon the earth in the sight of all who see you. And all who knew you among the nations will be saddened over you; you have become perdition, and you will be no more for ever.") Since we have learned who the prince of Tyre is and how he fell through pride, let us come to know the lamentation over him for his former glory. First he is reminded of what he was, so that he may grieve that he has lost what he had: You, he says, the seal of likeness, according to what John the evangelist says properly of the Savior: For him God the Father has sealed, and of men: He has sealed that God is true, and in the Psalms: The light of your countenance has been sealed upon us, O Lord, and in another place: Beloved, now we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, whence also it is said to God: Who will be like you?; for likeness is one thing, equality another. Hence that is a most savage heresy which confesses in Christ only the likeness of the Father and takes away his nature; but we say in the Son not only likeness but also equality — for this reason the Jews persecuted him: because not only did he break the sabbath, but he also made himself equal to God —; and where there is equality, there is the same nature and one substance. This is what the Apostle too says about likeness: 'My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you, that is, that you may recover his likeness, which you lost by your own fault'. And because in the Latin codices 'resignaculum' [unsealing] is read instead of 'signaculo' [seal] — since the one who translated, rendering word for word κακοζήλως [with misplaced zeal], set down 'resignaculum' for ἀποσφράγισμα [seal, seal-impression] according to the translation of the Seventy —, they accordingly understand it thus: that the king of Tyre unsealed and lost the seal of God and the figure that had been impressed as if in the softest wax, so that instead of a seal he made an unsealing, by no means having the image and likeness of God, according to which the first man too was formed, when God said: Let us make man according to our image and likeness; and it is to be noted that then only the image was made, while the likeness is completed in the baptism of Christ. And consequently to him to whom it was said: You, the seal of likeness, is joined: Full of wisdom and perfect in comeliness (or a crown of comeliness); for where the likeness of God is, there also is fullness of wisdom and perfect comeliness, or a crown of virtues, adorned and composed as if of various flowers, which the diligent man increases by his own effort while by industry he nourishes the good of nature, and the negligent man diminishes, according to what is said in Proverbs under the figure of a beautiful woman of bad character: As earrings in the nostrils of a pig, so is beauty to a woman of bad character. There follows: You were in the delights of the paradise of God — for which in the Hebrew there stands 'in eden' — which the history of Genesis also narrates — and 'eden' is rendered as 'delights' —, and fittingly, for distinction, he names the paradise 'of God', to show that there is also a contrary paradise, 'not of God', among those who change the truth into a lie and boast that they have paradise; by which word he shows that the one of whom it is written is by no means a man, but a contrary force that once dwelt in the paradise of God; although the Jews think that this is prophesied of Hiram king of Tyre through the τρόπον [figure of speech] which is called ὑπερβολὴ; and to him to whom it is said: You were in the delights of the paradise of God, or 'you were made', it shows what he had, and what he lost. Further, as to what is joined to the dwelling in paradise: Every precious stone was your covering (or 'your binding and encircling'): sardius, topaz and jasper, chrysolite and onyx and beryl, sapphire and carbuncle and emerald, or, as in the Seventy, twelve stones are contained in a different order and with other names, this is to be observed: not that the king of Tyre was surrounded with every precious stone — or 'covered' and, as Symmachus translated, 'bound' and 'built in' —, but that every stone which the prince of Tyre had was precious. Otherwise there are many precious stones which Scripture does not name in the present passage: chalcedony, sardonyx, chrysoprase, jacinth, crystal too, and the most precious pearl; but Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion also differ greatly in the present passage, both among themselves and from the Seventy translators, not only in order but also in number and in names; in the Revelation of John too, where Jerusalem is recorded as built of living stones, the same stones, with the order changed a little in the last parts, are set in its foundations, so that its gates are written to have been built of the light of crystal; but on the breast of the high priest also the same stones are described, in four rows on the breastpiece, and on his shoulders two onyx stones, on which the names of the twelve patriarchs are written, which the true high priest, of whom it is written: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek, bears on his breast, bears on his shoulders, so as to show in the twelve stones the number of the apostles, and in the two the mysteries of both testaments; of whom one, John the evangelist, reclined on his breast to drink in the streams of wisdom, and to be able to say: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God; these are the living stones of which the Church is built, and the apostle Peter writes: If you have believed that the Lord is sweet. Coming to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, honorable, you also yourselves, as living stones, are built up as spiritual houses, into a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual victims, pleasing to God through Jesus Christ. For the scripture says: Behold, I will lay in Zion a corner stone, chosen, precious; and he who believes in it will not be confounded, on which the vessel of election also agrees with like voice, saying: Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus our Lord himself being the corner stone; in whom the whole building, being constructed, grows into a holy temple of God; these are the stones of which we also read in another place: 'Holy stones roll upon the earth, like wheels, barely touching the ground and by their rolling hastening to heavenly things', of which Scripture also makes mention: Behold, I prepare your stone, the carbuncle, and your foundations, sapphire; and I will set your ramparts, jasper, and your gates with crystal stone, and your wall with choice stones, and all your sons taught by God, and your sons in much peace; and in righteousness you shall be built, on which we have said what seemed right to us in our explanations of that same prophet; of stones of this kind Psalm 20 (21) also sings: Lord, in your strength the king will rejoice, and over your salvation he will exult exceedingly. You have granted him the desire of his soul, and you have not cheated him of the will of his lips. For you have gone before him with the blessing of sweetness; you have set on his head a crown of precious stone; these are the pearls of the prophets and apostles which, in comparison with Christ, are all sold in the Gospel so that the most precious pearl may be bought, and the stone of which Zechariah writes that it has seven eyes, that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, read Isaiah, and it is laid by the apostle Paul in the foundation of the Church, upon which gold, silver, precious stones are to be built; whose colors and natures and the powers of each it is not for this occasion to discuss, but they require a volume of their own, so that in Ezekiel and in Exodus and in Revelation and in Isaiah all the stones and the orders of the stones, compared with one another, raise a great question both for the reader and for the expositor; on which the holy man Bishop Epiphanius also handed me in person a volume of his own, and the thirty-seventh book of the Natural History of Pliny Secundus, after a manifold knowledge of all things, discusses gems and stones; to the knowledge of these the diligent reader must be sent by us; further, the translation of Symmachus writes that this prince of Tyre was studded with stones like a most precious necklace. Indeed it calls it a tympanum of gold, in which the stones were set; whence also according to the Hebrew there follows: Gold, the work of your comeliness, and your openings were prepared on the day on which you were formed; for which the Seventy set down: With gold you filled your treasuries, and your storehouses, referring it to the sense and mind, that his thought lay open to the divine mysteries and gathered for itself spiritual riches, of which the Lord commanded: Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor worm destroys, nor thieves dig through and steal. For where your treasure is, there is your heart also; this is the hidden treasure of which he also speaks in the Gospel: The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field; which he who finds hides, and for his joy goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field; and the storehouses, or granaries, are those of which it is written in another place: Blessed are your storehouses and your remnants. After this it is said, according to the Hebrew: You, a Cherub stretched out and protecting — it is understood: the ark of God and the mercy seat; or, according to the Seventy, 'that he himself was anointed and created with the Cherub'; from which it is shown that this cannot apply to a man, the prince of the city of Tyre, but to a force once holy and preeminent, which was set as prince of the city of Tyre —; and I set you, he says, on the holy mountain of God — no doubt it signifies paradise, to which the apostle Paul says he was caught up after the third heaven —; now 'Cherub' is said in the masculine gender, singular number, and in the plural they are called 'Cherubim', which means 'multitude of knowledge', upon whom God rests and sits, and he uses this chariot, as the prophet says to him: You who sit upon the Cherubim, show yourself, and in another place: He ascended upon the Cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds; this Cherub, then, or the one created with the Cherub, stretched out and protecting the mysteries, was set on the holy mountain of God, of which we have often spoken and of which the apostle Paul speaks — if anyone, that is, accepts the epistle to the Hebrews —: You have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and thousands of angels; or certainly the holy mountain of God is to be understood, as we said, as paradise. He walked too in the midst of the fiery stones, of which it is written: Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire; and not only does God, who is called 'a consuming fire', consume hay, wood and stubble, but so do the angels, who are called 'fiery stones' and are fervent in spirit; whence the Lord too: Fire, he says, I came to send upon the earth, and how I wish that it may burn. And what follows: Perfect in your ways from the day of your formation (for which the Seventy set down: You were unblemished in your days, from the day on which you were formed), until iniquity was found in you, shows that every creature was formed good by God and had perfect virtue, and through this that the prince of Tyre too was unblemished, so that the blemish thereafter is not of nature but of will. 'Until', he says, 'iniquity was found in you — found by God —, which was held shut up in the treasury of your breast, through pride and the abuse of the power you had received'; in the multitude of his trading, too, his inner parts, or storerooms, were filled with iniquity — for while he seeks out many things, and is not content with the knowledge he had received nor with the power over which he had been set, he filled the storerooms and inner parts of his breast —; so that, sated and grown fat, he kicked against his Creator: for Jacob ate indeed and was sated, and the beloved kicked back; he grew fat and was fattened and was enlarged, and forsook God who had made him, and: Out of the heart proceed the worst thoughts, on account of which God says: You sinned. And I cast you out from the mountain of God (or you were wounded from the mountain of God); reading this, we are compelled to fear: for if a Cherub stretched out and protecting, set on the holy mountain of God and in the midst of the fiery stones, perfect and unblemished, on account of the multitude of his trading filled his inner parts with iniquity, and sinned, and was cast out from the mountain of God — that is, from the dwelling of paradise — or was wounded from the mountain of God — which is plainly understood as Christ —, or certainly, while placed and dwelling on the mountain of God, was wounded by himself, and pricked by the evil of his conscience when he understands himself to be unworthy of dwelling on the mountain, what must be thought of us? For this reason it is said to him: 'And I destroyed you, O protecting Cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones, so that you should by no means stand among the fiery stones, but perish; O Cherub yourself, or the Cherubim who protected you, I led you out from the midst of the fiery stones', according to what is also written of Adam: He cast out Adam, and set him over against the paradise of delights. And he gives the reasons why he was led out, or cast out, from the midst of the fiery stones: 'For lifted up indeed was your heart in your comeliness, while you think yours what is God's'; whence the Apostle too says he received a goad of the flesh and an angel of Satan to buffet him, lest he be proud through the multitude of revelations and fall into the judgment of the devil. And therefore: 'Your learning has been corrupted', he says, 'with your comeliness (or you have lost your wisdom in your comeliness), so that, while you wish to be more than you were formed and to be wiser than you had received from God, you lost even what you had, and instead of beauty and learning, deformity and folly possessed you; whence you were cast down to the earth, you who formerly dwelt on the mountain of God — of whom Isaiah also writes: How has Lucifer fallen, who rose in the morning?, and the Savior in the Gospel: I was watching, he says, Satan like lightning falling from heaven, which Jeremiah also says to Jerusalem: How the Lord in his anger has darkened the daughter of Zion, has cast down from heaven to earth the glory of Israel —, and cast down in the sight of all kings so that they might be terrified by your example, whether the good kings, whose heart is in the hand of God, or the evil ones, whose kingdoms the devil showed to the Savior, who went to meet the Babylonian king, saying: You too have been taken as we were, and are counted among us'. Wherefore he also polluted his sanctification, which he had had when he dwelt on the mountain and lived in the midst of the fiery stones. There follows: I will bring forth fire in your midst which may devour you; this fire would be kindled in the heart of the king of Tyre by him whose darts are fiery, and of whom it is written: All adulterers, their hearts are like an oven, of which fire Isaiah also speaks: Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame which you have kindled, so that, going forth outward, it may devour its possessor, according to what is written in the same Isaiah: It will devour the matter like hay; on that day the mountains and hills and forests will be quenched, and it will devour from the soul even to the flesh; this fire, which is called strange, Nadab and Abihu had offered at the altar of the Lord, and therefore they were consumed by divine fire; whence Moses too says: This is the word which the Lord spoke: In those who draw near to me I will be sanctified; and the sanctification of God is the punishment of sinners. After this it is said: And I will make you ashes, so that the fire may consume all that you have built upon your evil conscience; you who, though you ought in the rest and the sabbath by no means to do servile work, gathered wood on the sabbath, so that the blaze might have something to devour in your breast. It is profitable too that all evil works be turned into ashes, so that the harmful fire may be utterly extinguished, and all may see and be astonished that the Tyrian king has perished and been made nothing, not for many ages, but for one, or certainly for ever, so that what is written may be fulfilled: I will not spare you, and I will not have mercy. The Hebrews, among their other fables and γενεαλογίας [genealogies] and endless questions, are accustomed to understand these things as spoken against Hiram king of Tyre, although from Solomon to Ezekiel there are a great many years, which it is evident men did not live at that time; and to pronounce it thus, as if the prophet were speaking to him in irony: 'Are you the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and perfect in comeliness, you adorned with all stones, you a Cherub, or created with a Cherub, when on the contrary you have sinned and are to be dissolved into ashes?'; and they add to their fable a marvel, so that, against the authority of Scripture, or rather without the authority of Scripture, they say: Hiram lived a thousand years. But how forced this interpretation is, the prudent reader understands without our judgment.

28:20-26

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set (or make firm) your face against Sidon, and you shall prophesy concerning it, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Sidon, and I will be glorified in you (or in your midst), and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have executed judgments in it (or in you) and have been sanctified in you (or in it). And I will send upon it (or into you) pestilence and blood in its streets (or your), and the slain (or the wounded) shall fall in its midst by the sword (or by swords) round about, and they shall know that I am the Lord. And there shall no longer be for the house of Israel a stumbling block of bitterness and a thorn bringing pain on every side round about, from those who oppose them (or who were doing them insult), and they shall know that I am the Lord God. Thus says the Lord God: When I have gathered the house of Israel from the peoples (or from the nations) among whom they have been scattered, I will be sanctified in them before the nations, and they shall dwell in their land which I gave to my servant Jacob; and they shall dwell in it secure (or in hope), and they shall build houses, and plant vineyards, and dwell confidently (or in hope), when I have executed judgments upon all who oppose them round about (or have done them insult), and they shall know that I am the Lord their God. (And what follows according to the Seventy: And the God of their fathers, is not found in the Hebrew.) Consequently, after Tyre, the word is addressed to Sidon; for both cities belong to one province, and in the Gospel Tyre and Sidon are named together: If in Tyre and Sidon had been done the mighty works which have been done in you, whence also the Canaanite woman, whose daughter was troubled by a demon, because she went out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, obtained what she had asked. Now the divine word foretells that it too is to be taken by the Babylonians, and that by the weight of its evils it is to know that he is the Lord, when he has judged it and been sanctified in it and consumed it by famine and pestilence and the sword, so that it falls in its streets and is no longer a stumbling block to the people of God, nor assails them frequently; and when this has been done, the people of Israel, whom he had scattered among various nations, are to return to their own land, and he is to be sanctified in them, not, as in Sidon, in the bad sense but in the good, when he has had mercy on them, and they have dwelt in the land which he gave to their father Jacob; and they have dwelt secure and trusting in the Lord, and have built houses and planted vineyards, when he has fulfilled his promises; and then they are to know that he is the Lord, whose promises are most firm. Many refer this to the time of Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah, when the people of Israel returned and dwelt in the land of Judea; but others hope that it is to be fulfilled in the last time and in the thousand years. Further, according to the spiritual understanding, this seems to us the sense. 'Sidonians' means 'hunters', of whom it is also written in the Psalms: Our soul has been snatched like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters, and again: For he will rescue me from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word, and in Proverbs the eye of a harlot is the snare of a sinner; but there are also hunters in the good sense, contrary to these, of whom Jeremiah writes: Behold, I will send fishers and hunters who will hunt you from every hill and mountain, whom the Lord also sends to fish, and makes them from fishers of fish into fishers of men; whence the little village of Peter and Andrew too is called by this name — for 'Bethsaida' means in our tongue 'house of hunters' —. Against these, then, the worst hunters, the word of God is directed, and the prophet is commanded to set, or make firm, his face against Sidon, and by no means to waver with every wind of doctrine, but, standing firm in the truth, he will slay the hunters. What, then, are the things with which the Lord threatens Sidon?: 'Behold, I myself will come to you, and I will be glorified in you when I have slain you; and all who live will know that I am the Lord, when I have repaid you what you deserve. And I will send pestilence and blood into your streets' — and rightly are the streets said to be Sidon's: for broad indeed and spacious is the way that leads to death —; and those who stood badly will fall slain by the sword round about, that sword which the Lord came to send upon the earth to separate what was badly joined; and those who remain will know that he is the Lord. And when they have ceased, there will no longer be a stumbling block of bitterness and a thorn of pain pricking and wounding the people of God. All these things, moreover, are said against the adverse powers: that in the last time they are to be destroyed, and there will be eternal security, when the Lord has gathered the house of Israel, those who discern God with the mind, and has been sanctified in them, and that will be fulfilled which is written: Be holy, for I am holy, and they have dwelt in their own land, of which we also read elsewhere: I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, which he had given to Jacob, who had supplanted his elder brother and had deserved to receive his birthright; and they will dwell in it secure, or in hope, and they will build houses and plant vineyards, and they will dwell a second time in hope, according to what is read in Isaiah: You who have been weaned from milk, who have been drawn from the breast, expect tribulation upon tribulation, hope upon hope; and they will build houses, such as he builds in the Gospel who laid his foundations not upon the sand but upon the rock, of which it is written: Unless the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it, and in Exodus, according to the Seventy: Because the midwives feared the Lord, they made houses for themselves, and many things of this kind; and when the Lord has executed judgment against those who oppose Israel round about, or treat it with insults, then every creature will know that he is the Lord, whose judgments are true and justified in themselves.

29:1-3a

In the tenth year (or, according to the Seventy, the twelfth), in the eleventh month (or, according to the Hebrew, the twelfth), on the first (or one) day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set (or make firm) your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and you shall prophesy concerning him, and concerning all Egypt you shall speak, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God. After Sidon, which itself too is situated on the coast of Phoenicia, the word comes to the prophet in the tenth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin, and in the twelfth month, and on one day of the month, that he should set his face, or make it firm, against Pharaoh king of Egypt and speak concerning all, or to all, Egypt; and that the province of Egypt, situated on the same coast on the other side of Judea, should be described, and the things that are to come upon it be prophesied. But if something must be said about the numbers: the place that one holds among ten days — whence also at the beginning of Genesis it is not said: There was evening and morning, day 'first', but 'one', so as to teach that the same day always comes round again — that same rank the tenth number will hold among ten decades, that is, the number one hundred, the tenth on which the lamb is taken up for the victim, to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day; and in this way, up to a thousand and ten thousand and a hundred thousand and beyond, the order of numbers proceeds by its decades; and after the tenth year the 'twelfth' month is set down, so that the perfect number of the twelve apostles and of the prophets — who are contained in one volume — may be shown; further, according to the Seventy, the 'tenth' month, which in Hebrew is called 'tebeth' and among the Egyptians 'tybi', and among the Romans is called 'Ianuarius' [January] because among them it is the door [ianua] of the year, holds the first place of winter's cold, all heat having been taken away; let it suffice to have said this about the numbers. But this above all must be inquired: whether it is the same Pharaoh who is named in Exodus and in Isaiah and Jeremiah and Ezekiel and in many other places, and in the Song: To my cavalry among the chariots of Pharaoh I have likened you, my near one, or one and then another; and it seems to me that he is not one, but that among the Egyptians the royal dignity is indicated by this word, just as among the Romans their kings are called 'Caesars' and 'Augusti' — from the first, Gaius 'Caesar', and the second, his adopted son Octavian, who was afterwards named 'Augustus' —, and among the Syrians 'Antiochuses', among the Persians 'Arsacids', among the Philistines 'Abimelech', and, after Alexander, in Egypt 'Ptolemies' down to Cleopatra, at whose defeat at Actium Egypt was made a Roman province; therefore at present the word of the Lord is spoken against any one whatever of the kings of Egypt, who is interpreted as διασκεδάστης, namely 'slayer' and 'mangler' and 'one who cuts down and divides all things with the sword'. This, according to the mystical senses, is to be referred to that power to which Egypt is subject; for a man would never dare to say: The rivers are mine and I made them, nor would he be called a 'dragon', 'great and sitting in the midst of his rivers'; now Egypt is called 'mesraim' in Hebrew, and into our language it is rendered ἐκθλίβουσα, that is, 'straitening' and 'afflicting' those who are subject to it, and not allowing them to lift their eyes to heaven but — according to the Gospel and the example of that woman whom the devil had bent over for eighteen years — always plunging them down toward earthly things. Let us see, then, what the threat is against Pharaoh and all Egypt.

29:3b-7
