And strangers and cruel men will cut it down (or the pestilent among the nations) — so that that which is written may be fulfilled: When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser, and again: Already the axe is laid to the roots of the tree —, and they will cut it down upon the mountains, so that it falls in its pride. In all moreover the valleys its branches will fall, so that all who were in his retinue are led down to Tartarus and withdraw from its shade and leave it, so that the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, which before had been under it and were covered by its shade, afterwards become partakers of its punishment. And when the other trees of the forests, or of paradise, see that Assyria the cypress has fallen by the sentence of the Lord, they will not be lifted up in pride, nor will they think themselves anything, nor will they consider the watering of their waters their own riches: because all the branches and the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth which were under the rule of Assyria are led down to death, to the lowest land — of whom it is written: In his sight all who go down into the earth will fall, and in another place: They will go into the uttermost parts of the earth —, and they will be by no means with the angels, but with the sons of men: Who go down into the pit (or into the ditch) everlasting. But when he has gone down into the uttermost part of the earth and has become the portion of foxes, by which he is to be torn, then there will be mourning, either of all his allies or of the holy powers, who will grieve that he has gone down to the underworld; whence the Lord says: I covered him with the deep, by whose waters he had before been nourished, and I held back its rivers, that is, the deep's, and restrained many waters, so that they would not water him but rather overwhelm him; Lebanon was saddened over him, in which he had been exalted, and all the trees of the field were shaken, dreading a like cutting down. At the sound of its fall I shook the nations, so that no one would be ignorant of his destruction and of his being led down to the underworld with his other allies; and all the trees of pleasure, that is, of paradise, received consolation, while they see evil things repaid to the evil and good things to the good — and these are the trees of Lebanon, watered by the waters of the rivers of the Lord, with which that tree too which fell had been watered; or all the trees which once were good and were watered by waters and dwelt on the height of Lebanon will receive consolation when they see their prince suffer like torments —; for they too will go down to hell to those slain by the sword of the Lord, and all the strength of the trees will dwell under its shade, that is, in punishment, in the midst of all the nations which will be held by the bars of hell. After this the discourse is turned to Pharaoh himself, to whom it had been said at the beginning: Whom have you become like in your height?, and it is said to him: To whom have you been likened, O renowned and lofty one among the trees of pleasure? — to the Assyrian, of course, who fell —: 'You too were renowned and lofty among the trees of Eden — that is, of delights and of paradise —, and behold, you have been led down like the Assyrian, with all the trees that were once in delights, to the lowest land and to the underworld; and you will sleep not in rest but in punishments, in the midst of the uncircumcised — that is, the unclean — and with those who fell by the sword of the Lord'; and so that we may know who it is to whom he said: O renowned and lofty one among the trees of pleasure, he puts it more openly: He is Pharaoh and all his multitude (or, according to the Seventy: So is Pharaoh and all his multitude), so that, as the Assyrian above was cut down and fell, so also the Egyptian may be overthrown.

32:1-16

And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month (or the tenth), on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lament over Pharaoh king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: You have been likened to the lion of the nations, and to the dragon that is in the sea; and you tossed with your horn in your rivers, and you troubled the waters with your feet, and you trampled their rivers (or your rivers). Therefore thus says the Lord God: I will spread my net over you in a multitude of many peoples, and I will draw you out in my dragnet (or I will draw you out on a hook); and I will cast (or I will draw) you onto the land, upon the face of the field I will throw you (or the plains will be filled with you), and I will make dwell (or sit) upon you all the birds of the sky, and I will glut the beasts of the whole earth with you; and I will put your flesh upon the mountains, and I will fill the hills (or the valleys) with your gore (or with your blood). And I will water (or the land will be watered) with the stench of your blood (or with your dung) upon the mountains, and the valleys will be filled with you; and when you have been extinguished I will cover the sky, and I will make its stars grow black: I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light; all the lights of the sky I will make mourn (or they will grow dark) over you, and I will put darkness upon your land, says the Lord God. And I will provoke the heart of many peoples, when I bring your destruction (or your captivity) among the nations upon a land (or in a land) which you do not know. And I will make stand astonished (or there will be saddened) over you peoples (or many nations), and their kings will tremble over you with exceeding horror, when my sword begins to fly over their faces, and each one will be suddenly dumbfounded for his own life on the day of his ruin (or awaiting their own ruin from the day of your ruin). For thus says the Lord God: The sword of the king of Babylon will come to you; by the swords of the mighty (or of giants) I will cast down your multitude (or your strength) — all of them invincible nations (or pestilent ones from all the nations) —, and they will lay waste (or destroy) the pride (or the insolence) of Egypt, and its multitude will be scattered (or all its strength). And I will destroy all its beasts that were beside many waters (or from many waters), and the foot of man will trouble them no more, nor will the hoof of beasts trouble (or trample) them; then I will make their waters most pure (or so that their waters may at length be at rest), and I will lead their rivers like oil (or so that they flow like oil), says the Lord God, when I have made the land of Egypt desolate (or ruined): and the land will be deserted of its fullness (or with its fullness) when I strike (or scatter) all its inhabitants, and they will know that I am the Lord. It is a lament, or they shall lament him; the daughters of the nations shall lament him; over Egypt and over its multitude (or all its strength) they shall lament him, says the Lord God. We mingle both editions, only in those places in which they disagree; otherwise, where there is one sense, we follow the Hebrew. In many copies, moreover, according to the Seventy 'the twelfth year' and 'the tenth month' is set down, but according to the other translators 'the tenth year' and 'the twelfth month', so that either Jerusalem has already been taken, and Pharaoh's joy, with evils hanging over him, is taken away, or at any rate it is about to be taken, and he should grieve more over his own miseries than rejoice at the captivity of others; and meanwhile, briefly laying down certain foundations of the history, let us run through what the Hebrews understand concerning this passage. Pharaoh is compared to a lion — not of one nation but of many nations — or to a dragon in the sea, so that he possesses land and waters; he was lifted up into 'pride' by the watering of the rivers — which he calls 'horn' — and, by the multitude of his army, passing through all the waters, he was able to trouble them. Therefore he says that he will spread his net over his multitude and draw him out with his dragnet — or hook —, and cast — or stretch — him out upon the land, him who like a serpent had been wound in many coils, so that he may be devoured by all the birds of the sky. And when not only the birds but all the beasts of the earth have torn him, the rest of his flesh will fill the mountains and valleys and plains, so that all things swarm with worms — and he says this by way of metaphor, so that, after the birds of the sky and the beasts have been glutted with his flesh, that is, his army and the whole multitude, the remaining part may be turned into worms and gore —: 'Then,' he says, 'the heavens will be wrapped in darkness: the sun and the moon and the other lights will not give their light, but over you all things will grow black, and nothing will be joyful for you. And at your destruction all peoples and all their kings will tremble with exceeding horror, seeing my sword flying this way and that and sparing no one, and in your ruin they dread a like ruin. But so that you may know what this sword is, hear it more plainly: The sword of the king of Babylon will come to you; by the swords of the mighty (or of giants) I will cast down all your multitude — which giants are the invincible nations that were held in the army of the Babylonian king —; these will lay waste (or will destroy) the pride of Egypt and all its multitude, and nothing will remain in Egypt, but together with the men the beasts and brute animals too will be carried off alike. And so great will be the desolation in Egypt that its waters will be troubled neither by the foot of man nor by the hoof of beast, but all things will be quiet; and the waters of its rivers will flow like oil, most pure and shining, with no one passing through them nor troubling their streams' — and this will come about because of the desolation of Egypt, which will be reduced to a desert, stripped of all its multitude, when the Lord has struck its inhabitants, so that those who remain may understand that he himself is the Lord —. Therefore it is a lament for Pharaoh, and the daughters of the nations round about will lament him, and not only over him, but also over his multitude which, as the Lord laid it waste, was blotted out. Let it suffice to have said these things in passing on the simple letter, so that we may come to the spiritual understanding. Nor do I think one must labor greatly to know who Pharaoh king of Egypt is, since we have spoken of it more fully above: namely that power to which Egypt was entrusted, whether one province or the Egypt of the whole world, which was not created a lion but by its own vice was likened to the lion of the nations — for Man, indeed, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts, and was made like them; of this lion Peter also speaks: Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, and in Psalm 9 (10) it is written: He lies in wait in secret like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor, and Jeremiah says by the Holy Spirit: A lion from the forest has struck them —; but that the devil is called a dragon — for which Aquila translates Leviathan, setting out the name of the dragon — I have shown in the earlier explanation with many testimonies, he who had said: The rivers are mine and I made them. This dragon, then, tossed very many nations with his rivers as with horns; which we can understand of Marcion, Valentinus, Arius and Eunomius, and the other leaders of heresies, who imitate churchmen saying to the Lord Savior: In you we will toss our enemies with the horn, and they do not toss them unto salvation, to lift them from earth to heaven, but to cast them into the deep. Then follows: And you troubled the waters with your feet — according to that saying of the Apostle: But he who troubles you will bear the judgment —; for he does not wish to drink the waters of Siloam, which go in silence, but the 'turbid' and 'muddy' waters of Egypt, which, before they were trampled by the dragon's feet, were pure and flowed in their own order, but after they were troubled by his feet, lost the order of their course — for the heretics do not use testimonies of the Scriptures that cohere with one another, but they trouble everything —; and, because he himself is the enemy and the avenger, the Egyptian dragon not only troubles other people's waters with his feet, but tramples his own rivers, so as not to spare those whom he has once brought under his power — which the righteous man, desiring to avoid it, prays: Let not the foot of pride come against me; and in another place, having been trampled, he asks not to be trampled again: Have mercy on me, O Lord, for man has trampled me; and the enemy man is the devil, of whom another psalm also speaks: That man may no more be magnified upon the earth —. Therefore thus says the Lord God: I will spread my net over you, in a multitude of many peoples; the Lord's net, woven by the plan of the Old and New Testament, is cast over the dragon — who dwells in the multitude of peoples, and delights in crowds and multitude —, so as to draw him out in his dragnet, or on his hook — this is the dragnet that is cast into the sea of this world and draws out many fish, some to be chosen and others to be thrown away; or this is the hook of which it is written in Job: But you will draw out the dragon with a hook and put a halter around his nostrils, for which Aquila translates: Drawing out Leviathan with a hook, and with cords you will bind his tongue —; and the dragon — or Leviathan — is drawn out of the sea with the hook — or the Lord's dragnet —, so as to be cast — or stretched out — upon the land, and all his coils, in which he used to hide his snares, may be opened and brought out into public and thrown down upon the land, and he may lie prostrate who had set his mouth in heaven and boasted that he was like the Most High; hence there follows: And I will make dwell (or sit) upon you all the birds of the sky, and I will glut the beasts of the whole earth with you — according to what is written: You gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians —, who are called either birds or beasts of the earth: birds, which, as we have said, snatch the seed beside the way; beasts of the whole earth, made savage by vices; which can be referred to heretics and Gentiles; and what follows: And I will put your flesh upon the mountains, and I will fill your hills with your gore (or I will fill the valleys with your blood), has this sense, that we should understand the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth as the peoples of the deceived and the cruelty of the Gentiles, and refer the mountains to the leaders of heresies — such as Valentinus and Marcion were —, and the hills to their successors who are glutted with the dragon's gore, or the valleys which are filled with the dragon's blood to all the lower sort of believers; or certainly the mountains are the hostile powers that roam about in the air, and the valleys those which penetrate the underworld and have been consigned to eternal punishments. Further, what is said: And I will water the land with the stench of your blood upon the mountains (or the land will be watered with your dung upon the mountains), and the valleys will be filled with you, signifies this, that all the pride and arrogant swelling of the heretics is filled not so much with living and pure blood as with putrid and stinking blood — according to what is written: Make them like the dung of the earth, from which the holy man is delivered by the Lord: Who raises the needy from the earth, and lifts the poor from the dung, to set him with princes, with the princes of his people —; and the valleys, sunk into the depths, as we said above, signify either the underworld or the lowly mind of the heretics, who do everything for the sake of pleasure and earthly wealth; and what is joined: And when you have been extinguished I will cover the sky, and I will make its stars grow black: I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light; all the lights of the sky I will make mourn (or grow dark) over you, and I will put darkness upon your land, says the Lord God, if we follow the letter, cannot be understood at all: for when, after Pharaoh — or the dragon — was slain, did the sun and moon and stars not give their light, and the sky was covered with darkness — according to that poetic line: And the impious ages feared eternal night —? This, then, must be said: that when Pharaoh has been extinguished — who transformed himself into an angel of light, of whom it is written in another place: The light of the impious will be extinguished —, the sky, or the heavens, will be covered with darkness — of which Paul also speaks: And the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places —; and the Lord made its stars grow black, whether the dragon's or the sky's — concerning whom Jude the apostle also writes: Wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved forever —; the sun too is covered in a cloud: the sun of iniquity — which is the opposite of the sun of righteousness —, and with a cloud: either by the Lord Savior himself — who descends into Egypt upon a light cloud, weighed down by no burden of sins —, or by the prophets and apostles — of whom we read: I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it, and in the Psalms: Your truth reaches to the clouds —; and when the sun of iniquity has been darkened, the moon — which we take to be the church of the heretics, and which was thought to receive its light from the sun of iniquity — will not give its light, nor will it deceive believers with the knowledge falsely so called; all the lights also, and whatever of doctrine seems to be among the heretics, will be blinded when the dragon has been extinguished, or they will mourn the loss of their prince, so that the Lord himself covers the land of the heretics with darkness, namely ignorance of the truth, so that the blind lead the blind into a ditch and the inhabitants of the land are sent into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. After this it is said: And I will provoke the heart of many peoples, when I bring your destruction (or your captivity) among the nations upon a land which you do not know, so that those who formerly served Pharaoh are angered against him, seeing that his captivity has been led away to another land, which the dragon did not know. Nor ought we to doubt that the lands which Pharaoh does not know are good, namely when the captivity of Pharaoh is exchanged for another captivity — of which it is said to the Savior: Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he received (or, according to the Apostle, gave) gifts among men —. And I will make, he says, many peoples stand astonished over you, so that those who formerly admired Pharaoh's power may afterwards marvel at him for having fallen from his summit; the kings of the peoples, too, will tremble over him with exceeding horror — whose kingdoms the devil showed to the Lord, and of whom it says in the psalm: The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together —; and this will come about when the sword of the Lord begins to fly over their faces, understood as those of the kings, or of the peoples — and the sword of the Lord is to be understood as the word of God, living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, which flies and darts about and dazzles the eyes of those who behold it and frightens their faces —, so that, astounded at the ruin of Pharaoh, they may see themselves cast down in him; and indeed the sword of the Lord — of which it is written: Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many — raises those who lie fallen and by humility changes those wrongly lifted up. But the sword of the king of Babylon will come upon the Egyptian dragon, so that by the swords of the mighty — or of giants — the Lord may cast down his multitude, which followed the king of Egypt: Invincible, he says, (or pestilent ones from the nations) are all these, so that the evil are handed over to worse ones to be punished — of whom it is written: A sending by most evil angels, and the Apostle: Whom I have handed over, he says, to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme, or for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved —. And when by ministers of this kind the pride of Egypt has been cast down and its multitude scattered, all its beasts that were beside many waters will perish, and the foot of man will trouble them no more — for if Blessed is he who sows upon the waters, where ox and ass tread, conversely unhappy is he who will be able any longer to hold the simple by his terror, so that the foot of man does not tread in them, whereby the Egyptian waters seem not to have in them even a sign of wisdom and reason —; nor will the hoof of beasts trouble them, so as to make them 'turbid and muddy' instead of most limpid and shining. Then the waters that had been troubled by the dragon's dominion will be rendered most pure, not by another but by the Lord himself, so that their rivers are rendered like oil and are the nourishment of the true light; and these things will come about when the Lord has made the land of Egypt desolate and has destroyed its fullness and all its inhabitants have been struck, so that by this progress they may be able to know that he himself is the Lord. And what is joined: It is a lament, and they shall lament him; the daughters of the nations shall lament him; over Egypt and over its multitude they shall lament him, says the Lord God, makes it plain that the souls of all the nations which had formerly been oppressed by him, or of those nations which by no means dwelt in Egypt but in the region of the living, lament the slain dragon and all his multitude: not in hope of salvation, but because from so great a power, by his own vice and pride, he has been cast down into eternal punishments.

32:17-32

And it came to pass in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, sing a dirge over the multitude of Egypt, and drag it down, it and the daughters of the mighty nations, to the lowest land with those who go down into the pit. Than whom are you more beautiful? Go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised. In the midst of those slain by the sword they shall fall; the sword has been given; they have dragged her away and all her peoples. The mightiest of the strong will speak to him from the midst of hell, they who went down with his helpers; and they have slept uncircumcised and slain by the sword. There is Assyria and all her multitude, round about her are their graves, all of them slain, and they who fell by the sword; whose graves have been set in the uttermost parts of the pit, and her multitude is round about her grave; all of them slain and falling by the sword, who once had spread dread in the land of the living. There is Elam and all her multitude round about her grave; all these slain and falling by the sword, who went down uncircumcised to the lowest land, who set their terror in the land of the living, and they have borne their shame with those who went down into the pit. In the midst of the slain they have set his bed, among all his peoples; round about him is his grave, all these uncircumcised and slain by the sword; for they had spread terror in the land of the living, and they have borne their shame with those who go down into the pit; they have been set in the midst of the slain. There is Meshech and Tubal and all her multitude, round about her are her graves, all these uncircumcised and slain, falling by the sword, who set their dread in the land of the living; and they will not sleep with the mighty who fell, and the uncircumcised, who went down into hell with their weapons and set their swords under their heads, and their iniquities were in their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. And you therefore will be crushed in the midst of the uncircumcised, and you will sleep with those slain by the sword. There is Edom and all her kings and her leaders, who were given up with their army with those slain by the sword, and who have slept with the uncircumcised, and with those who went down into the pit. There are all the princes of the north and all the Sidonians (or 'hunters'), who were led down with the slain, trembling, and confounded in their strength, for they have slept uncircumcised with those slain by the sword, and they have borne their confusion with those who go down into the pit. Pharaoh saw them and was comforted over all his multitude which was slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his army, says the Lord God, for I have set his terror in the land of the living; and he has slept in the midst of the uncircumcised with those slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God. (In this place the edition of the Seventy translators disagrees greatly both in order and in translation, and some things in it have been added from Theodotion; hence we have found it necessary to set it down too, by no means sparing length, and serving the diligence of the studious reader. LXX: "And it came to pass in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, lament over the multitude of Egypt, and the nations will lead her daughters down dead into the depth of the earth, to those who go down into the ditch." — Moreover, under asterisks there has been added: ※ From the most beautiful water go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised ⁚. Again the sequence follows: — In the midst of those wounded by the sword they shall fall with him, and all their strength will sleep. And the giants will say to you: Go down into the depth of the ditch. Than whom are you better? Go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised in the midst of those wounded by the sword. There is Assyria and all her congregation. — And what is joined: ÷ All the wounded have been set there, and his grave is in the depth of the ditch, and his congregation came to be ⁚, is not found in the Hebrew, but was added by the Seventy. Again it is said: — Round about his grave, all the wounded who had fallen by the sword. — And again from the edition of Theodotion there has been added under asterisks: ※ Who had set graves for them in the sides of the pit, and the congregation came to be round about his grave; all these wounded and falling by the sword ⁚. After which the Seventy set down: — Who set their fear in the land of life. There is Elam and all her strength round about her grave; all wounded and falling by the sword, and who go down uncircumcised into the depth of the earth, who set their terror in the land of life, and they received their torment with those who go down into the ditch, in the midst of the wounded. There have been set Meshech and Tubal and all their strength, round about his grave, all his wounded, all uncircumcised and wounded by the sword, who set their terror upon the land of life; and they did not sleep with the giants, who had fallen from of old, who went down into hell with the weapons they used for wars and set their swords under their heads, and their iniquities came to be in their bones, because they had terrified giants in their life. And you in the midst of the uncircumcised ※ will be crushed, and ⁚ will sleep with those wounded by the sword. There is Edom, ※ her kings and all ⁚ the princes of Assyria, who gave his strength to the wound of the sword; these have slept with the wounded, with those who went down into the ditch. There are all the princes of the north, all the magistrates of Assyria, who go down wounded with their terror, and confounded in their strength; they have slept, uncircumcised too, with those wounded by the sword, and they have carried off their torment with those going down into the ditch. Pharaoh will see them and will receive comfort over all their strength ※ wounded by the sword, Pharaoh and all his strength ⁚, says the Lord God, for I have set his dread upon the land of life, and he will sleep in the midst of the uncircumcised with those wounded by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God.) I am not unaware that so great a discrepancy between the two editions will be tiresome to the fastidious reader; but what am I to do with my slanderers, who, if I take away anything from the translation of the Seventy translators, cry out that I am sacrilegious and without the fear of the Lord — especially those who, though they disagree with me in the truth of the faith and follow the errors of the Manichaeans, stir up the minds of the unlearned on this very point, if they can show that anything of the old has been changed against established custom, preferring to err rather than to learn anything true from a rival. Meanwhile, according to the history the sense is plain. For in the same twelfth year, and in the same month, as we think, but not on the first of the month, as above, but on the fifteenth day, a lament is taken up not over Pharaoh, but over the strength — or multitude — of Egypt, which is dragged down from its pride with all its daughters — or those of the mighty nations — to the lowest land, that is, into the depth of hell. And it is said to the king of Egypt: 'Than whom are you better, that you should deserve to escape death? — for since Assyria and Elam — that is, the Persians —, and Meshech — who are interpreted as the Cappadocians —, and Tubal — whom some take to be the Iberians, others the Italians —, the Edomites also and the princes of the north and the Sidonians, with all their armies by whose help they struck horror into all the nations, have died and been slain by the sword, and have set their swords under their heads — which saying is to be taken ἐμφατικώτερον [more emphatically, as an expressive figure] —, will you alone be able not to endure the same things? Rather, when you see so great a multitude of sleepers with you among the dead below, and your grave surrounded by the memorials of princes once most mighty, you will have consolation, reckoning your torments lighter through the fellowship of very many —'. Let it suffice for the present to have said these things briefly according to the simple sense. Now, with the same brevity, so far as the difficulty of the explanation permits, let us gather the chief points of the spiritual understanding. Above, the word of the Lord came to the prophet on the first day of the month; here, on the fifteenth — now on the first day, that is, on the calends, is the beginning of the month; on the fifteenth, when the whole orb of the moon is filled; and if it was the first month, it is the first day of Unleavened Bread, but if the seventh, of Tabernacles, when the tents are pitched, which feasts are among the very greatest among the Hebrews —; and the lament is made over the strength of Egypt, so that he who is strong in evil may cease to be so and take on weakness, and when he is weaker, then he may be stronger. For the 'strength' of Egypt, the Hebrew has 'multitude' — For wide and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many enter by it, just as, on the contrary, it is said to Israel: But you are few among all the nations; for virtue is always rare, and: Narrow and strait is the way that leads to life, and few are those who enter by it —. And that Egypt is lamented, and its dead daughters — 'her' daughters according to the Seventy, or those 'of the mighty nations' — are led down to the lowest land into the deepest pit — or ditch —, signifies the souls dwelling in the Egypt of this world — which have lost him who says: I am the life, and, dead in sins, are dragged down to the underworld by their weight, as the sinner says: For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they weigh upon me; these are the ones of whom it is also written in another place: They go into the lower parts of the earth; they will be given over into the hands of the sword; they will be portions for foxes. He who, indeed, digs a ditch, falls into it; whence we also read: He opened a pit and dug it out, and he will fall into the ditch which he made —. And what follows: Than whom are you more beautiful? Go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised, the word is properly addressed to Pharaoh king of Egypt — or, as was added in the Seventy from Theodotion, to Egypt itself: From the most beautiful water go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised; which pertains especially to him who, reborn in the baptism of Christ, hearing with the Church: Who is she that comes up made white, leaning upon her kinsman?, afterwards, defiled either by fornication or by other vices, is cast out of the Church, and it is said to him: From the most beautiful water go down, and sleep 'with the uncircumcised', that is, 'with the unclean', according to that sense which the Apostle sets down: We are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit, and glory in the Lord, and put no confidence in the flesh —. All these will fall with Pharaoh in the midst of the wounded — or the slain —, by that sword which is the opposite of the sword which the Lord came to send upon the earth: for just as the sword of Christ separates the good from the evil — as he says: I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword —, so the sword of the heretics cuts down all peoples and leads the wounded down to the underworld; these are the giants, most mighty and rebellious and setting their mouth on high, and the more they raise themselves up to the heights through pride, the more they are dragged down to the depth of the ditch and the uttermost parts of hell, all of whom have been slain by the sword. And so that either Pharaoh or the whole strength of Egypt, which has been dragged down to the underworld, might know whom he had as companions in punishment, the following word shows: There is Assyria and all the multitude (or synagogue) of her; for the prince of the heretics is the devil — whose congregation is truly a synagogue, of which it is said in the Revelation: Who are the synagogue of Satan —. But the following short verses, which are marked in front with an obelus, I think should be passed over, and what is found in the Hebrew should be stated: Round about her are their graves, namely of those deceived by him, who are all wounded (or slain) by the sword, and therefore have fallen; whose graves have been set in the uttermost parts of the pit — and that hell is called a pit is plainly shown by that psalm in which the penitent says: I have been likened to those who go down into the pit; which we ought by no means, according to the proper sense of the Latin word, to understand as that which in Greek is called λίμνη [lake] — such as the lake of Tiberias, and lakes Larius and Benacus, and many others —, but as what we are accustomed to call cisterns; which pits, because they chill the waters and take from them all the warmth of the spirit, sinners and all heretics dig; and, so far as my memory goes, Scripture testifies that none of the saints dug a pit — that is, a cistern — but all sinners — among whom was Uzziah, the leprous king, who also fell through his pride, of whom it is written that he was a man brooding over the works of the soil, and that he built many towers of pride in the corners, and that he dug pits —; on the contrary it is said to the righteous man: Drink waters from your own vessels and from the springs of your wells, and again: Let the fountain of your water be your own, whence the Lord also says: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves pits (that is, cisterns) which cannot hold water —. There follows: And her multitude is round about her grave; all these surround the Assyrian, and their multitude is very great, all of whom have been wounded and slain and are falling by the sword — for none of them can stand with Moses, or hear: You who stand in the house of the Lord; but all have been wounded and slain and are falling —: who once had spread dread in the land of the living; and dread to those who were set over the churches, lest in the land of the living they should make peoples of the dead and deceive all the simple — whence Paul also said: But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve in his malice, your minds be corrupted through the simplicity that is in Christ; but this fear is softened by hope in the Lord, as the man of the Church says: The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? —. After this it is said: There is Elam, and all her multitude round about her grave, no doubt the Assyrian's. 'Elam' is rendered into our tongue as 'their ascent'; for all who, despising the humility of Christ, have ascended to the pride of the devil and have thought themselves to be something in the knowledge falsely so called, are to be named Elamites, who go round the grave of the Assyrian king and have been slain and wounded by the sword; and although they set their mouth on high, yet they went down unclean and uncircumcised to the lowest land, so that the more loftily they had been raised up, the more heavily they might fall; these set their terror not once but a second time in the land of the living — for who among the churchmen is safe from the terror of Elamites of this kind and has not lost someone of his flock? —; and beautifully the Church of Christ is called the land of the living, so that, on the contrary, the conventicles of the heretics may be believed to be the land of the dead. And they have borne, he says, their shame (or their torment) with those whom they dragged down with them into the pit and the depth of hell, whose bed is in the midst of the slain; namely of those whose throats they cut with their blade, and they are surrounded by peoples of this kind; these peoples are the peoples of the Assyrian king, and although they boast that they are circumcised, yet they are uncircumcised and slain by the sword, and a third time they have spread terror and dread in the land of the living; hence they have borne their torment and punishment in the midst of those whom they deceived by their frauds. There also is — that is, beside the Assyrian — Meshech and Tubal and all her multitude, round about her grave, all uncircumcised and slain and falling by the sword, who had set their dread in the land of the living. For 'Mosoch and Thubal', Symmachus and Theodotion translated 'their bed', to show that the beds of the heretics, or rather their everlasting ditches, are the punishments of the Assyrian king; 'Mosoch' means 'madness', 'Thubal' 'conversion' — not to good from evil but from good to evil — or 'all things', to show that all heretics are mad and with equal zeal are turned to worse things; nor is it surprising if those who are mad and heaped together for evil have a multitude, since they are companions of the Egyptian king, who rejoices in multitude; all these have been slain by the sword, who set their dread, not once nor a second time, but a third time, in the land of the living, of which we have spoken more fully above. There follows: And they will not sleep with the mighty (or the giants) who fell, and the uncircumcised, who went down to hell with their weapons and set their swords under their heads, and their iniquities were in their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. 'These,' he says, 'who stood out as leaders of the heretics, have come to such a summit of malice and of torment, that they do not deserve to bear like punishments even with the mighty and the giants who fell from the beginning; who, having by no means done penance for their error, went down to the underworld with their weapons, rebels against God and his Church, carrying their spirit with them' — of whom it is written: Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows —, 'and they set,' he says, 'their swords under their heads, resting in a hostile spirit, and, as their supreme victory, embracing the darts of their opinions, to such a degree that their iniquities were in their bones — that is, their strongest fabrications —, and holding fast the doctrines of their error: Because they became the terror of the mighty in their life (or in the land of the living)', which is said for the fourth time, that by their perversity they terrified even the mightiest, and those who had knowledge of the Scriptures and who were of the region of the living, while they go down to hell with their weapons and set their swords under their heads and their iniquity reaches to their bones. After this it is written: 'And you therefore will be crushed in the midst of the uncircumcised' — which is said either to Pharaoh or to the strength, or multitude, of Egypt, that it too is crushed, according to what is written: But may God crush Satan under your feet swiftly — 'and you will sleep,' he says, 'with those slain by the sword, in perpetual sleep'. There, with the Assyrian and with the Egyptian multitude, will be Edom and her kings, all who have served earthly works or delighted in blood — for 'Idumaea' [Edom] sounds both 'earthy' and 'bloody' —; all the kings and all the princes — of whom the Apostle also frequently speaks: 'brooding over earthly works and daily shedding the blood of those whom they have deceived by their fraud' — have slept with the uncircumcised and unclean and with those who went down into the pit, of whom we have spoken above. In the same company will also be the princes of the north, from which evils blaze up upon the earth — and from which, whether in Jeremiah or in this same prophet, that pot full of flesh and bones is set alight —, and not only the princes of the north, but every magistrate of 'Assur' — for which in the Hebrew is more truly set down all the 'Sidonians', whom we have rendered as 'hunters', according to what is written: Our soul has been snatched like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters (for which in the Hebrew is set down of the Sidonians); which Sidonians — or hunters — will be led down to the underworld trembling, who once trusted in their own strength; and they will sleep unclean, and they will bear their confusion — or torment —, having the everlasting remorse of an evil conscience, so that their fire is not quenched and their worm does not die. When Pharaoh has seen all these, he will be comforted, either still having his former malice and seeing that he has many companions of his punishment, or at any rate he was comforted seeing that they too are confounded in their punishments and their terrors, over all his multitude which was slain by the sword: that is, Pharaoh's, or that of all his companions, and especially of the Assyrian king and Meshech and Tubal and the Edomites, and of the princes of the north and of the Sidonians; for these had set their terror in the land of the living — which is said for the fifth time, so that we ought to beware of and flee all nations of this kind, which have deceived us in all our senses, and know that they are dreadful and cannot easily be avoided unless we keep our heart with all vigilance —. 'He has slept,' he says, 'Pharaoh himself too, with his companions slain by the sword', which companions are his multitude, going by the wide and spacious way to everlasting punishments.

33:1-9

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the sons of your people, and you shall say to them: A land, when I bring the sword upon it, and the people of the land take one man from the last of them (or one man from among them), and set him over themselves as a watchman, and he sees the sword coming upon the land, and sounds the trumpet and announces it to the people; but whoever he is who hears the sound of the trumpet does not take heed for himself, and the sword comes and takes (or seizes) him: his blood shall be upon his own head; he heard the sound (or voice) of the trumpet and did not take heed for himself, his blood shall be upon him. But if he guards himself, he has saved his soul. But if the watchman sees the sword coming, and does not sound the trumpet, and the people do not guard themselves; and the sword comes and takes a soul from among them: that one indeed has been taken in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from the hand of the watchman. And you, son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Hearing therefore the word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked: Wicked one, you shall die by death; you have not spoken so that the wicked may guard himself from his way, that wicked one shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from your hand. But if, when you announce to the wicked that he should turn from his ways, he has not turned from his way, he shall die in his iniquity, but you will deliver your soul. Again the word of the Lord comes to the prophet — the word which had for a time been silent, because the prophet cannot, nor can human frailty, sustain within itself an unceasing and continuous prophesying —, and it speaks the same things that are contained in the earlier passages: 'Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel, and hearing the word from my mouth, you shall also threaten them from me; in that I shall say to the unrighteous: You shall die by death, and you did not announce it to him, nor did you speak so as to announce it to the unrighteous, that he might turn from his ways and live, that unrighteous man shall die in his iniquity and his blood I will require from your hand. And you, if you announce it to the unrighteous, and he has not turned from his iniquity and from his way, that unrighteous man shall die in his iniquity, and you will deliver your soul'; if you examine these words carefully, you will understand that they are indeed similar, but not the same, since they disagree in a great many points — and this we ought to observe in all the holy Scriptures: where there seems to be some similarity of meaning, not everything is said identically, but a great many things are either taken away or added, and the difference between the individual words has its reason —. And meanwhile, before we come to higher things, the sense must be briefly explained: 'If a watchman has been appointed among the people to announce the sword of the Lord and the wrath that is coming, and, when he announces it, the people are unwilling to hear, the watchman will be free, and he who has been overwhelmed by the sword will himself bear the guilt of his own blood; but if he has heard, he has saved his soul; if, however, the watchman has not sounded the trumpet and the people, not knowing that the sword is coming, have by no means taken heed for themselves, the people indeed will die in their iniquity; yet I will require the blood of the dying from the watchman's hand'; and so that the prophet Ezekiel might know that this general discussion pertained above all to himself: 'And you,' he says, son of man, not by the land and by the people of the land, as I said above, but by me you have been appointed watchman for the house of Israel: If therefore, when I say to the wicked: Wicked one, you shall die by death, you have not spoken to him so that he may guard himself and be delivered from destruction, he indeed will die in his iniquity, which he had committed before and from which, had you announced it, he could have been delivered: but his blood I will require from your hand. But if you declare it to the wicked, and command him to turn from his most evil ways, and he is unwilling to do this, he indeed will die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul from the destruction of negligence'. From these words we learn: that a man, though unrighteous and wicked, can be saved from his wickedness if he hears the words of the teacher and repents; and no less, that the teacher incurs peril if he is unwilling to teach, whether from fear of peril or from despair of the sinner, since he is guilty of the blood of one who could have been delivered and rescued from death, had he not fallen through the teacher's silence; and that in both free will is preserved, since it lies both in the teacher's will either to keep silent or to speak, and in the hearer's choice either to hear and do and be saved, or to despise and perish by his own contempt. Nor does it immediately follow that, because a prophet foretells something, what he foretold comes — for he does not foretell it so that it may come, but so that it may not come —; nor, because God speaks, must what he threatens necessarily happen; rather he threatens for this reason: that the one whom he threatens may turn to repentance, and that what is to come if the words of the Lord are despised may not happen. We can, however, discuss this passage in a threefold way: so that the land which appoints a watchman for itself is either, according to the letter, the land of Judea, or, according to the spiritual understanding, the Church, which often chooses a watchman from the last of its people — namely that one whom the Apostle too, writing to the Corinthians, takes as judge —, or certainly the soul of the believer, which sets the mind and reason over the people and crowd of its thoughts — so that it may not admit every incitement of the thoughts, but may judge and discern which things it should pursue and which it should flee —. The watchman of the land of Judea can be understood as either the king or the prophet; but the watchman of the Church as either the bishop or the presbyter, who has been chosen by the people and, knowing and foreseeing through the reading of the Scriptures what is to come, is to announce it to the people and correct the one who goes astray. Hence we must greatly fear lest we approach this office unworthy, and, having been taken up by the people, give ourselves over to negligence and sloth, and, what is worse than these, serving delicacies and the belly and leisure, think that we have received an honor, not a ministry: For the Son of man did not come to be ministered to, but to minister, and he washed the feet of the disciples, to show that all the filth and vices in the disciples ought to be washed away and cleansed by the teacher; nor let us at once reply: 'What use is it to speak, if the hearer is unwilling to do what you have taught?', for each one is judged by his own intention and office: you, if you have not spoken; he, if he has been unwilling to hear; of negligent teachers Solomon speaks: Wisdom hidden and treasure hidden, what profit is there in either?; something of the kind is signified also in the Gospel: that for one who has caused one of the least of the Church to stumble, it would be better that a donkey's millstone be tied to his neck and he be cast into the deep, than that, set in the watchtower, he should harm very many.

33:10-20

You therefore, son of man, say to the house of Israel: Thus you have spoken, saying: Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and we are wasting away in them; how then shall we be able to live? Say to them: As I live, says the Lord God; I do not want the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn back from his way, and live; and turn from your most evil ways; and why will you die, house of Israel? You therefore, son of man, say to the sons of your people: The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins, and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness; and the righteous shall not be able to live in his righteousness on whatever day he sins. Even if I say to the righteous that he shall live by life, and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity; all his righteous deeds shall be consigned to oblivion, and in his iniquity which he has wrought, in it he shall die. But if I say to the wicked: You shall die by death, and he repents of his sin, and does judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge, and gives back what he has robbed, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust, he shall live by life, and shall not die: all the sins which he has sinned shall not be imputed to him; he has done judgment and righteousness, he shall live by life. And the sons of your people have said: The way of the Lord is not of equal weight; and it is their own way that is unjust. For when the righteous withdraws from his righteousness and commits iniquities, he shall die in them; and when the wicked withdraws from his wickedness and does judgment and righteousness, he shall live in them. And you say: The way of the Lord is not right. I will judge each one of you according to his ways, house of Israel. If we read carelessly, it seems to us to be the same prophecy as the one above, in which it is said: Do I willingly desire the death of the unrighteous, says the Lord, and not rather that he turn from his evil way and live?, and at the end of the same prophecy: Turn and return from all your wickednesses, and they will not be to you a torment of iniquity; for there the word is addressed to those who wish to repent and would blot out their sins with righteousness, so that they may turn with confidence and repent with a full heart; here, however, he speaks to those who, because of the greatness of their sins, or rather of their wickednesses, despair of salvation and say: Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and we are wasting away in them; how then shall we be able to live?; and the sense is: 'Since death has once been set before us, and no medicine can restore health to our wounds, what need is there to toil and be worn out in vain, and not to pass the present life in desperation, so that at least we may enjoy this one, since we have lost the future one?'; to them God answered that he does not want the death of the wicked, but that he turn back and live, and he makes an apostrophe to the despairing wicked: Turn from your most evil ways; and so that we may know who the wicked are to whom he speaks, the following word shows it: Why will you die, house of Israel? — but the life and death signified in this place is not this one by which all of us, by the law of nature common with the beasts, either live or are dissolved by death, but that of which it is written: I will please the Lord in the land of the living, and: The soul that sins, it shall die —. And from the particular admonition with which he was speaking to the house of Israel, he passes to a general discussion: that past acts of righteousness do not save the righteous man if he has become taken up with new crimes, and old sins do not destroy the sinner or the wicked if he has amended his old errors by works of righteousness, and that God in both cases judges not past things but present ones: 'If I say,' he says, 'to the righteous: You shall live by life, and promise him the rewards of righteousness, and he, trusting in this, sins, all his former righteous deeds will be consigned to oblivion and he will die in his present iniquity; nor has my sentence changed, since I cannot render to the same man, now a sinner, what I had promised to the righteous man; on the contrary, if I threaten the sinner and the wicked — and say: Yet three days and Nineveh shall be overthrown —, and he repents and amends his old error by good works, so that he does judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge, and gives back what he has robbed, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust: ought he not to live by life, which is Christ, and by no means die, since the threat made to the sinner ought not to punish the righteous man?' — something of the kind the divine word says to Jeremiah when he goes down into the potter's house and hears that God's promises or threat aim at this: either to call men forth to salvation or to deter them from sin — 'hence those who say: The way of the Lord is not fair, are convicted of this, that it is their own judgment that is unfair, since they have a most evil eye and judge by no means the new things but the old'. By all these things it is shown that neither ought the sinner to despair of salvation if he repents, nor the righteous to trust in his righteousness if he has carelessly lost what he had acquired with great labor. We pass quickly over what is plain, in order to linger over what is more obscure; but in what points the present prophecy differs from the earlier one, and in what it says similar things, a comparison of the two will be able to show. Moreover, what it is to do judgment and righteousness, to restore the pledge, to give back what was robbed, to walk in the commandments of life, and the rest, we have said above in this same prophet.

33:21-22

And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the tenth month, on the fifth of the month of our exile (or captivity), there came to me one who had fled (or who had been saved) from Jerusalem, saying: The city has been laid waste (or taken). Now the hand of the Lord had come upon me in the evening, before he who had fled came; and he opened my mouth until he came to me in the morning, and, my mouth being opened, I was silent no longer. In the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah, in the fifth month, the city of Jerusalem was taken. But this prophecy is dated the twelfth year, the tenth month, the fifth of the month, of the captivity or exile, when he was taken captive with Jeconiah. From this it is shown that one year, four months and twenty-five days after Jerusalem was taken, one of the citizens of Jerusalem came to Babylon to report that the city had been taken and laid waste. One day before the one who was to tell these things came, in the evening the hand of the Lord came upon the prophet Ezekiel, and it opened his mouth, which had long been closed; and whatever that man was going to say, this one recounted beforehand as already done, and he was silent no longer, seeing his prophecy fulfilled in deed, and that the people who were in Babylon, or those who were captives, by no means doubted the prophetic oracle; for the mouth of the prophet is opened at the moment when he has shown accomplished in deed what he had announced before; and he proclaims with all freedom who points out not future things at all, but things either present or past. This is according to the letter; but according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense]: if 'Hiezechiel' [Ezekiel] means 'strength of God' — and Christ, moreover, is the power of God and the wisdom of God! —, this is to be understood: that, Jerusalem having been taken and overthrown, whoever has been able to escape the faithlessness of the Jews — such as were the apostles and the remnant that was saved —, he himself announces to Christ that all the ceremonies of the Jews have been overthrown — which certain people think must be observed even to this day, not hearing that saying of the Apostle: You have fallen from grace, you who are justified in the law. And I marvel at the obstinacy of men in wishing to defend in word what they do not dare to fulfill in deed, unless perhaps Jewish wolves are hiding under the skin of sheep, that is, of Christians. Why does a defender of the Synagogue make his voice resound in the churches of Christ? —. Jerusalem, therefore, having been taken and overthrown, the mouth of the Lord is opened through the apostles and apostolic men — who can say: My mouth is opened to you, O Corinthians, and: A great and effective door has been opened to me, and that saying: I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit —, a mouth which will never be able to keep silent, nor to hear — along with Israel: Hear, Israel, and be silent —, but will resound in the whole world and will lay open the Gospel of Christ to the nations. Hence, according to this sense, the 'twelfth year' refers to the twelve tribes, and the 'tenth month' to the time of the Jewish propitiation, which in Greek is called ἱλασμὸς, and the 'fifth day of the month' to the fleshly senses — all of which, Jerusalem having been taken and the Gospel succeeding, we have shown to have been abolished and to have passed away —, and 'in the evening', that is, at the consummation of the world, to the hand of the Lord having come upon the true Ezekiel, who had sung of the future ruins of the city through the prophets and in the morning showed that they had been fulfilled.

33:23-33

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, those who dwell in these ruins upon the soil of Israel speak, saying: Abraham was one, and he possessed the land; but we are many, to us the land has been given as a possession. Therefore you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: You who eat in blood, and lift up your eyes to your uncleannesses, and shed blood, shall you possess the land by inheritance? You have stood upon your swords, you have done abominations, and each of you has defiled his neighbor's wife, and shall you possess the land by inheritance? These things you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: As I live, those who dwell in the ruins shall fall by the sword, and he who is in the field shall be given to the beasts to be devoured, but those who are in strongholds and in caves shall die of pestilence. And I will give the land into solitude and into desert, and its proud strength shall fail, and the mountains of Israel shall be made desolate, because there is no one who passes through them; and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have made their land desolate and deserted, because of all their abominations which they have wrought. And you, son of man, the sons of your people talk about you beside the walls and in the doorways of the houses, and they say one to another, a man to his neighbor, speaking: Come, and let us hear what is the word that comes forth from the Lord. And they come to you as if a people were entering (or as a people is accustomed to gather), and my people sit before you; and they hear your words and do not do them, for they turn them into a song of their mouth, and their heart follows its avarice. (or, as is contained in the Seventy, for they make a lie in their mouth, and their heart walks after their abominations. It follows:) And you are to them like a musical song which is sung with a sweet and pleasing sound, and they will hear your words and will not do them. And when what has been foretold comes — for behold, it is coming —, then they will know that you prophesied in their midst. First it must be known that some eight lines, more or less, from the place we have set down: You who eat in blood, and lift up your eyes to your uncleannesses, up to the place where it is written: These things you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God, are not found in the Seventy, who omitted these too along with many others; or else, having been translated by them, they were gradually removed through the fault of copyists. And our Latins, or rather envious Christians, and, to speak more openly, heirs of the Grunnian faction, bark against us: why do we expound according to the Hebrew — as though food were to be forced upon the unwilling, and the banquet were not being prepared for those who receive it with thanksgiving; surely, if they do not trust us, let them read the other editions: of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion; let them question Hebrews — not of one place, lest they keep boasting that they were bought by me, but of different provinces; and when they see that all agree with my error or inexperience, then let them understand that they are excessively wise, and desire to sleep rather than to learn —, and let them dwell in the seventy little cells of the Alexandrian Pharos, lest they lose the sails from their ships and sigh over the loss of their ropes. So much against the envious; now let us discuss what we have set before us. Jerusalem having been taken, as we have said, and the temple overthrown, the poor of the land, of whom Jeremiah writes, had alone been left in Jerusalem, to tend the vineyards and the fields and to dwell in the ruins of the burned city; and though they ought to have repented over the things on account of which the captivity had come, deceiving themselves with an empty hope, they said: 'Our father Abraham was one, and yet he possessed this land by inheritance — not that he himself possessed it, but that his seed received the land of promise; if therefore that one man was multiplied into such great peoples, we, who are many more, who have been left in the land of Judea and dwell in deserted and ruined cities, shall surely be multiplied much more, so that we, being many, may possess what that one man possessed'. To them the Lord answered that Abraham, one man, had possessed the land of promise by faith — For Abraham believed, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness —, but that these, taken up with unbelief and crimes, even if they are more, cannot possess it; and at the same time he enumerates by what deeds they offend God, namely six kinds of sins: 'You who eat in blood, and lift up your eyes to uncleannesses, that is, to your idols, and shed blood, that is, commit homicide; doing these things, will you be able to keep the land by inheritance? Nor are you content with this limit of crimes, but you stand upon your swords daily, ready to kill and imitating Esau, who stood, and lived by his sword; you do incredible abominations, namely the foulnesses of lusts; and each one defiles his neighbor's wife, so that he is the more wicked in this, that he had defiled the wife of a friend and neighbor. Would you do these things,' he says, 'and suppose that you will hold the land by inheritance? Answer them therefore, O prophet, and bring forth this sentence upon them from my word: I swear by myself that those who dwell in the ruins and the crumbling walls shall fall by the sword, and those who are in the fields — or in the open country — shall be devoured by beasts, and those who are in walled places — or in strongholds — and in caves shall not be able to escape the wrath of God, but shall die by famine and pestilence. And I will give,' he says, 'the land of Judea into solitude, and its proud strength shall fail — which had once been strength: The proud, however, God resists, and gives grace to the humble —; the mountains too and everything shall be deserted, and they shall come into such solitude that no one passes through them; and then the few who had remained shall by no means trust in their multitude, but shall know, by the greatness of the solitude, that I am the Lord, who gave the land into desert because of all the abominations which they have wrought'. Let these things be said against those who, Jerusalem having been taken and the whole region of the Jews laid waste, dwelt, a few of them, in the ruined and deserted cities and little villages. Now let us come to the tropology and, according to our custom, draw the broad discussion together rather than spread it out. Every heretic dwells among crumbling walls and in deserts, and thinks that he possesses the land of Israel: 'If Abraham, one man, by his faith came to such great blessedness that his seed was multiplied like the sand of the sea and like the stars of heaven, how much more shall we, being many, possess the land of 'Israel', that is, 'of those who see God', and 'Iudaea' [Judea], 'of the Lord's confession'?'; to them the Lord answered: 'He possessed the land by the merit of faith; but your unbelief, or rather blasphemy, will not be able to possess the land of Israel, that is, the Church. For first, you eat in blood, pouring out the blood of those whom you cause to stumble; next, you lift up your eyes to uncleannesses or to your abominations which you have fabricated out of your own mind — when you ought to have imitated the man of the Church and said: To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens —; third, you shed blood, not giving life to those whom you have led astray, but killing them; nor is it enough for you to have done these three things, but you stand upon your swords, that is, you persevere in the depravity of your opinion, and are ready for slaughter; and you have done abominations, doing in bedchambers things that are shameful to speak of; and you have defiled the wife of your neighbor, hastening, namely, to snatch away daily from the embrace of Christ, by deceiving them, those of the Church's way of life. And when you have done these things, do you think that you will hold the land of Israel by inheritance?' To them God says that whoever has dwelt in the ruined conventicles of the heretics shall fall by the sword of the Church — of which it is written: And two-edged swords in their hands, and in the Gospel: I did not come to send peace, but a sword, and: 'The servant who gives himself over to luxury and leisure shall be divided, that is, shall be struck with the blade, and his portion shall be placed with the unbelievers' —, and he who is in the field, or in the open country, shall be given to the beasts to be devoured — the beasts which the prophet, desiring to avoid them, prays against: Do not give to the beasts the soul that confesses to you —, but he who is in strongholds and in walled places — of which it is written: The righteous man went up against the strongest cities and destroyed their fortifications, in which the wicked trusted — and lingers in caves — of which it is said: It is written: The house of my Father shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers —, that one shall die by famine of the word of the Lord and by pestilence; and the whole land of the heretics shall be given into solitude, so that their pride may be broken and the mountains which promised themselves the loftiness of knowledge may be reduced to solitude — mountains that are called of Israel because under the name of Christ they trip up all whom they deceive —, and no one shall pass through them — nor will anyone be able to say what Moses said: Passing over, I will see this great vision; for they are inhabitants of the perverse mountains, not pilgrims and sojourners —, so that, when they have suffered these things, they may then know that he himself is the Lord, who has given their land into solitude because of the abominations which they have wrought. There follows — on the same day indeed and at the same time, that is, in the twelfth year, the tenth month, on the fifth of the month, when the one who had fled from Jerusalem came, and when the prophet spoke to those who were in the land of Judea and promised themselves the hope of an everlasting possession — and he commands the prophet to speak to the people that lives in Babylon and dwells with him, and to rebuke them for their flattering snares, those who desire to hear the words of the prophet not for the salvation of the soul but for the pleasure of the ears; these walk beside the walls and in the doorways of the houses, by no means desiring to enter into the prophet's meaning, but they urge one another on and say: Come, and let us hear what is the word that comes forth from the Lord. 'And so they come like a people entering the Church of God, and they sit before you, my people, which says that it is mine, and they are unwilling to do what they have heard; people of this sort seem to me like those who are beguiled by theatrical songs and listen either to tragedians or to comedians and are there caressed with pleasure, so that, when they have gone out from you, they repeat these things and sing them over and deceive themselves with the sweet sound: And they will hear,' he says, 'your words and will not do them'. Such, even to this day, are many in the churches, who say: 'Come, let us hear this man and that man', as he rolls out the words of his preaching with marvelous eloquence; and they stir up applause and shout and wave their hands; and the things they had neglected in deeds, once they learn that these have come — for what the prophet pronounces by the word of God must come —, then they will begin to acknowledge, and to know that all that they had heard were not the words of a man, but of the Lord, who spoke through the prophet and the man of the Church.

Book Eleven

The eleventh book of the explanations on Ezekiel will contain, in its last part, the prophecy against Gog and Magog, and it will come as far as the beginning of the city set on the mountain, Jerusalem, and of the temple situated in it. If, with the Lord helping and expounding his own mysteries, I am able to bring it all the way to the end, I shall have to hesitate long and much whether I ought to set my hands to the spiritual temple or openly confess my ignorance, especially since, both among the Jews and among us, there is a great silence over its interpretation: some judge that it is to be built in time to come; others, with a good intention indeed but an unskilled one, know that the things said are spiritual, and yet do not know how those spiritual things themselves ought to be expounded. And in the meantime, so that the care of the present work may hold us, know also, O virgin of Christ Eustochium, that you must pray for us. In a most difficult prophecy I will briefly point out this: that a man of our own age, by no means undistinguished, writing to the emperor, said concerning this nation: This Gog is the Goth; by what reasoning everything that is written in it can be fitted to him is not mine to expound, but theirs who think so.

34:1-31

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy concerning the shepherds (or to the shepherds) of Israel, prophesy and say to the shepherds: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who were feeding themselves (or O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds feed themselves); are not the flocks fed by the shepherds (or do not the shepherds feed the sheep)? You ate the milk and covered yourselves with the wool, and what was fat you slaughtered, but my flock you did not feed; what was weak you did not make firm (or strengthen), and what was sick you did not heal, what was broken you did not bind up, and what was cast off (or was straying) you did not bring back, what had perished you did not seek, but you ruled over them with harshness and with power (or and what was strong, you afflicted with toil). And my sheep were scattered, because there was no shepherd (or shepherds); and they were made to be devoured by all the beasts of the field, and they were scattered. My flocks (or sheep) had wandered over all the mountains and on every high hill, and over the whole face of the earth my flocks (or sheep) were scattered; and there was none who would seek, there was none, I say, who would seek (or who would bring back). Therefore, O shepherds, hear the word of the Lord: As I live, says the Lord God, because my flocks (or sheep) have become a prey, and my sheep have been made to be devoured by all the beasts of the field, because there was no shepherd (or shepherds); for the shepherds did not seek my flock, but the shepherds were feeding themselves, and were not feeding my flocks. Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself, against the shepherds, will require my flock at their hand, and I will make them cease, so that they no longer feed my flock, nor shall the shepherds feed themselves any more (or the sheep); and I will deliver my flock (or sheep) from their mouth, and it shall no longer be food for them. For thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will seek out my sheep, and I will visit them. As a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep (or when there is gloom and cloud in the midst of his separated sheep), so will I visit my sheep, and I will deliver them from all the places into which they had been scattered in the day of cloud and gloom. And I will lead them (or them) out from the peoples (or from the nations), and I will gather them (or them) from the lands (or regions), and I will bring them (or them) into their own land, and I will feed them (or them) on the mountains, Israel, by the streams and in all the dwelling places of the land. In the richest pastures I will feed them (or them), and on the high mountains of Israel shall be their pastures (or their folds); there they shall rest in green grass, and in fat pastures they shall feed upon the mountains of Israel. I will feed my sheep, and I will make them lie down (or rest), says the Lord God. What had perished I will seek, and what had been cast off (or had strayed) I will bring back, and what had been broken I will bind up, and what was weak I will make firm (or strengthen), and what is fat and strong I will guard, and I will feed them in judgment (or with judgment). But you, my flocks (or my sheep), thus says the Lord God: Behold, I judge between cattle and cattle, of rams and of he-goats. Was it not enough for you to graze down the good pasture? Moreover you will also trample the remnants of your pastures with your feet, and when you drank the purest water, you fouled the rest with your feet; and my sheep fed on what had been trampled by your feet, and drank what your feet had fouled. Therefore thus says the Lord God to them: Behold, I myself judge between fat cattle and lean (or between strong cattle and weak): because you thrust with your sides and shoulders and tossed all the weak cattle with your horns, until they were scattered abroad, I will save my flock and it shall no longer be a prey, and I will judge between cattle and cattle (or between ram and ram). And I will raise up over them (or them) one shepherd to feed them (or them), my servant David, he shall feed them (or them), and he shall be to them for a shepherd. But I the Lord will be to them for God, and my servant David prince in the midst of them: I the Lord have spoken. And I will make with them a covenant (or testament) of peace, and I will make the most evil beasts cease from the land, and those who dwelt in the desert shall sleep secure in the woods; and I will make them, round about my hill, a blessing, and I will bring down (or give) the rain in its season: there shall be rains of blessing. And the tree of the field shall give (or the trees of the plains shall give) its fruit, and the earth shall give its shoot (or strength), and they shall be (or dwell) in their own land without fear (or in hope of peace), and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have broken the chains (or the collar) of their yoke, and rescued them from the hand of those who ruled over them (or who made them serve). And they shall no longer be a prey to the nations, nor shall the beasts of the earth devour them, but they shall dwell confidently (or in hope) without any terror. And I will raise up for them a renowned shoot (or a planting of peace), and they shall no longer be diminished (or perishing) by famine in the land, nor shall they bear any longer the reproaches of the nations; and they shall know that I am the Lord their God with them, and they my people, the house of Israel, says the Lord God. But you, my flocks, the flocks of my pasture (or sheep), are men, and I the Lord your God, says the Lord God. I have often pointed out that I mix the two editions so as to avoid making the books too large, at least in those places that do not differ much from each other in translation.
