He also measured the breadth of the threshold of the gate, of ten cubits, which is a perfect number and is contained either in the Decalogue or in the mystery of the four Gospels, which, beginning from one, so proceeds to I.II.III.IIII that it fills up the number ten; its length had thirteen cubits; in place of which, in the Seventy, breadth is put again — which seems to me to have been corrupted by the negligence of the scribes: for Scripture would not have said in one place breadth and again breadth, of ten or of thirteen cubits —; and the gate of the threshold, in which the number of the old and the new Testament is consecrated, can be understood either as the Lord himself, who says: I am the door, or certainly as all the saints through whom we enter into the knowledge of God, of whom the apostle Paul spoke: My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; be enlarged, you too; the thirteen cubits, after the number eight, contain the mystery of the books of Moses, which are shown both in the five loaves and in the Samaritan woman of the Gospel, who is reproved because she had had five husbands, and the sixth, whom she thought she had, she did not have; and yet the number eight and the number five are completed by one cubit, that is, the fourteenth, because in Christ all things are summed up; whence it is said: And one cubit the boundary on both sides, since one measure of Christ embraces both the old and the new testament, and one cubit encloses the height of thirty cubits of Noah's ark. And the cells, he says (or, as the Seventy put it, 'thau' or 'thee' — turning and changing the Hebrew names in each place as they pleased —), were of six cubits 'on either side', which is said as on this side and on that, and they by no means had the handbreadth, nor the reason added above, which might call our present way of life to the future blessedness, but only six cubits. Whence there follows: And he measured the gate from the roof of a cell to the roof (or wall) of it, and he found twenty-five cubits of breadth; and the number itself, though it is square, is nevertheless referred to the senses: for if you set five cubits against each other five times, you will produce the number twenty-five, which is between the roof of the cells and the roof; and yet both, set opposite each other, have from their highest parts door opposite door. Let these things not seem trivial to the reader — although they displease even me myself who say them, feeling that I am knocking at a closed door —, but they are to be read with indulgence; otherwise I could simply have confessed my ignorance and cut off every desire of the studious: for as we are far from perfect knowledge, so we judge it a lighter fault to say at least a little than nothing at all.

40:14-16

And he made fronts of sixty cubits, and at the front a court of the gate on every side round about; and before the face of the gate, which reached as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits; and slanting windows in the cells and in their fronts, which were within the gate on every side round about; and likewise there were also windows in the vestibules round about within, and before the fronts a painting of palm trees. (LXX: "And under the open sky the 'aelam' of the gate, sixty cubits, and the 'theïm' of the court of the gate round about; and under the open sky of the court outside, the 'aelam' of the inner gate, fifty cubits; and hidden windows over the 'theïm' and over the 'aelam', within the gate of the court round about; and likewise the 'aelamoth' and windows round about within, and on the 'aelam' palms on this side and on that.") Symmachus translated this place thus: And he made περιστάσεις, which we can call 'circumstantias' [things standing round], in place of which the Hebrew also has 'ulium', which Aquila translated κρίωμα [ram-work, a pilaster] and we have turned into 'front'; again, where the Seventy put 'theïm of the court', the Hebrew has 'ulim' in the singular number, which Symmachus translated 'beside the court', Aquila κρίωμα, that is, 'the front of the court'; 'under the open sky' too, 'the aelam of the gate', Aquila translated 'before the face of the posts of the gate', Symmachus 'before the face of the vestibule of the gate'; and the 'hidden' windows, which in Hebrew are called 'aetemoth', Symmachus translated τοξικὰς [arrow-like]; and where the Seventy said 'over the theïm' and 'over the aelam', the same Symmachus put 'posts' and 'circumstantias', Aquila 'cells' and 'their fronts', in place of which in the Hebrew is written 'tham' and 'aele'; further, 'aelamoth', which the Seventy and Theodotion translated alike, Symmachus translated 'circumstantias', Aquila 'fronts'; and 'aelam', in place of which in the Hebrew is written 'ul', is called either 'door' or 'portico'; 'palm' too is written in the Hebrew 'thamarim', in the plural number, because the singular number calls a 'palm' 'thamar'. I do not doubt that these things will be tiresome to a fastidious reader, but I wished to show briefly how far, through length of time, or rather through the fault of the scribes and, to speak more openly, through their fault and unskillfulness, the old translation differs from the Hebrew truth, and especially in the Hebrew words which we have rendered into the Latin tongue from the editions of others, simply indicating not so much an explanation of the words as our conjecture. And I think that between the wall of the temple, outside round about, and the house itself, in the court, that is, in the middle, certain things were set for ornament, which Symmachus translates 'circumstantias', that is, 'certain standing things', raised up on high from the ground of the earth, and that these occupied a space of sixty cubits; and again, for those going out from the inner gate to the face of the vestibule which looked toward the outer gate, that the place occupied fifty cubits, in which there were slanting windows, which the Seventy call 'hidden', Symmachus τοξικὰς; and these windows were in the cells, that is, in each of the rooms, and in the porticoes which extended before the rooms, occupying fifty cubits — these slanting windows, or τοξικαὶ, received their name from arrows for this reason, that, like arrows, a narrow light is let into the building; and within they widen —; and everything round about was full of windows of this kind. 'And before the fronts', he says, 'of the porticoes, a painting or carving of palm trees'; by which it is shown that, for those at the entrance of the gate and as soon as they enter the wall, sixty cubits meet them with various ornaments, which are referred to the creation of the world, so that the Creator may be understood from the creatures, and so that the variety of the world may show all things running in order and reason — the world which among the Greeks receives the name κόσμος from 'adornment', and was made in six days, so that for each day one decade may be reckoned, which we said above is a perfect number —; after this, as we enter the inner court, there meet us, before the very vestibule of the inner gate, cells with slanting windows, which occupy a space of fifty cubits, which itself too is a consecrated number: and after seven full weeks of festivity and joy, the first day of the ogdoad begins, which is the day of the resurrection, and brings us into the neighborhood of the temple — for when we have done all things, doing penance for our former error, then we are made neighbors and nearest to God, so that, in the outer court, the order and constancy of the creatures may teach us the knowledge of the Creator, and, in the inner, the true jubilee, in which all debts are forgiven us, may instruct us in θεολογίαν [theology, the knowledge of God]. It must also be noted that the inner court has many windows, not straight and even but slanting, narrow on the outside and widening within, so that through certain small openings we may be able to penetrate to the inner things and to come to the fullness of the brightest light which dwells in the temple —; finally, after the sixty and the fifty cubits, and the cells and the porticoes, the fronts of the porticoes and the very many windows round about, the carving or painting of palm trees is shown to us, so that, possessing the victory over the world, we may be made worthy to see the palms of the virtues.

40:17-19

And he brought me out to the outer court, and behold, chambers, and a pavement laid with stone in the court round about, thirty chambers round about the pavement; and the pavement at the front of the gates, according to the length of the gates, was lower. And he measured the breadth from the face of the lower gate to the front of the inner court outside, a hundred cubits toward the east and toward the north. (LXX: "And he brought me into the inner court, and behold, cells and intercolumniations of the court round about, thirty cells between the columns; and porticoes behind the doors, along the length of the doors, before the columns, lower. And he measured the breadth of the court from that place which was under the open sky of the outer gate to the inner place under the open sky of the inner gate, which looked toward the outer parts, a hundred cubits, and it faced toward the east.") In place of the thirty 'cells' which the Seventy rendered, or 'chambers', and 'storerooms', as Aquila translated, Symmachus put 'exedrae'; and in place of the hundred cubits of the outer part which extended as far as the eastern gate, in the Hebrew the same number of cubits is said to extend toward the north too, but in the Seventy the name of the north has been removed. That man, then, who had the masons' cord in his hand and the measuring reed, and stood in the gate, among the other things which he showed to his sight, after the court of sixty cubits and the other vestibule of the inner gate which occupied fifty cubits, brought the prophet out to the outer court or, as is contained in the Seventy, brought him into the inner court — and I wonder greatly, according to the letter and the Seventy, how, after the outer courts occupying sixty and fifty cubits, there is an inner court which extends over spaces of a hundred cubits in breadth, unless perhaps, according to the mystical senses and the progress of those who enter, the things which were more inward in teachings are broader —; and having been brought into the inner court, or led to the outer court, as is contained in the Hebrew, he at once beheld thirty 'cells' or 'chambers' and, as Symmachus translated, 'exedrae', which had been prepared for the dwelling of the Levites and priests, and the pavement laid with stones, or intercolumniations, so that it may be shown that the inner or outer court has before the doors a row of columns and a pavement at the front of the gates, or porticoes behind the back of the gates, in which porticoes I think the columns were arranged in order, so that before the chambers there were porticoes, and at the fronts of the porticoes columns sustaining the porticoes; and the pavement which was laid with stones and extended before the porticoes of the court was lower at the ascent of the porticoes, and had the same length which the building of the cells possessed. And the same man, in whose hand were the cord and the reed, measured from the face of the lower gate or, as the Seventy would have it, of the outer gate, to the front of the inner court or gate, a hundred cubits toward the east and, as is said in the Hebrew, toward the north too. From which we understand that the saying of the Gospel which the Savior relates, of the seed sent into the field onto good ground, which multiplies its fruits according to the variety of the virtues into the number thirty and sixty and a hundred, agrees with the prophecy of this place: here too the number thirty and sixty and a hundred is set, so that by these, as by steps, we may be able to come to perfect knowledge, yet only in such a way that the number fifty leads us to the inner house, which, when the sabbath of the seven weeks is finished, breaks forth into the day of the resurrection. And those are called 'gazophylacia' [chambers, literally treasuries] which are full of spiritual riches — of which it is written: The redemption of a man's soul is his own riches, and over which the apostle Paul too congratulates his disciples, that they are full in every word and in all knowledge; and in the language of the Persians 'riches' are called 'gaza' —, or certainly cells, which in Greek are called παστοφόρια [bridal chambers]: they show rooms prepared for the coming of the bridegroom; and they were thirty in number, to show the perfect age of those who dwell in them. And the 'pavement' was laid with stone, so that the footsteps of the inhabitants might not be defiled by the mud and earth and dust of sins, but that they might walk upon the living stones with which the temple of God is built; or there were 'intercolumniations' before the doors of the cells, which sustained the building laid upon them from above — these are the columns of which the apostle Paul also writes: They gave the right hand to me and Barnabas, Peter and John, who seemed to be columns, and in another place: The column and foundation of the truth; and in the Revelation of John we read: He who conquers, I will make him a column in the temple of my God, and he shall go outside no more —; so the 'pavement' which was at the front of the gates, of which we have already spoken, or the 'porticoes' behind the back of the gates, which protected the inhabitants of the cells from the rains, was lower: for the things which are lower are always placed in the higher ones, so that we may be able to come by ascent and by steps to the things that are mystical and secret and full of spiritual riches. And the full and perfect number is in the number of ten decades, which also multiplies the sowing of Isaac with a hundredfold crop; but because he was on earth and could still say: I am a sojourner and a stranger, as all my fathers were, he is related to have sown barley and reaped a hundredfold crop: for the grain of wheat had not yet died in the earth, to bear many fruits and to satisfy the Jewish people's hunger for hearing the word of God with that bread which came down from heaven; but how the hundred cubits were not only toward the eastern gate but also toward the gate of the north, the following testimony will show.

40:20-23

He also measured the gate which looked toward the way of the north of the outer court, as much in length as in breadth; and its cells, three on this side and three on that, and its front and its vestibule according to the measure of the former gate, its length fifty cubits, and the breadth twenty-five cubits. And its windows and its vestibule and carvings according to the measures of the gate which looked toward the east; and its ascent was of seven steps, and a vestibule before it. And the gate of the inner court opposite the gate of the north and the eastern one; and he measured from gate to gate a hundred cubits. (LXX: "And he brought me toward the north, and behold, a gate looking toward the outer court, and he measured it in length and in breadth; and its 'thee', three on this side and three on that, and the 'aeleu' and the 'aelamoth' — and what is not found in the Hebrew: — and its palms, and it was made according to the measure of the gate which looked toward the east, fifty cubits the length and the breadth twenty-five cubits. And its windows and the 'aelamoth' and its palms as in the gate which looked toward the east; and by steps they went up to it, and the 'aelamoth' within. And the gate of the inner court looking toward the gate of the north — and what is not found in the Hebrew: — as the gate which looks toward the east; and he measured the court from gate to gate, of a hundred cubits.") What the Hebrew words 'thee' and 'aeleu' and 'aelamoth' signify we have said more fully above, but in the present passage too our translation will teach it by their placing. And the man in whose hand was the cord measured the gate of the north too, of the outer court, or brought the prophet in through the gate of the north to the outer court — in which it must be considered that he is brought in first through the gate of the north, second through the gate of the south, third through the eastern gate — From the north, for, evils blaze up upon the inhabitants of the earth, and fittingly he who is an inhabitant of the earth, and not a sojourner and a stranger, lies open to the darts of him who comes from the north, whose darts are fiery, which, according to the Apostle, are quenched by the shield of faith —; and toward the north the court is called outer, but toward the midday, that is, toward the south, not outer but inner — for Scripture says: And he brought me into the inner court, to the southern gate, which is found written likewise of the eastern court too —: for the first entrance to virtue is to tread the north underfoot and, through the number fifty and twenty-five, to come to the summit of the hundred; then to be brought into the southern quarter and to drive out the cold of the north; then to come to perfect virtue, that is, to the eastern gate, in which the sun of righteousness rises and through which the high priest alone enters — and this is to be observed, that, though there are four quarters, the western gate is passed over in silence, of which it is written at the beginning of that psalm: Make a way for him who ascends over the setting: the Lord is his name, so that, after we have prepared the way for the Lord and have fulfilled what John the Baptist cries in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight, we may be able to hear what is said in the last part of the same psalm: who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east —. And that the cells are said to be three on this side and three on that teaches this, that both the letter and the spirit, and each understanding, that of history and that of tropology, pertain to the mysteries of the Trinity. And what is said: And its front and vestibule according to the measure of the former gate, signifies the eastern gate, which is called former not in order but in merit. 'And they had', he says, 'fifty cubits in length and twenty-five in breadth', so that in the fifty, after seven weeks, the eternal rest may be shown, extending through the day of the resurrection to the kingdoms of heaven, in which there is true rest, and in the twenty-five, of which number we have spoken before, the five senses may be kept, through five rows, in the measure of a square, one of which is fitted to the length, the other to the breadth, so that in the length may be shown the rest and delight of a more sacred knowledge, in the breadth the reason of present things which pertains to the senses. And what is added: And the windows and the vestibules and the carvings (or, as the Seventy have handed down, the palms) were according to the measure of the gate which looked toward the east, indicates this spiritually: that whoever, placed at the entrance of the virtues, has entered the three and three cells and has recognized the front and the vestibule of the measure of the former gate, may also come to those things, and behold those, which he is going to receive most fully in the eastern gate. Further, what follows: And its ascent was of seven steps, and a vestibule before it (or within), has this sense: that through the seven steps of the week, and of the pot which is kindled from the face of the north, and of the ceremonies of the Jews, to whom God gave precepts that were not good and ordinances in which they should not live in them, we climb to higher things and to its vestibule, that is, the vestibule of the gate, in place of which the Seventy translated 'aelamoth', which vestibule is before the gate, or within. Nor is there only one gate of the north, which above is called the outer gate, but another which has the likeness of the eastern gate, as the Seventy said more plainly: And the inner gate of the court looking toward the gate of the north, as was the gate which looked toward the east; and he measured from the outer gate of the north to the inner gate of the same north a hundred cubits, so that by these as by steps, withdrawing from the outer gate, we may be able to come to the inner one, concerning the mystery of which number it has been spoken.

40:24-31

And he led me to the southern way, and behold, a gate which looked toward the south; and he measured its front and its vestibule according to the measures above, and its windows, and the vestibules round about it, like the other windows, in which there was a length of fifty cubits and a breadth of twenty-five. And by seven steps one went up to it, and a vestibule before its front, and there were carved palms, one on this side and another on that, on its front. And the gate of the inner court on the southern way; and he measured from gate to gate on the southern way a hundred cubits. And he brought me into the inner court at the southern gate, and he measured the gate according to the measures above, its cell and its front, and its vestibule with the same measures, and the windows of the vestibules round about: fifty cubits of length, and of breadth twenty-five cubits, and the vestibule round about, in length twenty-five cubits and in breadth five cubits, and its vestibule toward the outer court, and palms on the front, and there were eight steps by which one went up through it. (The Seventy agree in the same words, except for 'thee' and 'aeleu' and 'aelamoth' and 'aelam', in place of which in the Hebrew is put 'ulam'; and 'thee' means 'threshold' or 'front', 'aeleu' 'around it' or 'supports', 'aelamoth' 'propyla' [gateways] or 'vestibules', 'ulam tritilon' 'round about', that is, 'before the doors'. But what we have put according to the Hebrew: And the vestibule (or πρόπυλον [gateway]) round about, of a length of twenty-five cubits and of a breadth of five cubits, is not found in the Seventy. But this too is to be noted, that at the southern gate, according to the Seventy, 'way' is not said, but simply: And he led me toward the south, and behold, a gate which looked toward the south.) Through each of the entrances, then, Ezekiel, whom God strengthened — for this is what his name means —, is led, and he passes from the gate of the north to the southern gate, whose fronts and thresholds, πρόπυλα or vestibules, and windows round about had similar measures: a length of fifty cubits and a breadth of twenty-five cubits. And by seven steps one went up to it, that is, to the southern gate, and its vestibule, that is, the 'aelamoth', was before its doors; there were also two carved palms, of which we spoke at the northern quarter of the gate. And let it suffice to have advised only this, that what is set there according to a lowlier understanding, that is, according to the letter, we understand at the southern gate according to the spiritual sense: for history and tropology run along the same lines, but the former is humbler, the latter more sublime; the former clings to the earth, the latter flies up to heavenly things. And round about, through the windows, all things were full of light — for the several προβλήματα [questions] have their own limits —, and through them its own light enters the soul of the one who sees, especially if the length of his life has been prolonged by the mystery of the fiftieth year, that is, of the jubilee, and he has been able to come to the breadth of the more divine sense; in which breadth and streets wisdom acts confidently and cries aloud with a lofty voice. He enters by seven steps so as to come to the vestibule, and through the palms of his purpose and effort to hold the everlasting victory. And lest we should think there is one court toward the southern part, it is said of a second court: And the gate of the inner court on the southern way; and he measured from gate to gate on the southern way a hundred cubits, so that after the mysteries of the week and of the old Testament he might come to the good land and to the grace of the Gospel. Nor is there only a second court at the southern gate, but a third, of which it is now said: And he brought me into the inner court at the southern gate, and he measured the gate according to the measures above, and the rest: for each court has its own measures and orders, and in the same measures there is a different grace, since we know the same things in one way at the beginning, in another in our progress, in another at the end. But this, which is not found in the Seventy: And the vestibule (or πρόπυλον) round about, in length twenty-five cubits and in breadth five cubits, seems to raise a question, on account of which it was also not set down in the translation: how, after the progress of the third step, twenty-five cubits and five are set; but what follows removes the ambiguity: And its vestibule toward the outer court, and the palms on its front, namely, that this court, which has twenty-five cubits in length and five in breadth, belongs not to the inner but to the outer court, so that the length of the outer court possesses the breadth of the former court, that is, twenty-five cubits, and holds five cubits in breadth; which measures, that is, twenty-five and five, we refer to those senses, namely sight, hearing, taste and smell and touch, which, if we climb to higher things, we double five times, and out of carnal senses we shall make spiritual ones — as in that saying: Lift up your eyes and see, for the harvests are white for reaping, and: He who has ears to hear, let him hear, and: Taste and see that the Lord is sweet, and: We are the good odor of Christ among those who believe; and in the epistle of John it is said: What we have heard and seen, and our hands have handled, concerning the word of life —. And at the last they make not, as at the northern quarter, only seven steps, but after the seven the number eight is set, so that we may pass from the Synagogue to the Church, from the old testament to the new, from earthly things to heavenly ones.

40:32-34

And he brought me into the inner court by the eastern way, and he measured the gate according to the measures above; the cell and its front and the vestibules as above, and its windows and its vestibules round about, the length fifty cubits and the breadth twenty-five cubits; and its vestibule, that is, of the outer court (in place of which the Seventy and Symmachus put inner), and carved palms on its front, on this side and on that, and its ascent by eight steps. From the northern quarter, into whose court one went up by only seven steps, he passes to the southern gate and to the court of the same quarter, to which one ascends not only by seven steps, as we said above, but by eight: namely, so that through the old things we may pass to the new and, to speak more plainly, through the patriarchs and prophets we may come to the apostles: so that in the one there is the hebdomad, in the other the ogdoad. But now he comes to the last, or rather to the highest, and brings the prophet in by the way of the inner gate, or through the court to which one goes by the eastern way — 'way', according to the Seventy, is found in this place only: at the northern and the southern quarter it is wholly passed over in silence, so that we may understand that at the eastern gate alone is that way to be understood which says: I am the way and the truth and the life; for through him we come to the Father, and of him it is written: Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who think nothing sinister about Christ, but whose faith is pure and in no way polluted with the filth of heretics —; and there is the same number of cells, of fronts and vestibules and windows and of their light, and the same measure of length and breadth, preserving, namely, the mysteries of fifty and of twenty-five cubits; and the vestibule of its gate, or of the inner court, which according to the Hebrew is set down as outer, so that all things may be held enclosed by the eastern light — according to that which is written: Nor is there anyone who hides himself from its heat —; but if we take the court as both outer and inner, it is to be understood thus: that God is both poured around and poured in, saying through the prophet: Who holds the heaven in his palm and the earth in his fist, so that all things may be seen to be enclosed by him, and again: Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet, so that he is to be believed to be within all things — according to that passage of Vergil: In the beginning the heaven and the lands and the liquid plains, the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars, a spirit within nourishes, and mind, poured through the limbs, moves the whole mass and mingles itself with the great body —; and when, through the weapons on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through good report and bad, through praises and reproaches, we have won the victory over this world, then palms are given to us on both sides, whom neither joys have changed nor grief, neither prosperity nor adversity has overcome; and by no means through seven steps, as in the quarter of the north, nor through seven and eight, as is contained also at the midday, but through eight steps only we climb to the summit, because the number eight, that is, the mystery of the Gospel, suffices for us, and we may say, according to the Apostle: Even if we had known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer, understood: according to the flesh.

40:35-43

And he brought me to the gate which looked toward the north, and he measured according to the measures above its cell, its front and its vestibule and its windows round about, in length fifty cubits, in breadth twenty-five cubits. Its vestibule looked into the outer court, and a carving of palms on its front on this side and on that; its ascent was by eight steps. And by each chamber a door at the entrances of the gates; there they washed the holocaust. And in the vestibule of the gate two tables on this side and two tables on that, that the holocaust may be sacrificed upon them, and for sin and for trespass. And at the outer side which goes up to the door of the gate that leads toward the north, two tables; and at the other side, before the vestibule of the gate, two tables. Four tables on this side and four tables on that: along the sides of the gate there were eight tables, upon which they sacrificed. And four tables for the holocaust, built of squared stones, of a length of one cubit and a half, and a breadth of one cubit and a half, and a height of one cubit, upon which they are to put the vessels in which the holocaust and the victims are sacrificed; and their lips of one handbreadth, bent back inward round about, and upon the tables the flesh of the oblation. In this testimony the Hebrew truth disagrees greatly with the edition of the Seventy translators: for what we have said: There they washed the holocaust. And in the vestibule of the gate two tables on this side, and again: That the holocaust may be sacrificed upon them, and for sin, is not found in the Seventy, but in most manuscripts it has been added from Theodotion; again, where we said: And their lips of one handbreadth, bent back inward round about, the Seventy translated: And having a 'gisum' of a handbreadth, hewn inward round about — which word, whether it is Hebrew or Greek, we cannot know, except only this, that in place of 'gisum' Symmachus and Theodotion translated 'lips', the first edition of Aquila ἐπιστάσεις [ledges] in the plural number, the second 'lips', in place of which in the Hebrew there is 'asaphanaim' —; and where we said: And upon the tables the flesh of the oblation, the Seventy put of their own: And on the tables, coverings above, that they might be covered from rain and from drought; and as for what they rendered with Hebrew names, 'thee' and 'aeleu' and 'aelamoth' and 'aelam', what it signifies we have both advised above, and our translation, set over against it, can show, nor is there any need to advise the reader often about this and to distrust his prudence and diligence. He is brought, then, again to the gate which looked toward the north, but by no means, as above, to the outer court, but to the inner — for in what is said in what follows: Its vestibule looked toward the outer court, it is shown that this court was within —; by which the progress of the one entering is shown, since in each place the names and measures are its own, and the windows round about show all things full of the light of knowledge; and through the fifty and the twenty-five cubits the mysteries of remission and of the divine senses are set, so that, placed in the vestibule of the inner court, we may see the outer things, and, contemplating the knowledge of things past and present, through which we may come to the double palms and victories, may know the mysteries of the eight steps, having gone into the chambers, in which the riches of the temple are contained and our prayers are washed from every stain of sin. And two tables were set on each side, so that first the holocaust may be sacrificed, which the sacred fire consumes wholly, then the offering for sin, and lastly that for ignorance: for what we have committed either knowingly or in ignorance. At the outer side too, according to the Seventy, there was a skillfully made channel which carried outside the ashes of the holocausts and the putrid matter of the flesh, or: there were two tables; and at the other side of the vestibule of the same gate two tables, that is, four on each side. Four on this side and four on that, and behind them or at their side another eight tables, so that together they make sixteen tables; by which number the mysteries of the prophets are shown, so that whatever we offer through the condescension of the Gospel we may prove to have been foretold by their prophecies. And as for the four tables that are brought in, built of squared stones, and these too for the sacrifice of the holocaust: these are the living stones which roll upon the earth and have with them the cornerstone by which the walls of the old and the new Testament are held together; and the number four shows the mysteries of the Gospel; having in length and breadth one cubit and a half, that is, in a square, which joined together make three cubits, and these three cubits have one cubit in height, so that the measure of one cubit, that is, of the divine majesty, may preserve the mysteries of the Trinity, as the Lord says to his disciples: Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: and the name of God is, as it were, the one cubit of height, which embraces three properties and always takes up the holocausts of our offerings; and upon these four tables of the holocausts, built of living stones, whose length and breadth and height have been described, are put the vessels in which is sacrificed the holocaust of the martyrs, of whom it is said: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints, and the victims of those who by continence and holiness of body sacrifice their souls to the Lord; and I think the names of these tables are contained in the apostles Matthew and Luke and Mark and John; their rim, bent back inward from above, went round the edges round about, so as to hold the holocausts within and not allow them to flow everywhere, and to hold the flesh of the oblation; or, as the Seventy translated: And the tables themselves were covered above, because of the violence of the rains and the excessive drought of the summer sun, so that the flesh placed upon them may say with the prophet: By day the sun shall not burn us, nor the moon by night, of which the one dissolves the offerings with excessive rains and storms of tribulations, the other makes whatever has been offered dry up in the fierce heat of persecutions. Pardon, reader, the difficulty of the passages, or, if you can find something better, teach me: we gladly learn what we do not know.

40:44-49

And outside the inner gate the chambers of the singers in the inner court, which was at the side of the gate looking toward the north, and their faces toward the southern way, one at the side of the gate which looked toward the way of the north. And he said to me: This is the chamber which looks toward the way of midday, for the priests who keep watch in the charges of the temple. Further, the chamber which looks toward the way of the north shall be for the priests who keep watch for the ministry of the altar: these are the sons of Zadok, who from the sons of Levi come near to the Lord to minister to him. And he measured the court, in length a hundred cubits and in breadth a hundred cubits, in a square, and the altar before the face of the temple. And he brought me into the vestibule of the temple; and he measured the vestibule, five cubits on this side and five cubits on that, and the breadth of the gate, three cubits on this side and three cubits on that; and the length of the vestibule twenty cubits and the breadth eleven cubits, and by eight steps one went up to it, and their columns on the fronts, one on this side and another on that. In place of 'chambers' the Seventy translated 'exedrae'; and what we said, exedrae or chambers 'of the singers', was passed over by them; and again, after the measure of the vestibule of five cubits on this side and five cubits on that, they added of their own: And the breadth of the gate of fourteen cubits, whereas in the Hebrew there is set only: And the breadth of the gate of three cubits on this side and three cubits on that. I have advised the reader of these things so that he may not be disturbed by the diversity of the translations, but that, in the present place and especially in the measures of the temple, he may be content with the Hebrew truth. So, after the wall, which the Seventy translated περίβολον, which went round the whole temple in a square round about, we read that the prophet was brought into the inner court, and then to the north and to the south and to the eastern gate and again to the north, of which we have spoken as best we could, and in whose diversities, whether of names or of measures, our past discourse has shown what seemed right to us — whose sense the testimony of the Savior briefly shows, saying: In my Father's house are many mansions —. These things completed, he enters the temple, that is, the Holy of Holies, of which it is now spoken, and within the inner gate are the chambers or exedrae of the singers — to whom that command is given: Sing to the Lord a new song, who cry aloud with the angels: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among men of good will —, which inner court was situated at the side of the gate which looked toward the north, and toward the south and toward the east, so that the singers of the Lord, and those who are held in the office of the angels, may always remember by what steps they have come to the summit, and may diligently recognize the mysteries of each place. Then that man, in whose hand were the cord and the reed, brings the prophet into the inner court which looked toward the way of midday, and spoke these words: This is the chamber (or exedra, and, as Theodotion put it, cell) which has been set apart for the dwelling of the priests who keep watch in the vigils of the temple. Further, the chamber which looks toward the way of the north shall be for the priests who keep watch for the ministry of the altar. In which it is to be noted that the priests to whom the guarding of the temple has been delegated dwell in the chamber which looked toward the way of midday, in which the light is fullest, but those who keep watch for the ministry of the altar, on which the victims for sin are offered, are in the chamber which looks toward the way of the north, desiring to receive and save those who come from the north and offer victims for sin: and both of these, serving the Lord according to their offices, are called sons of 'Sadoc' [Zadok], which means 'righteous' or 'justifying', namely the almighty God — of whom it is written: The Lord is righteous and has loved righteous deeds; his countenance has beheld equity —; and these sons of Zadok are from the sons of 'Leui' [Levi], which means 'taken up', and they too are taken up by the Lord, so that they may come near to him — and it is by no means said of Moses alone: Moses came near to the Lord, while the others did not come near, but all who serve him and minister to him are said to draw near to the Lord —. And this man, who brought Ezekiel into the outer court and, so to speak, to the Holy of Holies, measured the court itself, in which were the two exedrae or chambers assigned as dwellings for the guardians of the temple or of the altar, and found a hundred cubits each of length and of breadth, in a square, so that the priests serving in the ministry of the Lord, who had entered by the strait and narrow way, may have very broad walks and may abide in the perfect and complete number of the virtues; and in the court itself was the altar before the face of the temple, so that the prayer of the saints to the Lord may never cease. The aforesaid man also brought Ezekiel into the vestibule, or πρόπυλον, of the temple, which he measured at five cubits on this side and five on that, since he who was brought in had been instructed in the divine senses, and knew neither the right hand nor the left, but walked by the royal road; and the breadth of the gate itself, through which was the entrance to the vestibule of the temple, had three cubits 'on this side and on that' — in which the elegance of holy Scripture is to be observed, that it did not say 'on the right and on the left', lest it should seem to name anything sinister in the Holy of Holies, but 'on this side and on that', that is, on either side —, and at once the prudent reader understands that the number three pertains to the mystery of the Trinity, which is the gate of those who enter to God, since the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both; and this threefold number is the one gate of those who, after the baptism of the Trinity, come to salvation. But what follows: The length of the vestibule twenty cubits and the breadth eleven cubits, seems to raise a question: how the dual number, which is referred to two decades, and the eleventh, which lacks one to fill up the sacred number twelve, can be said to be in the vestibule of the temple; which most people solve thus: although the priests are holy and placed in the ministries of the temple and daily offer victims to Christ, yet, because they dwell in this mortal and frail little body — and one which is subject to sicknesses and vices —, they have the number twenty and the eleventh — whence the apostle too said: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?, not that we should believe, according to a most savage heresy, that bodies are to be abolished, but that it is for us to be clothed over, not stripped, and for this mortal to receive immortality and for the corruptible to put on incorruption —. But what follows: And by eight steps one went up to it, that is, to the inner gate, is a great difficulty for those who know the Hebrew language: in fact Symmachus, whom we have followed in this place, put 'by eight steps', the Seventy 'ten', Theodotion and the second edition of Aquila 'eleven', but the first put no number, but says absolutely: And by steps by which one went up to it, so that we should understand either, according to the custom of the earlier gates, 'eight' 'steps', as Symmachus also understood, or certainly those steps which the inner gate had, whose number Scripture did not state: because in the Hebrew there is set 'urob' — that is, 'and the breadth' — 'ast-hesre' — which, if it is read so, signifies 'eleven', but if instead of 'hesre', that is, 'ten', we read 'heser', it does not signify 'ten' but a pronoun —; which may seem ravings to those who have no experience of the Hebrew language. But now we are not writing disputations or orations, in which one is accustomed to play with the arrangement of words, but explanations and commentaries on the Hebrew volumes; but let us return to our undertaking. By eight or ten steps, which is a perfect number, or eleven, of which we have already spoken, one went up to the gate of the holy places, on whose fronts were columns, one on this side and another on that: he did not say 'two', lest he should run into the dual number, but 'one and one', which is a perfect number and is taken from the oneness of God — and these were its columns, of which it is also said in the Revelation: He who conquers, I will make him a column in the temple of my God, and he shall not go outside; and Peter and John are called columns of the Church, through whom we enter into the Holy of Holies, and by whose teaching is our entrance to Christ —.

41:1-2

And he brought me into the temple, and measured the fronts: six cubits of breadth on this side and six cubits of breadth on that side, the breadth of the tabernacle. And the breadth of the gate was of ten cubits, and the sides (or shoulders) of the gate of five cubits on this side and five cubits on that side; and he measured a length of forty cubits and a breadth of twenty cubits. After many mysteries and various entrances and the particular features of each place, at long last the man in whose hand were the masons' line and the measuring reed brings the prophet Ezekiel into the temple, and he measured the front of the temple — for which the Seventy translated 'aelam', and Theodotion 'aelim', and Symmachus 'round about' —, and each breadth of the tabernacle was of six cubits, containing the mystery of all creatures — for in six days the world was founded —, through the knowledge of which, and of the causes and the principle of their founding, we enter into the temple of God, and from the order and constancy of creatures we know the Creator. The breadth of the gate of the temple, moreover, was of ten cubits — which is a sacred and perfect number, and the one on which, in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, there is the fast and the propitiation; and on the tenth day of the first month, which is called Nisan, the lamb is taken for the sacrifice and preparation of the Passover. In the seventh month, therefore, tithes are offered into the granaries of God, or, as Scripture is accustomed to call them, the winepresses; whence the Apostle also says: Be enlarged, you also —, so that, after someone has entered the temple through the ten cubits of the gate, its sides on either part, or, as it is properly said in the Hebrew, its shoulders, are measured, which always refer to works — whence also: Issachar desired the good, resting among the middle lots; and he saw rest, that it is good, and the land, that it is fat: he put his shoulder to labor and became a husbandman; and in the garment of the high priest the shoulder-piece is bound together with the rational, so that works may be completed by reason, and the churchman may say: From your commandments I have understood —, which shoulders of the gate had five cubits each on either side, so that through the earthly senses and the divine, about whose difference we often write, we may enter the innermost recesses of the temple; of which that man, who was the prophet's guide, measured the length of forty cubits and the breadth of twenty cubits, or, as is better, the length and breadth of the gate, because above he had spoken only of its breadth and its shoulders. Now that twenty times forty makes the number eight hundred, which is akin to the number eight, is doubtful to no one — whence also in Ecclesiastes it is commanded: Give a portion to seven, give also to eight —, and I know that I have often discussed the mystery of that number; or else, because it is through the tribulations and straits of this world that we enter into the sanctuary of the Lord, therefore the length of the gate had forty cubits, a number that is always set in labor — whence both Moses and Elijah for forty days do not eat bread and do not drink water, and for forty years the people of Israel is harassed and tested in the wilderness and after many labors enters the land of promise, and the Lord and Savior, according to the frailty of the body he assumed, is tempted for forty days in the wilderness, so that after the victory angels might come and minister to him —. But when, after tribulations and straits, we are able to say that apostolic word: In all things troubled, but not straitened, and the prophetic one: In tribulation you have enlarged me, then a most wide entrance is opened to us, which has a breadth of twenty cubits, so that, having overcome the contests of the world and of earthly things, which itself also is a dual number, we may enter the inner places of the temple, and hear the Lord commanding the disciples: Take courage, I have conquered the world.

41:3-4

And having entered within (or into the inner court) he measured in the front (or 'aelam') of the gate two cubits, and the gate of six cubits, and the breadth of the gate of seven cubits (or and the shoulders of the gate seven cubits on this side and seven cubits on that side). And he measured its length (or of the doors) of twenty cubits and the breadth of twenty cubits before the face of the temple, and he said to me: This is the Holy of Holies. However much we advance, a greater advance always opens before us. Hence, after the entrance of the temple, we again enter within, or, as the Seventy translated, the inner court, in whose 'front' or 'ael' — for which Symmachus translated 'around the gate', Theodotion 'aelam', the Hebrew 'ul', Aquila 'on this side of the door', we 'front' —, there were two cubits, so that, according to the sense given above, through the dual number we may enter that place where the Holy of Holies is; whence also the gate itself was of six cubits, through which, having entered, we possess eternal rest, which is shown in the number seven: for which the Seventy translated: And the breadth of the gate of seven cubits on this side and of seven cubits on that side, whereas in the Hebrew and the other editions the cubits in the breadth of the gate are set down only once. What follows, however: And he measured its length of twenty cubits (or, as is contained in the Seventy, forty), the breadth also of twenty cubits before the face of the temple, signifies this: that before the face of the temple and at its entrance the measure of past labor and contest always meets us; for the same meaning that the double number holds among the single numbers, the two decades have. And this must be considered: that, having entered within through the gate of two cubits in front, which has six cubits and seven in breadth on either side and twenty cubits in length and as many in the very doors of the temple, the prophet is taught what that place is, or by what name it is called: for he said, he says, to me: This is the Holy of Holies. But if before the temple, or, as Scripture names it, before the face of the temple, there is the Holy of Holies, how great a blessedness ought we to reckon there is in the innermost recesses of the temple and in its interior — of which the prophet speaks: This is labor in my sight, until I enter into the sanctuary of God; I shall understand in their last things —! But this too must be noted, that in the description of the tabernacle Sancta sanctorum [holies of holies] is said in the plural number, but here Sanctum sanctorum [holy of holies] in the singular number, so that after the holy things we may come to the Holy — just as after many songs we arrive at the Song of Songs, which is the song of all songs and singing which we are joined in the embraces of the Bridegroom —.

41:5-12

And he measured the wall of the house, six cubits, and the breadth of the side, four cubits, round about the house on every side; and the sides, side to side, twice thirty-three. And there were projections which entered through the wall of the house in the sides round about, to hold and not to touch the wall of the temple. And there was a broad way going upward in a round by a spiral, and it led into the upper room of the temple by a circuit. Therefore the temple was wider in the upper parts, and so from the lower parts one went up to the upper into the middle. (But what is set down in the Seventy, and from the middle parts to the tristega — that is, 'to the third upper rooms' and 'thrael', is not found in the Hebrew; and for 'thrael' too, which I do not know what it signifies, for it is not found in the Hebrew, there is read among them 'uraithi', which both we and the others translated 'and I saw', so that the order of the testimony may follow:) And I saw in the house a height round about, the sides founded to the measure of a reed with a space of six cubits; and the breadth through the wall of the side outside of five cubits, and the inner house in the sides of the house, and between the chambers a breadth of twenty cubits round the house on every side. And the door of the side for prayer (which is not found in the Seventy), one door toward the way of the north, and one door toward the southern way; and the breadth of the place for prayer (which the Seventy likewise did not translate) of five cubits round about. And the building which was separate and turned toward the way looking to the sea, of a breadth of seventy cubits, but the wall of the building five cubits of breadth round about, and its length ninety cubits. After he came to the Holy of Holies, of which we spoke above, that venerable man measured the wall of the Holy of Holies, which, on account of the fabric of the world and all the visible creation that was founded in six days, had six cubits, and the breadth of one side, four cubits: not on one side only, but round about the house was the breadth; and the breadth held four cubits round about the house, so as to show the four elements from which all things are compacted, and especially human bodies, against which the saints, fighting and subjecting them to the power of the soul, merit to enter the inner places and to know the secrets of the Lord. The sides themselves, which were round about the house and were separated from the wall of the temple by a space of four cubits, were joined to one another, so that one side touched another side and had in length not thirty-three cubits but twice thirty-three, that is, sixty-six. The Old Testament speaks in Leviticus about the birth of a male, that after one week both she who bore and he who was born fulfill thirty-three days so that they may come to purification; but if she bears a female, she is to observe a double number, that is, sixty-six; and because, in order to come to the Holy of Holies, we need not only the first birth but also the second, so that, born in the flesh, we may be reborn in the spirit, therefore not the number sixty-six but twice thirty-three is set down, so that each birth may be owed to God as author and to his clemency, and that the sides of the house which support the building of the temple may go round it with a double wall. And what follows according to the Hebrew: And there were certain projections which entered through the walls of the house through the sides round about, to hold and not to touch the wall of the temple, signifies this: that holy men in the multitude of believers break forth through the wall of the temple, that is, through all the sides round about, and hold the foundations of the Church, and yet do not touch the wall of the temple, content only to have seen and from afar to have adored the unspeakable mysteries: for now we see through a mirror in an enigma, and we cannot touch and comprehend the fullest truth. But as for: There was a broad way going upward in a round by a spiral, and it led into the upper room of the temple by a circuit, and: Therefore the temple was wider in the upper parts, and so from the lower parts one went up to the upper and the middle, I think it is clear to the reader that the things below are always narrower, in fasts, in sleeping on the ground, in restraint of diet, and that little by little, as we climb to the heights, a wider way is opened to us and that is fulfilled which is written: In tribulation you have enlarged me; and by the round and the spiral we climb to the upper room of the temple, a figure which among all σχήματα [shapes, figures] is approved as the more beautiful even by the philosophers of this world, since the sky and the sun and the moon and the other stars and the point of the earth, and in human bodies too the eyes, like other stars, and the shape of the head, which is the receptacle of all the senses, and the rounded fingers and thighs and arms display this roundness; moreover, the upper room of the temple, to which one climbs from narrower things to higher, I think is that which Elijah and Elisha had in the volume of Kings, and which our Tabitha — that is, δορκάς and doe — possessed in the Acts of the Apostles, she who by good works had climbed to the heights; but the apostle Peter, upon whom the Lord made firm the foundations of the Church, went beyond the upper room and came to the roof — which is more expressively called δῶμα in Greek — that is, the sun-terrace of the roof —, and came to know the mysteries of the Church previously unknown to the world; the Savior of the human race also made the Passover in an upper room, and in a large and broad upper room, purged of all filth and spread and prepared for the spiritual banquet, where he handed on to his disciples the mystery of his body and blood and left us the eternal festival of the spotless lamb. And what he adds: And from the middle parts to the tristega (that is, third upper rooms) and 'thrael', seems to me fit to be marked beforehand with an obelus: for what need is there to discuss doubtful things that are not written, when we ought to apply ourselves to the things contained in the books of the Hebrews? There follows: And I saw in the house a height round about, the sides founded to the measure of a reed with a space of six cubits; and the breadth through the wall of the side outside of five cubits; and between the chambers (which Symmachus calls ἐξέδρας [exedras]) a breadth of twenty cubits round the house, by which numbers it is shown that from this world and from the earthly senses and from the dual number of two decades, which is referred to twenty, we may merit to ascend not only into the Holy of Holies but also into its upper rooms, and may always keep in memory that through the six days of our creation and through the five senses and through the twenty cubits of breadth we have ascended to the upper room of the temple and, leaving behind earthly lowliness and the sense of the letter, have crossed over to the summit of the Church, and rejoice in the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. And the door, he says, of the side for prayer facing the way of the north: From which evils blaze forth upon all the earth, and which the Lord promises he will drive away from us, saying: And him who is from the north I will drive away from you; and beautifully at the door facing the north is the place of prayer, so that according to the Apostle we may pray without ceasing, and say with Jeremiah: Let not the pupil of my eye be silent, either desiring to avoid present evils or giving thanks for past ones — for as long as we are in the tabernacle of this body, we groan and say: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? —; but toward the southern way too there was a door, and it also, according to the Hebrew, had a place of prayer and extended five cubits round about — for after the cold of the north let us cross over to the warmth of the south —, and yet once more we seek a place of prayer: at the door of the north, that we may escape dangers; at the southern one, that we may give thanks for past things and that the possession of victory may be secure for us; and the five cubits in this place too indicate the divine senses, through which we climb from earthly things to higher. And the building, he says, which was separate and turned toward the way looking to the sea, of a breadth of seventy cubits, so that, after labors and dangers and the waves and shipwrecks of this world, and the seventy years of which Jeremiah writes, and Daniel and Zechariah, we may attain the true and lawful sabbath of seven decades, and there may be eternal rest for us; and that through the breadth of five cubits we may come to the length of ninety cubits, the age at which Sarah bore a son by the promise, she who at ninety years, that is, of nine decades, gave birth to Isaac, joined to Abraham the hundred-year-old, who held the mystery of ten decades — what this number signifies, the Scripture that follows will show.

41:13-22a

And he measured the length of the house, a hundred cubits, and the building that was separate and its walls, of a length of a hundred cubits; but the breadth before the face of the house and of that which was separate toward the east, a hundred cubits. And he measured the length of the building facing that which was separate at the back, ἔκθετας (that is, 'projections') on either side, a hundred cubits; and the inner temple and the vestibules of the court, the thresholds and slanting windows, and ἔκθετας round about on three sides facing each threshold, and it was laid with wood in a ring round about; and earth up to the windows, and the windows closed above the doors. And up to the inner house and outside, over the whole wall round about, within and without, by measure. And Cherubim and palms were wrought, and a palm between Cherub and Cherub; and a Cherub had two faces: the face of a man next to a palm on this side, and the face of a lion next to a palm on the other side, fashioned through all the house round about. From the ground up to the upper parts of the gate Cherubim and palms were carved on the wall of the temple. A four-cornered threshold, and the face of the sanctuary, aspect facing aspect. Of the wooden altar the height three cubits, and its length two cubits, and its corners and its length and its walls of wood. (LXX: "And he measured ÷ facing ⁚ the house, a length of a hundred cubits, and the remaining parts and the separating parts and its walls in length a hundred cubits; and the breadth facing the face of the temple and the remaining parts opposite, a hundred cubits. And he measured the length of the separating part facing the face of the remaining parts which were behind the back of that house, and the remaining parts on this side and on that, a length of a hundred cubits; and the temple and the corners and the 'aelam' outside laid with wood, and windows made in the manner of a net, three, for giving light, so that one might see through them; and the house and the things that were next to it laid with wood round about, and the pavement, and from the pavement up to the windows, and the windows opened in threefold manner so that one might look out through them. And up to the inner and the outer house and over every wall round about, within and without, measure; and carved Cherubim and palms between Cherub and Cherub: the face of a man toward the palm on this side, and the face of a lion toward the palm on that side, every wall carved round about: from the pavement up to the ceiling Cherubim and palms carved. And the sanctuary and the temple opened by four corners. Facing the face of the holy things a vision like the appearance of a wooden altar, its height three cubits and its length two cubits and its breadth two cubits, and it had horns, its base also and its walls of wood.") The word 'facing', which the Seventy translated at the beginning of the testimony, where it is written: And he measured 'facing' the house, is not found in the Hebrew, and therefore it must be marked beforehand with an obelus, so that it may read more rightly and more truly: And he measured the house, a length of a hundred cubits, and the rest. There are described, moreover, the Holy of Holies and the inner temple, which after ninety cubits is said to have a hundred cubits on three sides: the perfect number, namely, of ten decades, so that we may serve God with mind and speech and works, remembering that apostolic example in which he says: That we may be able to know what is the breadth, and length and height and depth. But what the Hebrew calls 'the separate building and its walls', the Seventy render 'the remaining parts' 'and the separating parts', which do not cling to the walls of the temple but have walls near at hand and their own. The temple itself also and its corners and the 'aelam' (that is, πρόπυλον or 'vestibule') were laid with wood outside, namely with wisdom, which Scripture records as the tree of life set in paradise. The windows also were made in the manner of a net, like lattices, so that they were closed not with transparent stone nor with glass, but with wood cut in openwork and worked in wavy patterns — for which the Hebrew has 'slanting windows' —; and they were on three sides of the temple only, namely to the right and the left and behind the back, that is, toward the south and the north and toward the west; but the eastern side had no windows, because the entrance itself let clear light in within, and all the interior of the temple was filled with the light of the doors, so that through the individual windows and the openings of the lattices one could look inside. And not only were the outer parts laid with wood, but so great was the abundance of wood round about that both the pavement and, from the pavement up to the windows, everything was joined with wood; and these windows, according to the Seventy, opened in threefold manner, so that, when they were opened, a threefold understanding might be shown in the temple of God — according to what is said elsewhere: But you, write them threefold —; and one might look out through them not only inward but outward, so that we may recognize the inner things as invisible and the outer things as visible; so that one shows the mind, another the flesh, one the spiritual understanding, another the simple history. And over all the walls round about, both within and without, there were measures of their own: for nothing was made by God without reason and measure in the temple of God, and especially in the Holy of Holies. Carved also were Cherubim, no doubt on the wood reaching from the pavement up to the windows, and the carvings were so skillfully wrought that they seemed not carved but applied. 'Cherubim' means 'multitude of knowledge'; therefore within, in the interior of the temple, after the multitude of knowledge, palms also are carved — in which is the sign of victory, as the Apostle says: But I press on toward the appointed goal, toward the prize of the upward calling of God in Christ Jesus —, which palms: Palms were between Cherub and Cherub, so that each Cherub was fenced in by the flanks of two palms; and this Cherub by no means had four faces, as we read at the beginning of this prophet, namely of a man and of a lion and of a calf and of an eagle, but only two, that is, of a man and of a lion, of which the first pertains to reason, the next to fury — which is more expressively called θυμός in Greek —: but by fury we mean not that which is next to perturbation and vice, but that which firms up the softness of the mind and makes the spirit of the one fighting stronger; for at the beginning we are subject also to desire, which is referred to the calf because of the works of the earth, and some things are carnal and others spiritual, the last of which is assigned to the eagle; but when we have entered the Holy of Holies and come into possession of the interior of the temple, we need nothing else but reason and fortitude, of which the one is referred to sense and prudence, the other to perseverance of spirit. Every wall, therefore, round about the temple, from the pavement up to the ceiling, had Cherubim and palms carved with wonderful art; after these the sanctuary was opened by four corners facing the face of the holy things: for first we have the multitude of knowledge, through which we gain the victory over the enemy, and afterward the sanctuary is opened to us, and the temple, which has four corners, a most firm station, and one that leans toward no side; for this is the nature of the measure of a quadrangle, that it stands on a stable base and, in a mystical number which is clear to the prudent reader, possesses the four elements, of which all things consist, solid and perpetual. And all things looked toward the face of the sanctuary; before which sanctuary, or in which sanctuary, there was: The appearance of a wooden altar three cubits in height and two cubits in length and two cubits in breadth, which joined together make seven cubits. This altar had horns, and both its base and its walls, that is, its sides, were wooden: in which the human tongue cannot unfold the mysteries of Holy Scripture: how an altar on which fire was to be kindled, namely the table of incense, suffers nothing from the fire but, so to speak, becomes purer than fire; for just as the works of the saints — of which the Apostle writes: The fire will test what sort each one's work is — do not perish but are shown purer through fire, so too the wood of the altar, which is of the trees of paradise, is not burned by the neighboring fire but is rendered purer — nor is it a wonder to believe this of the sanctuary and the interior of the temple and the altar of incense, since even ἀμίαντον [amiantus, asbestos] — it is a kind of wood, or one having the likeness of flax — is found the cleaner the more it has burned —. Forgive, reader, the difficulty, and grant pardon to a poor understanding: for through windows that are slanting and made in the manner of a net and always closed, we can scarcely send the eye of our heart in as far as the inner house, so that all that we discern we see in shadow and image — and let us cry out with the Apostle: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! And who has known the mind of the Lord? except him who is the angel of great counsel and can open his mysteries to the worthy —. Now at Rome they call Ἔκθετας 'solaria' [sun-balconies], jutting out from the walls of upper rooms, or 'maeniana' [balconies], after him who first invented them; some of the Greeks call them ἐξώστρας [projecting galleries].

41:22b-26

And he spoke to me: This is the table before the Lord. And there were two doors in the temple and in the sanctuary; and in the two doors on either side there were two little doors each, which folded into one another; for there were two doors each on either side of the doors. And there were carved on the very doors of the temple Cherubim and sculptures of palms, just as they were also fashioned on the walls; wherefore the timbers also were thicker on the front of the vestibule outside. Above which were slanting windows, and the likeness of palms on this side and on that in the little shoulders of the vestibule, along the sides of the house and the breadth of the walls. (In this place the edition of the Seventy disagrees much with the Hebrew truth. Hence I will point out only this: that for 'thicker timbers' they translated σπουδαῖα, that is, 'necessary' or 'worthy of care', and for 'slanting' windows, 'hidden', and what is placed at the end of the testimony: And he measured on this side and on that the ceilings of the lintel — or of the vestibule — along the sides of the house, compacted — or joined, which they called ἐζυγωμένα, for which we can render 'of equal weight' —.) That man, therefore, who had brought the prophet into the innermost recesses of the temple, and among other things had shown him the wooden altar, which had corners, and horns according to the Seventy, and wooden walls, said to him: 'This altar which you behold: This very one is the table before the Lord', which in the likeness of the bush burns and is not consumed — of which the holy man speaks to the Lord: You have prepared a table in my sight against those who afflict me —. Two also doors were in the temple and in the sanctuary itself, through which the mysteries of both Testaments are shown. And in the two doors on either side there were two little doors each, which folded into one another, so that we may have both the spiritual understanding in the history and the truth of the history in the tropology; each of these needs the other, and if one is lacking, perfect knowledge is wanting. What follows, however: There were two doors each on either side of the doors, is clear according to the letter: for in larger dining halls two doors are wont to adjoin each other and be joined together, so that the greater entrance is closed or opened not by two huge leaves but by four smaller ones. On which doors of the temple (or of the Holy of Holies) were carved Cherubim — of which we spoke above — and sculptures of palms, so that after the multitude of knowledge victory might be granted to those who enter; and this sculpture of palms was also on all the walls of the temple. And he gives the reasons why Cherubim were carved on the doors themselves and likenesses of palms fashioned: Whence also the timbers were thicker in the vestibule of the gate outside, so that they might have firmness and also be able to receive carving; and beautifully, according to the spiritual understanding, the doors are firmer and carved, so that they may have both firmness and beauty, lest anyone like Uzziah should be able to burst into the Holy of Holies and claim the priesthood for himself. Above which doors there were slanting windows (or hidden), so that the very light that was given within might not have perfect knowledge, nor a clear light open to all, but for most might be hidden in part — for now we see in an enigma, and we do not yet know as we ought to know; but when that which is perfect has come, then what had been in part will be destroyed —. And there was a likeness of palms on this side and on that: elegantly, in the interior of the temple and in the Holy of Holies, he did not put 'right and left', lest he seem to say anything sinister in things that are great and secret, but 'on this side and on that' — according to what is written in the Gospel: Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also. Could he not have said 'and the left'? But when the right is struck, another right is offered, because in a holy man both are right, both are perfect —. And: In the little shoulders of the vestibule, along the sides of the house and the breadth of the walls (for which the Seventy translated: In the ceilings of the 'aelam' — that is, πρόπυλον [gateway] — and the sides of the house of equal weight — or measure —), by which it is shown in a hidden way that the posts of the lintel or of the vestibule — for this is what the little shoulders seem to signify —, and the sides of the house, and the breadth of the walls are all full of reason and measure, and that nothing is found in the temple of the Lord which has been established without measure and wisdom.

Book Thirteen

The thirteenth book of the explanations on Ezekiel is the second book of the explanation of the temple; and this book, together with the fourteenth, I desire, with the help of our Savior, to dictate right through to the end, singing with David that verse of the same number in Psalm 14 (15): Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? or who shall rest on your holy mountain? This we ought to take as something both difficult and impossible; hence in another place too, as a man of desires, he prays more earnestly and says: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the delightfulness of the Lord and visit his holy temple, and again: How beloved, he says, are your tabernacles, Lord of powers. My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord. I forestall the curses of my rivals, who consider not what they themselves can do but what I cannot do, and who, while they pass judgment on our works, do not offer their own to be judged, never fighting in the contest themselves but judging those who fight with an idle, nay rather a proud, mind: it is easy to hand out instructions from among the crowd, and to find fault with every single blow, and to laugh at another man's blood, and, where a wound ought to have been dealt, to hold forth in the manner of an unskilled trainer of gladiators. For my part, in the explanation of Ezekiel's temple and of the other matters that belong to the end of the volume itself, I confess that I write nothing worthy of the greatness of the subject, and that in the few things, if indeed I shall have deserved to receive any, I give thanks to the Savior; for it is written: Unless you believe, you will not understand, and in another place: If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, and say to this mountain: Move away and be transplanted into the sea, it will be done; and just as the Apostle recalls that the grain of mustard seed is not a small portion of faith but the whole of faith, saying: And if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, so then this grain of mustard seed, even if it be small: grows up into a great tree, and the birds of heaven dwell in its branches. Wherefore I wish this to stand solemnly attested to you, my daughter Eustochium, who gladly receive our works, whatever they may be; and I briefly remind you of that saying of the rhetorician Victorinus, so that you may know that the obscurity of books arises from three things: either from the greatness of the subject, or from the inexperience of the teacher, or from the dullness of the hearer. Of these, the first and the second I shall plainly confess in this work; the third the keenness of your mind and your desire for the Scriptures easily reject, you who, by the privilege of virginity and the continence of your way of life, possess God as a guest, I will not say frequent, but constant. Let us therefore take up the thirteenth book on Ezekiel, whose beginning is this:

42:1-12

And he brought me out into the outer court by the way leading to the north; and he brought me into the chamber that was opposite the separate building, and opposite the house facing toward the north. In front of the length, a hundred cubits, of the door of the north, and of the breadth fifty cubits, opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court, and opposite the pavement laid with stone of the outer court, where there was a portico joined to the threefold portico. And before the chambers a walk of ten cubits in breadth, and looking toward the inner parts of the way of one cubit; and their doors toward the north, where the chambers were lower in the upper parts, because they supported the porticoes which projected from them, from the lower and from the middle seats of the building. For they were three-storied, and they did not have columns as were the columns of the courts; therefore they projected from the lower and from the middle, from the ground, by fifty cubits. And the outer peribolus alongside the chambers which were in the way of the outer court before the chambers; its length of fifty cubits, because the length of the chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits, and the length before the face of the temple a hundred cubits.
