And beneath these chambers there was an entrance from the east for those entering into them from the outer court. In the breadth of the peribolus of the court which was opposite the eastern way, in front of the separate building, and there were chambers before the building. And a way before their face according to the likeness of the chambers which were in the way of the north; according to their length so also their breadth, and all their entrance and likenesses and their doors according to the doors of the chambers which were in the way looking toward the south; a door at the head of the way which was before the separate vestibule, for those entering by the eastern way. (LXX: "And he brought me out into the outer court ÷ toward the east ⁚ opposite the gate of the north; and he brought me in, and behold, five exedrae next to the wall of the building and beside the separate building toward the north, and opposite, a hundred cubits of length toward the north and of breadth fifty cubits, laid out like the gates of the inner court and like the columns of the outer court, in order opposite the face of the threefold portico. And opposite the exedrae a walk of ten cubits of breadth, for a hundred cubits of length — into the inner way of one cubit —; and their doors toward the north. And the walks of the upper rooms likewise, since columns projected from the lower columns, and the space was similar. And the porticoes were threefold, and they did not have columns like the columns in the outer parts; therefore they projected from those which were below and in the middle, from the ground — of fifty cubits —. And the light outside, like that of the exedrae of the outer court which looked opposite the exedrae of the north, in length fifty cubits; for the length of the exedrae looking onto the outer court was fifty cubits, and these are opposite their own face: all of a hundred cubits. And the doors of these exedrae toward the eastern entrance, so that one may go in by them from the outer court according to the light which was at the beginning of the walk — toward the south, opposite the midday and the face of the remaining and separate building. And the exedrae and the walk opposite their own face according to the measures of the exedrae and the way toward the north, and their length and their breadth and all their exits and entrances and lights and the doors of the exedrae opposite the midday, and the entrance from the beginning of the walkway to the light at the space of a reed, and so that one might go to the east by them —.") This which the Seventy translated, 'toward the east', is not found in the Hebrew, and it is plain that it is superfluous — for how is he led out to the outer gate 'toward the east', when there follows 'opposite the gate of the north'? —; and that which we set down both above and in this place, And he brought me into the chamber that was opposite the separate building, and opposite the house facing toward the north, for which there stands in the Seventy, And he brought me out, and behold, five exedrae joined to the remaining building and beside the separate one toward the north: for 'separate', which Aquila and Symmachus translated, the second edition of Aquila and Theodotion set down the very word 'gazera', rendering it in the same way in all places; and many other things which are set forth in the present place disagree between the Hebrew and the Seventy not only in order but also in number and in the rendering of the words, so that, if we wished to linger over each one and to seek out and explain the reason for their difference, we would stray far from our purpose; and I had wished, out of despair and because of the magnitude of the matter, to pass over the present passage in silence, but I judged it better to say something, whatever it might be, than to say nothing at all, taking up that Socratic saying: 'I know what I do not know'; for it is a part of knowledge to know what you do not know. After the prophet, then, had contemplated more carefully the things that were within, the man in whose hand were the cord and the reed led him out into the outer court by the way leading to the north, which he had already seen above as well, before he penetrated the inner parts — but we see in one way when we have perfect knowledge, in another at the beginning of instruction; and it is necessary that one who has beheld the inner parts according to the same form and measures and hidden mysteries should also see the things that are outer —; and he was led out into the chamber — or, as Symmachus says and the Seventy translated, 'exedra', and Theodotion παστοφόριον, which is rendered 'cell' — that was opposite the separate building; but what the Seventy added in place of the chamber, 'five exedrae', is not found in the Hebrew —, which chamber was opposite the separate building — concerning which we said above, 'gazera' —: and it was separate, receiving those who came from the north, and it was opposite the house facing toward the north, that is, looking indeed toward the parts of the north but not situated in the north, so that the passage might be easier for those who were leaving behind the cold of the north, from which evils blaze up over the earth — we read in the book of Numbers that the tribes of Dan and Naphtali and Asher, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, the handmaids of Rachel and Leah, held their camp on the northern quarter —. Now too, in front of the length of the north door there were a hundred cubits, and of breadth fifty, so that, by the square and perfect number made of ten decades, and by the number made of seven hebdomads, which is the number of remission and breaks out into the beginning of unity, that is, of the ogdoad, the priestly spaces in the temple of God might be shown; and that which is joined according to the Hebrew, Opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court, for which the Seventy translated, They were laid out like the gates of the inner court, has this sense: that the number one hundred and the number fifty of the outer court have the same force as the number twenty of the inner court: for if you reckon four times five in the number twenty, you will find both testaments, so that the law is held within the Gospel and the Gospel is born from the root of the law; in place of this number the Seventy translated 'the likeness of the inner court', perhaps fearing to place in the inner court the number twenty — in which gifts are offered to Esau. There follows: And opposite the pavement laid with stone of the outer court, where there was a portico joined to the threefold portico, for which the Seventy translated: And like the columns of the outer court, set in order opposite the face of the threefold porticoes: and it signifies that the pavement of the outer court was laid with living stone, so that the footsteps of the priests might be defiled neither by the dust of summer nor by the mud of winter — whence also the Lord, about to ascend to the Father, washes the feet of the apostles, so that with clean and purified footsteps they may climb to the kingdoms of heaven, and he commands the apostles that, whatever city they have entered and they have not received them, they should shake off the dust of their feet, so that, namely, they may suffer nothing of earthly gifts from them to remain with them —; and not only was the pavement laid with stone, but there was also a portico joined to the threefold portico: one portico protecting the priests from rain and heat and joined to the threefold portico, and it shows the mystery of the Trinity, which, though it is divided into the names of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, is nevertheless joined to itself in one divinity. There was also before the chambers — or exedrae, or cells — a walk ten cubits in breadth, looking toward the inner parts of the way of one cubit — and what was added by the Seventy, For a hundred cubits of length, is superfluous, because it is not found in the Hebrew; and in setting it down they removed what is found in the Hebrew, Looking toward the inner parts of the way of one cubit, which we translated from the Hebrew truth —: and it signifies that before the doors of all the chambers, or exedrae and cells, there was a walk having a breadth of ten cubits, which is itself also a perfect number, either because of the Decalogue of the law or because of the mysteries of the Gospel: for if you go from one through two and three to the fourth number, the number ten is produced, and the number of the Gospels —, in whose breadth the priests walk about, stepping before each of the chambers, only in such a way that they always look toward the inner parts of that way which leads to one cubit, namely to the worship of one divinity — as the Son says to the Father: I have revealed your name to men. For this is the way looking toward the inner parts which will be in the Gospel: I am the way and the life and the truth, for no one comes to the knowledge of the Father except through the Son —. There follows: And their doors toward the north, where the chambers were lower in the upper parts, because they supported the porticoes which projected from them, from the lower and from the middle of the building. For they were three-storied, and they did not have columns as were the columns of the courts; therefore they projected from the lower, and from the middle, from the ground, by fifty cubits. In what is joined, 'their doors', there is understood 'of the exedrae' or 'of the chambers', of which there was talk above; which chambers were lower in the upper parts, that is, in the upper rooms — the upper rooms which Elijah and Elisha climbed, and the Lord with his disciples when he was about to keep the Passover, and Tabitha, who was raised up both by the faith of the apostle and by the merit of her own virtues; these are the upper rooms of which it is also written in the psalm: He who waters the mountains from his upper rooms: for unless someone has been made a mountain and has risen to higher things, he will not be watered by the rains of the Lord, he who according to the diversity of merits is watered from the first and the second and the third upper room; these very chambers too, that is, the treasuries of the riches of the Lord, are lower in the upper parts: for the more exalted someone has been, the more is he cast down in humility with the apostle, who says: I who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God —; and these chambers were lower in the upper rooms because they supported the porticoes which projected from them, from the lower and from the middle of the building: he gives the reasons why the chambers placed in the upper rooms were lower: 'Because they supported' he says 'the porticoes which enjoyed the freedom of the air, and projected from the lower and from the middle of the building', so that the second upper room stood out above the pavement of the inner house and the third upper room was higher than the second, and the higher someone climbed, the loftier the upper room he would use, which grew by humility — as the Lord says: Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him become the least of all —. For they were not carried by other columns, as we read of the columns of the courts, but they projected from the lower, and from the middle, from the ground, by fifty cubits, the number of the remission of all debts — and these are the three-storied things of which it is commanded: Describe it threefold with counsel and knowledge, so that you may answer words of truth to those who are set before you —. The lower and outer things, then, need columns, but those which are higher and inner have no use for the help of columns, that is, of another. After this it is said: And the outer peribolus alongside the chambers which were in the way of the outer court before the chambers; its length of fifty cubits, because the length of the chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits, and the length before the face of the temple a hundred cubits. 'Peribolus' signifies 'a wall', which was outer and surrounded the chambers in the way of the outer court, having in length fifty cubits, a number of whose mystery we have often spoken; moreover, the length before the face of the temple was by no means of fifty cubits, as before the chambers, but of a hundred cubits, so that after the remission of all sins we may await perfect rewards in the number one hundred; for 'peribolus' or 'wall', which in Hebrew is called 'gader', the Seventy translated 'light', which comes from outside and is to illumine the eyes of our heart, since our nature is not sufficient for the light that dwells in the understanding to have the perfect brightness of knowledge, unless it enters from outside through the grace of God: which first illumines the eyes of our heart and makes the whole outer court, which extends with a breadth of fifty cubits, grow bright; but afterwards, when we have come before the face of the temple, we are to receive the perfect rewards in the number one hundred. And there was beneath the chambers an entrance from the east for those entering into them from the outer court. For we must possess the riches of God, and from the outer court find the entrance of the east beneath the chambers, and through the height of the peribolus which looks toward the way of the east come to the building which is set apart for the saints; before which are the chambers. And in that very way there is the likeness of the chambers which were in the way of the north: for although we arrive at the entrance of the east, yet the likeness of the greater things is in the lesser, and we cannot arrive at the light of the east except by the way of the north, that is, unless through lesser and humbler things we strive toward greater and higher ones. And in the entrance itself the length was like the breadth, that is, the same measure in a square, and every entrance and the likenesses and the doors had the same measure and likeness as the chambers which were in the way looking toward the south: for, leaving behind the cold of the north, we arrive through the east at the south, in which the bridegroom reclines at midday and dwells in full light; and at the head of that same way, that is, the eastern one, which lies open to those who enter, there is a door — which is not opened unless it has been opened by him who says, I am the door, and who has the key of David —, to the vestibule set apart for the virtues of the saints; and that which receives those coming from the north we cannot reach. It is superfluous to discuss each word of this passage according to the Seventy, since both the things that have been said are not free of obscurity, and those about which we keep silent are nearly similar to those that we have said.

42:13-14

And he said to me: The chambers of the north and the chambers of the south which are before the separate building, these are the holy chambers in which the priests eat who draw near to the Lord in the Holy of Holies: there they shall place the Holy of Holies and the offering for sin and for trespass, for the place is holy. And when the priests have entered, they shall not go out from the holy places into the outer court, and there they shall lay up their garments in which they minister, because they are holy; and they shall be clothed with other garments, and so they shall go forth to the people. That man who was the prophet's guide, after he had led him into the outer court and shown him all the things which the preceding discourse has narrated, the chambers too, or exedrae, in which he lingered a very long time, said to him: 'These are the chambers, or exedrae and cells, toward the north and toward the south which are before the separate building, and they are called the holy chambers in which the priests eat who draw near to the Lord in the Holy of Holies' — from which we learn that there are many differences of foods which the priests are or are not permitted to eat, and that of those very ones which it is permitted to take as food, they are not taken in all places, nor by all, nor at every time —; I think the chambers of the north and of the south are those which contain either the simplicity of the history or the mysteries of spiritual understanding, so that through the north we may come to the midday: for neither is the letter to be read and the foundations of the history to be laid in such a way that we do not come to the summits, nor are roofs to be set on top of a most beautiful building in such a way that the foundations are by no means solid; and the priests who eat in the storerooms in which many riches are contained are those who draw near to the Lord — of whom Scripture testifies that Moses drew near to the Lord and the rest could not approach —: in the building of the mystical temple and in the mystery of the Church there are many priests and apostolic men who approach the Lord, and not in just any place, but in the Holy of Holies — and what is said according to the Seventy, The sons of 'Sadoc' [Zadok], which means 'righteous', is not found in the Hebrew —. 'There' he says 'the priests shall place the Holy of Holies and the offering, that is, the victim of the holocaust, and for sin and for ignorance', so that they may not only offer the perpetual sacrifice, but may know how to appease the Lord according to the diversity of times and the quality of the sin and of the ignorance: 'Because the place itself is holy', and the priestly dignity dwells in it, which is able to make petition for the rest: 'But when one must go forth to those who cannot penetrate the inner sanctuaries of the temple nor know the secrets of divine knowledge, let the priests go out' he says 'outside to them into the outer court, by no means with those garments with which they had been clothed within' — namely, the bowels of mercy and the Lord Savior, of whom it is written: Put on Christ Jesus; nor do they use those words of which God speaks: My mystery is for me and for mine; nor should they incur what the Savior forbids, saying: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine —, 'but they shall lay down their garments within, with which they are clothed when they minister in the inner sanctuaries of the temple: for they are holy, and they ought not to be brought out to those who do not have perfect holiness; and they shall receive other garments, and so they go forth to the people': 'So' he says 'they shall speak to the people, as the people is able to hear' — whence also the apostle spoke to the Corinthians — among whom fornication was heard of, and such fornication as is not even among the nations —: I gave you milk to drink, not food — that is, solid food —: you were not yet able to take it; to whom again he says: My little children, with whom I am in travail again until Christ be formed in you: for to little ones and sucklings solid food, which befits men of mature age, not only does no good but kills them —. But that which was added by the Seventy, Therefore the priests shall not go out into the outer court, so that those who offer may always be holy, let us mark beforehand with an obelus, because it is not found in the Hebrew.

42:15-20

And when he had completed the measures of the inner house, he brought me out by the way of the gate which looked toward the eastern way, and he measured it on every side round about (or the likeness of the house round about in order). And he measured toward the east wind (or and he stood behind the back of the gate looking toward the east) with the reed of measure round about five hundred reeds, by the reed of measure all around. And he measured toward the north wind five hundred reeds by the reed of measure all around. And toward the south wind he measured five hundred reeds by the reed of measure round about. And toward the west wind he measured five hundred reeds by the reed of measure. By the four winds he measured its wall on every side round about, the length of five hundred cubits, and the breadth of five hundred cubits, dividing between the sanctuary and the place of the common people. It should be known that, after the east wind and the north, in the south wind and the west the order in the Seventy is reversed: for they put first the west — that is, the sea — and afterwards the south, whereas among the Hebrews the south wind is put first and afterwards the west. And what Scripture now says, And when he had completed the measures of the inner house, he brought me out by the way of the gate which looks toward the eastern way, shows that all the things which were said above, both outside and inside and in the inner parts of the temple — that is, the Holy of Holies —, belong properly to the building of the temple, and of the inner temple. Hence there now follows: He brought me out by the way of the gate which looked toward the eastern way, and he measured it on every side round about (or the likeness of the house), by which it is shown that it is not the house itself but the likeness of the house that is seen — because: Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; but when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be destroyed; whence also Moses in the tabernacle, and Solomon in the building, made not the truth of the tent and of the temple but a likeness and figure —, so that through these things which are lesser and earthly we might be able to understand those which are in the heavenly places and in the spiritual building. Now the man who had led the prophet out, by no means into the outer court but by the way of the gate which looked toward the eastern way, measured first toward the east wind — that is, toward the eastern quarter — five hundred reeds all around, second toward the north, third toward the south, fourth toward the sea — that is, toward the west —: by the four winds, namely, the wall round about, as much in length as in breadth, that is, in a square: which wall had in all two thousand reeds: but if the reed was of six cubits and one παλαιστῇ [handbreadth] — which παλαιστής is the sixth part of a cubit —, it is clear that the outer wall had round about two thousand reeds: which make twelve thousand three hundred and thirty-three cubits and a third, out of the two thousand — let the prudent and diligent reader read the book of Joshua son of Nun, and he will find how this measure is kept in the suburbs; whence also the Legion of demons chose this number in the choking of the swine, so that what by the Lord's command was set apart for those who serve God might be turned, in the opposite direction, to the perdition of those who pursue a life worthy of mud and filth. And the whole wall, which is outer and has a most spacious length and breadth in a square, contains the number of the apostles, that is, of twelve thousand — so that a thousand may be assigned to each apostle —, and yet it would not come to the measure of the fullness of Christ and of the perfect man unless the παλαιστής too is joined to it: which makes three hundred and thirty-three cubits and a third part of a cubit: by which things the mystery of the holy and venerable Trinity is shown, which girds and walls in all things and renders the inhabitants of its temple most secure; whence also Noah's ark has a length of three hundred cubits and a height of thirty cubits, which is finished off in one cubit — and that fifty cubits in breadth are added there signifies, as we have often said, the mystery of remission —; whence also the Lord came to baptism at thirty years of age; and this very prophet at the beginning of his volume sets down the thirtieth year; and this thirtieth and three-hundredth number is completed by the addition of three and a third part —. But what, through simplicity of rendering, while we paid too little attention in the speed of dictation, both the Seventy have and our translation, Its wall on every side round about, the length of five hundred cubits, and the breadth of five hundred cubits, the Hebrew language does not contain, but simply 'the length of five hundred and the breadth of five hundred', so that 'of reeds' is understood — just as was said four times above: toward the east wind and toward the north and toward the south and toward the sea, five hundred 'reeds' each —, and that the wall of the individual sides was measured by him who held the reed — and that the number five hundred, because it is close to fifty, pertains to the remission of all sins, not only the old Scripture but also the words of the Savior in the Gospel show, when he says: There were two debtors to a certain moneylender; one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty —; and the wall divides between the sanctuary and the place of the common people, from which we understand that the whole description of the temple above was assigned to the ministries of the priests — who are the sons of Zadok —, but that this wall — which is extended over so great a space and goes around everything — separates the sanctuary and the place of the common people.

43:1-9

And he brought me to the gate that looked toward the eastern way, and behold, the glory of the God of Israel was entering by the eastern way, and its voice was like the voice of many waters, and the earth shone from his majesty. And I saw a vision according to the appearance that I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and the appearance according to the aspect that I had seen beside the river Chebar, and I fell upon my face. And the majesty of the Lord entered the temple by the way of the gate that looked toward the east. And the spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord. And I heard one speaking to me from the house, and the man who was standing beside me said to me: Son of man, the place of my throne and the place of the footprints of my feet, where I dwell in the midst of the sons of Israel forever; and the house of Israel shall no more pollute my holy name, they and their kings, by their fornications and by the ruins of their kings and in the high places: who built their threshold beside my threshold, and their posts beside my posts, and there was a wall between me and them, and they polluted my holy name by the abominations that they committed; for which reason I consumed them in my wrath. Now therefore let them put far away their fornication and the ruins of their kings from me, and I will dwell in the midst of them always. (LXX: "And he brought me to the gate that looked toward the east ÷ and he led me out ⁚, and behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming by the way of the east, and the voice of the camp like the voice of many redoubling, and the earth shone out like lightning from the glory round about. And the vision which I saw, according to the vision that I had seen when I was entering to anoint the city, ÷ and the vision of the chariot that I saw ⁚ according to the vision that I had seen over the river Chebar; and I fell on my face. And the glory of the Lord entered the house by the way of the gate that looked toward the east. And the spirit took me up and brought me into the inner court, and behold, the house full of the glory of the Lord. And I stood, and behold, a voice from the house of one speaking to me, and the man was standing beside me and said to me: Son of man, you have seen the place of my throne and the place of the footprint of my feet, in which my name shall dwell in the midst of the house of Israel forever; and the house of Israel shall no more defile my holy name, they and their leaders, in their fornication and in the murders of the leaders in their midst, when they set my threshold in their thresholds, and my posts beside their posts, and they made my wall as if joined between me and themselves, and they defiled my holy name by their iniquities which they were doing; and I crushed them in my fury and in slaughter. And now let them cast away their fornication and the murders of their leaders from me, and I will dwell in the midst of them forever.") First we must speak about the variety of the translation. What the Seventy put, And he led me out, is not found in the Hebrew — for if he had been brought to the gate that looked toward the east, what need was there for him to be led out, since he had been brought in for this very purpose, to see what was happening at the eastern gate? —; next, where it is said, There was a voice (doubtless God's) like the voice of many waters — which John too confirms in his Revelation —, the Seventy put: And the voice of the camp like many redoubling; third, in the Hebrew we have: A vision according to the appearance that I had seen when he came to 'destroy' the city: and there came that one who at the beginning of this prophet was clothed in linen and had an inkhorn at his loins, together with six others, to 'destroy' the city, not to 'anoint' it, as the Seventy translated; and they, fourth, said: And the vision of the chariot that I had seen, which is not found in the Hebrew. Let us speak briefly on each point, as far as the difficulty of the explanation allows, lest, while we strive for brevity, the veil not only of Moses but also of the prophet Ezekiel remain upon us who desire to contemplate the truth of the Lord with unveiled face. The glory, therefore, of the God of Israel enters by the eastern way, by which it had also gone out when the city of the Lord was struck by fury; and it enters, or rather returns, to it because he had shown the temple of the Lord built upon the mountain. And yet what is said in what follows is much more: The spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord: for here only the glory of the God of Israel enters, but there it is said that the fullness of the glory of the Lord was in the temple — of which Isaiah too writes: I saw the Lord upon a throne high and lifted up, and the house full of his glory — by which, when with unveiled face we contemplate the glory of the Lord, we are re-formed into the image of the Creator. The voice of God also was like the voice of 'many' waters: that is, of all the peoples in the whole world, as John the evangelist interprets; or: Like the voice of a 'camp' and as the voice of many redoubling: so that he might know the mysteries of the army of God — understanding which, Jacob too called the name of that place Camps; of which it is also written elsewhere: The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those rejoicing —; and one 'voice' is spoken of, of the camp and of the multitude, because of the one accord in the praise of God; and the voice 'is redoubled' of those singing to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth; the earth is full of his glory. There follows: And the earth shone from his majesty, which was properly fulfilled at the coming of Christ, when the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world; and it is fulfilled daily in believers and will be completed to perfection when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has been clothed with immortality. But what is added, And I saw a vision according to the appearance that I had seen when he came to destroy the city, for which the Seventy translated, When I entered to anoint the city, though it is clear according to the Hebrew, according to the Seventy it holds very great obscurity: how Ezekiel entered to 'anoint the city' for his prophecy — unless perhaps we say this, that the rebuke of the prophet is the anointing of the city, and the anointing with the oil of gladness, priestly and royal, and those who have willingly received it and been willing to hear become anointed ones of the Lord — of whom it is written: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets —; but that one can, according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], anoint the city — of which it is written: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God — who has seen the vision of the chariot and of the mysteries of God which Ezekiel beheld over the river Chebar — which signifies 'burden and weight': for what is 'heavier' than the Babylonian rivers, by which David sat and wept when he remembered Zion — of which it is written: For the form of this world is passing away —? and I think that nothing in the confusion of this age is lasting, but that all things pass away and flow —; and whoever has considered these things will fall upon his face, understanding how far he is from the majesty of God, and will bend his knees to the Father in the name of Jesus Christ. 'And when', he says, 'I had fallen down, the majesty of the Lord entered the temple by the way of the gate that looked toward the east; and at once the spirit lifted me up — for lying down I was not able to go on — and brought me into the inner court — for I had fallen outside —; and behold, I who had earlier beheld the glory of the God of Israel coming by the eastern way saw his house filled with the glory of the Lord, and I heard the voice of one speaking to me from the inner house' — what it said, Scripture does not relate, unless perhaps that saying of the apostle: And I heard unspeakable words which it is not lawful for men to speak —. But that man, he says, who was standing beside the prophet spoke to him; and we plainly understand him to be the Lord: for to whom could what follows apply, Son of man, the place of my throne and the place of the footprints of my feet, where I dwell in the midst of the sons of Israel forever, except to him who dwells in the Church in the midst of the sons of Israel who see God? — and 'he dwells forever', not as in the temple of Solomon, for a time; and 'his place' is that of which it is written: And his place was made in peace, which surpasses all understanding; and 'the place of the footprints of his feet', as the apostles say: Let us worship in the place where his feet stood, and he said 'stood' beautifully: for in the Church the feet of the Lord stand, in the Synagogue they walk and pass by —; and so that we may know that this is said of the Church, there is joined: And the house of Israel shall no more pollute my holy name, which properly pertains to those who, being of holy life, abide in the Church; but who those are who earlier polluted the holy name of God, he sets out more plainly: They and their kings, the people as much as the priests, by their fornications, by which they committed fornication away from God, and by the ruins of their kings, who vainly take to themselves the royal name through pride; finally there follows: And in the high places — for an arrogant mind offends God, a humble one calls forth mercy —: who, after pride, or rather through pride, built their threshold beside the threshold of God, and their posts beside his posts. Let the silly women laden with sins, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth, hear these things according to the letter: that it is a mind joined to God, not nearness to the churches and a dwelling close to God, that calls forth clemency upon itself, and that rather the indignation of the Lord is stirred up when there is an unworthy inhabitant in consecrated places. They built, he says, their threshold beside my threshold, so that there was no difference between sacred and profane, and their posts beside my posts, so that there was one entrance for laity and priests — whence the apostle too says: But let a man prove himself, and so approach the body and blood of the Lord —; and to make what he was saying weightier, he joins in the following verse: And there was a wall between me and them, so that a very short wall divided the priestly sacrifices and the places of the sacraments of the body and blood of Christ. And they polluted, he says, my holy name by the abominations that they committed. What does nearness of dwelling profit, and a wall standing between our cell and the altar of the Lord, when in the things we do in secret, which it is shameful even to speak of, the name of the Lord is defiled and polluted? I think this: that no one pollutes the name of the Lord except him who has seemed to believe in his name and to be reckoned by his title; and as he who earlier believed in Christ takes the members of Christ and makes them members of a harlot, so he pollutes the name of the Lord who earlier received faith in his name — otherwise the heathen and the Jew, since they are polluted and defiled, or rather defilement itself and pollution, cannot pollute and defile the name of the Lord; but those pollute it to whom it is said: Through you my name is blasphemed among the nations —; for these causes, therefore, I consumed them in my wrath, because they did these things that we have described. And yet the merciful Lord again commands the prophet to bid them remove their former fornications far from themselves, and to abandon the ruins of their kings and princes and drive them away, not so much from themselves as from God; and he at once promises the rewards of good work, saying: And I will dwell in the midst of them — of whom it is said in the Gospel: There stands in the midst of you one whom you do not know —; and he will dwell not for a short time, as in the Synagogue, but forever, which is borne out in the Church of Christ.

43:10-12

But you, son of man, show the house of Israel the temple, and let them be confounded by their iniquities, and let them measure the structure, and let them blush for all that they have done. The figure of the house and of its structure, its exits and entrances, and its whole design, and all its precepts, and its whole order and all its laws, show them; and you shall write it in their sight, that they may keep all its distributions and its precepts and do them. This is the law of the house on the summit of the mountain: all its bounds round about are the Holy of Holies; this therefore is the law of the house. (LXX: "And you, son of man, show the house of Israel the house, and they shall cease from their sins, and its vision and its arrangement, and they themselves shall bear their torment for all that they have done. And you shall describe the house and its preparation, and its exits and its entrances, and its substance, and all its precepts, and all its ordinances and all its laws you shall show them; and you shall describe it before them, and they shall keep all my justifications and all my precepts and do them. And the description of the house on the top of the mountain: all its boundaries round about the Holy of Holies; this is the law of the house.") It is no small task to demonstrate to hearers what you have beheld with the eyes of the flesh or with the mind, so that they too may seem to have seen it with you — for which reason Josephus writes that those who were sent by Joshua son of Nun to describe the land were γεωμέτρας [geometers, land-surveyors], and possessed in the proper sense the art of geometry, which belongs to philosophers —. To the house of Israel, therefore — of those who behold God with the mind — the house is shown, that is, the temple which Ezekiel beheld situated on a mountain, and not only on a mountain but, as is now said, on the summit of the mountain; and let us by no means think it to be that one which is related in the books of Kings and Chronicles to have been built by Solomon: for that one is of another order and measure, and has great diversity in every detail, and is so far inferior to the temple which is now shown to Ezekiel that not only its worshipers and sacristans, but even its builder Solomon himself sinned and offended the Lord — although afterward he did penance, writing the Proverbs, in which he says: At last I did penance, and I looked back so as to choose discipline —; but this one, which is shown to Ezekiel and through Ezekiel to the house of Israel, is such that whoever has beheld it with the mind ceases from his iniquities, not from some but from all — or, as is contained in the Hebrew: is confounded —, and bears his torment for all that he has done — and he bears the torment of his iniquities who has ceased to commit his past sins —. And it greatly profits him who has sinned before to see the house of God and to know the principles of its whole structure — let him both desist from sinning and, having a longing for it, say to the Lord: 'Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place of the dwelling of your glory', and again: 'One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, when I have begun to live and to be with Christ, who is the life of believers' —. There follows: Its exits and entrances, 'of the house' being understood — the exits, that is, of those who go out to those who are outside, and the entrances of those who through the discipline of teachers penetrate to the inner parts —. 'And all', he says, 'its design (or substance, as the Seventy translated: which pertains not so much to the nature of the house as to its furnishings and riches), and all the precepts, and the whole order and all the laws of the temple you shall show them, who have borne the torment of their iniquities and have ceased, or been confounded, over the things they had done before; and for this reason you shall show them, that they may keep all that has been commanded: for it profits nothing to know the design of the house and all its distributions — of which it is written: Many mansions with the Father, and again: He set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the sons of Israel (or of the angels of God) — unless you do what has been commanded'. But the house, and the law of all the precepts of God, and the city which is established on the summit of the mountain, must be believed to be that one of which it is written: A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, and: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God: which plainly refers to the Church of God, and it is situated on that mountain which is at the peak of all mountains and by which the prince of Tyre was wounded; and all the bounds and boundaries of this house are the Holy of Holies — in that house, that is, in the tabernacle that was made by Moses and in the temple that was built by Solomon, only the inner parts, where the Cherubim were and the mercy seat and the ark of the covenant and the table of incense, were called the Holy of Holies; but in this house, which is shown to Ezekiel and which is established on the summit of the mountain, all its boundaries are reckoned among the Holy of Holies —; and what is added, This is the law of the house, pertains either to past matters, of which we have already spoken, or to those which are to be spoken of afterward.

43:13-17

And these are the measures of the altar in the truest cubit, which had a cubit and a handbreadth (or palaesten [handbreadth]): in its bosom was a cubit, and a cubit in breadth, and the delimitation up to its lip, and round about one handbreadth: this also was the trench of the altar. And from the bosom of the earth to the lowest ledge two cubits, and the breadth of one cubit; and from the lesser ledge to the greater ledge four cubits, and the breadth of one cubit. And the 'ariel' itself of four cubits, and from the 'ariel' upward four horns. And the 'ariel' twelve cubits in length by twelve cubits of breadth, squared with equal sides. And the ledge fourteen cubits of length by fourteen of breadth in its four corners; and the crown round about it of half a cubit, and its bosom of one cubit round about; and its steps turned toward the east. (LXX: "And this is the measure of the altar in the perfect cubit — a cubit and a παλαιστῆς [handbreadth] —: its bosom in height by a cubit, and a cubit of breadth, and a 'gisus' along its lip round about of one handbreadth. And this is the height of the altar: from the depth of the beginning in its bosom up to the great mercy seat which is beneath, of two cubits, and the breadth of a cubit; and from the lesser mercy seat up to the greater mercy seat four cubits, and the breadth of a cubit. The 'ariel' of four cubits, and from the 'ariel' up to the upper parts of the horns one cubit. And the 'ariel' itself had twelve cubits in length, and twelve cubits in breadth, of four corners on each of its sides. And the mercy seat of fourteen cubits in length by fourteen cubits in breadth on its four sides; and its 'gisus' round about, encircling it by half a cubit, and its circuit by a cubit round about; and its steps looking toward the east.") It is written: The abyss and wisdom, who will search them out? and: O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God!: whose depth is profound, and who will find it? It is a great matter if we wish to compare the temple of Solomon with this temple, and all its parts and those of the tabernacle; and since that is most difficult, for the present let us compare, in a small part, the altar which was shown to Ezekiel with the altar which we read of in Exodus: there an altar of five cubits in length and five cubits in breadth, that is, square, and of three cubits in height is described; here, departing from the five senses, it tends toward unity, in which a perfect or truest cubit is set down, to which a handbreadth is joined, that is, a παλαιστής, having, as we said above, the sixth part of a cubit; and in its bosom, that is, the altar's, there was a cubit, namely the one that received the things which were consumed by fire, and in its breadth another cubit, so that the inner parts too, that is, the secret places and spaces of the altar which are shown in breadth, might be bounded within one cubit. And as for what follows, And the 'delimitation' up to its lip — for which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion put 'boundary' —, the Seventy again translated 'gisum' — of which word, as I already said before, I cannot know the reason, nor say confidently to what language it belongs, except to advise the reader of this, that where I have now translated 'delimitation', above I rendered 'crown'; and this is briefly shown, that round about the altar itself, that is, at its margin and circle, there was a lip bent back and, as it were, a crown in the manner of a lily, having very great beauty in appearance —; which 'delimitation', or 'gisus', extended round about in the breadth of one handbreadth, or παλαιστοῦ. But the 'pit' of the altar, or 'depth' and 'height', for which in the Hebrew 'gab' is set down, was of two cubits from the bosom of the earth up to the lowest ledge, or up to the greatest mercy seat, and its breadth of one cubit: for the lower parts, deep and clinging to the earth, are contained in the dual number — which was also set down for the unclean animals —, but the upper parts, reaching to the ledge or mercy seat — which Theodotion called by the Hebrew name itself, 'azara' [ledge, enclosure] — have a breadth of one cubit, so that the dual number passes over to the single, and the good of marriage, which is lower, attains to the blessedness of unity. And as for what follows, And from the lesser ledge up to the greater ledge four cubits, and the breadth of one cubit — for which in the Seventy is set down: And from the lesser mercy seat up to the greater mercy seat, and Theodotion in both places translated 'azara' —, this is to be understood: that the lesser mercy seat is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, and the great mercy seat is the stone itself which grew into a great mountain and filled the whole world; or, according to another sense, the lesser mercy seat is when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and the great mercy seat when he received back the glory which he had with the Father before the world was made: for first we come to know the humbler things of Christ, and so we arrive at the height of his divinity; and yet the mercy seat of both natures, that is, of the lesser and the greater, pertains to the mystery of one altar. And between the two mercy seats, the lesser and the greater, there were four cubits, signifying the four elements of the world, which themselves too arrive at the breadth of one cubit — and this is to be noted, that in the measure of the altar the first cubit in breadth is coupled to none but is perfect in its own unity, while the second cubit of breadth grows to the top after two cubits, and the third cubit, after the lesser and greater mercy seat, tends through the four elements to the mystery of one cubit: so that the one and the second and the third cubit in the altar of the Lord are by no means said to be first, second and third, but one and one and one —. And the 'ariel' itself was of four cubits, and from the 'ariel' upward four horns (or, as is said in the Seventy, and from the 'ariel' up to the upper parts of the horns one cubit): 'ariel', as most suppose, means 'my light is God' — about which we have spoken more fully in the prophet Isaiah too, where it is written: Woe to you, city 'ariel', which David stormed (or surrounded) —, but, as I think, 'lion' or 'strong one of God' — a name which refers properly to the altar, in which there is either the illumination of God, or the lion and his strength, as Jacob says to Judah: A lion's whelp, my son, Judah; to the prey, son, you have gone up. Resting you lay down as a lion, and as a lioness: who will rouse him? —; and it is of four cubits and has four horns, or the upper parts of the four horns are bounded by one cubit: so that the measure of the Gospels and the strength running out into the whole world may be shown under the illumination of God and the strength of the lion, and may pertain to the one cubit of the divine confession. And so that the obscurity of the present passage may little by little become clearer, there follows: And the 'ariel' twelve cubits in length by twelve cubits of breadth, square with equal sides, which no one doubts pertains to the twelve tribes which are written in the Revelation of John, and to the number of the apostles, about whose mystery I remember having spoken above; along the four sides — the sides of the world — twelve cubits each together make forty-eight cubits — of the priestly cities —, so that, with these as it were foundations distributed through the whole world, the strength of the Church may be made firm. Furthermore: The ledge (for which the Seventy translated mercy seat, Theodotion, as above, 'azara', Symmachus περίβολον, that is, 'circuit') was of fourteen cubits of length by fourteen of breadth, in its four corners; and the 'crown' round about it of half a cubit (for which again the Seventy translated 'gison'), and the bosom (or, according to Symmachus, 'consummation') of it (and 'perfection') of one cubit round about: this covertly shows that our Lord, who is truly called the mercy seat, not only for our sins but for the whole world, came through fourteen generations from Abraham to David, and again through another fourteen to the captivity of Jeconiah, and by the mystery of the same number descended to earthly things, so that in the third tesseriscedecade [set of fourteen], and by the mystery of the divine number, he might save the four corners of the world — of which it is written: Many will come from the east and from the west and from the north and the south, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven —. And what follows, And the crown (or gisus) round about it — 'of the mercy seat' being understood — had half a cubit, and the 'bosom' of the mercy seat itself (or consummation and perfection, which Symmachus translated περιγραφήν [outline, circumscription]) had one cubit, signifies this: that both sinners and the righteous are saved by the propitiation of the Lord — as the apostle Paul says: We have been reconciled to God in the blood of his Son —; and of sinners it is said that they have the measure of half a cubit round about: who nevertheless are saved by the mercy of the Creator — according to what is written in the psalm: For nothing you will save them —; of the righteous: that they are saved in the one number, single and perfect and imitating the one divinity — as the apostle says: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself —. But as for what is set down at the end of this testimony, And its steps turned toward the east, by the steps of this mercy seat we ought to understand either the twenty-four books of the Old Testament, which had harps in the Revelation of John and crowns on their heads, or the mystery of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, in which true propitiation is given to us; and to speak more openly: the number of the steps is left uncertain for this reason, that with however much zeal we may have been able to climb to higher things, we may think that we are still to be placed in the inner things, and may ponder that saying of the psalm: They will go from strength to strength.

43:18-22

And he said to me: Son of man, thus says the Lord God: These are the rites of the altar on whatever day it shall have been built, that a holocaust may be offered upon it and blood poured out. And you shall give to the priests and Levites who are of the seed of Zadok, who approach me, says the Lord God, that they may offer me a calf of the herd for sin. And taking some of its blood, you shall put it upon the four horns, and upon the four corners of the ledge, and upon the crown round about, and you shall cleanse it and expiate it. And you shall take the calf that has been offered for sin, and you shall burn it in a separate place of the house outside the sanctuary. And on the second day you shall offer a he-goat of the goats without blemish for sin, and they shall expiate the altar as they expiated it with the calf. (LXX: "And he said to me: Son of man, thus says the Lord God: These are the precepts of the altar on the day on which it shall have been made, that holocausts may be offered upon it and blood poured out upon it. And you shall give to the priests and Levites who are of the seed of Saddoch, and who draw near to me, says the Lord God, that they may minister to me a calf of the oxen for sin. And they shall take of its blood, and shall put it upon the four horns of the altar, and upon its base round about, and they shall cleanse and expiate it. And they shall take the calf for sin, and it shall be burned in a separate place of the house outside the Holy Place. And on the second day they shall take two kids of the goats without blemish for sin, and they shall expiate the altar as they expiated it with the calf.") After he had shown the prophet the altar and its cubit and two cubits, and again a cubit and four cubits and, thirdly, a cubit, and also twelve cubits by another twelve, and the four horns of the altar, and the 'ariel' of twelve cubits by twelve cubits, and the ledge, that is, the mercy seat, of fourteen cubits by fourteen cubits, and also its crown and bosom of half a cubit and one cubit round about, and the steps toward the east whose number is uncertain, the man in whose hand were the reed and the cord spoke, and he teaches him how, once the work of the altar is completed, the altar ought to be expiated and consecrated. And first a victim is offered, and it is given to the priests of the race of Levi who are of the seed of 'Sadoc' — why the Seventy name him 'Saddoch' I am not able to know. And 'Sadoc' means 'righteous' —. And there is offered, according to the Seventy and Theodotion, a 'calf', according to Symmachus a 'bull', which in Hebrew is called 'phar' — and many passages of the Scriptures, and especially the epistle of Barnabas, which is held among the apocryphal scriptures, name him who was sacrificed for us a 'calf' —; and a he-goat of the goats is offered on the second day: whence also those who are to keep the Passover take from the flock a lamb and a kid, and those who could not keep the first Passover keep it in the second month: of which the one pertains to the righteous, the other to the penitent. But if the translation of the Seventy pleases us — who said: And on the second day they shall take two kids without blemish for sin —, what we are about to say is bold indeed, but nevertheless the opinion of others must be set down plainly, who say that two kids without blemish were offered at the altar of the Lord after the passion of the Lord: James and Stephen, of whom the one was of the number of the apostles, the other was the chief of the seven chosen for the ministry of the Lord — this is the James who saw the Savior transfigured on the mountain, who with the Lord and Peter and John beheld the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue rising, who in the κατάλογῳ [catalogue, list] of the apostles — in which the names are joined in pairs — is placed before his brother: him Herod killed, and as it were sacrificed as a kid without blemish on the second day after the passion of the Savior; Stephen too, whose wisdom and teaching no one could resist, and who saw the Son of man standing at the right hand of the Father, and said, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, the Jews overwhelmed with stones; and as the apostle names certain of the believers the firstfruits of Achaia and of Asia, so these too were the firstfruits of the martyrs, whom the confession of Christ afterward crowned —. And this is to be noted, that the calf is offered whole as a holocaust, and the fatness of its body is consumed by divine fire — for even if we had known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him according to the flesh —, but James and Stephen, who were offered on the second day, or the he-goat, which according to the Hebrew is related to have been offered, is indeed offered as a victim, but the holocaust is reserved to the preeminence of the Lord. And that the blood is taken — of which Peter speaks: We have been redeemed from our vain manner of life of paternal tradition by the precious blood of Christ; and the apostle Paul teaches: You have been redeemed with a price, and in another place: Making peace through the blood of his cross, whether on earth or above the heavens — signifies this: that by the blood of the Savior the four horns of the altar are purified — that is, the four regions of the world —, and the crown of the mercy seat, or the bases round about, is sprinkled, so that all things may be cleansed and the propitiation may be firm. And for this reason, on the second day, either two kids — of which we spoke above — or a he-goat is taken, because it is an animal always hastening to the heights and suffering no danger on precipices, and it finds a way there where for the other animals there is destruction — whence also in the Greek language 'a flock of she-goats and he-goats' is called 'the dwelling of the lofty', that is, 'αἰπόλιον', as if 'αἰπυ-πόλιον': since αἰπύ signifies, as it were, 'lofty', and πολεῖν 'dwelling' —. Furthermore, the altar of Christ is expiated with blood, so that the prayers of the saints may reach God clean. This too is to be noted, that according to the Hebrew Ezekiel himself, as a priest, is ordered to take the calf and to make the holocaust and to sprinkle its blood round about, on the altar as well as on the corners and the crown, or base; but the Seventy translators show that other priests do this, of whom it was said: And you shall give to the priests and Levites who are of the seed of Zadok, who approach me.

43:23-27

And when you have finished expiating it, you shall offer a calf of the herd without blemish, and a ram of the flock without blemish; and you shall offer them in the sight of the Lord, and the priests shall cast salt upon them, and shall offer them as a holocaust to the Lord. For seven days you shall make a he-goat for sin daily, and a calf of the herd and a ram of the flocks without blemish they shall offer. For seven days they shall expiate the altar and cleanse it, and they shall fill its hand; and when the days are completed, on the eighth day and onward the priests shall make your holocausts upon the altar, and those which they offer for peace; and I will be appeased toward you, says the Lord God. (LXX: "And when you have completed the expiation, they shall offer a calf of the oxen without blemish, and a ram of the sheep without blemish; and you shall offer them before the Lord, and the priests shall sprinkle salt upon them, and shall offer them as holocausts to the Lord. For seven days you shall make a kid for sin daily, and a calf of the oxen and a ram of the sheep, without blemish, they shall make for seven days; and they shall expiate the altar and cleanse it, and they shall fill their hands; and they shall complete the days; and it shall be, from the eighth day and onward the priests shall make your holocausts upon the altar, and for your salvation; and I will receive you, says the Lord God.") After the altar and its measures on the top of the mountain had been shown, and again its expiation and consecration had been shown to the prophet through one calf without blemish and a he-goat or two kids, of which we have referred the first to the Lord Savior and the two following to the apostles and ministers, then, lest in the consecration of the spiritual altar, which properly pertains to the Church, the Law and the Prophets should seem excluded, for this reason, once the altar has been consecrated, a calf without blemish is taken, and a ram; and they are offered in the sight of the Lord, and the sons of Zadok, that is, the priests of the righteous, sprinkle salt upon their heads: so that both the Law and the Prophets may be seasoned with the savor of the Gospel; nor is there any sacrifice — according to the command of the Law and the interpretation of the apostle, who says: Let your speech be seasoned with salt — which lacks salt. And both are offered as a holocaust to the Lord, so that the fatter body — the letter, which is signified in the Law — and the cloud of prophecy may, by the fire of the Lord — that is, by the Holy Spirit, of whom Paul says: Fervent in spirit — be converted into a spiritual and fine substance. Do we wish to know more openly who is the calf of the herd without blemish, and the ram of the sheep with the purest fleece? Let us understand Moses and Elijah — of whom the first was the meekest among all men who dwelt on the earth, the other in ardor of faith was like Moses, whence he also dared to say: I alone am left —. But that in the Hebrew it is written, 'You shall offer' a calf, and in the Seventy, 'They shall offer', the priests, raises no question — for Ezekiel himself too, to whom these things are said, is of the number of the priests, of full and perfect age: and the grace of prophecy increased his priestly rank; and Moses and Elijah, that is, the Law and the Prophets, are seen on the mountain with the Lord, announcing to him what he was going to suffer in Jerusalem —. And when the altar has been expiated, for seven days a he-goat or kid is offered for sin daily, and a calf of the herd and a ram of the flocks without blemish, so that through these sacrifices over seven days the altar may be expiated to perfection: in the seven days is shown the sabbath rest which, according to the apostle, is reserved for the people of the Lord, in which we hope for eternal and true rest and may by no means do the servile work of sins; and in the he-goat and the calf and the ram are shown three general offenses to which the whole race of mortals is subject: for we sin either in thoughts or in speech or in deed — thought is referred to the ram, which is the first of all sins and from which the other two sins are born; and the kid, or he-goat, to utterance and speech, which always disputes about loftier things; but deeds are properly assigned to the calf, which is bound over to the plowshare and to labor and to earthly works —. These, therefore, without blemish, we ought to offer to God through the seven days of the true and perfect sabbath, and to expiate the altar, so that our prayer may reach God clean. And what is added, And they shall cleanse it, and shall fill its hand, as both the Hebrew and the other translators rendered it, signifies this: that the gifts of the altar itself too, for whose expiation the sacrifice is offered, must be filled up, just as it is offered for the priests and the people and the high priest, lest anything should seem to have stood empty in the sight of the Lord; for which the Seventy put: And they shall cleanse it, and shall fill their own hands, so that 'the priests' is understood, who, when they have been full of good works — for this is what full hands signify —, once the sabbath is past, may come to the eighth day of the resurrection — and say with the apostle: We have risen with Christ —, and beyond the eighth may tend toward heavenly things, and offer for us holocausts, or those offerings which are for the peace of our sins and for our salvation, so that, through the fire of the Holy Spirit, all that we think, speak and do may be converted into spiritual substance, and the Lord, delighted with sacrifices of this kind, may become placable toward us.

44:1-3

And he turned me back to the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary which looked toward the east, and it was shut; and the Lord said to me: This gate shall be shut, and it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered (or will enter) by it, and it shall be shut for the prince: the prince himself shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord; he shall enter by the way of the vestibule (that is, 'aelam') of the gate, and by its way he shall go out. (Where it is written in the Hebrew: It shall be shut for the prince, the Seventy translated: And it shall be shut, because the leader himself shall sit in it.) There are many gates which Scripture mentions in the description of Ezekiel's temple, both within and without; the preceding discourse also ran through the shape of the altar, its consecration and its sacrifices. That being finished, he comes to the gate of the outer sanctuary which looked toward the east, and it was shut; and at once that man who was the prophet's guide and was showing him everything spoke to him: 'This gate, which you see shut, will always be shut, and it will not be opened, and none of men will pass through it'; and he gives the reasons why it is always shut: Because the Lord of Israel has entered (or will enter) by it, and it shall be shut — according to the Hebrew — for the prince (whom the Seventy translated 'leader'): who, the prince (and leader, that is, 'nasi') shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord, and: By the way of the vestibule of the gate he shall enter, by the same he shall go out. What, then, is this gate which is always shut, and by which the Lord God of Israel alone will enter? Surely it is the one of which the Savior speaks in the Gospel: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, and: Woe to you, doctors of the law, woe, who take away the key of knowledge: you yourselves do not enter, and those who are entering you hinder — of this, under the name of a book, Isaiah writes: The words of this book shall be like sealed words; when you give it to a man who does not know letters, and say to him: Read; he will answer you: I do not know letters. And they will give it to a man who knows letters, saying: Read; and he will say: I cannot read, because it is sealed: and this is the book whose seals no one can loose and open, neither in heaven nor on earth nor under the earth, except him of whom it is said in the Revelation of John: Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, the root and offspring of David, to open the book and loose its seals: for before the Savior assumed a human body and humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, the law and the prophets and all the knowledge of the Scriptures were shut, paradise was shut; but after he hung on the cross and said to the thief: Today you will be with me in paradise, at once the veil of the temple was torn and all things were opened; and with the veil taken away we say: But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory. But if all things have been unveiled — for in Christ, according to the word of Paul, all things are unveiled — how is it: The gate shall be shut, and it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it? From this we learn — even though we may have come to the highest knowledge, by comparison with the divine knowledge — that now we know in part and understand in part: But when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away. Hence in another place too the Apostle himself says that he is imperfect and again perfect, which, if it lacks interpretation, seems to be a contradiction; for he says: Not that I have already received, or am already perfect. Brethren, I do not reckon that I have laid hold; but one thing: forgetting what lies behind, stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the appointed goal, toward the prize of the upward calling of God; and when we would think that by his own profession he is not perfect, and that he is seeking rather than has found what is true, he says that not only he himself but others with him are perfect: As many then as are perfect, let us be of this mind; and the sense of this place is: 'In comparison with the rest of men, who have no care for the knowledge of the Scriptures nor of the mysteries of God, I confess that I am perfect; but as regards the knowledge of the divine majesty, I now see in an enigma, and through mist and darkness, and I say with the prophet: Your knowledge has become wonderful to me; it is too strong, and I shall not be able to reach it' —. This gate, then, which is shut to all — for No man shall pass through it —: It shall be shut for the prince (or for the leader), and will be reserved for his coming: who shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord — of which he himself declares in the Gospel, saying: My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work —; he himself is prince and high priest according to the order of Melchizedek, both victim and priest, who in the sight of the Father eats the heavenly bread with us and drinks the wine — of which he speaks in the Gospel: I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father: namely in that kingdom of which the Apostle also writes: The kingdom of God is within you —; and the gate will be shut: for no one can know the mysteries of the Lord's passion and of his body and blood as the majesty of the thing deserves; and our prince is of such goodness and mercy that, although he alone sits in the gate which is shut and eats bread before the Lord, he wills to have many sharers of his table and banquet — and he says: Behold, I stand and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will come in to him, and I will sup with him, and he with me —; but he alone eats bread before the Lord, because his substance and divine nature is set apart from all the substances of created things. He himself enters and goes out through the same gate of the vestibule, because he is both within and without — that is, poured into all things and poured around all things —: entering through the gate to bring in with him those who cannot enter without his teaching and help, and going out to bring in others again, and to speak to those who do not grasp the more difficult things. — That the eastern gate beyond the bounds of the world is always shut and by no means lies open to human sight, the Gospel of John proves — when it says: No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known, as if he had said in other words: And it shall be shut for the prince: the prince alone shall sit in it to eat the bread 'of perfect and consummate knowledge': for No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him —. Some fittingly understand the shut gate, through which the Lord God of Israel alone enters, and the leader for whom the gate is shut, as the Virgin Mary, who remained a virgin both before giving birth and after giving birth — for both at the time when the angel was saying: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and that which will be born of you will be called Holy, the Son of God, and when he was born, she remained a virgin forever —, to confound those who think that after the Savior's birth she had sons by Joseph, taking occasion from his 'brothers' who are so called in the Gospel: on which little question I know that in my youth, at Rome, I wrote a book of no great size against Helvidius, a heretic of that time —.

44:4-5

And he brought me by the way of the north gate in front of the house; and I looked, and behold, the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord, and I fell on my face. And the Lord said to me: Son of man, set your heart, and see with your eyes, and hear with your ears all that I say to you concerning all the ceremonies of the house of the Lord, and concerning all its laws; and you shall set your heart on the ways of the temple, through all the exits of the sanctuary. The man who is the prophet's guide, and through whose showing he learns everything in the temple, after he had shown him the gate shut, never to be unbarred and yet open to him who entered through shut doors, leads the prophet to the way of the north gate, which itself too was in front of the house: no doubt this signifies the temple; and when the prophet, from directly opposite, had seen the house of the Lord full of the glory of the Lord — the same, namely, which he had beheld facing him when he was placed in the region of the north —, at once he fell on his face, not enduring to bear the majesty of the glory of the Lord. Therefore, because he had been cast down in humility, it is no longer the man but the Lord who says to him: Son of man, set your heart, and the rest: at the completion of the tabernacle and at the building of the temple which was erected by Solomon the glory of the Lord appeared, which afterward was done away by comparison with the glory of the Gospel — as the Apostle says: For what was glorified has not been glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory. For if what is done away was through glory, much more what remains is in glory —; and we must beware of thinking the doing away of the former glory to be its abolition, but must understand it thus: After that which is perfect has come, that which was in part will be done away — as if you were to compare a torch to the rays of the sun, or the light of a torch to a little lamp; for which reason it is also said of John the Baptist: He was a lamp shining in the house; but after the sun of righteousness came, the light of the lamp was hidden, as the prophet and Baptist himself says: He must increase, but I must decrease —; and the prophet fell on his face lest, while he longed to discern more than human frailty can behold, he should lose even the very light of his eyes; hence the Lord calls him more familiarly son of man, and commanded him to set his heart, and see with his eyes, and hear with his ears — for first the mind must be opened to understand what is said, second the eyes of the heart must be directed, of which it is said to Abraham: Lift up your eyes and see the stars of heaven, third one must hear with those ears of which the Savior says: He who has ears to hear, let him hear —, so that he may be able to understand all the ceremonies of the temple and its ordinances, and finally to set his heart on the 'ways' of the temple — because there are various entrances to it —, or the 'way' of the temple — it signifies the order of the ceremonies —, and the exits of the sanctuary. It is, then, a preface and a preparation of the prophet for understanding what he is afterward to learn concerning the order of the temple. And this too must be noted: that in the region of this world, which lies in the evil one and is set in the cold of the north, the order of the heavenly ceremonies is shown to us.

44:6-8

And you shall say to the house of Israel that provokes me: Thus says the Lord God: Let all your crimes suffice you, house of Israel, in that you bring in alien sons (or foreigners) uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary and to pollute my house; and you offer my loaves, the fat and the blood, and you dissolve my covenant (or you pass over my precept) in all your crimes. And you have not kept the precepts of my sanctuary, and you have set keepers of my observances in my sanctuary for yourselves. When he says: Let all your crimes suffice you (or your iniquities), he exhorts to repentance for former sins, lest we add sins to sins and prepare fuel for the fire to come — but let us hear what Isaiah says: Woe to those who draw sins as with a long cord, and iniquities as with the yoke-strap of a calf —. And the first sin is that they bring in alien sons — or foreigners — uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in the sanctuary of God and to pollute the house of the Lord — for A little leaven corrupts the whole lump, and in some copies of Proverbs there is found: Do not bring the wicked man into the tents of the righteous —. At this place the Jews and the Ebionites — who accept circumcision of the flesh — press us as to how we can explain the present passage: uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, meaning, that is, that after the spiritual understanding we ought also to undergo circumcision of the flesh; but — we who read Paul saying: And I testify to every man who is circumcised that, if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing, and that word of Jeremiah: Behold, your ears are uncircumcised, and you would not hear, and in Exodus: Moses spoke before the Lord, saying: Behold, the sons of Israel have not listened, and how will Pharaoh listen to me? But I am slow of speech (for which the Seventy said: Ἐγὼ δὲ ἄλογός εἰμι [But I am without speech], which is better rendered in the Hebrew: But I am uncircumcised of lips) —, let us question them — nay, let us compel them to circumcise their ears and cut off their lips, that they may be seen to fulfill the Scripture —: but if they begin to interpret circumcision of the 'ears' as when we allow ourselves to hear nothing base and unseemly, and circumcision of the 'lips' as when we speak nothing indecent, let us say to them: you ought to keep the same exposition also for 'heart' and for 'flesh': we circumcise the 'heart' with the knife of God, and the foreskin is removed from our heart, when base thoughts in no way go forth from our heart — and it is not said of us: The heart of this people has grown fat, and with their ears they have heard heavily —; so the 'flesh' too is likewise circumcised, so that we by no means do the earthly works which we are compelled to do for the necessity of the body — to take food and drink and sleep and to use clothing —, which we circumcise then, if we do all these things not for pleasure and for luxury and for idleness, but for the necessity of nature and the sustenance of this body — he who drinks a little wine for his stomach and his frequent infirmities and hates drunkenness circumcises his flesh; he who sleeps as much as nature allows will hear from Solomon: If you sit, you will be without fear; if you sleep, you will sleep sweetly: and you will not fear the terror coming upon you, nor the assaults of the wicked coming upon you;
