During the six days on which we work in the world, the eastern gate of the inner court is shut to us; but after we have come to the seventh day, that is, to the sabbath day on which there is eternal rest, or to the day of the kalends, when after blind night and dreadful darkness there is the beginning of light, the eastern gate is opened to us; and if any of us, through the merits of the virtues, has attained the name and dignity of a leader, he will enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate from outside, that is, through the labors of this world, and through the gate of the Church, which is still set within earthly bounds, not into the inner court — for this is what is written in the present passage — but to the threshold of the inner gate: and he will stand in it; but if the prince in the present scripture does not enter the inner court, but stands on its threshold, no one doubts that we now see in part and know in part, and do not yet contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. Then, while the prince stands on the threshold of the gate of the inner court, the other priests, to whom this office has been delegated — whom we can understand as the angelic powers —, will make for him the holocaust and peace offerings — for we need the mercy of God, and every creature, in comparison with the Creator, is unclean and must be purged by the divine fire, by which the lips of the prophet Isaiah too were purged —, so that, after he has received peace through the sacrifice, then, standing on the threshold, he may worship the omnipotence of God and confess himself unworthy of entering the inner court, and at once go out; but after he who is first has gone out, that very gate of the inner court will not be shut until the evening of this age, but will be open, so that the people of the land too may be at the entrance and worship toward him: by no means at every time, but when they have rested from sins and, the darkness of faith having been put to flight, have received the light of knowledge. And this very holocaust, which the prince offers through the priests on the sabbath day, is bounded by the number of six lambs without blemish — namely after the six days on which we work in the world — and a ram without blemish, which is the prince of the flock, so that for each ram an 'oephi' is offered in sacrifice, that is, the tenth part of a 'corus'; but in the sacrifice of the six lambs no fixed measure is laid down, but as much as the hand of the one who offers shall give, that is, according to the quality and measure of his works; and he will offer a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi' — that is, the oil which the five virgins prepared for themselves —, to anoint the fine flour or mix it, so that every offering to God may be full of the light of truth, and the face of the one who offers may be made glad with oil; but on the day of the kalends, that is, the thirtieth day, when the firstborn and the Levites are numbered according to the law apart from all Israel, of whom we spoke above, a calf from the herd without blemish is offered — about which we discoursed more fully in the previous chapter — and six lambs and a ram without blemish, and the rest that are offered on the sabbaths, so that we may attain eternal rest and may deserve to hear: Well done, good servant, because you have been faithful in a few things, I will set you over many: enter into the rest of your Lord, and may be able not only to come to the gate of the inner court but also to enter its innermost parts, and to possess in deed that saying: Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of our God.

46:8-11

And when the prince enters, let him enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate, and let him go out by the same way. And when the people of the land enter in the sight of the Lord on the solemn feasts, he who enters by the gate of the north to worship, let him go out by the way of the southern gate; and he who enters by the way of the southern gate, let him go out by the way of the gate of the north: he shall not return by the way of the gate by which he entered, but shall go out opposite it. But the prince in their midst shall enter with those who enter and shall go out with those who go out. And on market days and on solemn feasts the sacrifice shall be an 'oephi' for the calf and an 'oephi' for the ram, but for the lambs the sacrifice shall be as his hand shall find, and a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi'. That prince, of whom it was said above: And the prince shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate from outside, is both to enter by the same way and to go out by the same way: for he is of free will and has power to lay down his life and to take it up again, and, as much in coming to us as in ascending to the heavenly places, he uses the same freedom of his majesty. Then too, he does not seek market days or solemn feasts, nor does he observe any difference of days, because every time is a festival as well; but the people enter and go out only on market days and on solemn feasts, and not by the same way, but by one way and then another: for it is written: And when the people of the land enter in the sight of the Lord on the solemn feasts, he who enters by the gate of the north to worship, let him go out by the way of the southern gate; and he who enters by the way of the southern gate, let him go out by the way of the gate of the north: he shall not return by the way of the gate by which he entered, but shall go out opposite it — which is commanded not only to those who go out of Sodom, and to whom it is said: Do not look back, nor only to those who put their hand to the plow, that they not look back at the things that are behind their back, but those too who are set in the house of the Lord are commanded not to look behind their backs and return to the weak and beggarly elements, and, having begun in the spirit, be finished in the flesh, but to advance from spiritual things also to greater ones and to say with the Apostle: Forgetting the things past, and stretching myself out to the things before, so that they may by no means know in part and prophesy in part, but come to the perfect: yet according to that perfection which human nature can contain, so that we may understand that saying of the Gospel: And you, when you have done all things, say: We are unprofitable servants; what we ought to do, we have done; whence the Apostle too, in the same epistle, speaks of two perfections: for as one perfect he writes: Not that I have already received, and that I am already perfect; but I pursue, if I may lay hold of that in which I also have been laid hold of by Christ, and at once he speaks as one perfect: But one thing: forgetting the things behind, stretching myself out to the things that are before, I pursue according to the purpose toward the prize of the upward calling. As many therefore as are perfect, we are of this mind — for how can the statement stand, that he who had said: Not that I have already received or that I am already perfect, should dare to say: As many therefore as are perfect, we are of this mind? —, from which it is plain that every human being and the whole creation, although it has come to perfection, nevertheless needs the mercy of God and possesses full perfection from grace, not from merit —. And so the people of the land are commanded that, if they enter by the gate of the north to worship, they go out by the way of the southern gate. Who is this people to whom this is commanded? Surely that of the Gentiles: so that he who, leaving the gate of the north — from which: Evils blaze up upon the earth —, has entered the temple, should not go out except by the way of the southern gate, to the gate of light, to the gate of warmth, to the gate at which the bridegroom lies at noon; and indeed it is said in the same Song of Songs: Arise, north wind, and come, south wind. But he who enters by the way of the southern gate also goes out by the way of the gate of the north. Which people is that? Clearly that of the Jews, which, leaving the way of the gate of light, goes to the gate of the north — of which it is said: The north wind is a most harsh wind; for Jeremiah's pot too is kindled from the face of the north —. Let us say it another way too: he enters by the gate of the north who lets go of sins, and he goes out by the southern gate who follows the virtues; and conversely, if a righteous man has fallen into sins, he enters indeed by the southern gate, but goes out by the way of the gate of the north. But the prince, he says, in their midst will be, namely in the midst of those entering and going out, according to what is written: In the midst among you stands one whom you do not know, and the Apostle: Or do you not know that Christ is in you? — but if it is said to those who do not know that Christ stands in their midst, how much more to those who know; but when Christ has stood among those who know, then the body will become dead because of sin and the spirit living because of righteousness! —; and the prince enters with those who enter, and goes out with those who go out, standing by as witness of both, of virtue and of sin. Therefore on market days and on solemn feasts — namely of the sabbaths and kalends and of every festival, of which we have spoken earlier — both with the calf and with the ram a single 'oephi' will be offered in sacrifice; but with the lambs there will be no fixed number, nor is the choice left to the will, but one will use his strength and the good of his conscience, so as to offer as much as he can, not as much as he wishes; and over all, a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi', so that the fine flour may be anointed and the lamp lit in the sight of the Lord, and those who use it may be able to say: But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord.

46:12-15

But when the prince makes a spontaneous holocaust or voluntary peace offerings to the Lord, the gate that faces toward the east shall be opened for him, and he shall make his holocaust and his peace offerings as is usually done on the sabbath day, and he shall go out, and the gate shall be shut after he has gone out. And a yearling lamb without blemish he shall make as a holocaust daily to the Lord; morning by morning he shall make it. And a sacrifice (or manaa) he shall make with it morning by morning, a sixth part of an 'oephi' (or of a measure), and of oil a third part of a 'hin', to be mixed (or according to Symmachus sprinkled) with the fine flour; a sacrifice (or manaa) to the Lord, lawful, continual and perpetual. You shall make the lamb and the sacrifice and the oil morning by morning, an everlasting holocaust. Where we read 'without blemish' and in the Hebrew is written 'thamim', Aquila translates 'perfect'; and where the Seventy have 'manaa', Theodotion translated 'sacrifice', Aquila and Symmachus 'gift'; and for what we said, 'spontaneous', the Seventy rendered ὁμολογίαν, that is, 'confession'; and for 'prince', 'leader', for this is what 'basi' means. Moreover, the discourse is still about the prince — of whom Isaiah speaks: Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, a prince and instructor among the nations, and Ezekiel: And I the Lord will be their God, and David a prince in their midst —. When therefore this prince makes a spontaneous — and says: The voluntary (or spontaneous) things of my mouth make well pleasing, O Lord —: and a 'spontaneous' holocaust, so that he offers the whole to God, and 'voluntary' peace offerings — which is not found in the earlier passages, for it is written: And the priests shall make his holocaust and his peace offerings, and about the spontaneous and voluntary ones, of which it now speaks, there is complete silence —, so that he does it not by necessity but by will; after the holocaust let him offer peace offerings, and be reconciled to God — whence virginity too is greater than marriage, because it is neither exacted nor rendered, but offered —; for 'peace offerings', which in Hebrew are called 'selamim', the Seventy translate 'saving offerings': so that the very reconciliation of the peace offerings may be the salvation of the one who offers. When therefore the prince has done this: The gate will be opened for him (or, according to the Seventy, he will open the gate for himself) that faces toward the east — that gate, namely, of which it is written: This is the gate of the Lord, the righteous shall enter by it, and whence the sun of righteousness rises —. And he shall make, he says, his holocaust and his peace offerings — of which we have just spoken —; and 'he shall make': as being a spontaneous sacrifice, and not other priests 'shall make' it for him: namely as is usually done on the sabbath day; therefore at every time the holocaust and peace offering that is offered voluntarily has the gate of the Lord unbarred, and it does not observe the sabbath, but all days are reckoned to it as rest. Then, after he has offered the holocaust and peace offerings, at once: He goes out, and the door is shut after him (or he shuts the door), so that the prince's privilege may be kept for him and his sacrifices not be mingled with the people. And since he had said in general: A spontaneous holocaust or voluntary peace offerings to the Lord, and had not added bull or calf, ram or sheep, and a he-goat for sin, he teaches what this holocaust is: A yearling lamb, he says, without blemish he shall make as a holocaust; and not on fixed days, but: daily; nor at any other hour, but: morning by morning he shall make it: namely each 'morning', when, the sun having risen, there is the beginning of light — of which 'morning' David speaks in a psalm: In the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will stand before you, and will see, and in another place: In the evening weeping will linger, and in the morning gladness, and again: O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the morning. But who this lamb without blemish, or perfect, and yearling is, Isaiah teaches more fully, saying: As a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer, without voice and not opening his mouth, and Jeremiah: But I, like an innocent lamb led to the slaughter, did not know, and John the evangelist: Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world; this is the lamb that is sacrificed in Egypt and with whose blood the doorposts of faith are armed, and the destroyer is shut out; and a yearling, because: He proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord, the day of retribution. Nor let the reader wonder if the same one is both prince and priest and calf and ram and lamb, since in the holy Scriptures, according to the variety of circumstances, we read of him as Lord and God and man and prophet and rod and flower and root and prince and judge and righteous king and righteousness, apostle and bishop, arm, servant, ointment, shepherd, son and child, only-begotten and firstborn, door, way, angel, arrow and wisdom, and many other things, for all of which, if I wished to cite the testimonies, they would need a book of their own —. And so in the holocaust of this lamb, without blemish and a yearling, which is always offered in the morning: the prince himself shall make a sacrifice (or 'manaa', and fine flour or gift) morning by morning, a sixth part of an 'oephi', of fine flour being understood — and a sixth part of an 'oephi' is half a modius; for if an 'oephi' is the tenth part of a 'corus', that is, three modii, no one doubts that the sixth part of an 'oephi' makes half a modius —. Of the oil also, a third part of the measure 'hin' is offered, to be mixed (or sprinkled) with the fine flour; a sacrifice to the Lord, lawful, continual and perpetual, which is interrupted on no day but at every time, when the sun has risen, is always offered, so that what is set at the end of this chapter may be fulfilled: He shall make the lamb for a sacrifice, and the oil, morning by morning, an everlasting holocaust.

46:16-18

Thus says the Lord God: If the prince (or leader) gives a gift to any of his sons, his inheritance shall belong to his sons; they shall possess it by inheritance. But if he gives a legacy from his inheritance to one of his servants, it shall be his until the year of remission (for which Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, deror), but it shall return to the prince; but his inheritance shall belong to his sons. And the prince shall not take from the inheritance of the people by violence and from their possession, but from his own possession he shall give an inheritance to his sons, so that my people be not scattered, each one from his possession. Thus far the discourse about the prince; now precepts are given about his heirs, or rather about gifts, inheritance and legacies: to whom he ought to give, and whose the possession is, whether for a time or everlasting. 'If', he says, 'he gives either a gift or an inheritance to his sons, they will possess it, because it is owed to them by right of succession, and the possession cannot pass from one to another; but if he gives it to one of his servants under the name of a legacy, he will hold the possession only so long as until either the seventh year, of remission, which is called 'deror', or the jubilee, that is, the fiftieth, arrives, when every purchase and gift will return to its former owners: so that the servant has the use for a time, and the sons of the prince the ownership of the possession'. But what follows: And the prince shall not take from the inheritance of the people by violence (or, as the Seventy translated, so as to oppress them, or, as Aquila and Symmachus, afflict them and sadden them), but from his own possession he shall give an inheritance to his sons, censures not only the priests and princes of that time but also those of ours, who grow richer through the dignity of the priesthood and, beyond what is owed them by the Lord's ordinance, take from the poor by violence, or despoil the rich under the name of honor, so that even to their own sons, to whom the paternal inheritance is owed, they ought to leave nothing except what was left to them by their parents; therefore the priest who is richer than when he came to the priesthood ought to give whatever more he has, not to his sons, but to the poor and to the holy brothers and to those of the household of faith, who surpass the merits of his children, so that he may render to his Lord the things that are the Lord's — who speaks in the Gospel: Whatever you have done to one of these, you have done to me; for he himself, in the poor, is received in hospitality, visited in prison, clothed when naked, drinks when thirsty, is filled when hungry —: So that my people be not scattered from its possession: for if the prince has license either to take or to seize or to hold under the guise of honor what is not his and to leave it to his children, the people that had been gathered in the name of God will be scattered into parts and torn apart, or, according to the law, the inheritance of one may gradually pass to another and the cord of division perish, through which, as it happened, the inheritance came to each one; therefore he scatters the people of God and takes from it the everlasting possession of faith who leaves to his sons and brothers and kinsmen the goods of others, whether by plunder or by flattery or by blandishments or under the pretext of religion.

46:19-24

And he brought me in by the entrance that was at the side (or behind the back) of the gate into the chambers of the sanctuary for the priests (or exedras, and cells) that faced toward the north, and behold, there was a place sloping toward the west (or toward the sea, and, as the Seventy translated, separated); and he said to me: This is the place where the priests will cook for trespass and for sin (or for ignorance and for sin), where they will cook the sacrifice (or manaa, and gift), so that they do not carry it out into the outer court and the people be sanctified. And he brought me out into the outer court and led me around through the four corners of the court, and behold, there was a little court in a corner of the court, a little court in each corner of the court. In the four corners of the court little courts were laid out, of forty cubits in length and thirty in breadth: the four were of one measure. And a wall round about encircled the four little courts, and kitchens were built beneath the porticoes all around (or beside the couches, which Aquila translated στιβάδας [pallets], Symmachus περιφράγματα [enclosures], while Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, turoth). And he said, he says, to me: This is the house of the kitchens, in which the ministers of the house cook the victims of the people (or victim, for this is what zeba means in Hebrew). The man who held a reed in his hand and a mason's cord with which to measure the building: 'He brought me in', he says, 'by the entrance that was at the side of the gate (or behind the back of the gate) — and he did not state which gate, the eastern, the southern or that of another quarter, but left it uncertain —, so that I went to the place of the sanctuary and into the chambers, or rooms, of the priests, which faced toward the north and toward the sea': namely toward the northern quarter and toward the west, Holy Scripture having this custom, that by reason of the position of the land of Judah it always calls the west the sea — and it must be considered that the place of the priests where for trespass (or for ignorance) and for sin the sacrifices are cooked, lest they be carried out raw into the outer court, is set toward the north and the west, whence the coldest wind arises and where the light of the sun goes down; from which it is shown that whatever pertains to food is either for error or for sin: but if a sacrifice is offered even for ignorance, how much more for the consciousness of trespass!: whence Job too offered a victim every day in the morning for his sons, fearing lest they had transgressed through ignorance —. But what follows: 'So that they do not carry it out into the outer court and the people be sanctified, the people who had not been prepared for sanctification', signifies this: that we should not readily give holy things to the unsanctified; that we should not, according to the Gospel, cast pearls before swine nor give what is holy to dogs — indeed Moses wishes the people to be sanctified for three days from all uncleanness and from the embrace of wives, so that they may approach Mount Sinai and, sanctified, receive holy things. But if those about to approach to hear and receive the words of God are commanded to be sanctified from their wives, it is manifest that that apostolic saying too is contained in the law: Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by consent for a time, that you may be free for prayer; and that by consent one must abstain from wives, that we may be free for prayer —. After this it is written: And he brought me out into the outer court and led me around through the four corners of the court, and behold, there was a little court in a corner of the court, a little court in each corner of the court; in the four little courts of the corner, little courts laid out; that man whom he often mentions brought him out of the place of the priests which sloped toward the north, or which was separated, where the priests cook for trespass and for sin or ignorance; and he brought him out into the outer court: from which we understand that the court from which he went out was the inner one, and that there are many courts in the holy Scriptures — of which we read: You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, and in John: And other sheep I have, which are not 'of this court'; and them too I must bring: and they will hear my voice, and there will be one 'court' and one shepherd — for this is what the Greek αὐλή means, which Latin simplicity translated as 'fold' —: for when he says 'of this court', he shows that there is another as well, which is pointed out either in the throng of the nations, as distinct from Israel, or in the heavens, as separate from the earthly court, and that to each office a court has been assigned according to the quality of merits, a subject that was argued more fully earlier —; and this court, of which the discourse now is, had four little courts, one in each corner — which the Seventy call 'lesser ones' and we, for ease of sense, have called ὑποκοριστικῶς [in diminutive form] 'little courts' —: they were of forty cubits in length and thirty in breadth, numbers which I remember having discussed in this same prophet: that the one refers to tribulations and straits, the other to the perfect age — whence Moses and Elijah and the Lord and Savior fasted forty days in the desert; and they come to the priestly office not, as the Seventy have it, after the twenty-fifth year of age, but after the thirtieth, for which reason the Lord too was thirty years old when he came to baptism, and in this same prophet the thirtieth year is set at the beginning. Where, therefore, there is food, there are also the straits and the temptation through which food is procured; and when we have come to the age of the perfect man, there everything must be trodden underfoot, and one must say: Having food and clothing, with these we are content, and: If the Lord gives me food to eat and clothing to cover me, or surely that saying: Food for the belly and the belly for foods: but God will destroy both it and them; for in the future we shall not eat and drink, but shall feed on that bread: Which came down from heaven, of which it is sung in the psalter: Man will eat the bread of angels, and: My food is to do the will of him who sent me —. And that the four little courts which occupied the corners of the greater court were of one measure signifies the four quarters of the world: that we eat bread in the sweat of our face and all our labor profits the belly and the dung. And these four little courts one wall also encircled: And kitchens were built beneath the porticoes all around, or they had couches nearby, so that where the food was, there was also the preparing of the tables. And lest the prophet perhaps not know what he was seeing, he said to him: This is the house of the kitchens, in which the ministers of the Lord will cook the victims of the people: victims of the people indeed, which are offered for trespass or for sin and ignorance, but nourishment and refreshment for the priests, so that they may remember that they ought to desire nothing else, since even in the temple refreshments for their flesh have been prepared.

47:1-5

And he turned me to the gate of the house, and behold, waters were going out beneath the threshold of the house toward the east; for the face of the house looked toward the east, and the waters were going down into the right side of the temple, to the south of the altar. And he led me out by the way of the gate of the north, and he turned me to the way outside, to the outer gate, the way that looked toward the east; and behold, waters overflowing from the right side. When the man who had a cord in his hand went out toward the east, he both measured a thousand cubits and led me across through the water up to the ankles (or he passed over in water, water of remission). And again he measured a thousand, and led me across through the water up to the knees (or and he passed over in water, water up to the thighs). And he measured a thousand, and led me across through the water up to the kidneys (or and he passed over the water up to the loins). And he measured a thousand, a torrent which I could not pass across, for the deep waters of the torrent had swelled, which could not be forded (for which the Seventy translated: And he measured a thousand, and he could not pass across, for the water was borne along like a headlong torrent which cannot be crossed). These waters which were going out beneath the threshold of the house, that is, of the temple, were not borne toward the north and toward the west but toward the east and on the right side of the temple, that is, toward the south, and that south not of just any place, but of the altar — from which it becomes clear that the waters are sacred and signify the teaching of our Savior, according to that which is written: Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and in another place: All things have been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as much water covering the sea; of these waters the prophet Zechariah too prophesied, saying: On that day living water shall go out from Jerusalem, and the middle of it into the first sea, and the middle of it into the last sea; of these waters the Lord too spoke to the Samaritan woman: If you knew who it is who says to you: Give me to drink, you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water, and again: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst forever, and in the temple he cried out and said: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly. But this he said of the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive; these are the waters of which the prophet spoke in the psalm: Beside the water of refreshment he has brought me up, and in Ezekiel: I will take you from the nations and from the lands, and I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleannesses. For there appeared the springs of waters, and in Psalm 92 (93) it is sung: The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices. From the voices of many waters, wonderful are the swellings of the sea; these are: The waters of Shiloah that go with silence, of which Isaiah speaks: You shall draw waters from the springs of the Savior, and the psalmist: Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel, and the same Isaiah of the Lord Savior: He, he says, shall dwell in a lofty cave of the strongest rock; bread shall be given him, and his water is faithful. For water has broken forth in the desert, and a valley in a thirsty land, and it is said to believers: Fear not, for I have redeemed you; you are mine. And if you pass through water, I am with you, and again: You who thirst, go to the water; and through Jeremiah God speaks: For my people has done evil things: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns, which cannot hold water. Just as, then, we read in a good sense the waters which go out from the threshold of the temple and are referred to the teaching of the Church, so there are bitter waters and most evil waters which the prophet Jeremiah forbids us to approach, saying: What have you to do with the way of Egypt, that you should drink of the waters of 'Geon'? — which in Hebrew is called 'Sior', that is, 'turbid' and 'muddy' —, of which God, angered over the heretics, speaks: Behold, I will feed them with distresses, and I will give them water of gall to drink; in which the Egyptian dragon reigns, who says: The rivers are mine, and I made them, who: Sees every high thing, and he himself is king of those who are in the waters; whence the man of the Church entreats the Lord and says: Save me, O Lord, for the waters have come in even to my soul. I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance; I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me, and again: May I be delivered from those who hate me and from the depth of the waters. Let not the tempest of water cast me down, nor the deep swallow me up; nor let the pit press its mouth upon me, and in another psalm: Unless the Lord had been among us, let Israel now say, unless the Lord had been among us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive; when their fury was angered against us, perhaps the water would have swallowed us up, and the bride in the Song of Songs: Much water will not be able to quench love, and rivers will not overwhelm it; this is the water of which Hosea says: Gilead has despised me, the city that works vanities, troubling the water, and its strength pirate men; which water is called by another name 'merra', that is, 'bitterness' — into which the wood of the Cross is cast, and bitter things are turned into sweet —; consider the law of Moses, if it is understood according to the carnal sense of the Jews, how bitter it is — digging out: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth —: the fornication of Judah with Tamar, and Hosea joined to a harlot, Jeremiah's περίζωμα [loincloth], Moses' Ethiopian wife, the killing of the Egyptian, and a thousand other things which, if we understand them according to the letter that kills and not according to the spirit that gives life, are bitter and do not so much edify their reader as destroy him —. These waters, then, which go out from the temple of the Lord, proceed toward the east and go down into the right side of the temple, to the south of the altar, where the bridegroom feeds his guests and reclines. But what follows: And he led me out by the way of the gate of the north, and turned to the way outside, to the outer gate, the way that looked toward the east, secretly shows that we cannot come at once to the eastern gate unless we come to it by the way of the gate of the north, by a long circuit: for unless we overcome the coldest wind by the heat of faith and trample its regions — so that that apostolic saying may be fulfilled in us: But God will crush Satan under your feet swiftly —, we are not able to enter the gate through which the waters enter and are on the right side; and note that these waters, which go out through the gate of the east, flee the left-hand parts to such a degree that they are described as proceeding from the right of the altar toward the south. 'But that man who had the cord in his hand, when he had led me through the gate of the north, outside, to the way that looked toward the east, and he himself too was in the same place, measured a thousand cubits of the same water'. And he led me across through the water up to the 'ankles' — which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated ἀστραγάλους [anklebones] — (for which the Seventy translated: But he passed over in water, water of remission), which we can understand to signify the first sins of men, which are remitted to us as we enter the waters of the Lord, and they show the saving grace of baptism, and are the beginnings of progress; finally, they reach as far as the ankles, which are neighbors to the sole and the heel — which lies open to the bites of the snake, as the Lord says: You shall watch for his head, and he shall watch for your heel; and in the Psalter it is said of Judas the betrayer: He who ate my bread has magnified tripping-up against me (or the heel: for this is what the Greek πτέρνα means). And after the thousand cubits which reach as far as the ankle: He measured another thousand cubits in the water and led me across up to the knees: since after the remission of sins and the beginnings of progress, when we strive to climb a little from earthly things to higher ones, we bend the knees to the Lord — as the Apostle says: That every knee should bend, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father —. Thirdly: He measured a thousand cubits, and led me, he says, across through the water up to the kidneys: for by these steps we come to the heights, which heights themselves, however, reach up to the loins and kidneys, so that all lust in us may be cut off, and we may possess the sanctification of the body without which no one will see God — whence also in this same prophet God is seen fiery from the feet up to the loins: for the works of the loins need fire and purgation, as the righteous man says: For my loins have been filled with illusions, through which the enemy mocks us both by day and in the phantasm of the nights; but from the loins up to the head and crown he shines with the brilliance of electrum, the most precious metal, so that he has in himself nothing of filth, nothing of baseness —. Whence now fourthly it is said: And he measured a thousand, 'cubits' being understood, a torrent — which the Seventy did not translate —, which I could not pass across (much better than the Seventy, who said: which he could not pass across): for the prophet, and all human nature, cannot after the loins pass across the torrent of thoughts and the incitements of vices; but that man: Who was clothed in 'baddi' [linen], and the guide of the prophet, clearly passes across: Who did no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth. And he gives the reasons why the prophet could not pass across the fourth thousand cubits: For, he says, the deep waters of the torrent had swelled, which cannot be forded — and how is it written, with the prophet glorying: Our soul has passed across the torrent? But it is easily resolved if we know that in place of this it is written in the Hebrew: The torrent has passed across my soul —. Of this torrent Isaiah too speaks: Behold, I incline upon them like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent glory, and in Psalm 35 (36) it is said of the saints: In the protection of your wings they will hope, they will be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and with the torrent of your delights you will give them drink; for with you is the fountain of life, and in Psalm 124 (125): Turn back, O Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south, and of the Savior: He will drink of the torrent on the way — for who of men can boast that he has a chaste heart?, or: Into whose mind has the death of concupiscence not entered through the windows of the eyes and, to say little, a tickling of the soul? For the world is set in the evil one, and: From childhood the heart of man is set on evil, so that from the very beginning of birth the human condition is not without sin for even a single day; whence David too confesses in the psalm: 'For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me, not by the iniquities of my mother or indeed my own, but in the iniquities of the human condition'; whence the Apostle too says: Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of the transgression of Adam —. That we say 'cubitos' [cubits] in the masculine gender and not, according to the rule of the grammarians, in the neuter 'cubita', I have also taught above: that we do this not from ignorance but from custom, for the sake also of the simple and unlearned, whose number in the congregation of the Church is the greater.

47:6-12

And he said to me: Surely you have seen, son of man; and he led me out, and turned me to the bank of the torrent (or of the river). And when I had turned (or he had turned me), behold, on the bank of the torrent (or of the river) a great many trees (or very many trees) on either side; and he said to me: These waters, which go out to the mounds of sand of the east and go down to the plains of the desert (or this water which goes out into Galilee, which slopes toward the east, and goes down to Arabia), will enter the sea; and they will go out, and the waters will be healed: and every living soul (or of animals) that creeps (or of creeping things), wherever the torrent (or the river) comes, will live, and there will be very many fish after these waters have come there, and all things will be healed and will live to which the torrent (or the river) comes. And fishermen will stand over them from En-gedi to En-eglaim; there will be a drying of nets; very many kinds of its fish there will be, like the fish of the great sea, of exceeding multitude. But in the places that go out beyond the banks and are marshy they will not be healed, but will be given over to salt-pits. And over the torrent (or river) there will rise on its banks on either side every fruit tree (or fruit-bearing tree); its leaf will not fall from it (or nothing will grow old from it), and its fruit will not fail: each month it will bring forth early fruits (or all things will be renewed), because its waters will go out from the sanctuary, and its fruit will be for food, and its leaves for medicine (or and its ascent for health). I wished to set down the whole passage together, although it is lengthy, so as not to break in upon the sense of the reader, and so that the order of the reading, divided into parts, might not confuse the understanding of the hearer. And first it must be said that for 'torrent', which in Hebrew is called 'nehel' and in the Greek tongue is named χειμάρρος, the Seventy translated 'river'; next, that for 'Galilee', which in Hebrew is called 'galila', Aquila translated θινάς, which means 'mounds' 'of sand', Symmachus μεθόριον, which we can translate 'border-region'; for 'Arabia' too Symmachus translated 'uninhabitable', Aquila 'low places' or 'plains', Theodotion 'arabas' [a transliteration of the Hebrew word]. Let us say, then, what seems right to us in each point. That man, who was Ezekiel's guide, admonishes the prophet to look more carefully and see, and to attend with the eyes of the mind to hidden mysteries; and he calls him 'son of man' either as a figure of the Lord Savior — for 'Hiezechiel' means 'strength' or 'dominion of God' —, or certainly as a reminder of human frailty — lest he forget his condition while great things are shown to him —; and having admonished him he leads him and turns him to the bank of the torrent so that, since he could not cross the middle depth, he might at least recognize the things that are on the banks. And when, he says, I had turned (or he had turned me, who was guide and admonisher), behold, on the bank of the torrent (or of the river) many trees (or a great many trees) exceedingly, on either side: this 'torrent', which on account of the abundance of its waters is borne along in the manner of a torrent and receives rains from heaven, of which we spoke in the preceding reading, is itself called by the Seventy 'river', because it has perpetual waters, not collected from rains here and there but abiding from a living and perpetual spring — of which river we read many things in the holy scriptures, but for the present a few things must be said, and first that: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God, and in another place: The river of God is filled with waters; you have prepared their food, for so is your preparation, and again in the plural: The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices. From the voices of many waters, wonderful are the swellings of the sea, and in Isaiah: I will make a way in the desert, and rivers in the pathless place, and in another place of the same it will appear more plainly that in Zion a river runs down, glorious in a thirsty land —; above this river there were very many trees on either side of the bank, so that, namely, the river ran enclosed between the two instruments, the old and the new; and the many trees, or the very many and exceedingly numerous trees, I take to be those which scripture records in paradise as abounding with various fruits. And the guide who goes before, the teacher, teaches the prophet and says: These waters, which go out (or into Galilee of the nations according to the Seventy, or, as is more truly contained in the Hebrew:) to the mounds of sand of the east and go down to the plains of the desert (or to Arabia), will enter the sea (or to the outlets of the sea), and the waters will be healed; we said long ago that the waters signify either the grace of baptism or the teaching of the Gospel, which, if they go out from the threshold of the temple of the Lord and hold to the apostolic discipline, make the mounds of sand, previously sterile and unfruitful, to be fruit-bearing, and so water all the plains and deserts as to express among themselves too the mystery of the spring of Jericho — which Elisha healed with the evangelic and apostolic salt, to such a degree that where there had previously been sterility and death, there was fertility and life —; nor did they heal the deserts only, but they enter the eastern sea — namely the 'Dead' sea, in which nothing living could exist, and the 'most bitter' sea, which in Greek they call λίμνην ἀσφαλτῖτιν, that is, 'lake of bitumen' —; and in a wonderful manner the dead waters are healed by the waters of the Gospel — which, from the fact that they have nothing living in them, have obtained the name of death: for they did not know him who says: I am the life; and in truth, according to the letter, up to now nothing that breathes and can move about can be found in this sea because of its excessive bitterness: not even little snails and small worms and eels and the other kinds of animals or creeping things whose little bodies we can know better than their names; finally, if the Jordan, swollen by rains, flowing in there, has carried fish along, they die at once and float on the fat waters —. Since, then, these waters have nothing of usefulness, as the plain account testifies, even if it should come about, as the foolish superstition of the Jews believes, according to the spiritual understanding, healed by the torrent of the Lord, they will have very many fish, and all things to which this torrent comes will live, so that fishermen stand over the banks from 'Engaddi' to 'Engallim' — of which the first means 'spring' or 'eye' 'of the kid', the next 'spring, or eye' 'of calves': En-eglaim is at the beginning of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan enters, and En-gedi where it ends and is consumed; and I think the Dead Sea is the one of which Zechariah speaks: On that day living water will go out from Jerusalem, and the middle of it into the first sea; Daniel too agrees with these words: I was seeing, and behold, the four winds of heaven were rushing into the great sea, and David: Wonderful, he says, are the upliftings of the sea, and in the person of the Savior in the psalm: I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me; the king of Egypt too, according to this same Ezekiel, is called a dragon who dwells in the sea and fans the rivers as with his horns, and again: This great and spacious sea; which, as long as it has not received into itself the water of the river or torrent, kills everything it has in itself: but the Lord — of whom it was said: He will strike: and he will heal after two days, and on the third day we shall rise and live in his sight — himself speaks in the same prophet Hosea: I bound Ephraim, I took him up in my arm, and they did not know that I healed them in the corruption of men — he who: Was wounded for our sins and made weak for our iniquities; the discipline of his peace is upon him, and by his bruise we have been healed —; he himself healed by his death this sea, which is most salty and dead from excessive bitterness, he who says through Isaiah: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to heal those who are contrite of heart, whence through Jeremiah too he cries out: Turn back, you turning sons, and I will heal your contritions — for the people, impatient and not enduring to bear the pain of its wounds any longer, had said: The summer has passed, the harvest has gone by, and we are not saved, whence the Lord also answered it: Is there no resin in Gilead, or are there no physicians there? Why has the healing of my people not gone up? —, and Jeremiah himself cries aloud and says: Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me and I shall be saved; finally the angels — who were the guardians of the Jews at that time when the foolish multitude cried out and said: His blood be upon us and upon our children, and the veil of the temple was torn and all the mysteries of the Hebrews were laid open — answered the Lord who commanded them, and said: We have treated Babylon and she is not healed; let us leave her, namely the city of confusion and of vices — whence Josephus too relates in his History that, after the Lord was crucified and the veil of the temple was torn, or the lintel of the temple broke and fell, a voice of the heavenly powers was heard in the inner shrines of the temple: Let us pass over from these seats —. Let all this have been said not superfluously but necessarily, because the Dead Sea is said to have been healed when the river of the Lord flowed into it —. Over this sea — from 'Engaddi', 'the eye and spring of the kid', which is always offered for sins, up to 'Engallim', 'the spring of calves', which are slaughtered to the Lord and imitate the calf that puts forth horns and hoofs, which are slaughtered at the altar in type of the Savior — there will be fishermen, to whom Jesus speaks: Come to me and I will make you fishermen, of whom Jeremiah too: Behold, I, he says, will send fishermen; and very many species, or rather kinds, of fish will be in the sea once dead, which fish Peter drew out on the right-hand side at the Lord's command, and they were one hundred and fifty-three, so that the nets were breaking because of their multitude — and those who have written on the natures of animals, and especially those who have published ἁλιευτικά [works on fishing] in the Latin as well as the Greek tongue — of whom Opianicus the Cilician is a most learned poet —, say that there are one hundred and fifty-three kinds of fish; all of which were caught by the apostles, and nothing remained uncaught, while both noble and ignoble, both rich and poor, and every kind of men is drawn out of the sea of this world to salvation —. But what follows: On its shores and in the marshy places (or in those which go out from the shore) the waters will not be healed, secretly shows that whoever was not in Noah's ark perishes while the flood reigns, and that those whom this river has not touched do not receive healing: But they will be given, he says, to salt-pits, according to that which is written: When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will be wiser — for the examples of the worse instruct the good —, or: They will be given to salt-pits, according to that which is written in the Gospel: Salt is good; but if the salt has become foolish, it is useful for nothing, so that they may lack crops and greenness forever — which a city too, sprinkled with salt after its ruin, demonstrates —. But over the torrent (or the river) there will rise on its banks on either side every fruit tree (or, as all have translated with one voice, βρώσιμον, 'that which provides food and nourishment' and 'that which can be eaten'; and in the Hebrew tongue it is called 'machal'). And: (nothing, according to the Seventy, will grow old in it, but its produce will be renewed daily, or:) its leaf will not fall from it, and its fruit will not fail, according to that which is written in Psalm 1: And he will be like the tree that is planted beside the runnings of waters, which will give its fruit in its season; and its leaf will not fall. Each month, he says, it will bring forth early fruits (or, as is written in the Seventy: its fruit in its renewal will give early fruits), so that all the fruits of believers may be firstfruits and the single months may be assigned to the single apostles; and this will come about: Because its waters will go out from the sanctuary: lest we think that so great an abundance of produce belongs to the banks or the trees or the months, he gives the causes of the fertility and adds: Because its waters will go out from the sanctuary — So then it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy —. The primacy among all these trees is held by the tree of life, which is understood as wisdom, of which it is written: She is a tree of life to all who believe in her. That which is said: And its fruit will be for food, and its leaf for medicine, shows the mysteries of the divine books, of which the one pertains to the letter, the other to the spirit, so that we understand the simple words in the leaves, but in the fruits the hidden sense: for just as the knowledge of the scriptures leads to the kingdoms of heaven and offers us the bread who says: I am the bread who came down from heaven, so its leaves, which contain moral teaching, bestow health, so as to heal the wounds of those who sin. For 'leaves', which in Hebrew are called 'ale', the Seventy, on account of the likeness of the word and of the sound, translated 'ascent', which itself too can be explained thus: that, after the food of the fruits, we may climb by the admonitions of the words to heavenly things.

47:13-14

Thus says the Lord God. This is the boundary by which you shall possess the land in the twelve tribes of Israel, because Joseph has a double cord; and you shall possess it — each one equally as his brother — the land which I lifted up my hand to give to your fathers; and this land shall fall to you as a possession. In place of what we said: Because Joseph has a double cord, the Seventy translated: Increase of the cord — for 'Ioseph' means 'increase —, understanding a thing in place of a name and confusing the mind of the reader: for when the Levitical tribe had been subtracted and assigned to the sacrifices of the temple, there remained eleven tribes, of which Joseph was divided into two, Ephraim and Manasseh, who said to Joshua son of Nun: Why have you given me a possession of one lot and one cord, though I am of so great a multitude and the Lord has blessed me?, to whom Joshua answered: If you are a numerous people, go up into the forest and cut down spaces for yourself in the land of the Perizzite and of Rephaim, since the possession of mount Ephraim is narrow for you, and again: And Joshua said to the house of Ephraim and Manasseh: You are a numerous people and of great strength; you shall not have one lot, but you shall pass over to the mountain and cut down and clear for yourself spaces for dwelling; and you will be able to proceed further when you have overthrown the Canaanite, who you say has iron chariots and is very strong; I have said this for this reason, because scripture now records that Joseph, that is, Ephraim and Manasseh, has a double cord. And the individual tribes receive equal spaces of land according to their multitude, by no means at the discretion of the one dividing but by lot, which rests in the power of the Lord. Finally Joshua himself too, who was the divider of the land, did not set apart his own land for himself, lest he should seem to have chosen the best, but received from the princes of all the tribes: Timnath-serah in mount Ephraim.

47:15-17

And this is the boundary of the land: toward the northern quarter, from the Great Sea, by the way of Ethalon, for those coming to Sadada, Hamath, Berotha, Sabarim, which is between the middle of Damascus and the border of Hamath, the court of Thicon, which is beside Hauran (or of Auranitis); and the boundary shall be from the sea up to 'the court of Enom' (or 'Aser-Enan'), the boundary of Damascus; and from north to north the boundary of Hamath, the northern quarter. Between the description of the holy land of the twelve tribes by Joshua son of Nun and the one which is now commanded to be made through Ezekiel there is this difference: that there the land is divided among the tribes by lot, here it is assigned by the discretion of the Lord who commands. In the book of Numbers, then, in which the whole land of promise is divided by four quarters in brief speech, this is the description from the north, that is, from the northern quarter: Moreover, on the northern side the boundaries will begin from the Great Sea, reaching as far as the Highest Mountain, from which you will come into Hamath, up to the borders of Sedada. And the borders will go as far as Zephrona and 'the village of Enan' (or 'Aser-Enan'). And the Hebrews say that the northern quarter begins from the Great Sea, which stretches along the shores of Palestine, of Phoenicia, and of the Syria which is called Coele, and of Cilicia, and extends through Egypt to Libya. But as to what he says: Reaching — the boundaries — as far as the Highest Mountain, the same Hebrews assert that it signifies either Mount Amanus or the Taurus — which seems truer to us —. From which, he says, you will come into 'Emath', which is now named 'Epiphania', its name having been changed by Antiochus, the cruelest of tyrants, for he had the surname Ἐπιφανής [Epiphanes, the Manifest]. Up to the borders, he says, of Sedada, which place is also set down in the present reading of Ezekiel. And the borders will go as far as Zephrona, which city they today call Zephyrium, a town of Cilicia. And what follows: And 'the village of Enan' (for which in the Hebrew is written 'Aser-Enon' or '-Enan'), the present passage also contains. And meanwhile let it suffice to have touched on it briefly according to the history and to have joined side by side the description both of Numbers and of Ezekiel, so that the prudent reader may understand in which points they record either the same or neighboring or different things; now, having interpreted the names of each, let us follow the ἀναγωγήν [anagogy, the higher sense], and let us set out, the Lord granting it, what seems right to us in each point. 'Ethalon' means 'cradle of grief'; 'Sedada', 'his side' — understand it from 'side', not from 'breadth'; 'Emath', 'fury', which in Greek is called χόλος; 'Berotha', 'wells'; 'Sabarim', 'circuit of mountains'; 'Damascus', 'blood of sackcloth' and 'of a kiss' or 'of a cup'; but the 'house' or 'court of Thicon' Symmachus translates 'the middle court', which goes on to the borders of 'Auran'; therefore 'Thicon' means 'middle'; 'Auran' — which the Seventy turned into the Greek tongue as 'Auranitis' —, 'wrath'; but 'Asar' '-Enon' — which is the boundary of Damascus — is called in our language 'court of the spring'. The northern quarter, then, begins from the Great Sea and goes by the way of 'Ethalon', which means 'cradle of grief'; through penitence it comes to 'Sadada', where there is a turning aside 'from the side': for we understand 'Emath', that is, the 'indignation' of God, impending over us, or, 'Emath' having been found to be 'truth', the 'wells' of 'Berotha' are opened to us, which the princes Abraham, Isaac and Jacob dug, and by a long 'circuit' we come to the 'mountains' of 'Sabarim', which are set between 'Damascus', that is, 'the blood of haircloth', and the border of 'Emath', that is, as we said above, 'of truth' — for just as through grief we turn aside impending evils and avoid them from the side, so after the blood and haircloth of a bloody life, before we come to the borders of Emath, we go around and come to the mountains of which it is written: Mountains round about it, and the Lord round about his people —, which place is called 'the court of Thicon', that is, 'the middle court', as Symmachus translated, beside the borders of 'Auran', which means 'wrath' — so that we may say with the prophet: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him —, and from the sea up to the borders of Damascus: in which the apostle Paul too, from Jewish fury and the shedding of the Church's blood, beheld the light through blindness and, having taken up the haircloth for his old persecution, preached the Gospel, so that he might come to the eternal 'court of the spring' and, once set in the north, might lay hold of the boundary of truth.

47:18

But the eastern quarter, from the midst of Hauran and from the midst of Damascus and from the midst of Gilead and from the midst of the land of Israel, the Jordan dividing, to the eastern sea; you shall measure the eastern quarter. For which in the book of Numbers I have found it written thus: Thence they shall measure the boundaries toward the eastern quarter from 'the village of Enan' (that is, 'Aser-Enon') as far as Sephama, and from Sephama the boundaries will go down to Rebla, opposite the spring; thence they will come toward the east to the sea of Chinnereth, and they will extend as far as the Jordan, and at the last they will be closed by the sea. Above he had said: And the boundary shall be from the sea up to Eser-Enon, the boundary of Damascus: from the end of the northern quarter, then, that is, from the court of Enan, the boundaries extend according to the book of Numbers as far as Sephama, which the Hebrews name Apamea, and from Apamea the boundaries will go down to Rebla, which is now called Antioch of Syria; and so that you may know that this Rebla signifies the city which is now the most renowned in Coele-Syria, there follows: Opposite the spring, which it is evident signifies Daphne, from which spring the aforesaid city enjoys most abundant waters — this place was planted by the military hand of Gnaeus Pompey, who first subjected Judea to Roman rule, and from him — following the fable of the poets — it received the name of Daphne, on account of the laurels and cypresses, trees which are very frequent in that very place too —. Thence, he says, the boundaries will come toward the eastern quarter to the sea of Chinnereth: as far as the lake of Tiberias; and it is called a sea although it has sweet waters, according to the idiom of the scriptures, which call gatherings of waters seas. And the boundaries, he says, will extend as far as the Jordan, and at the last will be closed by the sea: either by the Dead Sea or, as others think, by the tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Aila is situated, where a legion and garrison of the Romans is now stationed. Let this have been said according to the book of Numbers. But according to Ezekiel: from the midst of Hauran, which is a town of Damascus in the wilderness, and from the midst of Gilead, which, a mountain joined to the hills of Lebanon, fell into the lot of Reuben and Gad and of the half tribe of Manasseh, and is behind Phoenicia and Arabia — to which mountain Jacob came, having set out from Carrhae, and was overtaken by Laban; of which Jeremiah too speaks: Gilead, you are to me the beginning of Lebanon; which Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, took from the region of the Amorites —; and the end of this quarter: the river Jordan bounding it, and the eastern sea, which in this place they understand as the Dead Sea, not the tongue of the Red Sea. Let us speak according to tropology. After the boundaries of the north, by a long circuit through Ethalon and Sedada and Berotha, Sabarim too and Thicon and Auran and Damascus and the court of Enom, the eastern quarter reaches as far as Emath: from the midst of the 'wrath' of 'Auran', and from the midst of 'Damascus', namely of the 'blood' 'of penitence', and from the midst of 'Galaad', which means 'revelation' or 'mound of testimony': so that, after wrath and penitence, it may show the hope of salvation; and from the midst of the land of 'Israel', which contains the 'vision' 'of peace', it reaches to the most sweet streams of the Jordan, which, with the sea set far apart, attains the light of the east, so that it is ended by the 'river' 'Iordanis', which means 'stream of judgment', and by the boundary of the 'torrent'; but what is set down in the Seventy, 'phoeniconos', that is, 'of the palm grove', is not found in the Hebrew, for which we translated 'you shall measure': and the error is manifest, because for 'thamoddu' [you shall measure], deceived by the likeness of the letters 'daleth' and 'res' [d and r], they read 'thamorru' [palm].

47:19

But the southern quarter, the meridional, from Tamar up to the waters of contradiction (or to the waters of 'Mariboth' — for these mean 'contradiction' or διαδίκασμοι, that is, 'disputes' —) of Kadesh too, and the torrent up to the Great Sea; this is the southern quarter toward the south. For which in the book of Numbers it is written thus: It will begin from the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom, and will have as boundaries toward the east the sea. And they will go around the southern quarter by the Ascent of the Scorpion, so that they pass Senna and come into the south as far as Kadesh-barnea, whence the borders will go out to a village named Addar, and will extend as far as Asemona. And the boundary will go around from Asemona as far as the torrent of Egypt, and will be ended by the shore of the Great Sea. Which briefly signifies this — lest on the occasion of Ezekiel we seem to pass over to a very broad exposition of Numbers —: that the boundary goes around from the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom, and from the Red Sea, and, through the Ascent of the Scorpion and through Senna and Kadesh-barnea and the court of Addar and Asemona, reaches as far as the torrent of Egypt, which flows into the sea beside the city of Rhinocorura; but this boundary of the southern quarter, that is, the meridional, begins from Tamar — which is a city in the wilderness, which Solomon too built with wondrous works, and today it is named Palmyra, and in the Hebrew tongue it is called 'thamar', which in our language means 'palm' — up to the waters of contradiction of Kadesh, which beyond doubt is in the desert, and the torrent entering the Great Sea, this sea which stretches along the shores of Egypt and Palestine, and this is the southern quarter toward the south. After the quarter of the north, then, and of the east, when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, we receive the meridional quarter, when the whole light is poured upon us from above, and with Abraham we enter the banquet and are inebriated with wine — which makes glad the heart of man — with Joseph and his brothers; and this possession and these boundaries begin from 'Thamar', namely from the 'palm' and the victory over vices, up to the waters of contradiction: for virtues are always contradicted — whence the Jews too, disputing against Paul, assert that the preaching of the Gospel is contradicted in the whole world; and in the Gospel we read, as Simeon says: This one will be for the ruin and resurrection of many, and for a sign that will be contradicted —, but all contradiction is of 'holiness', which 'Cades' means — as the psalmist says: The Lord will shake the desert of Cades: which, namely, at first did not have the holiness of the Lord, but was shaken and moved, so as to receive God as its guest, who says: Upon whom will my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet and the one who trembles at my words? —; after the desert of Cades, up to the Great Sea, in the south of the southern quarter, is the torrent of which we spoke above, which has rains not from the earth but from heaven, collected from the variety of diverse virtues.

47:20

And the quarter of the sea, the Great Sea, from the border straight on until you come to Hamath; this is the quarter of the sea. Of which the book of Numbers writes more plainly and more briefly: But the western quarter will begin from the Great Sea, and will be closed by that same end, that is, from sea to sea: namely from the torrent of Rhinocorura, which flows into the sea, up to that place which is opposite Hamath, the city of Syria, of which we spoke above. But the west, according to the laws of tropology, is always in the sea, always in the brine and the waves, where every day shipwrecks are stirred up, and the deaths of the wretched, and the loss of riches and merchandise; and yet, when we have broken all these things by patience, we come straight on to 'Emath', that is, to the 'truth' of the Lord, who, once persecutions are overcome, has promised us eternal rewards.

47:21-23

And you shall divide this land for yourselves by the tribes of Israel; and you shall cast it as an inheritance, for yourselves and for the strangers who have come to you, who will have begotten sons in your midst, and they shall be to you as natives among the sons of Israel: with you they shall divide the possession in the midst of the tribes of Israel; and in whatever tribe the stranger shall be, there you shall give him a possession, says the Lord God. Through this passage we learn — and the haughtiness of the Jews is struck down — that nothing is divided between Israel and the people of the Gentiles: for if the land is divided to strangers and foreigners together with those who are of the people of Israel, that is, the natives, no one doubts that the inheritance is the same for the people of the Gentiles and for the people of the Jews, if only they have been converted to the worship of the God of Israel — which properly possesses the name Christian —, the Jews having the letter of the law and we the spirit, they holding the parchments and we him who is written in the parchments; and with Moses the land is divided by lot, but here, as we said, it is assigned by the judgment of the Lord, and there is one possession for the stranger and for Israel, and in the individual tribes the inheritance is given, at the command of the Lord God.

48:1-7

And these are the names of the tribes: from the borders of the north, beside the way of Ethalon, for those going to Hamath, Court Enon, the border of Damascus toward the north beside Hamath; and its eastern side shall be the sea, Dan one. And from the border of Dan, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Asher one. And above the border of Asher, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Naphtali one. And above the border of Naphtali, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Manasseh one. And above the border of Manasseh, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Ephraim one. And above the border of Ephraim, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Reuben one. And above the border of Reuben, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Judah one. Now that the possession of the holy land has been described, both according to the present prophecy of Ezekiel and according to the book of Numbers, the possession of the individual tribes is now described, from the eastern side to the side of the west, that is, of the sea. And first they receive their boundaries from the north, beside the way of Ethalon, for those going to Hamath, 'Court' — or 'Aser' — Enon, the border of Damascus toward the north beside Hamath, of which we have already spoken before; and the tribe of Dan begins first, Asher second, Naphtali third, Manasseh fourth, Ephraim fifth, Reuben sixth, Judah seventh: that is, on the left side, and the number seven is completed. — Then the firstfruits of the priests and of the Levites, and the sanctuary of the Lord in the midst, and the Holy of Holies; the city itself also is described, foursquare, having four thousand and five hundred reeds on each side; the suburbs of the priests and of the Levites are also described in order, and the possession of the prince; and again on the right side follow five tribes, likewise from the side of the east to the side of the west, of which the first is Benjamin, the second Simeon, having its own possession specially and by no means mixed with Judah as before, the third Issachar, the fourth Zebulun, the fifth Gad; and the gates of the city, three on each side, and the name of the city itself, which is contained on the plate of gold on the forehead of the high priest — about all of which we shall discourse in their places —. This too is to be noted: that the names of the forty-eight cities which in the volume of Numbers are given to the Levitical tribe to dwell in, with their suburbs, are passed over in silence here, and so are the cities of the fugitives, of which three beyond the Jordan, namely Bezer and Ramoth and Golan, were given in the two and a half tribes, and three on this side of the Jordan, namely Kedesh and Shechem and Kiriath-arba: for there was no need, in a mystical description and in the dwelling of the saints and a perfect way of life, to describe the refuges of fugitives, which Israel needed while still set upon the earth and hastening through many labors and dangers to come to this city, and saying in each of the saints: I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were, and in another place: I have dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar; much has my soul sojourned.

48:8-9

And above the border of Judah, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, shall be the firstfruits which you shall set apart, twenty-five thousand in breadth, and in length as each of the portions from the eastern side to the side of the sea; and the sanctuary shall be in the midst of it. The firstfruits which you shall set apart for the Lord: the length twenty-five thousand, and the breadth ten thousand. It is superfluous to discuss again what has been discussed, and to labor once more, as though they had not been said, over things on which we labored above. After the boundaries of the seven tribes, the firstfruits are described from the east to the west, whose breadth is to hold twenty-five thousand reeds, but the length as much as the individual tribes hold from the east to the sea; the number of this length is uncertain, for no measure was set down in the description of the individual tribes; but if the breadth has twenty-five thousand reeds, one may infer that the number of the length, which is always greater than the breadth, is much greater. In the midst, moreover, the sanctuary is placed, beside the firstfruits which are set apart for the Lord, of a length of twenty-five thousand reeds and a breadth of ten thousand — reading which, we can say nothing else but that saying of the Apostle: O the depth of the riches and of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and untraceable his ways!, and in another place: That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, to know also the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God —. The number twenty-five, moreover, is referred to the senses — of which it was said: You shall possess a divine sense —, and that of ten thousand to perfect and consummate virtue — which by the decalogue of the old instrument reaches to the mystery of the Gospel; we touched on this briefly before, and here we shall recall it in part: for if, adding from one, you reach four, you will fill up the number ten, and so it will come about that the Old Testament is bound together in the New, and the New is expanded in the Old —.

48:10-12

These moreover shall be the firstfruits of the sanctuary of the priests: toward the north twenty-five thousand in length, and toward the sea ten thousand in breadth, and also toward the east ten thousand in breadth, and toward the south twenty-five thousand in length; and the sanctuary of the Lord shall be in the midst of it: the sanctuary for the priests, of the sons of Zadok, who kept my ceremonies and did not go astray when the children of Israel went astray, as the Levites went astray. And there shall be firstfruits from the firstfruits of the land, the Holy of Holies, beside the border of the Levites. The four sides of the firstfruits of the sanctuary are described — a portion which belongs not to the people or to the common crowd, nor to the Levites, a lower rank, but properly to the worship of the priests —: namely of the north and of the west and of the east and of the south; and part by part the order of progress is told: so that, leaving the cold of the north, we may come to the west, where, that is, our vices may set and perish, and thence pass over to the east, and, when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, come to the south, in which the light is brightest and perfect; and both from the north to the sea and from the east to the south there are to be twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth, so that everywhere the same measure of length and breadth may be kept. The sanctuary, moreover (that is, the temple) of the Lord, shall be in the midst of the priestly firstfruits, and it will be walled about on every part with equal sides; and because he had said: These moreover shall be the firstfruits of the sanctuary of the priests, lest under the common term all priests should claim for themselves the possession of this place and the ceremonies to be observed, he sets it down specifically, adding: The sanctuary shall be for the priests, of the sons of 'Sadoc' — which means 'righteous', of whom it is said: The Lord is righteous and has loved righteousnesses; his face has seen equity; for 'Sadoc' the Seventy write 'Saduc'. This Sadoc speaks in the Gospel: For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, and of him, under the name of Solomon, the prophet mystically sings: O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son —. Those priests, however, shall possess the sanctuary of the Lord and keep his ceremonies: Who did not go astray when the children of Israel and the Levites went astray, about whom there was discussion in the earlier parts: they do not offer victims but, content with the privilege of the name and with the humility of their error, always say in their heart: I know my iniquity, and my sin is ever against me — let the priestly rank hear this, and he who was overcome by the heat of the Arian persecution and afterwards bowed his neck to the true faith lest he lack wealth and power: let it be enough for him if he is not expelled from the temple, if he holds some shadow and image of his former name, and let him not, lolling back and belching up delicacies, as though spotless and pure, belch upon us from a most lofty throne the nausea of his ignorance and barbarous garrulity —. For there shall be, he says, for 'them' firstfruits from the firstfruits of the land — that is, for the priests, and for those Who did not go astray when the children of Israel and the Levites went astray; and firstfruits from firstfruits, as tithes of tithes —, and the Holy of Holies beside the border of the Levites, so that the Levites indeed may have the borders adjoining the priests, but may not be able to hold the navel, that is, its middle, and the possession itself.

48:13-15

And also for the Levites likewise, beside the borders of the priests, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth; the whole length twenty-five thousand and the breadth ten thousand; and they shall not sell of it, nor exchange (or measure), nor shall the firstfruits of the land be transferred (or taken away), because they are sanctified to the Lord. But the five thousand that remain in breadth by twenty-five thousand shall be profane, of the city, for dwelling and for suburbs; and the city shall be in the midst of it. What we have rendered as 'profane', for which Aquila translated βέβηλον, Symmachus and Theodotion λαικόν, the Seventy said προτείχισμα, which we can call 'outer wall'; but 'profane' and 'lay', that is, 'common', is what all the people may dwell in anywhere; and what they said: Nor shall it be measured nor taken away, for what we said: It shall not be exchanged nor transferred, plainly has no sense.
